fields.text:
It is said that Lord Hanumān had performed tapas at this kshethram. When the Lord appeared in front of him, Lord Hanumān asked the Lord to re-enact the scene of Gajendra Moksham.

The story of Gajendra Moksham is as follows. King Indradyumna was a renowned ruler of the Pandya Dynasty. It is said that he was the one who constructed the Puri Jagannath Temple. One day, the King was engaged in deep meditation when Sage Agastya visited the Kingdom and sought hospitality from the king. The King was so deep in his meditation that he overlooked the Sage. The sage got irritated and cursed the king, saying he would be reborn as an elephant. Similarly, a Gandharva named Huhu was cursed by Sage Devala to turn into a crocodile as he attempted to break the Sage's penance. Many years passed, and King Indradyumna reincarnated as an elephant who had once been the ruler of an elephant herd on the Mountain of Trikūṭa. Gajendra used to visit a lake on the mountain daily and offer the Lord a lotus as dakshina every day. On one such visit to the lake, a crocodile caught Gajendra's leg. This crocodile was none other than the cursed Huhu. Gajendra started to wail in pain and called out to the Lord by holding up a lotus that he had just plucked to give to the Lord. Gajendra referred to the Lord as "Ādimūla" and called out a plea for help. All the gods saw Gajendra's plight, but when they heard the call, Ādimūla refused to help him as they were not qualified to do justice to that title. It is said that as soon as Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa heard the call of the devotee, he didn't even wait for Garuḍa. He ran at the top of his speed, and soon Garuḍa caught up and took the Lord to the Trikūṭa mountain, where the Lord's Sudarshana Chakra had already taken off, even before he could release it. The chakra killed the crocodile and released Huhu from the curse. It is also said that the lotus held by the Lord is the same Lotus that Gajendra presented to the Lord that day. Following this, Gajendra was granted moksham.

fields.text:
Legend has it that Devī Lakshmī was born as Vanchulavalli at the foot of a Vanchula tree to Medhavi Muni. Lord Vishṇu is believed to have manifested himself in the Pancha Vyūha forms and married Vanchulavalli Thāyār. In the sanctum, one finds the idols of the deities – Sankarshaṇan in the east, Pradyumnan in the south, Aniruddhan in the west, Purushottaman in the north, and Vāsudevan in the center.
It is said that the Lord had performed Pancha-Samskāram for Tirumangai Āzhwār at this kshethram. The story is as follows:
Tirumangai Āzhwār wanted to marry a woman named Kumudhavalli. She placed two conditions, namely, 1) to get Pancha-Samskāram done, and 2) to perform tadhiyararadhanam (annadhanam) for a thousand people for one year. Tirumangai Āzhwār satisfied the second condition, but when it came to fulfilling the first condition, no acharya was ready to perform Pancha-Samskāram, as Tirumangai Āzhwār was a very fierce personality. Thus Tirumangai Āzhwār approached the Lord here, and the Lord himself performed the Pancha-Samskāram. Hence, we can see the Lord holding his arms out with the Pānchajanyam in His right hand and the Sudarshanam in His left hand.


***This temple is regarded as a Mani Mada Mantapam, which means the temple is divided into partitions known as mantapams, wherein one must climb up a flight of stairs to move from one mantapam to the next to reach the garbha griha, which is placed internally. As one moves closer to the main garbha griha, we can see a shrine outside the garbha griha dedicated to Kal Garuḍan. There is a peculiarity with Garuḍan here. At any other kshethram, one can find a Garuḍa Vahanam made of wood or panchaloha, but at this kshethram, we see a Garuḍa made of saligrama shila. Another peculiarity is when Garuḍar comes out for uthsavam. As Kal Garuḍan comes out of the shrine, we see that four people hold up Garuḍar. As the first mantapam is crossed, eight people are required to carry Garuḍar. Similarly, by the time Garuḍar reaches the temple gates, sixty-four people carry Garuḍar. As Garuḍar makes his journey back to the shrine again, only four are needed to place Garuḍar back in the shrine.

Anyone afflicted by sarpa-dosham is said to be relieved of those impediments by the Garuḍan here at this kshetram.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Hiraṇyāksha's brother Hiraṇyakashipu was a great demon emperor who dominated the earth. He performed great penance to Lord Brahmā. After centuries of penance, Brahmā finally appeared in front of Hiraṇyakashipu and told him that he had appeared to grant him a boon for the penance that Hiraṇyakashipu had performed. Hiraṇyakashipu asked for immortality. Brahmā said it was against the law of nature and that it was not in his power to grant this boon and asked him to rethink what he desired. Hiraṇyakashipu thought for a while and asked for a boon that would be equivalent to immortality. He asked that he shouldn't be killed by man nor animal, not be killed inside the house nor outside, not be killed at day nor at night, not be killed in space nor on the surface of the earth. Further, he should not be killed by anything which was created by Brahmā. Brahmā granted this and disappeared.

Soon Hiraṇyakashipu became a tyrant and became a ruthless king. He soon had a son by the name of Prahlāda. Prahlāda was a great devotee of Lord Vishṇu. Hiraṇyakashipu considered Lord Vishṇu as his mortal enemy as he had incarnated himself to kill his brother Hiraṇyāksha. When Prahlāda was in his mother's womb, Sage Nārada had narrated tales of the Lord to his mother. As the mother heard the stories, so did the fetus.

When Prahlāda was admitted to Gurukulam, he changed the views of all his teachers and all the students to advise them to praise the Lord instead of praising his father. When Hiraṇyakashipu came to know of the events that were taking place in the Gurukulam, he took measures to try and kill his son. He tried to get him trampled by an elephant, feed him poison, imprison him without food, throw him into a ravaging flame. None of his methods produced the results that he wanted. He then brings Prahlāda to his royal court. He asked him how he was surviving all the deadly situations. He said the Lord was protecting him. He also said that the Lord is within everyone, including his father. Hiraṇyakashipu then drew his mace and pointed out to a pillar and asked him if his Lord was present in that particular pillar. When Prahlāda said yes, Hiraṇyakashipu smashed the pillar, and from that pillar, the Lord emerged in the form of a man-lion. The incarnation had the face of a lion and the body of a man. The Lord's rage knew no bounds. He dragged Hiraṇyakashipu to the doorstep and sat on the separating junction, which is neither inside nor outside the home. The Lord placed Hiraṇyakashipu on his lap, which was neither in space nor on Earth. Then the Lord used his nails at a time of sunset, which was neither day nor night, and dug into the stomach of Hiraṇyakashipu, ripping out his intestines and putting an end to the tyrant.

The legend has it that Garuḍa was desirous of seeing Lord Vishṇu in His Narasimha avataram; thus, he meditated upon Him at the Ugra Sthambham, and the Lord manifested Himself as nine forms of Narasimha.

1. Bhargava Narasimha Svāmi

The Bhargava Narasimha Svāmi is situated at a distance of two kilometers from the Lower Ahobilam, on a hill, near the sacred pond, known as 'Bhargava Tīrtham,' where Bhargava Rāma (Parashurāma) performed his penance. Hence the Lord of the temple is known as Bhargava Narasimha Svāmi.

2. Yogananda Narasimha Svāmi

This temple is to the southeast of Lower Ahobilam at a distance of 2 kilometers. The popular legend is that after killing Hiraṇyakashipu, Lord Narasimha taught Prahlada several yogic postures. Therefore, the Lord in this aspect is called Yogananda Narasimha.

3. Chatravata Narasimha Svāmi

About three kilometers from lower Ahobilam, the image of the deity is installed under a peepal tree, surrounded by thorny bushes. Hence, the Lord is called Chatravata Narasimha Svāmi. The Lord can be seen putting thaalam with one of His hands. It is said that the Lord is enjoying the musical service of two yakshas named Haha and Huhu.

4. Ahobila Narasimha Svāmi

The temple, situated on the Upper Ahobilam, at a distance of eight kilometers from the Lower Ahobilam, is the main temple and the earliest of all the nine temples there. The Lord here appears in his fierce aspect, called Ugra Narasimha, who is the presiding deity of the temple and is known as Ahobila Nṛisimha Svāmi. It is firmly believed that Lord Narasimha was 'Swayambhu' (self-manifest) here.

5. Krodakara (Varāha) Narasimha Svāmi

The temple of this Lord is one kilometer away from the main temple of Ahobila Nṛisimha Svāmi on the Upper Ahobilam. The image of the deity has the face of a boar (Varāha or kroda), and the Lord is seen along with his Consort, Lakshmī. Hence the Lord of the temple is known as Krodakara (Varāha) Narasimha Svāmi here.

6. Karanja Narasimha Svāmi

This shrine is situated at a distance of one kilometer from the Upper Ahobilam and one furlong from the road leading to Lower Ahobilam. The image of the deity is installed under a tree called 'Karanja Vruksham.' Hence this Lord is called Karanja Narasimha Svāmi. The Lord here is prathyaksham to Hanumān. It is said that when Hanumān performed tapas here at this kshethram, Lord Narasimha appeared with a bow and arrow, signifying that He is Rāma.

7. Malola Narasimha Svāmi

Nearly two kilometers from the main temple of Upper Ahobilam is the famous shrine of Malola Narasimha Svāmi. The deity here appears in 'Soumya' (graceful) form. As Lord Narasimha is seen with his consort, Lakshmī, He is known as Malola Narasimha Svāmi. The word 'Malola' means beloved to Lakshmī (Ma=Lakshmī, Lola= beloved). It is said that the 'utsavamoorthi' of the Lord appeared to Srimath Adivan Satakopa Jeeyar, the first Jeeyar of Ahobila Mutt. Right from the founder, i.e., the first Jeeyar of Ahobila Mutt down to the 44th pontiff, Shrīvan Satakopa Shri Vedānta Desika Yatīndra Mahadesika, the present jeeyar, the utsavamoorthi of Malola Narasimha Svāmi is worshipped, and it is taken by them whenever they are on religious tours, visiting the villages every year. Recently, the 45th Jeeyar Shrīvan Satakopa Shri Nārāyaṇa Yatīndra Mahadesikan has taken over the worship.

8. Jwala Narasimha Svāmi

The temple of Jwala Nṛisimha Svāmi lies higher up the above temple, on a hill called 'Achalachaya Meru.' This is about four kilometers from the Upper Ahobilam temple. This place is said to be the actual spot where the fierce anger of the Lord reached its culmination when he tore Hiraṇyakashipu.

9. Pavana Narasimha Svāmi

Nearby the above temple is the shrine of Pavana Narasimha, on the banks of the river, Pavana, and it is about six kilometers from the Upper Ahobilam temple. Hence the Lord of the shrine is known as Pavana Narasimha Svāmi. It is said that Mahālakshmī reincarnated Herself as Chenchulakshmi into one of the local tribes that resided here. When Lord Narasimha was roaming the land in enraged after killing Hiraṇyakashipu, Chenchulakshmi is said to have pacified the Lord and married Him.

Ugra Sthambham

At a distance of eight kilometers from the Upper Ahobilam temple, we can see a cleft of the mountain dividing it into two visible parts. It is a long-held view that from the cleft, the Lord appeared in the form of Narasimha, and this cleft is known as 'Ugra Sthambham.'

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The idol as we see it today is said to have originated from the milky oceans of Shri Vaikuṇṭham. Lord Brahmā then took the idol to worship, and for many eons, was worshipped by Lord Brahmā in Satyalokam. A time came when the great king Ikshvaku approached Lord Brahmā and asked him to install the idol of the Lord in Bhūlokam. Considering the king’s request, Lord Brahmā obliged and installed the idol of the Lord along with the Praṇavākāra Vimānam at Ayodhyā, along the banks of the river Saryu. The Lord then remained in Ayodhyā even till Lord Rāma was the king of Ayodhyā. After the battle with Rāvaṇa, the Lord returned to Ayodhyā to be coronated formally. Here, he gifted all his army generals with something unique and meaningful. When Vibhīshaṇa’s turn came during the distribution of divine gifts after Lord Rāma’s victory over Rāvaṇa, he humbly requested Lord Rāma to give him the idol of Shri Raṅganāthar so that he could take it back to Lanka for worship. Lord Rāma, recognizing Vibhīshaṇa's unwavering devotion and righteousness, agreed without hesitation. Thus, the divine idol, along with the Pranavakara Vimānam—a sanctified structure shaped in the form of the sacred syllable Praṇavam (a-u-m)—was entrusted to Vibhīshaṇa, who then began his journey southward aboard the Pushpaka Vimānam. As Vibhīshaṇa reached the sacred banks of the river Kāvēri, it was the auspicious month of Pankuni. According to the ancient traditions upheld by Lord Rāma and his Ikshvaku lineage, this period marked the celebration of the grand Brahmotsavam festival. In reverence to this dharmic custom, Vibhīshaṇa paused his journey and conducted a nine-day festival in honor of the Lord on the riverbank. During the course of these festivities, the idol and the Pranavakara Vimānam were placed at a site later known as Shesha Peetam, near the sacred tank Chandrapushkarani. As the nine days drew to a close and Vibhīshaṇa made ready to resume his journey, a Chōḷa king named Dharmavarman fell at his feet and begged him to leave the Lord there on the banks of the Kāvēri. Vibhīshaṇa then asked the Lord Himself whether He wished to continue on to Lanka or to remain on the banks of the Kāvēri. But when Vibhīshaṇa attempted to resume his journey, he found the Vimānam immovable—it had firmly anchored itself to the earth. Overcome with grief and confusion, Vibhīshaṇa was then graced with a divine vision of Lord Vishṇu, who appeared before him. The Lord consoled His devotee, declaring that He had chosen this very spot to be His eternal abode. He assured Vibhīshaṇa that although He would remain in Bharata Varsha, He would face southward toward Lanka as a mark of blessing and everlasting connection. Touched by this revelation, Vibhīshaṇa accepted the divine will with devotion and humility. It is believed that to this day, Vibhīshaṇa comes at midnight to offer his prayers to Lord Raṅganāthar in an invisible, celestial form. Thus, the reclining Lord of Shrīraṅgam, ensconced in the Pranavakara Vimānam that embodies the essence of the Praṇavam (a-u-m), took His place on the banks of the Kāvēri by His own will. This sacred event established Shrīraṅgam as the foremost among the 108 Divya Desams—a sanctum where divine grace, eternal dharma, and boundless devotion converge. This temple is enormous in size and is the largest temple complex, spanning 156 acres, surrounded by seven concentric walls (the outermost wall has a perimeter of over 3 km) and 21 gopurams. It has seven Prakarams or Tiru Veedhis surrounding the sanctum, with a total length of approximately 9 km. The 236-foot-high, thirteen-tiered Rajagopuram, built at the southern rampart, is a notable recent addition. It is significant that Rāmānuja completely overhauled the administrative system in this temple. The physical remains of Rāmānuja, who lived for nearly 120 years, are still preserved in a sitting posture in the sannidhi dedicated to him on the southwest corner of the fifth prakaram. Furthermore, Arayar Sevai, an ancient art form that involves rendering and expressing the Naalaayira Divya Prabandham through dance, originated at this kshethram under the auspices of Nāthamuni. *Swayamvyaktha kshethram, according to the Shri Vaishṇavas There are certain idols of the Lord that nobody has carved, or there is no godly origin, sagely origin, or humane origin to the idols, as the Lord Himself has incarnated into these places. The list of these kshethrams is as follows: 
1) Vanamamalai 
2) Shri Raṅgam 
3) Shri Mushnam 
4) Tirumala 
5) Naimisharanyam (as a forest)
 6) Pushkar (as water) 
7) Badri 
8) Muktinath

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
This kshethram is the avatara sthalam for both Periya Āzhwār and Shri Āṇḍāl.
In the then Pandya kingdom, there was a small town called Putthoor, where great scholars and pundits were residing. Nearby, there was a forest where hunters were living. The chief of these hunters had two sons named Villi and Kandan. One day, Villi and Kandan went to the forest for hunting as usual. They spotted a tiger, and it escaped the arrows from their bows. Kandan started chasing vigorously and went deep into the forest. After some time, the tiger hid behind a tree and pounced on Kandan, killing him. Villi waited for his brother for a long time and started searching for him. When he spotted the dead body of his brother, his heart almost stopped with grief, and he cried heavily and fell unconscious on his brother's body. During his unconsciousness, he had a scene in front of his eyes; Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa, along with Mahālakshmī, appeared and instructed Villi to stop lamenting. They told him that They would bring his brother back to life. The two brothers would then search for a giant banyan tree in the middle of the forest, where they would find Lord Vatapatrashayee, who had been lying there for a very long time. The divine couple also told Villi that they would find a cave nearby with treasures that one could never even dream of. They further instructed that the brothers were to use that wealth to deforest the area and construct a magnificent temple that had never been seen before. Saying this, the Divine couple disappeared. When Villi came back to consciousness, he did not know whether what he saw (in his unconscious state) was true at all, and was confused. But suddenly, Kandan got up alive as if he had just woken up from sleep (without any wounds even). Villi explained the whole thing to his brother, and both of them hugged each other for having been blessed by the Lord and having been chosen by the Lord to establish the temple.

Soon, many Vaishṇava scholars began to migrate towards Putthoor, among them Mukunda Bhattar and his wife, Padmavalli. The couple was ardent devotees of Shri Vatapatrashayee. On an auspicious day, the couple was blessed with a son, named Vishṇuchittar. The child lived up to his name by constantly finding ways to contemplate how to find the Lord's days. As time passed, he would perform pushpa-kainkaryam to Shri Vatapatrashayee. As he aged, he sold his property. He purchased a small plot of land near the temple, which he converted into a Nandavanam, where he cultivated various creepers, vines, fragrant flowers, and tulasi plants. The plot also featured a small pond with crystal-clear water. Vishṇuchittar would spend his time cultivating his garden, plucking the flowers, and making garlands for the Lord. Over time, his small plot was allowed to expand and transform into a vast, flourishing garden with a lovely scent due to all the flowers that bloomed within it. Soon, he married a woman who shared his ideals of serving the Lord.

During that time, there was a king named Vallabhadevan, whose capital was situated in Madurai. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishṇu and wished to learn the meaning of the Vedas and Upanishads. He enquired with his chief minister as to how he could achieve this goal. The minister suggested that the king call all the Vedic Scholars present in his kingdom to debate and question all the matters present in the Vedas and Upanishads. The one who could solve all the questions posed by the king would be rewarded dearly. The king agreed with the minister's suggestion, and soon an announcement was made throughout the kingdom saying there would be a grand meeting of all the Vedic Scholars in the land. The scholar who would impress the king with their answers would be rewarded with gold coins, which would be hung in a divine binding. The coins would present themselves to the person who would aptly answer all of the king's questions. Many scholars came before the king, but none gave satisfactory answers that the king desired. One night, Lord Vatapatrashayee appeared in Vishṇuchittar's dreams and instructed him to go to the king's court to claim the prize that was being offered. Vishṇuchittar told the Lord that he knew nothing about the Vedas or Upanishads. All he knew to do was to make garlands and present them to the Lord. The Lord then told Vishṇuchittar not to worry and to go to the royal court. The Lord said He would speak through the mouth of Vishṇuchittar. That same night, the Lord also appeared in the dreams of the chief minister and asked him to make royal arrangements to receive Vishṇuchittar and escort him to the king's court.

The next morning, a royal elephant with palanquins arrived and carried Vishṇuchittar to the royal court. As he entered, all the scholars began to murmur and pass sarcastic comments about him, knowing that his knowledge was limited. Vishṇuchittar prostrated himself before the king and the gathered scholars, and then began his speech on the Vedas and Upanishads. As and when the king questioned, it was almost as though the answer to the question was pre-prepared and ready. Finally, to close his speech, Vishṇuchittar made a final statement that said, "Shrīmān Nārāyaṇane Paramporul." This translates to "It is Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa who is the only protector, and it is with His blessing that the universe is surviving. It is He and only He who is the underlying principle that is mentioned in the four Vedas and Upanishads. When this statement was made, the binding came undone, and the gold coins showered into Vishṇuchittar's hands from above. The king was overcome with joy and ecstasy. All the gathered scholars lowered their heads in shame. The king then asked Vishṇuchittar how he had spoken about all the Vedas and Upanishads in such simple language. Vishṇuchittar then told the king that truly it was he who had spoken and that the Lord himself intended for this to perspire. The king was deeply moved by what Vishṇuchittar said and fell to his feet. He arranged for complete royal honors and sent him around the kingdom in a royal procession. At one point, when Vishṇuchittar looked up at the sky, he saw the Lord along with Mahālakshmī seated atop Garuḍan, granting their blessing to him. It was at that moment that, with eyes filled with tears of joy, he said the words"pallaandu, pallaandu pallayiratthandu palakodi noorayiram." These words are still sung to date during sathumorai seva every day, whether it may be at a temple or within a household.

Periya Āzhwār being taken on the royal procession and seeing the Lord and Mahālakshmī

Life went back to normal for Vishṇuchittar, and he continued his pushpa-kainkaryam for Lord Vatapatrashayee. Once, while plucking flowers in the garden, he found a child on a flower in the garden and named her Āṇḍāl and brought her up in the service of the Lord. One day, Periya Āzhwār(Vishṇuchittar) found Āṇḍāl wearing the garland meant for the Lord. Discarding that garland, he prepared fresh garlands and offered them to the Lord. PeriaAzhwar was surprised to see the Lord refusing to accept the garland except the one used by Āṇḍāl. Hence, Āṇḍāl is called Shoodi Kudutha Nāchiyār. As per the wishes of the Lord, Periya Āzhwār gave Āṇḍāl in marriage to Shri Raṅganāthar in Shri Raṅgam, and Āṇḍāl, on entering the sanctum, merged with the Lord.

Shri Āṇḍāl Nāchiyār

Shri Āṇḍāl is said to be the reincarnation of Bhūdevi. When Lord Varāha saved Bhūdevi from the grasp of Hiraṇyāksha, He is said to have delivered various Brahmā-gyanam to Bhūdevi. It is noted that Bhūdevi came in this form to provide that knowledge to the people in a way that they would understand it simply. Thus, Shri Āṇḍāl wrote 30 Pāsurams known as Tirupavai and Nāchiyār Tirumozhi, which contain 143 Pāsurams that convey all the knowledge that was given by Shri Varāha Perumāl to Bhūdevi on that day.
Even to date, on the tirunakshtram of Shri Āṇḍāl, Tiruaadipooram Utsavam is observed on a very grand scale. This is the time when brahmotsavam is done here, and a massive number of devotees throng to see this grand celebration.

Tiruaadipooram Celebration

fields.text: It is said that Chandran was the husband of the twenty-seven nakshatras, who were the daughters of Daksha Prajapati. It is noted that Chandran showed more affection towards Rohini and was ignoring his other twenty-six wives. Thus, Daksha Prajapati was angered by Chandran's behavior and cursed him, saying he would suffer from Kshaya-Rogam(tuberculosis). It is said that to relieve himself of the curse, Chandran came here to this kshethram and prayed to the Lord after taking a dip in the temple's pushkariṇī. The Lord is then said to have appeared here and relieved Chandran of his curse.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend is said to have taken place in Kṛta Yugam. Parāshara Maharshi was said to have been performing tapas when three demons by the name Thanjakan, Dhandakan, and Gajamukhan started to interrupt him. It is then that Parāshara Maharshi asked Lord Vishṇu to intervene and help him. The Lord mounted Garuḍan and first released his Sudarshana Chakram to deal with Thanjakan. On his deathbed, Thanjakan asked the Lord to name the land where he died to be named after him. Thus the land where he died became Tanjavur. Next, the Lord went after Dhandakan. The Lord took the form of Varāha and bore his teeth into Dhandakan and dug through the land, emerging out of Shrīmushṇam. Dhandakan asked for the land where he was buried to be named after him. Thus emerged the Dhandaka Vanam. The last demon Gajamukhan was killed by the Lord in his Narasimha form. Thus the three temples were put together to form one kshethram known collectively by the name of Tanjai Mamanikoyil.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend tells the story of Salihotra Maharshi, who had his hermitage in this place. He used to grind rice for a living and offered half of the flour to the seekers, while he consumed the rest himself. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishṇu. To test his devotion, the Lord appeared as a guest to him one day. He requested Salihotra Maharshi to offer him food, which the sage did. The guest felt hungry and requested the sage to provide more food. The sage offered the other half of the flour, which he used to consume himself. The guest asked for a place to rest(Evvul), and the sage readily offered his hermitage. On arriving at the hermitage, the guest revealed His true form and blessed the sage.

*** This kshethram has a few specialties. It is said that if one bathes in the Hruthapanashini Pushkariṇī on Thai Amāvāsyā, all of their ailments will be cured. Another belief that has seen fruit here is when a person takes a handful of jaggery and dissolves it in the water on any Amāvāsyā, all their wishes come true.
When Lord Shiva had Brahmahatyā dosham for killing Daksha Prajapati, it is said that after he bathed in this Pushkariṇī, all his sins were absolved.
Another story tells the story of the Lord's marriage to Vasumathi Thāyār. It is said that Thāyār belonged to a village called Dharmasenapuram, located near Tiruvallūr. Vasumathi Thāyār was the daughter of the king of Dharmasenapuram. She wanted to get married to the Lord. Her father agreed, but he had a condition: his Son-in-law should not leave his kingdom and take his daughter with him. The Lord agreed to this condition and promised the king that He would never leave Tiruvallūr.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
This kshethram is said to be one of the eight Swayam Vyaktha kshetrams. The other swayam Vyaktha kshethram are Shri Raṅgam, Shrīmushṇam, Salagramam, Thotadri (Vaanamamalai), Tirupati, Pushkaram, and Badri.
This Naimisharanya kshethram is said to be regarded as a Tapovanam. There are 9 tapovams. They are Daṇḍakāraṇyam, Saindhavāraṇyam, Jambhukāraṇyam, Pushkarāraṇyam, Utpalāraṇyam, Badrikāraṇyam, Gurujāṅgalāraṇyam, Aruputhāraṇyam and Naimishāraṇyam. It is believed that the perumāl is found in the form of a forest. And this Naimisharanyam is viewed as a holy forest.This Naimisaranya kshethram is said to be regarded as Tapovanam. There are nine tapovams. They are Daṇḍakāraṇyam, Saindhavāraṇyam, Jambhukāraṇyam, Pushkarāraṇyam, Utpalāraṇyam, Badrikāraṇyam, Gurujāṅgalāraṇyam, Aruputhāraṇyam and Naimisaranayam. It is believed that the perumāl is found in the form of a forest, and this Naimisharanyam is regarded as the holiest forest. The Emperumaan of this sthalam is giving his seva as the entire form of the Vanam (forest). In their old age, all the Maharshis, along with Sownakar, went towards Lord Brahmā and asked him which is the best place suited for doing Yajña and tapas. As the answer, Lord Brahmā took a dharbai grass and made it into a wheel shape, and rolled the dharbai grass. Lord Brahmā said that after he rolls the grass, the place where it stops is considered the ideal location for performing tapas and yagam. He rolled the wheel, and it stopped at a particular place on Earth. That place is said to be Naimisharanyam. Nemi means a wheel, and Naimisham means the place where the wheel landed. Aaranyam means forest. Since Nemi, the Chakkaram that landed in Aaranya's forest, the sthalam is called Naimisharanyam. This Naimishāraṇyam is said to be the place where most of the rishis performed sacrifices, tapas, and meditation, and explained the meaning of the old Puranas and Vedas. The Lord gives his seva in the form of Nature. The Lord here gives his seva with the name as Shri Devaraja Perumāl along with Shri Hari Lakshmī and gives his audience (prathyaksham) to Devendran, Sudharma, Devarishis, Soodhapuranika, and Vedavyāsa.

Chakra Tīrtham

It is said that taking a bath in the Chakra Tīrtham absolves all sins.
Gayāsura did tapas in this sthalam. Shrīmān Nārāyaṇan gave His audience to him as his tapas fulfilled him. The Lord asked him what boon he wanted as a result of complete tapas. But Gayasooran answered the Almighty that he didn't want any boon from him, as he was already so powerful. He asked that anyone who met him should be entitled to get moksham. The Lord did not want immoral souls to attain moksham just by meeting him. The Lord said that the boon that Gayāsura was asking for could not be fulfilled in the way he was asking. Gayāsura then asked the Lord to present the souls for whom shraadham is performed upon his body to be given moksham. The Lord then said that this would be possible. Thus, Gayāsura grew to an enormous size, and the Lord sent his chakram to kill the asura, and his body was cut into three parts. The three parts are Siro Gayā (the head part), Nabhi Gayā (the middle part), and Charana Gayā (the foot part). This sthalam, the Naimishāraṇyam, is said to be the Nabhi Gayā. The Gayā kshethram is said to be the Charana Gayā, and Badri is said to be Siro Gayā. Offering shraadham to departed souls in all these three sthalams is said to grant moksham to them.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: Once there was a dancer who wanted to impress the goddess, Maha Lakshmī. The dancer performed a very intricate set of dances, and soon the goddess appeared before her, presenting the dancer with a garland. Soon after this, it is said that Sage Durvāsa was passing by and saw the lovely garland on the neck of the dancer. The dancer offered the sage the garland and left the scene. It is said that the garland possessed a very fragrant smell that attracted bees. Soon, the sage started to get irritated by the buzzing of the bees and was looking to dispose of the garland when Indra arrived atop his mount, Airāvata. Durvāsa presented the garland to Indra. Airāvata took the garland, but instead of throwing it on Indra, it crushed it beneath its legs. Durvāsa was immensely angered by this insult and cursed Indra, saying he and the world would lose all their wealth. As the phrasing of the curse was vague, all wealth-bearing substances and creatures, such as the Kalpa Vriksha, Kamadhenu, and even the Goddess Lakshmī, disappeared. To retrieve all his lost wealth, Indra prayed to Raṅganāyaki Thāyār, who instructed him to perform the Samurda Manthanam and attend her marriage to Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa. By doing so, he would regain his lost wealth. Another story tells that Kamadhenu had performed tapas here, as well as Agni had performed worship to the Lord here. From the following story, we can see that this temple predates even Shri Raṅgam.

fields.name: travelNote

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
One day, Kadrū and Vinatā were arguing about the color of Uchchaihshravas' tail. Vinatā claimed that the divine horse was a pure white color throughout, but Kadrū said the horse's body was white, but the tail was black. Thus, the two had a bet to see who was right. The one who would lose the bet would become the other's slave. Kadrū knew very well that the tail of Uchchaihshravas was pure white, and knowing she would lose the bet, she told her sons to wrap themselves around the tail of Uchchaihshravas so that she could win the bet. One day, in the presence of Kadrū and Vinatā, Uchchaihshravas passed by with a black tail. Thus, Kadrū won the bet, enslaving Vinatā. For five hundred years, Vinatā was a slave to Kadrū. After five hundred years, Vinatā's second egg hatched, and from that egg was born Garuḍan. As soon as he was born, he went straight to his aunt and demanded that his mother be freed from slavery.
To this, Kadrū put a condition, saying that if Garuḍan could bring the Amrutakalasham (the divine pitcher that contained the sacred nectar of immortality) for her and her children, she would release Vinatā from slavery. Thus, Garuḍan immediately left for Svargalokam and defeated all the Devas in battle, successfully retrieving the Amrutakalasham. After retrieving the Amrutakalasham, Garuḍan returned to Bhūlokam. On Bhūlokam, Lord Vishṇu was very impressed with Garuḍan for his strength and dedication. The Lord then offered Garuḍan a boon. Garuḍan asked that he should always be soaring far above the Lord; thus, Garuḍan is present in the Dhvajasthambham outside the temple. The Lord also then told Garuḍan that he wanted Garuḍan to be constantly under his command; therefore, he asked Garuḍan to become his vaahanam. The Lord also relieved Vinatā from slavery and took the Amrutakalasham. The Lord is said to have taken the Amrutakalasham, placed it on His head, and danced. Hence, he got the name Kudamaadukoothan.
Another story tells us that, after the Mahābhārata battle, as the Lord was on his way back to Dvārakā from his tour of South India, the Lord reached Arimeya Vinnagaram, where Utaṅka Maharshi's ashram was situated at the time. Utaṅka Maharshi, upon seeing the Lord, is said to have stopped the Lord's chariot and asked him to visit his Ashramam. When the Lord reached the Ashramam, Utaṅka Maharshi began to pose indirect questions to the Lord about how He ensured the Pāṇḍavas won the battle. The Lord sensed that the Maharshi had other intentions and asked him what he had in mind. Utaṅka Maharshi then told the Lord that he desired to see the Vishwaroopa Darshanam as He had shown Arjuna. The Lord then showed the Maharshi His Vishwaroopam.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Before Lord Athi Vardar was presented the havis to the yajña, Sarasvatī Devī presented many interruptions to stop the yajña from reaching completion. Sarasvatī Devī is said to have summoned many different types of demons, ghosts, and ghouls to attack the yajña-kundam. Lord Brahmā is said to have appealed to Lord Vishṇu to appear and protect the yajña so that it would achieve its completion. The Lord is said to have appeared with eight hands (Ashṭabhujar), holding weapons in seven hands and a lotus in one hand, symbolizing that he would attack his enemies while also protecting his devotees. The Lord is said to have vanquished all the interruptions placed by Devī Sarasvatī in her first attempt to foil the performance of the yajña.
The Lord here is referred to as Gajendravaradhan, as He is said to have shown Pey Āzhwār the sight of Gajendra Moksham here at this kshethram.

*** A peculiarity of this kshethram is that this is the only temple in all the Divyadesams at Kāñchipuram to house a Vaikuntha Dwaram. Usually, if the entrance of the temple is east-facing, the Vaikuntha Dwaram is placed in a west-facing direction. But here, the Vaikuntha Dwaram and the temple entrance are both facing in the easterly direction.

The legend has it that Lord Vishṇu extracted Ayodhyā, a part of Vaikuṇṭham, and presented it to Lord Brahmā, who then gave it to his son, Swaayambhuva Manu, who brought it to Bhooloka and placed it on the banks of the Sarayū River. The original temples, on which the Āzhwārs composed the Divya Prabhandam, were destroyed by invaders. Now, there are shrines for Raṅganāthar and Rāma in the Ammaji Temple, located on the banks of the River Sarayū as well as the newly constructed Ayodhyā Ram Janmabhoomi Mandir.

This temple for Lord Hanumān is known as Hanumān Gadhi. The Lord here is said to be the protector of Ayodhyā.
Performing go-dhaanam on the banks of the Saryu River is said to give the person performing dhaanam moksham.

fields.text:
According to legend, it is said that Gandaki Nadi performed tapas to the Lord. When the Lord appeared before her, she asked that He stay in her womb always. The Lord told her that, as she is a river, her riverbed represents her womb. He told her that He would reside in the stones at the bottom of the river in the form of Shalagramam. To date, whenever a devotee visits this kshethram, they take back with them the various kinds of shalagramams.


Surrounding the temple, there are 108 springs called Sahasradhara, which are perennial and have pure water throughout the year. The water is considered to be holy; thus, whenever a devotee visits this kshethram, they perform prokshanam of this water at each of the 108 springs.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
During the Mahābhārata war, on the fifteenth day of the war, Bhīma and Drishṭadyumna attacked Dronacharya in full fury, but it had no avail. Droṇa still had many divine weapons left in his Astra-Bhandara. Then Krishna devised a plan wherein Droṇa would voluntarily drop his weapons, thereby presenting the opportunity for the Pāṇḍavas to kill him. Krishna told Bhīma to kill an elephant named Ashvatthāma, and then told everyone on the battlefield to announce that Ashvatthāma was dead. As instructed, Bhīma immediately killed Ashvatthāma, the elephant, and all the warriors in the Pāṇḍavas' army started screaming, saying Ashvatthāma was dead. When Droṇa heard these words, he was in disbelief. He immediately went to Yudhishṭhira and asked what all the warriors were saying was true. Yudhishṭhira was put in a spot at that moment. He went into deep thought about how to convey the information. He says aśvatthāmā hataḥ which translates to Ashvatthāma is dead. As soon as he had lied, the chariot, which always used to hover four inches above the ground, immediately fell to the ground. Droṇa was heartbroken and laid down his arms, renouncing war. He assumed a yogic stance and prayed to Lord Vishṇu, then instructed Karna to take charge of the army and protect Duryodhana.
As soon as Droṇa had laid down his arms, Drishṭadyumna came and beheaded Droṇa.
It is said that Yudhishṭhira came to this kshethram, bathed in the Chitraaru river, and performed tapas to the Lord here. The Lord appeared in front of Yudhishṭhira and gave him atonement for his sin of lying to Dronacharya.

*** An interesting point that can be seen here is that the Lord holds the Pānchajanyam in the right hand and the Sudarshanam in the left hand.

fields.name: azhwarPasuram
fields.text:
Nam Āzhwār: 11 Pāsurams

*** This is the second Pancha-Pāṇḍava Kshethram. Yudhishṭhira established this temple. Thus, this temple is referred to as Dharmaputra Prathista Kovil.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
According to legend, it is believed that Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi and Kāvēri Thāyār meditated upon Lord Vishṇu. It is also believed that Brahmā made a clay pot to rescue and preserve the Vedas during pralaya, but none of the pots made by Brahmā would last. Thereupon, he was directed by Lord Vishṇu to proceed to Tirucherai (Saarakshethram) and make a pot out of the clay on the banks of Kāvēri, and thus the Vedas were protected in a pot made out of tough mud at this place. Another legend recounts a feud between the Gaṅgā and Kāvēri rivers. It is said that seven rivers were meditating at the foothills of the Vindhya hills. At this moment, a Gandharva is said to have appeared and paid his respects to the devis. The question then arose: seven women were present, but to whom did the Gandharva pay his respects? Gaṅgā and Kāvēri started to argue. Gaṅgā claimed that she was a greater entity than Kāvēri. To solve this feud, both of the devis went to Lord Brahmā. Lord Brahmā, in a bias, declared that Gaṅgā was a greater entity than Kāvēri. Kāvēri wanted to be the greatest river and hence performed penance to the Lord here at Tirucherai. The Lord appeared and showed her Vishwaroopa Darshanam, but this did not satisfy her. The Lord then showed her His form as He appears in Shri Vaikuṇṭham and told her that soon He would lie in Bujanga Shayanam at Shri Raṅgam, and she would flow by His Tiruvadi (His holy lotus feet) until the end of Kāli Yuga, thereby making her a greater entity than Gaṅgā.

*** Here, the Lord can be seen with five of his spouses, namely, Shri Devī, Bhūdevi, Neela Devī, Mahālakshmī, and Saraṇāyaki Thāyār.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is located in Nāṅguṇēri on the way to Nagarkoil from Tirunelvēli.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
There are multiple legends associated with this temple. Let's go through them one by one.
How the Lord appeared:
Lord Mahā Vishṇu is said to have defeated the demon brothers, Madhu and Kaiṭabha. When He defeated them, their blood is said to have spilled over the earth, causing the world to smell with a very foul odor. Bhūmi Devī is said to have performed tapas at this kshethram to relieve Herself of the odor. The Lord is said to have answered Her tapas and appeared here for the first time. Vishvakarma is said to have designed the temple here. Over time and improper maintenance, the Lord is said to have gotten buried under the earth. Many years passed, and the Lord was forgotten. Then came a king named Karya Maharaja, who had no children. The king was growing anxious as he grew older, and he did not have any children.
One night, the Lord appeared in the king's dream and told him that He wanted to be reestablished in the temple. The Lord directed the king to Nāṅguṇēri and told him where He lay buried below the earth. The king began digging and, at one point, saw that the tip of one of his tools had blood on it. Upon closer inspection, the king found the Lord, Shri Devī, Bhūmi Devī, Sūryan, Chandran, Bhṛgu Maharshi, Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi, Urvashi, Thilothama, Vishvaksenar, and Garuḍan. (Among all the Swayam Vyaktha Kshethrams, this is the only kshethram where there have been 11 vigrahams that have emerged.) The king was bamboozled by the blood and did not mean to hurt the Lord in any way. The king immediately begged for the Lord's forgiveness. The Lord told the king not to be worried and asked him to apply some gingelly oil, and the wound would heal. The king followed the Lord's instructions. To date, this tradition is still observed, where the Lord is massaged with a mixture of gingelly oil and sandalwood oil, along with a blend of medicinal herbs, and abhishekam is performed daily.

Yennai Kannar

After the abhishekam is performed, all the oil is collected and poured into a well that is 25 feet deep. This well is known as the yennai kannar. The oil from this well ages over time and undergoes multiple chemical reactions when exposed to sunlight. All devotees who visit this kshethram take some amount of this oil with them to their households without fail. This oil has multiple medicinal benefits, including the ability to alleviate arthritis symptoms, and it can also be used to treat leprosy.
Another legend goes that once upon a time, there was a righteous king in the kingdom of Sind named Gunaseelan. In his usual pastime, he went out hunting, followed by his attendants on horseback. The King missed his companions in the trackless forest, and when he was feeling the pinch of thirst and hunger, he could locate a mysterious animal in the form of a deer with eight legs. This phenomenon diverted the king's mind, and he pursued it. But alas! The deer, with its swift legs, quickly disappeared, drawing the King deep into the forest. At its disappearance, the King felt dejected and retraced his steps to find his companions. By then, he felt thirsty and hungry. He noticed at a distance a small hermitage made of mild leaves. He halted in front of it and, finding the door wide open, alighted from his horse and entered it. He could not find the owner of the hermitage. There was no temple there till then. But the sanctity of the place gained significant prominence. It was a dense mango forest where many sages, including Roma, Nārada, Vaikhānasa, Dadhichi, Angeerasa, Jabali, Kalavar, Kanva, and others, were engaged in deep meditation and penance. But to his utter surprise, he found in a corner food and drink spread over a leaf as if offered to somebody. His acute thirst and hunger did not allow him to wait long. He unceremoniously helped himself to the food and drink. When he had finished the meal, he realized he was an intruder in the hermitage.
Sage Kusasanan, who had been to the river for his daily ablution, was entering the hermitage. The Rishi became angry and immediately cursed the intruder to turn into a dog for his canine actions, as only dogs sneakily creep into households and desecrate food. The intruder had not only desecrated the hermitage through his actions but had also violated the country's moral code. The curse became immediately effective, and the King turned into a roaming mongrel. Gunaseelan begged the Sage to take back his curse in place of his entire domain and wealth, but the words of the sage, who had already attained Vak Siddhi, were irrevocable. But seeing the humility, distress, and penitence of the King, Sage Kusasanan retorted to lighten the cruel rigor of the curse by saying that in due course of time, he would come across a holy place where he would regain his original form after a bath. In the form of a mongrel, the King had to roam around the earth, how long none could say. Once, during his wanderings, a juggler came before him and, finding him relatively healthy and plump, utilized his services to demonstrate sleight-of-hand tricks in the art of juggling.
Time passed, the mongrel in the company of the juggler roamed around the earth and, at last, reached Nāṅguṇēri. Before starting his show, the juggler took his bath in the temple tank and bathed the mongrel too. But to his surprise, the mongrel stood transformed as a king after the holy dip. People thronged around the juggler to see the wonderful jugglery of God. Such is the power of the holy waters of the sacred tank at Nāṅguṇēri.

*** The Vanamamalai Jeeyar Mutt headquarters are situated here at this kshethram. It is said that Manavaala Maamunigal used to preach here at this kshethram, and the Mutt was founded by Ponnadikaal Jeeyar, who was one among Manavaala Maamunigal's eight sishyas.

fields.text:
It is said that Garuḍa and Ādisheshan were once mortal enemies, engaging in a fierce battle due to the injustice committed by Ādisheshan's mother against Garuḍa's mother. The story is as follows. Kadrū ( Ādisheshan's mother) and Vinatā ( Garuḍan's mother) were both wives of Kashyapa Maharshi. One day, Kashyapa Maharshi asked his wives to ask him for a boon each. Kadrū asked that she be blessed with a thousand sons. Vinatā asked for two sons who would be brighter and stronger than all of Kadrū's sons combined. Thus, both Kadrū and Vinatā were blessed. Slowly, all of Kadrū's children were born. Five hundred years passed, but neither of Vinatā's eggs hatched into a thousand nagas (snakes). In desperation, Vinatā opened one of the eggs manually.
The offspring in the egg was still half-formed and, in anger at Vinatā's impatience, cursed her, saying she would become Kadrū's slave. But he also told her that in another five hundred years' time, his brother would hatch, and he would be extremely powerful, and he would relieve Vinatā of this curse. This offspring is known to us by the name of Arunan, the charioteer of Sūryan. Even though he was half-formed, he had extreme tolerance and power. Hence, he was taken by Sūryan as a charioteer. As time passed, the curse came into effect. One day, Kadrū and Vinatā were arguing about the color of Uchchaihshravas' tail. Vinatā claimed that the divine horse was a pure white color throughout, but Kadrū said the horse's body was white, but the tail was black. Thus, the two had a bet to see who was right. The one who would lose the bet would become the other's slave. Kadrū knew very well that the tail of Uchchaihshravas was pure white, and knowing she would lose the bet, she told her sons to wrap themselves around the tail of Uchchaihshravas so that she could win the bet. One day, in the presence of Kadrū and Vinatā, Uchchaihshravas passed by with a black tail. Thus, Kadrū won the bet, enslaving Vinatā. For five hundred years, Vinatā was a slave to Kadrū. After five hundred years, Vinatā's second egg hatched, and from that egg was born Garuḍan. As soon as he was born, he went straight to his aunt and demanded that his mother be freed from slavery.
To this, Kadrū put a condition, saying that if Garuḍan could bring the Amrutakalasham (the divine pitcher that contained the sacred nectar of immortality) for her and her children, she would release Vinatā from slavery. Thus, Garuḍan immediately left for Svargalokam and defeated all the Devas in battle, successfully retrieving the Amrutakalasham. After retrieving the Amrutakalasham, Garuḍan returned to Bhūlokam. On Bhūlokam, Lord Vishṇu was very impressed with Garuḍan for his strength and dedication. The Lord then offered Garuḍan a boon. Garuḍan asked that he should always be soaring far above the Lord; thus, Garuḍan is present in the Dhvajasthambham outside the temple. The Lord also then told Garuḍan that he wanted Garuḍan to be constantly under his command, and thus asked Garuḍan to become his vaahanam. The Lord also relieved Vinatā from slavery and returned the Amrutakalasham to the Devas.
In one of the battles between Garuḍan and Ādisheshan, Ādisheshan is said to have hidden in the pushkariṇī and performed tapas to the Lord to save him. Thus, the Lord appeared on the bank of the pushkariṇī and made Ādisheshan his recliner. Hence, the Lord made sure that as long as He is present, both of His bhaktas do not fight amongst themselves.
It is said that if one prays to the Lord here, they will be relieved of all and any sarpa-dhosham.
***There is an interesting story that Vyagrapadar, who obtained a boon from Lord Shiva to possess the legs, hands, and eyes of a tiger, worshipped Lord Vishṇu at this kshethram, and hence it gained the name Sirupuliyur.

fields.text: This kshethram is located in the Naṭarāja temple at Chidambaram.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend has it that Lord Shiva and Devī Pārvatī once engaged in a competition to determine who was the better dancer. When the world was asked, they all responded, saying Lord Shiva was the better dancer. In hopes of getting a second opinion, Devī Pārvatī suggests that the divine couple go to Vaikuṇṭham and ask Lord Vishṇu for his opinion, as His opinion was supreme, and nobody could question Him. When the question was put before the Lord, he said he would watch the divine couple dance and would decide then who among them was a better dancer. Thus, a maṇḍapam was constructed by Vishvakarma, known as the Chitra Maṇḍapam. The Lord descended from Vaikuṇṭham along with Shrīdevī and Bhūdevi reclining on Ādisheshan. Lord Shiva appeared as Naṭarāja at the forefront of the Chitra Maṇḍapam. All the devas and Lord Brahmā descended to Bhūlokam to witness the spectacle of Lord Naṭarāja and Devī Pārvatī's dance. Thus, Lord Naṭarāja and Devī Pārvatī began dancing, and all those present to witness the spectacle watched in awe as the duo danced at a level never before seen. After the divine dance performance was concluded, Lord Vishṇu asked everyone present at the event who they thought performed better. Everyone voted in favor of Lord Naṭarāja, and Lord Vishṇu simply obliged by lifting his head. Devī Pārvatī, in anger, fled the scene and took the form of Devī Kāli outside Chidambaram. Thus, one can still see a temple of Devī Kāli here outside Chidambaram.

*** The Lord here is said to be a direct reincarnation of Tirumalai Shrīnivāsa Perumāl. The Lord here is reclining on the seven-headed serpent Ādisheshan, whereas the Lord standing at Tirumalai is standing atop seven hills. Govindarāja Perumāl is depicted with Shankham and Chakram, one hand supporting his head and the other hand displaying the Varada Mudra. Similarly, Shrīnivāsa Perumāl can be seen with Shankham, Chakram, one hand tucked inside and another hand showcasing Varada Mudra.
This temple has a rich history. During the Chōla rule, Kulothunga Chōla II was said to have uprooted the presiding idol of the Lord from the Shrine at the Naṭarāja temple to show Shaiva dominance. It is said that Bhagavat Rāmānujāchārya took the utsava moorthy (Paartasarathy Perumāl) to Govindrajapatnam at Tirupati. When the kings changed over time, Krishnappa Nayaka of the Madurai Nayaka dynasty played a crucial role in reinstalling the Lord in this temple. There was considerable resistance from the Shaivaites present at Chidambaram at the time to reinstalling an idol of Lord Vishṇu in a temple dedicated to Lord Shiva. However, the king remained unmoved and reinstated the idol of the Lord, as seen in modern times.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend has it that Lord Krishna built the city of Dvārakā with the assistance of Vishvakarma. After Lord Krishna had killed Kansa, his two wives became widows. Kansa's wives were the daughters of Jarāsandha. Jarāsandha swore to exact revenge against Lord Krishna, who had caused his daughters to suffer a cruel fate. Jarāsandha attacked Mathura seventeen times. Each of these seventeen times, Lord Krishna defended Mathura. After all these attacks, Lord Krishna deemed that Mathura was no longer fit for stay as Jarāsandha would continue to attack the state. Lord Krishna orders Vishvakarma to claim land from Samudraraja and convert it into a grand city that would be safe from any form of invasion. Thus, Dvārakā came into being. Dvārakā is among the Mukthi Kshethrams along with Ayodhyā, Mathura, Maya (Haridwar), Kashi, Kāñchipuram, and Avantika (Ujjain).
Apart from this divyadesam, there are four other Dvārakā. Together, the five kshethrams are collectively known as PanchaDwarka.
The five Dvārakā include:
Dvārakā
Rukmiṇī Dvārakā
Beyt Dvārakā
Dakor Dvārakā
Shrīnāthji Dvārakā


Rukmiṇī Dvārakā:
This kshethram is located 3.1 km from Dvārakā. This Dvārakā houses Rukmiṇī Devī, whom Durvāsa Maharshi cursed to stay away from Lord Krishna. Performing neer-daanam at this kshethram is of importance. Even the prasadam offered here is that of water

Beyt Dvārakā:
This kshethram is located on an island off the coast of mainland India. To reach this kshetram, one must travel by boat from Okha Port or by road using the Sudarshana Setu. This kshethram was once connected to the mainland. It is said that after Lord Krishna left this world for Paramapadam, the land that connected the mainland to this kshethram was reclaimed by Samudraraja. This is the kshethram where Sudāmā visited the Lord to ask for alms. Sudāmā never asked for anything from the Lord, but he was presented with more than he could ever have asked for. It is said that Meerabai attained moksham here at this kshethram when she merged with the Lord.

Dakor Dvārakā:
This kshethram is located near Anand in Gujarat. The Lord is called Ranchodraiji. It is said that in the seventeenth encounter with Jarāsandha, the Lord started to run from the battlefield when He was faced against an asuran called Kaalayavanan. It is said that the Lord left the battlefield near Mathura and ran till the Junagadh district in modern-day Gujarat. Here, there was an ancient sooryavanshi king named Muchukunda who lay asleep after gaining a boon from Indra. There was once a great battle between the devas and the asuras. To win the battle, Indra took the help of Lord Ram's ancestor, King Muchukunda. After winning the battle for the devas, Indra gave Muchukunda the boon that he could sleep for a long time to take a rest after the long and drawn-out battle. When Muchukunda would awake from this sleep, the first thing he would lay his eyes would turn into ash. Lord Krishna ran into the cave and awoke Muchukunda from his sleep in such a way that the first person he would lay his eyes on would be Kaalayavanan. When Kaalayavanan came in Muchukunda's line of sight, he turned to ash. The idol of the Lord present at Dakor Dvārakā is said to have originally been in Dvārakā. After the idol was brought to Dakor, another idol that Devī Rukmiṇī was worshiping was installed in the temple at Dvārakā.

Shrīnāthji Dvārakā:
This kshethram is located in Nathdwara, Rajasthan. This kshethram was established by Shri Vallabhacharya. The idol is said to have been installed in this temple by Meerabai. The idol is said to be a swayambhu moorthy, which is believed to have originated from the Govardhana Parvatham and became the object of worship in the Mevar Royal family, where Meerabai was born.

fields.text:
According to legend, it is said that during the Kṛta Yugam, two demons by the name Madhu and Kaiṭabha stole the Vedas from Lord Brahmā and disappeared into the Pralaya Samudram (Ocean of Deluge). It is said that Lord Maha Vishṇu took the Matsya Avataram and retrieved the Vedas. It is also said that the Vedas had lost their fragrance as they were robbed. The Lord is then said to have taken the form of Parimala Ranganathan, restoring their fragrance and returning them to Lord Brahmā. It is said that Gaṅgā Devī is present near the head of the Lord. As seen at Tirucherai, Kāvēri Devī was deemed greater than Gaṅgā Devī. Hence, it is said that Gaṅgā comes to this kshethram and bathes here in the Kāvēri river to rid herself of her sins.

*** A peculiarity seen here with Lord is that he is seen in the Veera Shayanam. Anywhere one goes and sees the Lord in Shayana Kolam, one can see that the Lord will not be holding His shankam and chakram. However, here at this kshethram, as He carries His weapons and is in a reclined posture, He is said to be in the Veera Shayanam.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: There is no explicitly known sthala purāṇam for this particular kshethram. The presiding deity Karunakara Perumāl is so named because of his character of showing karunai or daya. The Lord here is compared to a cloud. This is for two reasons: one being his color, and the other being that he showers affection on all his devotees. This kshethram is called Kaaragam. This is because Kaara means karunai or affection, and agam means place. Thus, at this kshethram, the Lord showers his affection on all his devotees as Karunakara Perumāl.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: This kshethram again does not have a particular sthala purāṇam of its own. This kshethram is closely related to Tiruneeragam and Tirukaaragam. Kaarvaanam means a sky filled with clouds. The world cannot survive without water, and clouds play a crucial role in bringing water to the world. Thus, the Lord standing here is an embodiment of rain clouds bringing rain to the world, helping it survive.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text:
Next, we will see the Divyadesams located in and around Kāñchipuram.
This Divya kshethram is located in Vishṇu Kanchi, Kāñchipuram. This is one of the celebrated Vaishṇava Divya Desams. The first prakaram of the temple is on the Hastigiri hill. In Vishṇu Kanchi, there are other shrines Ashtabhujakaram, Tiruttanka, Tiruvelukkai, and Tiruvegkaa. In Shiva Kanchi, there are Tiru Oorakam, Tiru Neeragam, Tiruppaadagam, Nilaattingal Tundam, Tirukkaragam, Tirukkaarvaanam, Tirukkalvanur, Tiruppavalavannam, and Parameswara Vinnagarm shrines.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
According to temple history, the Lord first appeared in the Satya Yuga. The first account of the Lord is mentioned in the Rāmāyaṇa. As we know, the great King Dasharatha performed the Putrakāmeyishṭi Yajña to obtain children. The Putrakāmeyishṭi is a supplement to the Ashvamedha Yajña. It is said that Dasharatha first performed the Ashvamedha, and the origin of the Lord is believed to be found in this act. It is noted that Dasharatha asked his son-in-law, the sage Rishyashringa, to make arrangements to perform the Ashvamedha, where he recounts the story of an Ashvamedha Yajña performed by Lord Brahmā. The story states that Lord Brahmā once performed an Ashvamedha Yajña in a very sacred place that would yield a multifold increase in merit. In his research, he decided to perform this Yajña at a place known as Hasthigiri. It is said that he sat atop Hastigiri and prepared the sacrificial altar. According to Vaideeka Shāstram, Goddess Sarasvatī had to accompany Lord Brahmā to perform this Yajña. At this point, he was faced with two problems. The first being that Goddess Sarasvatī was not present, and the second being that there was no image of Lord Vishṇu present at the sacrifice. Lord Brahmā decided to address the second problem first. To address this problem, Lord Brahmā summoned Vishvakarma, the architect, and had him design an image of Lord Vishṇu for the Devas. Lord Brahmā wanted this idol to be useful for generations to come. He hence sought to make the idol of the Lord from a material whose properties would be beneficial to anyone who sought the Lord's blessings. Lord Brahmā's four heads signify each of the four Vedas. That is when Lord Brahmā recollected that in the Atharvana Veda, there was a mention of a tree known as Udhumbara, which, when worshiped with devotion, has the power to annihilate any forces of enmity to the worshiper. So, what is Udumbara? Udumbara is a tree known as Ficus racemosa, which belongs to the fig family (athi tree). Brahmā selected this tree because it offers numerous benefits, as per Ayurveda. Hence, Vishvakarma crafted the wood from the fig tree into a resplendent idol of the Lord. So the second problem was solved. To address the first problem, Lord Brahmā decided to call upon his second wife, Goddess Savitri, to take Goddess Sarasvatī's place. It is said that Goddess Sarasvatī had gotten into a tussle with Lord Brahmā and had decided to seek solace to contemplate what had gone wrong. When Goddess Sarasvatī learned what Lord Brahmā was doing, she became furious. In a fury, she decided that she wanted to destroy the sacrificial altar and hence put a stop to the Yajña in totality. It is said that the Goddess Sarasvatī took the form of a river known as Vegavathy and began to flow at a rapid speed towards the altar. Before Goddess Sarasvatī could reach the altar, she witnessed the idol of Athi Vardar and decided to flow beneath his feet as a mark of respect to her father-in-law. Thus the Yajña reached a conclusion. During the culmination of the Yajña, a resplendent Vimānam, known as the Punyakoṭi Vimānam, rose from the sacrificial altar. In the shade of this Vimānam stood a beautiful utsava moorthy of the Lord, known as Perarulaalan or Varadarajan.


Modern Day
Around the 1520s, the Vijayanagara empire was the ruler of South India. They contributed immensely to the temple. One such contribution is the "Noor-Kaal Maṇḍapam," or a Hundred Pillared Maṇḍapam, which Achyutha Deva Raya, the brother of the great Krishna Deva Raya, built. Around the 16th century, a significant shift occurred in the Delhi Sultanate when the Mughals gained control of North India and began expanding south. Towards the end of the Mughal Rule, when Aurangzeb took over, he began to plunder the temples and loot their wealth. The Vaishṇavas of Kāñchipuram sought to protect both the Mūla Vigraham and the Utsava Mūrti from the invasion. To protect the Utsava Mūrti, the idol was carried by palanquin to a remote place called Udayarpalayam, where the local chief agreed to host and protect the Lord. Now, protecting the Mūla Mūrti was a herculean task, as the idol was nearly 9 feet in length. Thus, a place had to be discovered where the Lord could be kept safe. The Vaishṇavas then dug a giant pit within the temple tank (Ananthasaras) and embalmed Athi Varada, placing him alongside Ādishesha to protect the Lord.
Over a while, the temple did not have a Mūla Mūrti or a Utsava Mūrti. After Aurangzeb's invasion, the temple was in ruins, with the Punyakoṭi Vimānam destroyed. Thus, the temple was reconstructed, but the daily rituals of the temple couldn't be performed in the absence of the Lord. Hence, after major tussles with the chief of Udayarpalayam, the Utsava Mūrti was brought back to the temple. But the Mūla Mūrti was lost as the people who had dug the pit were either very old or had passed away. Thus, the temple needed to install a Mūla Mūrti in the temple. Hence, an idol of the Lord, known as Devaraja, found in a hamlet called Pazhayasheevaram, was brought to Kāñchipuram and installed in the temple. Later, sometime in the 18th Century, when the temple tank was being cleaned, the idol of Athi Varada was found. At this time, the scholars came to the consensus that the idol would be preserved, and the idol of the Lord would be displayed for the devotees for 48 days, after which it would be returned to the temple tank to remain there for 40 years.

According to legend, Pundareeka Maharshi, desirous of worshipping Lord Vishṇu with lotus flowers, proceeded eastward and attempted to drain the waters of the ocean to make his way. The Lord came in the guise of an old man and asked for some food. The Maharshi went to fetch him some food, and when he returned, he found Lord Vishṇu adorning Himself with the flowers and giving darshan as Ananthasayanam. Hence, this place gained the name Sthalasayanam.

*** A peculiarity of this kshethram is that one can see the Lord in reclining posture without Ādisheshan. The Lord is reclining on the ground; hence, he is known as Sthalashayana Perumāl (Sthala meaning 'ground'). The Lord can be seen with four hands. His left hand displays the aahwaana-mudra, welcoming his devotees, and his right hand is seen in the varada-mudra along the left and right lengths of his bed.

fields.text:
It is said that Mahābali Chakravarthy had offered Lord Vāmana three paces of land from where the Kapila Tīrtham pushkariṇī now stands. As the Lord took the three steps, with the first step, the Lord measured the entire earth; with the second step, He measured the heavens and hell. By the time he could take the third step, there was no more space where He could place His foot. Thus, He placed His foot on Mahābali Chakravarthy's head upon his request, sending him to Pātāla-lokam. It is said that Mahābali then asked the Lord to come back one day to the world of the living to see his subjects. To fulfill this wish, the Lord let Mahābali visit his subjects on the day of Onam in the month of Avanni. It is said that Kapila Maharshi had performed tapas at this kshethram to see the Lord in His Vāmana form.
*** There is a very peculiar story of how the Nendram Vazha, a local variety of plantain, started to grow in this area. It is said that there was once an orchard that used to grow plantains. The yield of the orchard was terrible. The owner of the orchard came to this temple and prayed to Lord Vāmana, offering Him a plantain made of gold. Lord Vāmana is said to have opened His eyes upon seeing the golden plantain, which is said to have triggered an excellent yield of plantain henceforth. As the Lord opened His eyes, the fruit came to be known as Nethra Vazha, which over time has become Nendram Vazha.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend has it that Pārvatī Devī, standing on one foot, meditated upon Lord Shiva under a mango tree to be united with him in marriage. She sought the blessings of her brother Lord Vishṇu, and her prayers were answered. There is another story that Parvarti Devī sighted Lord Vishṇu, overhearing a conversation between her and Lakshmī, upon which she addressed Him as Kalvan.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
During Samudra Manthanam, Mahālakshmī appeared from the Ksheerasagaram. Upon appearing, she was searching for Lord Vishṇu so that she could be reunited with him once again. She sees the Lord but is embarrassed to put the Varamala around his neck as there were thirty-three crore gods(men) who were present there at the time. She thus decided to seek the Lord in private and went to Tirukanamangai, where she performed penance within the Darshana Pushkariṇī to bring the Lord there in solitude. The Lord appeared, and as Mahālakshmī was about to put the Varamala around the Lord's neck, all the Devas appeared once more to witness the spectacle of the Lord's marriage. The Lord thought that if the devas continued to stay in the form of men, Mahālakshmī would once again run away in embarrassment. Hence, he changed all the Devas into bees. As soon as this was done, Mahālakshmī married the Lord.

***Even today, outside the shrine of Abhishekavalli Thāyār, one can find a hive of bees buzzing around, symbolizing the presence of the Devas at the temple to date.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Bhṛgu Maharshi, Gautama Rishi, and Brahmā worshipped Lord Vishṇu at this kshethram. It is also believed that Vasishṭhar created an image of Lord Krishna out of butter and meditated upon it. Lord Krishna is said to have appeared one day when Vasishṭhar was performing aaradhanam for the butter idol. When the Lord saw the butter idol, he was tempted and gobbled it up. When Vasishṭhar started to look for the butter idol, he saw a boy running away, saying he had eaten up the butter. Vasishṭhar began to chase the child. As the Lord was being chased by Vasishṭhar, a group of sages who were meditating under a Magizha tree caught sight of the boy, recognizing Him to be the Lord. The Lord is then said to have taken the form of Damodaran( the one who was tied up). Thus, this kshethram became the home of Lord Krishna. Hence the name Tirukkannankudi.

Thirukannangudi Divyadesam and Tirumangai Āzhwār

Once, when Tirumangai Āzhwār was building the massive outer walls of the Shrīraṅgam temple, he ran out of money. To find a way, he went to the Buddhist Vihara at Nāgapaṭṭinam. There, he sang a verse saying that for Buddha, it was enough to have a statue made of iron, wood, brass, or any simple metal—there was no need for it to be made of gold.

As he sang, something strange happened. The gold from the Buddha statue started to melt and flowed towards him, turning into gold bars. With that gold, he set off to Shrīraṅgam.

On the way, he became tired and rested under a tamarind tree. Before lying down, he buried the gold near the tree and told the tree to wake him up if anyone came by. The tree, taking his words seriously, stayed alert all night and didn't "sleep." That's why it's known as Urangaa Puli—the Tamarind Tree That Didn't Sleep.

The next morning, a landlord from that area came by. The tree dropped a few leaves on Āzhwār, waking him up just in time. Seeing the gold, the landlord claimed that since it was found on his land, it belonged to him. But Tirumangai Āzhwār told him the land actually belonged to him and that he had the documents to prove it in Shrīraṅgam. He said he would go there, bring back the papers, and settle the matter. But he never came back. The issue was never resolved and is still said to be "pending." That's why it's called Theraa Vilakku—the Case That's Still Not Settled.

On the journey, Āzhwār became very thirsty. He saw a few women near a well and asked them for some water. But since he had an argument with the landlord from their village, they refused to give him any. Angry at this, Āzhwār cursed that the wells in that village would go dry forever. That's why the place came to be called Oorak Kinaru—the Village of Dry Wells.

Tired, thirsty, and hungry, Tirumangai Āzhwār lay down under a Maghizham Tree. The tree gently fanned him with its cool breeze and gave him some comfort. At that moment, Lord Pārthasārathy (Paranthaman) appeared in the form of a Brāhmiṇ. He gave Āzhwār some food and water. After eating, when Āzhwār looked around, the Brāhmiṇ had disappeared. He then realized it was the Lord Himself. Feeling blessed and happy, he gave a boon to the tree that it would never dry up. From then, that tree has been called Kaaya Magizhai—the Maghizham Tree That Never Dries.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend has it that Uparisravas, a Fisherman King, performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and begot a daughter named Padmini, whom he offered in marriage to Lord Vishṇu at this shrine. It is believed that Neelamegha Perumāl vanquished a demon called Veekatakshan with His chakram, and hence the presiding deity is found with the prayoga chakram. It is also thought that the Lord in the sanctum miraculously showed the growth of hair to protect the words of a devout priest, Raṅgabhaṭṭar. It is said that the local king was visiting the temple on a given day, and Raṅgabhaṭṭar had already given the garland the Lord adorned to his lover. When the king arrived at the temple, there was no garland to perform the required honors. He requested the king to perform pradakshinam of the temple, by which time he would arrange for a garland. He sent a boy to fetch the garland from his lover. When the garland was presented to the king, he found a strand of hair in it. The king then questioned Raṅgabhaṭṭar as to where that hair had come from, to which Raṅgabhaṭṭar said the hair was that of the Lord's. When the king came to examine the same in the morning, he found hair behind the crown that was placed atop the Lord's head. Hence, the Lord attained the name Sowrirajan.

***Tirumangai Āzhwār is believed to have been initiated with the ashtaakshara mantram at this temple.

fields.text:
The name of the kshethram is Tirukarambanur. This is because the Lord showed Himself to Maharshi Kadambha. Additionally, the Lord had taken the form of a Kadambha tree, to which Lord Brahmā used to perform aaradhanam by pouring holy water from his kamandalam. Another story associated with this kshethram is similar to that of Tirukandiyoor. It is said that Lord Brahmā once had five heads. In a rage, Lord Shiva once slapped Lord Brahmā's fifth head, as he also had five heads, and it stuck to his hand as a curse. The only way the Bramhakapalam falls from one's hand is to beg for alms, and for that to fill up the kapalam. In his search for alms, Lord Shiva reached Karambanur. Here, when he begged Pūrṇavalli thāyār for alms, the kapalam burst, and Lord Shiva was free of the curse. Thus, it is said that people without a means of obtaining food can come here to pray to Pūrṇavalli Thāyār to gain her blessings.
* This is said to be the only temple where one can see the Trinity with their wives all under the same temple. There are temples where one can see Lord Vishṇu, Lord Brahmā, and Lord Shiva together. However, this is the only temple where you will see Lord Vishṇu with Pūrṇavalli Thāyār (Lakshmī), Lord Brahmā with Sarasvatī, and Lord Shiva with Pārvatī.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend is that Lord Vishṇu blessed Romesa Maharshi with a vision of Trivikrama with his left foot raised in the gesture of dominating the three worlds. Romesa Maharshi had once performed tapas here to seek the Lord. When the Lord appeared before Romesa Maharshi, he asked the Lord to bring down the pride and arrogance possessed by Lord Brahmā, as he was the creator of the three worlds. The Lord told Romesa Maharshi that as and when a hair would fall from his head, the lifetime of Lord Brahmā would be reduced by one year. It is said that Lord Brahmā soon lost all of his pride and served his purpose diligently. After seeing the Lord, Romesa Maharshi requested to see the Lord in His Trivikraman form. Thus, the Lord showed Romesa Maharshi the form in which He was ready to measure the world by raising His left foot.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend recounts the story of how the Lord appeared at this kshetram as the Saptarshis performed tapas, with the intention of seeing the Lord in the form of Shri Nṛisimha. The rishis requested a local ruler to protect them from the prevailing demons in the area while they performed the necessary yajñas to please the Lord. The king tried his best to keep the rishis safe, but was defeated after some time. At this point, Lord Rāma had just defeated Rāvaṇa and was on his way back to rule Ayodhyā. Thus, He instructed Hanumān to go and protect the rishis from all and any danger that was prevalent in the area. It is said that Hanumān held the Shankham and Chakram at this kshethram to protect the rishis from every possible risk. After successful completion of the tapas and yajñas, Lord Nṛisimha emerged seated in padmasana as Yoga Nṛisimha.
*** Another name of this kshethram is Gadikachalam, as Gadika means 24 minutes. It is said that if one spends 24 minutes at the top of the hill, it absolves all sins that one has committed throughout one's life. There are two hills at this kshethram: one large hill with 1,300 steps, which houses Shri Yoga Nṛisimha Perumāl, and a smaller hill with 750 steps, which houses Shri Yoga Añjanēya Perumāl. This is the only place where one can see Añjanēyar with Shanku and Chakram seated in padmasana. Shri Añjanēyar faces Lord Nṛisimha. It is said that Lord Nṛisimha constantly blesses Lord Añjanēyar. It is said that if one visits both of these temples, they will never be plagued by any kind of ghosts, spirits, or ghouls of any kind.

Legend tells the story of Kubera losing all his wealth because he had inappropriately seen Devī Pārvatī. When he asked for Her forgiveness, Devī Pārvatī asked him to go to Tirukkolur and perform tapas towards Lord Vishṇu, and he would regain his wealth. Thus, Kubera is said to have come to this kshethram, and after performing tapas, the Lord appeared as Vaithamanidi Perumāl, who brought all of Kubera's wealth. The Lord is said to have kept Kubera's wealth under Ādishesha and slept over it. Thus, Kubera received their kripa-kataksham in the form of keeping his wealth safe and also gaining interest over time. The Lord's left-hand houses kajal. The Lord is said to be looking at this hand to find more wealth for Kubera's treasury.
Another story tells the tale of pralaya-kalam. Dharma is said to have taken a human form and prostrated at the Lord's feet to fight against adharma. The Lord is said to establish dharma by defeating all factors causing adharma at the time.

*** This kshethram is the avatara sthalam of Madhurakavi Āzhwār.
