fields.text:
It is said that Ambarīsha was such an ardent devotee that the Sudarshana Chakra had made himself self-obligated to rush for Ambarīsha's protection. One day, the great sage Durvāsa decided to pay a visit to Ambarīsha. Ambarīsha had undertaken the Dvādashī-Vratam, in which one must break the fast after Ekadashi and feed their people at the start of Dvādashī. Durvāsa Maharshi told Ambarīsha that he would take a bath and then join him in the Dvādashī-Vratam. Ambarīsha agreed to wait for Durvāsa Maharshi. Hours went by, but Durvāsa Maharshi was nowhere to be seen. On the advice of Sage Vasishta, Ambarīsha broke his fast by taking holy water. At this moment, Durvāsa Maharshi arrived and, in his temper, threw a lock of his hair to the ground. This hair grew into a monstrous demon that chased Ambarīsha to devour him. At this moment, the Sudarshana Chakra of the Lord came to Ambarīsha's rescue and cut the demon into tiny pieces. Further, the Chakra started to chase after Durvāsa Maharshi. Durvāsa Maharshi began to run and sought refuge with Lord Brahmā, Lord Shiva, and ultimately at the heavenly abode of Lord Vishṇu himself. Still, the Chakra continued to pursue Durvāsa Maharshi. Lord Vishṇu instructed Durvāsa Maharshi to go and fall at Ambarīsha's feet and ask for his forgiveness. Durvāsa Maharshi then falls at Ambarīsha's feet for his forgiveness. Ambarīsha forgives Durvāsa Maharshi, and the Sudarshana Chakra stops going after Durvāsa Maharshi. It is said that
Ambarīsha used to pray to this Lord, and with this Lord's grace, he was protected.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend has it that the Devas came together (goshti) to worship the Lord at this kshetram to rid the universe of the demon Hiraṇyakashipu. This temple is also considered Dakshina Badri. This is probably the most important kshetrham according to the Shri Vaishṇava Parampara, as it is the kshetram where Svāmi Bhagavad Rāmānujar first performed the Ashṭākshara Mantropadesham. Let us see the story. Svāmi Rāmānujar came here to this kshethram to seek education from Shri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal. Shri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal is said to have rejected giving Svāmi Rāmānujar education seventeen times, sending him back to Shri Raṅgam. When Svāmi Rāmānujar came back for the eighteenth time, Shri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal is said to have revealed the ashtakshara mantram and the charama shlokam to Svāmi Rāmānujar and instructed him to keep it a secret. Svāmi Rāmānujar realized that this mantram and shloka were the means to Shri Vaikuṇṭham. Thus, Svāmi Rāmānujar is said to have climbed up to the top of the Ashṭāṅga Vimānam and openly revealed that he possessed the ashtakshara mantram as well as the charama shlokam and was willing to pass it on to anyone who so wished to listen to him. When Shri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal learned of this, he immediately pursued Svāmi Rāmānujar. He told him that he was destined to go to hell because he had not listened to his guru's wishes. Svāmi Rāmānujar is then supposed to have said that he was more than ready to go to hell if he could provide the means for so many people to go to Vaikuṇṭham. Shri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal then realizes his mistake and is said to have asked for forgiveness of Svāmi Rāmānujar after seeing his broad outlook.

Ashṭāṅga Vimānam with the arch from where Svāmi Ramnujar performed mantropadesham

fields.text:
It is said that the Lord is said to have taken this form when asked by Mrugandu Maharshi asked to see the Lord as Trivikramar. The Lord present here is an exact mirror image of the Lord standing at Tirukazhicheerama Vinnagaram. One peculiarity of the Lord standing here is that the Lord is holding the Shankham in the right hand and the Chakram in the left hand.

***
The first three of the Āzhwārs — Poigai Āzhwār, Bhūtath Āzhwār, and Pey Āzhwār — came to Thirukkovilur on a rainy night. First to arrive was Poigai Āzhwār, from Kāñchipuram, who sought refuge for the night at the ashram of Mrugandu Rishi. The rishi told him that there was a place for just one person to sleep and that he was welcome to stay for the night.
Bhūtath Āzhwār, from Māmallapuram, followed shortly, and he too requested that he stay at the ashram for the night. PoigaiAzhwar welcomed him, saying there was a place for one to sleep and two to sit, and took him inside.
Pey Āzhwār, from Mylapore, too, reached the ashram. He was told that there was a place for one to sleep, two to sit, and three to stand. It is explained as a slogan by
"Oruvar Padukka – Iruvar Irukka – Moovar Nirkalam".
 The three of them stood there through the night, sharing their experiences with each other.
A little later, the three Āzhwārs sensed the presence of a fourth person, and with space only for three to stand, they felt uncomfortable. Through their exceptional vision, the three Āzhwārs realized that the fourth person was none other than Lord Vishṇu himself. Delighted at this, they showered praises on the Lord.
This is the first temple where the first three Āzhwārs sang praises (Pāsurams) of Lord Vishṇu, the compilation of which later came to be known as the Naalayira Divya Prabhandham.
It is believed that this ashram, where the 3 Āzhwārs stayed that rainy night, is the one where one, today, finds the sanctum. The first of the three Āzhwārs also finds a place inside the Sanctum.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
There was once a Chozha king by the name Dharmavarman who lived in Kumbakoṇam. Once, when the king had gone on a hunting trip, he found that a few rishis were distressed by the attack of demons and sought the king's help to kill them. The king bravely defended the rishis and stayed in the forest for some time to look after the welfare of the rishis. At this time, the king was saddened by his inability to father any children. The rishis then performed a yajna to help the king in his time of difficulty. As the rishis were performing the yajna, a voice boomed from the sky, stating that if the king wanted children, he must pray to Goddess Lakshmī. Thus, the king prayed to Goddess Lakshmī. One day, as he was going through the forest, he noticed a very peculiar lotus blooming in a pond. Upon further inspection, he saw that the lotus had a thousand petals, and in the center, a beautiful baby girl was nestled. Goddess Lakshmī had answered the king's prayers by reincarnating herself as the baby girl. As she was found in a lotus, Dharmavarman named the child Kamalavalli.
Here, the meaning of Kamala can be interpreted as Ka meaning Paramathma, Ma meaning the Jeevathma, and La meaning the one who helps reach. Therefore, Kamala means she who leads the Jeevathma to the Paramathma to attain moksham. Soon, a time came when Dharmavarman began to seek a suitor for Kamalavalli. Among the men in the swayamwaram, Lord Raṅganāthar of Shri Raṅgam was present. Seeing the Lord, Kamalavalli immediately garlanded the Lord. The Lord then left a form of Himself in the form of Shri Azhagiya Māṇavāḷan there in his stead. Thus, all the people gathered at the event witnessed the grand spectacle of the wedding of the Lord with Goddess Lakshmī.
During the Pankuni Brahmotsavam in Shri Raṅgam, on the sixth day, the Lord travels to Urayur to marry Shri Lakshmī. Thus, between the two kshethrams, there is only one utsava moorthy. This kshethram does not conduct Brahmotsavam on its own.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The rishis, headed by Kashyapa, began to perform a sacrifice on the banks of the Gaṅgā. Sage Nārada visited them and asked them why they were performing the sacrifice and who would be pleased by it. Unable to answer the question, the rishis approached Sage Bhṛgu to find a solution through direct ascertainment of reality.
Bhṛgu first went to Satyalokam, the abode of Lord Brahmā. At Satylokam, he found Lord Brahmā reciting the four Vedas in praise of Lord Nārāyaṇa, with each of his four heads, and attended upon by Sarasvatī. Lord Brahmā did not take notice of Bhṛgu offering obeisance. Concluding that Lord Brahmā was unfit for worship, Bhṛgu left Satyalokam for Kailāsham, the abode of Lord Shiva.
At Kailāsham, Bhṛgu found Lord Shiva spending his time pleasantly with Pārvatī, unaware of his presence. Pārvatī drew Shiva's attention to the presence of the sage. Lord Shiva was furious at Bhṛgu's intrusion and tried to destroy him. The sage cursed Lord Shiva and left for Vaikuṇṭham. At Vaikuṇṭham, Lord Vishṇu was reposing on Ādishesha with Shri Mahālakshmī in service at His feet. Finding that Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa also did not notice him, the sage became infuriated and kicked the Lord on his chest, the place where Mahālakshmī resides.
At once, Lord Vishṇu hastened to apologize to the angry sage and pressed his feet to allay the pain caused to Bhṛgu's leg. In doing so, the Lord removed the eye in the foot of the sage, which gave Bhṛgu power to defy the Devas. Thereupon, the sage decided that Lord Vishṇu was the most supreme of the Trimūrtis and informed the rishis accordingly. Thereupon, they decided that Lord Vishṇu was the fruit of the yaga. Shri Mahālakshmī was angered by the action of her Lord in apologizing to Bhṛgu, who committed an offense. She, therefore, left Vaikuṇṭham without heeding the entreaties of the Lord. She furiously ran to Kolhapur and began to perform tapas to get the Lord's attention once more. At the same time, the Lord had taken the form of Shri Shrīnivāsa and was marrying Devī Padmāvatī. When Mahālakshmī found out what was happening, she rushed to take her anger out on the Lord. The Lord is said to have run to Kumbakoṇam and hidden in the temple as Pathala Shrīnivāsar. Mahālakshmī was determined to be reunited with the Lord; thus, she stayed in Kumbakoṇam and performed tapas to fulfill her desires.
At around the same time, Bhṛgu Maharshi had reincarnated as Hema Maharshi and was residing in Kumbakoṇam. One day, in the temple, a pushkariṇī found a baby girl among thousands of lotus flowers blooming in the tank. Hema Maharshi realized that this child was none other than the incarnation of Mahālakshmī and decided to adopt her. As she came of age, She desired to get married to the Lord. During Makara Sankranthi, the Lord descended from Shri Vaikuṇṭham in a grand chariot, and after marrying Komalavalli, Thāyār stayed in Kumbakoṇam along with his chariot. Even today, when we visit this temple, we can see that the garbha griha features a grand chariot in which the Lord is reclining in the Udyoga Shayanam posture.
 Udyoga Shayanam is a peculiar posture, as the Lord is neither completely asleep nor completely upright. It is said that Tirumazhisai Āzhwār was once having a conversation with the Lord. The Lord then was about to get up to greet Tirumazhisai Āzhwār when he told the Lord that he looked notably different and lovely in that position. Hence, the Lord is said to have permanently taken that posture.
***This kshethram is credited for the resurfacing of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal (compilation of all the Āzhwār Pāsurams). At one point, all of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal were lost except for ten Pāsurams that were being sung at this temple. Here, Nāthamunigal heard this, and the verses told ten out of a thousand Pāsurams. This had Nāthamunigal intrigued as to where the other nine hundred and ninety Pāsurams had disappeared. These ten Pāsurams also spoke of Kurugūr (present-day Āzhwār Tirunagari) and Sadagopan (Nam Āzhwār). Thus Nāthamunigal went in search of Nam Āzhwār. Upon reaching Kurugūr and inquiring about these ten Pāsurams, the locals denied knowing of the ten Pāsurams he had asked for, but they were familiar with eleven other Pāsurams. Nāthamunigal recited these eleven Pāsurams twelve thousand times in front of the divine tamarind tree where Nam Āzhwār had once resided. Upon completion of the recitation, Nam Āzhwār is said to have appeared in front of Nāthamunigal and blessed him with the thousand Pāsurams sung by him as well as the three thousand other Pāsurams which were sung by the nine other Āzhwārs.

Hence, the deity is called Mayakoothan.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend says that this Lord is extremely ancient and is said to have appeared before the appearance of Lord Brahmā. When Lord Brahmā is said to have appeared and become conscious of the Lord, acknowledging Him is said to have asked for a place to establish His idol and perform tapas. The Lord is said to have directed Lord Brahmā to Kurugūr by giving him the command of tapas kuru. As the Lord commanded Lord Brahmā to perform tapas, this kshethram gained the name of Kurugūr. Lord Brahmā is said to have bathed in the Tāmraparaṇi River and performed tapas. The Lord is said to have emerged as a Swayambhu Mūrti ( self-established and not carved by anyone ). Lord Brahmā is said to have performed the prathishtapana of the Lord. Another legend tells the story that Indra was absolved of the curse given by his parents by praying to the Lord at this kshethram. It is believed that Lakshmī meditated on Lord Vishṇu when He was on a vow of celibacy. In response to Her request, He accepted Her in marriage in the form of a garland of flowers (Magizha malar maalai).
***

Svāmi Nam Āzhwār

This kshethram is said to be the avatara sthalam of Nam Āzhwār. As we saw in Tirukurungudi, Nam Āzhwār's parents prayed to Kuruṅgudi Nambi for a child who would be like the Lord Himself. It is said that Kuruṅgudi Nambi Himself reincarnated as Nam Āzhwār. We shall now see the story of Nam Āzhwār, one of the most revered gurus in the Shri Vaishṇava Parampara.
Forty-three days had passed since Lord Shri Krishna had ascended to Shri Vaikuṇṭham. A childless couple, Kari and Udayanangai, visited Tirukurungudi to pray for the birth of a child. It is said that they prayed to the Lord for a child who would be like Him. As none in this universe is comparable to Him, it is noted that Nambi Himself reincarnated as Nam Āzhwār. Thus, in the Vaikasi month, under Visakha, Nakshatram, Nam Āzhwār was born. As soon as he was born, he exhibited very peculiar behavior in the form of not crying or suckling. The couple, out of concern, is said to have taken the baby to the Adinatha Perumāl Temple to pray to the Lord for the baby's well-being. Nam Āzhwār is also said to be an amshavataram of Shri Vishwakshenar, who is said to be third in line in the Āchārya Parampara after the Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa and Mahālakshmī Thāyār. The couple is said to have tied a cradle near the Tamarind tree that was present in the temple courtyard.

Divine Tamarind Tree

The baby is said to have crawled out of the cradle and into a small, crater-like space within the tree, where it started a deep meditation. The baby is said to have stayed in this meditative state for sixteen years. At this time, Madhurakavi Āzhwār is said to have been at Ayodhyā and offering argyam as per his Nityakarmam when he saw a blinding light at the edge of the horizon. Recognizing the meditative nature of the divine light is said to have started to follow the light. In pursuit of the light, Madhurakavi Āzhwār is said to have traveled south, crossing Tiruvenkatam, then Tiruvallikeni, then Shri Raṅgam, then Madurai, and finally reaching Kurugūr. When Madhurakavi Āzhwār reached the divine tree, he saw a child in a deep meditative state and was worried if the child was still alive or not. Madhurakavi Āzhwār is said to have thrown a rock near the boy to test his consciousness. When the boy opened his eyes, Madhurakavi Āzhwār is said to have asked a question: "Sethathin Vayatrill Siriyadhu Pirandhaal Yeththai Thindru Enge Kiddakum?". Madhurakavi Āzhwār was referring to the Jeevaathma. Madhurakavi Āzhwār asked, "When the jeevaathma enters a lifeless body, how would it survive, what would it feed on, and how would it sustain itself?" This is when Nam Āzhwār is said to have first spoken by saying, "Aththaith Thindru Ange Kidakkum.". Nam Āzhwār's reply said that the lifeless body would experience the pleasures and pains of life before attaining paramapadam or moksham. Madhurakavi Āzhwār was so stunned by the boy's response that he begged to be his disciple. Madhurakavi Āzhwār composed 11 Pāsurams in praise of his Āchārya, Svāmi Nam Āzhwār, known as Kanninun Shiruthambu, which are included among the 4000 Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
When Nam Āzhwār was ready to attain paramapadam, Madhurakavi Āzhwār asked Nam Āzhwār with full of tears, what to do next. Nam Āzhwār advised Madhurakavi Āzhwār to boil the waters of Tāmraparaṇi, and he said that an idol would form during the boiling of the water. Madhurakavi Āzhwār followed Nam Āzhwār's advice. When he had boiled the waters of Tāmraparaṇi, He got an idol of Bhagavad Rāmānuja. He was surprised to see that the idol was different from what he had expected. He went to Nam Āzhwār with the idol, and the latter told him that this idol was that of a Bhavishyadhacharya (Future Āchārya) and that he would be born 4000 years from then. He again advised boiling the waters of Tāmraparaṇi. Madhurakavi Āzhwār once again boiled the waters of Tāmraparaṇi and finally got the idol of Nam Āzhwār.
Every year on the Tirunakashthram of Nam Āzhwār, the NavaTirupati Brahmotsavam is concluded, and the teerthavaari uthsavam is performed where the idol of Nam Āzhwār is brought to the Tāmraparaṇi River, and along with Shri Sudarshana ChakrathAzhwar, Nam Āzhwār's Idol is also dipped in the holy waters of the river.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
King Rukmangathan of the Suryavamsam is said to have offered flowers to the Lord daily as a form of kainkaryam. One day, the Devas saw the flowers and thought they were to be worshipped first by those beautiful flowers, and hence started to steal the flowers, making garlands for themselves and adorning themselves with them. One day, the king performed a yagam to reveal who was stealing the flowers. The king added numerous medicinal herbs to the divine flames of the yajña, which released a cloud of smoke that revealed the devas wearing floral garlands. The king told the devas that if they had asked for the flowers, he would have given them the flowers without any second thought. The king said to the devas that they could take the flowers at any time and asked them to return to Amarāvatī(Devalokam). The devas informed the king that they were unable to return, as their powers had been rendered useless by the divine smoke emanating from the yajña. The devas told the king that the only way they could return to Amarāvatī was if someone in the kingdom who was observing Ekādashī-vratham with a staunch following, without deviating from any of the rules, gave away the punyam that they gained by following the vratham. The king went searching throughout his kingdom and found a woman who was the only one in the entire kingdom who was religiously following the norms of the vratham.
The king explained the situation to her, and she gifted away all her punyam to the Devas, enabling them to reach Devalokam.

***There are also shrines for Krishna and Narasimhar.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
This kshethram shares many aspects of its Sthala Purāṇam with that of Srivilliputtur. We will see the story of Periya Āzhwār once again.
Periya Āzhwār ( Vishṇuchittar ) used to live in Srivilliputtur, leading a straightforward lifestyle, performing pushpa-kainkaryam to Shri Vatapatrashayee. During that time, there was a king named Vallabhadevan, whose capital was situated in Madurai. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishṇu and wished to learn the meaning of the Vedas and Upanishads. He enquired with his chief minister as to how he could achieve this goal. The minister suggested that the king call all the Vedic Scholars present in his kingdom to debate and question all the matters present in the Vedas and Upanishads. The one who could solve all the questions posed by the king would be rewarded dearly. The king agreed with the minister's suggestion, and soon an announcement was made throughout the kingdom saying there would be a grand meeting of all the Vedic Scholars in the land. The scholar who would impress the king with their answers would be rewarded with gold coins, which would be hung in a divine binding. The coins would present themselves to the person who would aptly answer all of the king's questions. Many scholars came before the king, but none gave satisfactory answers that the king desired. One night, Lord Vatapatrashayee appeared in Vishṇuchittar's dreams and instructed him to go to the king's court to claim the prize that was being offered. Vishṇuchittar told the Lord that he knew nothing about the Vedas or Upanishads. All he knew to do was to make garlands and present them to the Lord. The Lord then told Vishṇuchittar not to worry and to go to the court. The Lord said He would speak through the mouth of Vishṇuchittar. That same night, the Lord also appeared in the dreams of the chief minister and asked him to make royal arrangements to receive Vishṇuchittar and escort him to the king's court.

The next morning, a royal elephant with palanquins arrived and carried Vishṇuchittar to the royal court. As he entered, all the scholars began to murmur and pass sarcastic comments about him, knowing that his knowledge was limited. Vishṇuchittar prostrated himself before the king and the gathered scholars, and then began his speech on the Vedas and Upanishads. As and when the king questioned, it was almost as though the answer to the question was pre-prepared and ready. Finally, to close his speech, Vishṇuchittar made a final statement that said, "Shrīmān Nārāyaṇane Paramporul." This translates to "It is Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa who is the only protector, and it is with His blessing that the universe is surviving. It is He and only He who is the underlying principle that is mentioned in the four Vedas and Upanishads. When this statement was made, the binding came undone, and the gold coins showered into Vishṇuchittar's hands from above. The king was overcome with joy and ecstasy. All the gathered scholars lowered their heads in shame. The king then asked Vishṇuchittar how he had spoken about all the Vedas and Upanishads in such simple language. Vishṇuchittar then told the king that truly it was he who had spoken and that the Lord himself intended for this to perspire. The king was deeply moved by what Vishṇuchittar said and fell to his feet. He arranged for complete royal honors and sent him around the kingdom in a royal procession. At one point, when Vishṇuchittar looked up at the sky, he saw the Lord along with Mahālakshmī seated atop Garuḍan, granting their blessing to him. It was at that moment that, with eyes filled with tears of joy, he said the words, "Pallaandu, pallaandu pallayiratthandu palakodi noorayiram." These words are still sung to date during sathumorai seva every day, whether it may be at a temple or within a household.
*** One of the peculiarities observed in this temple is the presence of a Navagraha Sannidhānam. Usually, one does not observe Navagraha Sannidhānam in a Shri Vaishṇava temple.
Another specialty of this temple is the Ashṭāṅga Vimānam. It is one of the few temples in the country built in tiers. One can climb up and take a closer look at the Ashṭāṅga Vimānam, which enshrines Pallikonda Perumāl in one of its levels, and Sūrya Nārāyaṇan in a standing posture in the other. This aspect of a vimānam, consisting of three tiers enshrining three different postures of Lord Vishṇu — sitting, standing, and reclining — is unique in South Indian temple architecture. The shadow of the Vimānam never falls on the ground.

Ashṭāṅga Vimānam

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The Sthala Purāṇam of this kshethram is found in Varāha Purāṇam. It is known as Kaishika Maahathmiyam.
Kaishika Ekādashī is celebrated in the Tamil Month of Kaarthigai on the succeeding Ekādashī in the Sukla Paksham. This is named after the Kaishika Purāṇam, which is the 48th Chapter in the Shri Varāha Purāṇam. The message behind the day reinforces the fact that caste is not a hindrance in attaining the lotus feet of Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa, and true Bhakti alone is enough. This story took place in the Divyadesam of Thirukurungudi, one of the Nava Tirupati in Thirunelveli. Nambaduvaan was born in a low chandala kulam but was a devotee of Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa. On every Ekādashī, he observed Vratham, sleeping not a single night, singing the glory of the Lord, and thinking about Him. On one Karthigai Ekādashī, Nambaduvaan left for the Kuruṅgudi Nambi temple to observe his fast and recite some Pāsurams using various Paan on Shri Kuruṅgudi Nambi.On his way, Nampāḍuvān was confronted by a Brahmā Rākshasa. This Rākshasa, who has been starved of food, tells Nampaaduvaan that he would devour him. Nampāḍuvān humbly requests that he has the duty of nama sankeerthanam. Nampāḍuvān pleads with the rakshas that he would return after his vratham and darshan of Kuruṅgudi Nambi. He promises that he would indeed return; he mentions the various sins that he would incur if he were not to return. But for none of Nampāḍuvān's promises, Brahmarākshasa was not satisfied. At last, Nambaduvaan promised that "Whoever thinks/says that Supreme Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇan is equivalent/on par with or inferior to other devathas, that paaapam would catch me!" After hearing this, Brahmā Rākshasa was moved and impressed by such a firm promise and said, 'Now I believe in you; you can go now and return soon.' I will wait for you till your return." Nambaduvaan happily went to Shri Kuruṅgudi temple, observed his jakratha vratham, and completed his vratham with singular determination. He returned as stated to Brahmarākshasa. Nampāḍuvān went and offered himself to the Rākshasa. But his hunger had vanished, and instead, he was moved by the truthfulness of the Vishṇu devotee. The Brahmā Rākshasa then told his story – he was a Brāhmiṇ who had been cursed to become a Brahmā Rākshasa by his elders because he had not performed the yajnas carefully. The Rākshasa then asked Nampāḍuvān to give the reward of one of his prayers so that he could get liberation. Hearing the pleas of the Brahmarākshasa, Nambaduvan said that he never sang for any palam. However, he will still request Thirukurungudi Nambi to absolve the Brahmarākshasa of his sins. Nambi gives the palam of the last pāsuram and relieves Brahmarākshasa of its sins. This story strongly reiterates that true Bhakti is sufficient to attain Him, and a person's caste is entirely insignificant. It is believed that those who read or listen to 'Kaishika Purana' on that day will be showered with the Lord's abundant mercy! The story of Nampāḍuvān is narrated and acted in Vishṇu Temples in South India on the Kaishika Ekādashī. Shri Parasara Bhattar chanted the Kaishika Purāṇam before Lord Ranganatha, and this tradition continues to date with the descendants of Bhattar chanting the purāṇam on Kaishika Dvādashī day at Shrīraṅgam each year. Kaishika Ekādashī is considered even more significant to Vaishṇavas than Vaikuṇṭha Ekādashī, as it implies the steadfast Bhakti towards Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa and His abundant mercy on His devotees.


Vaishṇava Nambi Temple



Thirukurungudi Shri Vaishṇava Nambi Dhivya Sevai in Kaishika Maṇḍapam

This kshethram is one of the most important of all the Divyadesams.
The following summarizes the importance of this kshethram:
1) It is said that Svāmi Bhagavad Rāmānujāchārya wanted uniformity in the way rituals were conducted throughout South India. To achieve this, he is said to have traveled to Tiruvanantapuram to plead with the Nambudri priests to follow practices as per the Pancharatra Āgama Shāstras. It is said that the Nambudri priests pleaded with Ananthapadmanabha Svāmi to allow their prevailing traditions, which were being followed, to continue throughout Kerala. It is said that in the middle of the night, when Bhagavad Rāmānujāchārya was asleep, Kuruṅgudi Nambi Svāmi is said to have brought Bhagavad Rāmānujāchārya here to this kshethram. When Bhagavad Rāmānujāchārya awoke in the morning, he is said to have had a conversation with the Lord. The Lord tells Bhagavad Rāmānujāchārya that he has accomplished what He could not achieve in all His births. The Lord asks to be initiated into Shri Vaishṇavism by Bhagavad Rāmānujāchārya. Bhagavad Rāmānujāchārya is said to have performed the Pancha-Samskara for the Lord here, thereby bestowing upon Him the name Shri Vaishṇava Nambi.
2) It is said that Nam Āzhwār's parents came to this kshetram to pray for the birth of a child. The Lord is said to have had a conversation with Nam Āzhwār's parents, asking them what kind of child they desired. The parents are said to have asked for a child who is just like the Lord Himself. As none in this universe is like the Lord, it is said that the Lord Himself incarnated as Nam Āzhwār.
3) This is the kshethram where Tirumangai Āzhwār attained Paramapadam. There is a shrine here for Tirumangai Āzhwār.

Mahendragiri

There is a mention of this kshethram in the Rāmāyaṇa. It is said that Hanumān jumped from Mahendragiri Parvatham to fly to Shri Lanka in search of Sītā, the wife of Lord Rāma. Mahendragiri Parvatham is located within this kshethram. This is also the site of the Malai Mel Nambi Temple.

Legend has it that Yama, the lord of death, once undertook a pilgrimage. While visiting all the holy shrines, he was drawn to the serenity and beauty of Azhagar Malai and meditated on Lord Vishṇu, asking Him to reside in the beautiful surroundings for the benefit of the people. Responding to Yama's request, the Lord ordered Viswakarma, the architect of the celestials, to construct a temple for Him there. The Lord took this place as His permanent abode with his consorts, Shri Devī and Bhoo Devī. There is also an interesting story that the water used by Brahmā to wash the feet of the Lord in the Trivikrama Avatara passed through the anklets and fell at this kshethram. Hence, the nearby river is called Noopura Gaṅgā or Silambu Aaru. The river water is being used for Tirumañjanam to the deity.

Thotti Tirumañjanam

In the Tamil month of Aipassi, during the Shukla Paksham on the day of Dvādashī, a special utsavam known as Thotti Tirumañjanam is conducted. During this utsavam, the utsava murthy of the Lord is brought outside the temple to a small cave where the Noopura Gaṅgā flows. The Lord's hair is oiled with medicinal oils, and tirumanjanam is performed with Noopura Gaṅgā falling from a small height on the Lord's head.
Shri Āṇḍāl, in one of her Pāsurams, had written that she wished to present to Lord Kallazhagar 100 gangalams (a type of vessel made of copper and/or brass), each of butter and pounded rice. It is said that Bhagavad Rāmānujar read this pāsuram and decided to make her poetic wishes a reality, presenting the Lord with 100 gangalams, each made of butter and pounded rice.

Gangalam

fields.text:
It is said that this Lord was the first among the Tirunangur deities to appear to help Lord Shiva get relief from Brahmahatyadosham. The Lord is said to have given Tirukkoshtiyur Nambigal ( Guru of Shrīmad Rāmānujāchārya) the ashta-akshara mantram. Thus, one can find an idol of Tirukkoshtiyur Nambigal here at this kshethram.
Another story recounts how Indra was cursed by Durvāsa, a maharishi, which led to the Samudra Manthanam. Once there was a dancer who wanted to impress the goddess, Maha Lakshmī. The dancer performed a very intricate set of dances, and soon the goddess appeared before her, presenting the dancer with a garland. Soon after this, it is said that Sage Durvāsa was passing by and saw the lovely garland on the neck of the dancer. The dancer offered the sage the garland and left the scene. It is said that the garland possessed a very fragrant smell that attracted bees. Soon, the sage started to get irritated by the buzzing of the bees and was looking to dispose of the garland when Indra arrived atop his mount, Airāvata. Durvāsa presented the garland to Indra. Airāvata took the garland, but instead of throwing it on Indra, it crushed it beneath its legs. Durvāsa was immensely angered by this insult and cursed Indra, saying he and the world would lose all their wealth. As the phrasing of the curse was vague, all wealth-bearing substances and creatures, such as the Kalpa Vriksha, Kamadhenu, and even the Goddess Lakshmī, disappeared. Indra never knew a world without getting whatever he desired.
Thus, to regain his lost wealth, Indra is said to have performed tapas here. The Lord is said to have appeared here and given him the idea to perform Samudra Mathanam.
***Tirumangai Āzhwār, in his pāsuram, starts to address the Lord as nanda villake ananthakariyay, which translates to an Upanishad-Vaakyam which describes the Lord as satyam jñānam anaṁtam brahma. The word-for-word translation of this gives us:
satyam – The One who does not change and is the One true Universal Truth.
jñānam – The most knowledgeable. One who knows everything. Past, present, and future.
anaṁtam – The One who has no end by any cause.
Tirumangai Āzhwār refers to the Lord as Nanda Villake, which means a figurative burning lamp, signifying the Upanishad-Vaakyam.
***Another specialty of this temple is that it hosts the Annual Padhnor Garuḍotsavam. Find the picture attached below.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The deity Satyagirinathan is depicted in a reclining posture inside a rock-cut temple. Garuḍa, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Brahmā flank him, all witnessing the events that unfold around Him. According to tradition, the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha stole the Vedas and attempted to abduct Mahālakshmī. She is shown in the panel, frightened and hiding near the Lord's tiruvadi. In response, Ādishesha, who serves as the Lord's bed, emits poisonous fumes in the form of jwala (fiery orbs) to frighten the demons. The Lord is said to have retrieved the Vedas and protected Mahālakshmī from harm.
The panel shows both Madhu, who is soft by nature, and Kaiṭabha, who is fierce and aggressive, advancing toward the Lord. On one side, Bhoomadevi approaches the Lord seeking refuge at the Lord's tiruvadi. Shri Devī is seen near the head of Ādishesha, also seeking refuge. The Lord raises His hand to offer assurance to Shri Devī and lifts His gaze toward Bhoomadevi to reassure her.
Above the Lord, Ādishesha is seen releasing the jwala from his mouth, directed at the demons. At the top of the composition, Yama Dharmaraja and Chitragupta are depicted recording the moment in their ledger, signifying that the end of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is near.
The entire episode is captured within a single panel, carved in stone. It includes the fear of Mahālakshmī, the supplication of Bhoomadevi and Shri Devī, the aggression of the demons, the Lord's protective gestures, the fury of Ādishesha, and the presence of Yama and Chitragupta as cosmic witnesses. The depiction is dynamic and composed, presenting a complete narrative within a single visual frame.

The legend has it that Lord Vishṇu, in the form of Mohinī Avataram, distributed the celestial nectar Amritam to the Devas; hence, this place is also called Mohana-kshethram. It is also believed that Pulastya Muni performed tapas at this kshethram to have children. This Lord is believed to guide souls who have left the blazing body in the venture of Vaikuṇṭham. The Lord is said to throw water like a Megham (cloud) every step of the way so that the road to Vaikuṇṭham is cool.

ChakrathAzhwar

The worship of ChakrathAzhwar at this kshethram is very important, as He is believed to remove any hurdles in one's life or on the journey to Vaikuṇṭham. Devotees who come to this kshethram without fail take home with them a yanthram, which consists of the imagery of the Lord along with the Sudarshana Mantram engraved onto a copper or brass plate.

fields.text:
This shrine is associated with legends from the Rāmāyaṇa. Bharata, the brother of Shri Rāma and Lakshmaṇa, came to invite Shri Rāma, then in exile, to take over the reins of the kingdom, an angry Lakshmaṇa suspecting Bharata's intentions intended to kill Him; however, Bharata's innocence was very soon revealed, and then the two of them offered worship together at Tirumoozhikkalam.

***As per another legend, Hareetha Maharshi was performing penance at this place. Lord Vishṇu was pleased by his devotion and appeared to him. The sage requested the Lord to guide how all men can proceed with Varnashrama Dharma. Vishṇu uttered the sacred words, after which the place came to be known as Thirumoozhikkalam. The name Tirumoozhikkalam is said to have originated from the phrase tiru-mozhi-kalam, the place where sweet words were uttered.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This temple is located in the town of Nāgapaṭṭinam

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Modern-day Nāgapaṭṭinam was believed to be a dense forest back in the Kṛta Yugam known as Sundara-Aranyam. The town is said to have derived its name from Nāgapaṭṭinam, as Nagaraja Ādisheshan had performed tapas here in the Lord's honor.
 The Lord here is said to have shown Himself to Dhruva. The story is as follows.
Dhruva was the son of King Uttanapada. Uttanapada had two wives, named Suruchi and Suneethi. Suruchi was a very pompous and cruel person. She had a son named Uttama. Suruchi was hell-bent on outshining Suneethi in anything she did. On one occasion, when Uttanapada was sitting on the throne in the throne room, Dhruva approached Uttanapada and asked him if he could sit on his lap. No sooner had Dhruva asked than Suruchi dragged him away from his father and put Uttama on his father's lap. She told Dhruva that he was in no way blessed to sit on his father's lap and further went on to insult Suneethi by telling Dhruva that he wasn't destined for greatness as he was born in Suneethi's womb. She told him never to try approaching his father ever again. Dhruva innocently went to his mother and told her what had happened. She told Dhruva that if he couldn't sit on his father's lap, it was no big deal, as another father would accept anyone. She told Dhruva that Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa would never reject his requests. Hearing his mother's words, Dhruva went into the forests, committed to performing penance to see the Lord. When Dhruva went into the forest, he was greeted by Nārada, who described the Lord's appearance to Dhruva. Sage Nārada instructed Dhruva to visualize a dark-complexioned person with a conch-like neck, broad shoulders, slender hips, coral-like lips, lotus-like feet, and four hands holding the Shankha, Chakra, Gadha, and Padma in each hand.
Given the Lord's appearance, Dhruva, without any second thought in his head, started his penance to see the Lord. The Lord was soon impressed by seeing a five-year-old boy and appeared before Dhruva. The boy, upon seeing the Lord, was dumbstruck and didn't know what to say. The Lord then touched the boy's cheek with the Pānchajanyam and brought out the boy's voice. The innocence and devotion shown by the boy touched the Lord, who granted him and his mother a special position beyond the Brahmandam and told him that it would become known as the Dhruva Mandalam. When the boy could not get any attention from his father, he turned to see the Lord, who granted him far more than he ever asked for.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend tells the story of nine yogis who offered worship to the Lord present at this kshethram and attained moksham. According to the rules of prathistapana (the process of establishing the Lord in stone), the Lord is established, and all associated rituals are performed, sealing the Lord in the garbha-griha for eight days. Thus, the first yogi performed prathistapana of the Lord and opened the door of the garbha-griha after eight days. When he opened the doors, he found the Lord missing. Similarly, eight of the nine yogis found the Lord missing from the garbha-griha. The ninth yogi performed the prathistapana of the Lord, but instead of waiting eight days, he opened the door on the third day. The yogi found that the Lord was slowly sinking into the earth in the garbha-griha. The yogi then concluded that the Lords previously established by the other eight yogis must have also sunk into the earth in the same manner. Thus, the yogi asked the Lord to stop sinking into the ground and asked Him to remain there at the kshethram to serve all the devotees who would visit the kshethram. Thus, when one visits this kshethram, they can only see the Lord above the waist.
This is the only temple in the Malainadu Divyadesams that houses Lakshmī Devī separately in a shrine.

*** It is said the Lord here is prathyaksham to Gajendran and Shri Lakshmī. It is said that there was a competition between Gajendran and Lakshmī Devī as to who would present the Lord with a lotus first. One day, Gajendran asked the Lord to allow his devotee to perform kainkaryam (divine service to the Lord). Thus, the Lord requested Lakshmī Devī to come and sit next to Him and enjoy the divine service, and not to engage in any competition with the devotees.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: According to legend, Nandi had once visited Vaikuṇṭham to see the Lord, but the Dwarapalakas Jaya and Vijaya refused entry to Vaikuṇṭham. In a rage, Nandi insulted Jaya and Vijaya. Thus, Jaya and Vijaya cursed Nandi that he would experience excruciating heat and would perspire intensely. Jaya and Vijaya then felt sorry for cursing Nandi and suggested that Nandi go to Kumbakoṇam and meditate upon the Lord. Taking their suggestion, Nandi proceeded to Kumbakoṇam and began meditating on the Lord. Impressed with Nandi's tapas, the Lord appeared in front of Nandi and released Nandi from his curse.

fields.name: moolavar
fields.text: Gopalakrishnan, along with Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāma

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Narakasura was the son of Bhūmi Devī. Having allied himself with Bāṇāsura, Naraka became a force to be reckoned with. To show his power, Naraka had kidnapped 16001 maidens and was planning to offer them to Kamakya Devī. Naraka then attacked Amarāvatī, the heavenly capital of Indra. Naraka stormed into Amarāvatī and stole all of Indra's elephants, Varuṇa's Umbrella, and mother Aditi's earrings. As Naraka was to attack Indra, Indra mounted Airāvata and fled to Dvārakā to seek the help and protection of Lord Shree Krishna. Indra narrated what had happened at Amarāvatī and asked Krishna to bring back Mother Aditi's earrings. Lord Krishna, along with Satyabhāma, mounts the Lord's vehicle, Garuḍa, and leaves for Pragjyothisham (modern-day Assam), the kingdom of Naraka.
To stop intruders from entering his kingdom, Naraka had set up elaborate traps to take care of any who was daring enough to try and challenge him. Lord Krishna destroyed all the traps that were laid one by one. The first trap was a divine boulder that would crush anyone who tried to enter the border. The Lord destroyed the boulder with his mace. The second trap was a swirling pit of fire that would rise and engulf anyone who passed the first trial. The Lord sent his Sudarshana Chakra into the pit. The Chakra engulfed the flames and absorbed them. The last trap that was laid was a demon named Mura. Mura was the commander-in-chief of Naraka's army. Mura tried his best to keep the Lord at bay but was easily defeated. Following the death of Mura, his seven sons tried to avenge his death, but all of them were easily defeated. Finally, Naraka showed himself and had a long battle with the Lord. At the end of the battle, Lord Shree Krishna emerged victoriously. Naraka, in his dying breath, asked Krishna for a boon. He asked that one day in a year, to let Gaṅgā reach everyone so that they can atone for the sins that might have been committed by them knowingly or unknowingly. Lord Krishna granted the boon and said that day would henceforth be referred to as Naraka Chaturdashi. After Naraka's death, the Lord freed all the maidens and is said to have married all of them to protect them. He also placed Naraka's son Bhagadatta on the throne of Pragjyothisham and recovered Indra's elephants, Varuṇa's umbrella, and mother Aditi's earrings.
When Lord Shree Krishna and Satyabhāma reached Tirukavalampadi, Satyabhāma is said to have asked the Lord to bring her the divine Parijatham flower. Thus, the Lord went back to Indra and asked that he spare a flower for the sake of Satyabhāma. Indra promptly refused, saying the divine flower does not belong on Bhūlokam. Lord Shree Krishna is then said to have defeated Indra and established a Parijatham garden here at this Kshethram.
***The specialty of these eleven temples together is the Padhnor Garudothasavam(eleven Garuḍotsavam) that takes place together during Thai Maasam(January 15- February 15) on the day of Amāvāsyā.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: This kshethram is situated within the northern prakaram of the Ulagalantha Perumāl temple. This Lord is said to be a part of Ulagalantha Perumāl, symbolizing the first stage of Vāmana Avataram, which Neeramai, or a water-like behavior, characterizes. Just as water rushes towards the place where there is a small opening or hole, likewise, the Lord flows into the hearts of the bhaktas and fills their soul with bhakti.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is situated on the outskirts of Chennai near Pallavaram.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend tells the story of Tirumangai Āzhwār visiting this kshethram. When he visited this kshethram, the hill was surrounded by water, hence giving the kshethram the name Tiruneermalai. This kshethram features shrines for Ranganatha Perumāl, Ulagalantha Perumāl, and Shantha Nṛisimha Perumāl atop a small hillock. At the base of the hillock, one can find the temple of Neervana Perumāl and a shrine for Rāma, Lakshmaṇa, Bharatha, Shatrughna, along with Devī Sītā.
It is said that Maharshi Vālmīki visited this kshethram and paid his homage to the Lords atop the hill, but was not satisfied by his darshan of the Lords. Thus, he requested the Lords to show themselves as Lord Rāma. Therefore, the Lords collectively took the form of Rāma. Shrīdevī and Bhūdevi became Devī Sītā. Ādishesha, Shankham, and Chakra appeared as Lakshmaṇa, Bharatha, and Shatrugna, and Garuḍa as Hanumān.
*** As one enters the premises of the Neervana Perumāl temple, they can see that the Dhvaja-Sthambham is displaced and not in line with the entrance, and the same is true with the position of the garbha griha of Neervana Perumāl. This is because when Lord Rāma appeared, he assumed the primary deity of the kshethram, displacing the position of Neervana Perumāl. The Dhvaja-Sthambham is in line with Shri Rāmar.

fields.text: Shiva tested Parvathi's commitment to performing tapas by setting fire to the mango tree under which she was seated. Parvathi prayed to her brother, Lord Vishṇu, who caused waves of nectar to cool down the scorching rays. Lord Vishṇu, as Vāmana, continues to reside at this kshethram at the request of Pārvatī. It is also believed that at the request of Lord Vishṇu, the moon-adorned Shiva alleviated the discomfort caused by the heat that emanated during the churning of the milky ocean. Hence the name, Nilaatingal Tundattan.

fields.text: This kshethram is situated 25 km from Chennai, on the Chennai-Tiruvaloor Road.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend has it that Varuṇa and Samudraraja worshipped Lord Vishṇu at this kshethram. It is also believed that the Lord visiting this kshethram, followed by Lakshmī, made it His home, and hence the name Triu Ninravoor. It is said that Tirumangai Āzhwār, after worshipping at this shrine, left without singing a pāsuram. The Lord followed him to Māmallapuram, where he sang the pāsuram, referring to this kshethram.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
According to legend, when the Lord took Vāmana Avataram, Bali could not see the Lord as he was under the Lord's foot. Hence, after the Lord pushed Bali down to Pathalam, Bali requests the Lord to once again see Him as Ulangalanthan(The one who measured the three worlds). To fulfill his wish, the Lord revealed this form to Bali.

***
The Lord can also be seen here in a sarpam form(serpent form). It is said that if one prays here, one is relieved of all Sarpa-Dosham.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Shree Krishna told the Pāṇḍavas that he would, for the last time, visit the court of Hastinapur and try his hand at imploring reason to Duryodhana, trying to make him realize that nothing good could come out of a war. Shree Krishna arrived in Hastinapur and, instead of staying in the palace, chose to spend some time with Vidura. He stayed the night at Vidura's house and in the morning went to the court of Hastinapur to try and convince Duryodhana out of the idea of war. Krishna presented his argument, asking that if the Kauravas did not want to return the entire kingdom, then at least provide the Pāṇḍavas with five villages.
Duryodhana, in a crimson fury, snapped at Krishna, saying that he was not qualified to come to the court with such an issue and told him to go back to herding cattle. He further told Krishna that he would not give even a single needle-head's worth of land. He then instructed the guards to tie Krishna up and make him a prisoner. As the guards were tying Krishna, he started to grow to an immeasurable height and took his Vishwaroopam Form.
Vaisampayana Maharshi was narrating the Bhāgavatam to Janamejaya and was referring to Lord Krishna's visit to Hastinapuram as the Pāṇḍavas' Dhoota (Ambassador). Desiring to have the Vishwaroopa darsana, they performed Ashwamedhayagam at Kāñchipuram. On completion of the yagam, the Lord gave darshan as Pandavadhootar. There are shrines for Rāmānuja Āchārya and Manavaala Maamunigal.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
This kshethram is the ultimate destination for any jeevaatma. This kshethram lies beyond Tiruparkadal. Shri Vaikuṇṭham is described as a mesmerizing place from which there is no return, as specified in the Vedas and Upanishads as "na cha punara avarthathe na cha punara avarthathe na cha punara avarthathe." The Lord is seen as Shri Paramapadanathan, sitting alongside Him atop Ādisheshan are Shrīdevī, Bhūdevi, and Neeladevi. After the jeevaathma crosses Ksheerabdi, it will be guided to the borders of Shri Vaikuṇṭham. Here flows the Viraja River. The jeevaathma is allowed to bathe in the Viraja River, where the divine river washes away any residual sins. Upon entering Shri Vaikuṇṭham, the jeevaathma will see all the gods singing the praise of the Lord, which is described as "tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṁ padaṁ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ." After being mesmerized by all of this, the jeevaathma will go and finally see the Lord Himself. The Lord gives space on his lap and asks the jeevaathma what took it so long to reach Him. The jeevaathma has no response but to say it has finally attained Him. The jeevaathma then offers itself to become one with the Lord. It asks the Lord to give it space inside His Heart to attain moksham. The jeevaathma asks the Lord to imagine it to be a single grain of rice, and that grain is being offered solely and wholeheartedly to Him. The Lord then places the jeevaathma near His heart, merging the jeevaathma with Himself, the Paramātma, granting moksham. This is described in the Chandogya Upanishad as follows: "ahamannamahamannamahamannam; ahamannādo2'hamannādo2āhamannādaḥ; ahaṁ ślokakṛdahaṁ ślokakṛdahaṁ ślokakṛt; ahamasmi prathamajā ṛtā3sya;pūrvaṁ devebhyo'mṛtasya nā3bhāyi;yo mā dadāti sa ideva mā3vāḥ; ahamannamannamadantamā3dmi; ahaṁ viśvaṁ bhuvanamabhyabhavā3m‌;suvarna jyotīḥ; ya evaṁ veda; ityupaniṣat‌. ".
By attaining moksham, our journey is completed.

fields.text: Legend says the story of Bharadwaja Maharshi, who fell in love with a Gandharva Kanya. The union had children who became the heirs of the Pallava Dynasty, named Pallava and Villava. The Vimānam in this temple has three tiers. In the first tier, the Lord gives darshanam in the sitting posture. In the middle tier, He is depicted as Ranganatha in the reclining posture, accompanied by Shri Devī and Bhūdevi. In the top tier, He is shown in a standing posture.

fields.name: theertham
fields.text:
Paarkadal Tīrtham

This kshethram cannot be attained with the physical body. Only the jeevaathma can make the journey to this kshethram as well as Shri Vaikuṇṭham. Thus, these two kshethrams are referred to as Vinnulaga Tirupatigal.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The Lord present here is said to be a vyuha-roopam of Paravasudevan who resides in Shri Vaikuṇṭham. Empurumaan presents Himself as Vāsudevan, Sankarshaṇan, Pradyumnan, and Aniruddhan, who are said to be vyuha-roopam of the Lord. Vāsudevan is the creator, Sankarshaṇan is the sustainer, Pradyumnan is the destroyer, and Aniruddhan represents divine knowledge. These vyuha-roopam are further said to divide into three forms each. Vāsudevan is said to represent equivalence to Keshava, Madhava, and Nārāyaṇa. Sankarshaṇan is said to represent equivalence to Govinda, Vishṇu, and Madhusoodhan. Pradyumana is said to represent equivalence to Trivikrama, Vāmana, and Sridhara. Aniruddhan is said to represent the equivalence to Rishikesha, Padmanābhan, and Dāmodara.
The twelve of these forms are referred to as the 12 Sooriyars and Chandirans, who are found in all 12 directions. They are responsible for bringing all Jeevaathmas into existence, guiding their lives, and calculating their Paavam and Punyam.
The Ashṭākshara mantram is said to always resonate in this kshethram. To reach this kshethram, one must learn the ashtaakshara mantram from a guru and meditate upon Shri Ksheerabdi Nathan.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Once King Upamanyu (Pandya King) had gone hunting in the forest to hunt a rogue elephant, he accidentally killed a brahmin who was performing tapas by the banks of a river. In repentance for his act, the king renounced his throne and began roaming the vast expanse of his former kingdom. When the king reached Tiruperrnagar, Lord Shiva appeared in front of the king and told him to serve food to a thousand brahmins daily with appam. The king started to follow the instructions that he had received. One day, Lord Vishṇu decided to participate in the king's daily meal service. The Lord came in the disguise of a brahmin and approached the king, saying He was very hungry and asked that He be fed. The king asked the brahmin to wait until he had fed the remaining brahmins who had assembled before Him. The Lord was very strong with His claim and demanded that He be fed first. The king obliged and served the brahmin food.
To the king's astonishment, the brahmin ate all the food that was prepared for the gathered thousand brahmins. The king then asked the brahmin if he was satisfied with the meal. The Brāhmiṇ said he was still hungry and asked the king to give him an appam, as it had not been served to him. No sooner had the king obtained a pitcher (kudam) with the appam than the Brāhmiṇ snatched the kudam from the king's hands. Immediately, the Lord turned into an idol reclining on Ādisheshan, putting his hand inside the kudam. Hence, the Lord gained the name Appa Kuduthan. At the same time, Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi was directed by Lord Shiva to pray to Lord Vishṇu for the gift of longevity. When Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi reached the kshethram, the Lord removed his hand from the kudam and blessed him with the longevity of life and also relieved the king of his Brahmahatidosham.
Another story tells the tale of Kamalavalli Thāyār asking the Lord to get her Parijaatham flowers. Parijaatham flowers are divine flowers that grow in the gardens of Indra. When the Lord approached Indra to obtain some flowers for Thāyār, Indra refused to acknowledge that the Paarijatham was a divine flower and did not belong in Bhūlokam. He further tried to hurl the Vajrāyudham on the Lord when the Lord was persistent with His request. The Lord, in his shayanam, raised his left hand and plucked the Vajrāyudham from Indra's hand. Indra then provided the flowers, consisting of defeat at the Lord's hands. Thus, the vimānam and pushkariṇī here are named in Indra's honor as he provided the Parijaatham.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend states that this temple was established by Arjuna during his trip to South India, when he was in vanavaasam with the Pāṇḍavas. It is said that when Arjuna reached this kshethram, he was extremely thirsty and went in search of water. When he could find no water, he found Agastya Maharshi performing tapas. Arjuna paid his respects to the Maharshi and asked him if he had any water. Agastya Maharshi said all the water he could offer was that which was there in his kamandalam. After Arjuna drank the water, he asked the sage if he could direct him to a source of water, as he was still thirsty. Agastya Maharshi said there was no water in the area and told Arjuna to seek the help of Lord Krishna, as he always did. Arjuna then performs tapas to call Lord Krishna to this kshethram. When Lord Krishna arrived, he gave Arjuna a sword and asked Arjuna to dig the earth. When Arjuna dug the earth, a stream of water emerged, granting water to the area. This water source came to be known as Khaḍga Tīrtham( the water that came from the sword).


***Here, one can see Lord Pārthasārathy with four hands, as supposed to see him with two hands like at Tiruvallikeni(Chennai). Another specialty of this kshethram is that one can see the utsava moorthigal of both Lord Rāma and Lord Krishna standing in the same garbha-graham. We can see Kolavili Rāmar holding the shankam, chakram, bow, and arrow.

fields.name: moolavar

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
This kshethram comprises two temples, namely Pachivannam and Pavalavannam. The presiding deity is said to be prathyaksham for Bhṛgu Maharshi and Ashwini Devatas here.
*** This kshethram is special for Lakshmī Devī, as she is seated atop the Shri Yantram.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is one of the Nava Tirupati temples and is located 5 km from Āzhwār Tirunagari on the way to Tiruchendur from Tirunelvēli.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
According to legend, Durvāsa Maharshi is said to have once visited Karya-Vaikuṇṭham, but Bhūdevi ignored his arrival and did not perform the required athithi-sathkaaram. Thus, Durvāsa Maharshi is said to have cursed Bhūdevi, stating that she would become like Shrīdevī. When the Lord takes His avatars, He stands, sits, lies down, and performs all His activities on Bhūdevi, whereas He has allocated a small position in His heart for Shrīdevī. Upon hearing this curse, Bhūdevi pleads with the Maharshi to forgive her. Durvāsa Maharshi tells Bhūdevi that once a curse is delivered, it cannot be taken back, but she could attain atonement if she performed tapas at Tirupperai. Thus, Bhūdevi is said to come to this kshethram and perform tapas by chanting the ashtakshara mantram. One day, when Bhūdevi went to bathe in the Tāmraparaṇi River before offering her daily penance, She is said to have found a pair of kundalam (earrings) in the shape of makaram (a type of fish). She is said to have presented this makara-kundalam to the Lord, thus relieving Herself from the curse and giving Him the name Makara Nedunkuzhaikkadan.

*** The importance of this kshethram lies in the practice of Varuṇa Japam. It is said that if one performs Varuṇa Japam at this kshethram, it will bring rain as desired. It is noted that Varuṇa sought the help of Makara Nedunkuzhaikkadan Perumāl in his time of need.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is located in Joshimath en route to Badrināth in Uttarakhand.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The shrine that we see today is said to have been established by Shri Ādi Shankaracharya. We can see that Lord Narasimha is holding his chakram, which is said to be a prayoga-chakram that is spinning. During the winter season, Lord Badrinarayan's Utsavar Mūrti is brought to this temple and worshipped here, as it becomes very cold, and Badrināth closes its doors after Deepavali.
According to Tirumangai Āzhwār's pāsuram, we can understand that the temple and Lord being described is not the Lord Narasimha who we see today. Tirumangai Āzhwār describes the Lord to be reclining in the bujanga shayanam on Ādishesha bearing a thousand heads. According to the pāsuram, the kshethram could be situated at Manasarovar.
However, since time immemorial, all our acharyas have been visiting this kshethram, situated in Joshimath.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is part of Nava Tirupati and is located approximately 4 km from Shrīvaikuṇṭham.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend tells the story of a brahmin named Yajña Sarma. It is said that one evening, when Yajña Sarma and his wife were in a jovial state, Shakthi Maharshi(son of Vasishta Maharshi) is said to have visited their hermitage. Yajña Sarma and his wife failed to recognize that the sage had come to their doorstep and did not perform any kind of athithi-sathkaaram(service to the guest). Shakthi Maharshi, in a fit of rage, cursed Yajña Sarma that he would become a demon. Yajña Sarma begged for the sage's forgiveness and asked him if there was any way out of this curse. The sage then tells Yajña Sarma that Indra would perform a yajña at Tiruppulingudi, and he is to go and try to disrupt this yajña. When this would happen, Indra would hurl his vajra-aayudam, releasing him from the effects of the curse. As the sage predicted, Yajña Sarma went in his demonic form to disrupt the yajña, and Indra hurled his vajra-aayudam at the demon, killing Yajña Sarma. Indra was performing a prayashchita-yajña as he had unknowingly killed a sage who was performing tapas in the form of a deer. When the yajña reached its completion, the Lord is said to have appeared, granting atonement to Indra and moksham to Yajña Sarma.
Another story tells that there was a feud between Bhūdevi and Shrīdevī. Bhūdevi claimed that the Lord spends too much time with Shrīdevī and does not spend enough time with Her. The Lord is said to have solved the problem by placing Bhūdevi on one side of His tiruvadigal(His lotus feet) and Shrīdevī on the other, and constantly looking at both of them, showing that in His eyes, both of them are equal. Thus, when one stands outside the garbha-griha, they cannot see the Lord's tiruvadigal. To see the Lord's tiruvadigal, there is a small window on the outside of the garbha-griha through which we can see His tiruvadigal while performing pradakshinam.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: During the Rāmāyaṇa period, when Rāvaṇa abducted Devī Sītā and started to fly away in the Pushpaka Vimānam, a vulture by the name of Jaṭāyu stood in his way and put up a valiant battle against Rāvaṇa until Rāvaṇa cut off Jaṭāyu's wings, causing him to fall in the Panchavati forest. Jaṭāyu held on to his life till he could see Lord Rāma and tell him what had transpired so far. After relaying the information of Devī Sītā's kidnapping to Lord Rāma, Jaṭāyu lost his life. Lord Rāma is then supposed to have cremated Jaṭāyu, offering him salvation(moksham). The Lord here is assuming a sleeping posture after performing the final rites for Jaṭāyu. The Lord shows this entire scene to Tirumangai Āzhwār.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is located 5 km from Cheṅgannūr in Kerala.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
As Bhīma had also participated in deceiving Dronacharya during the Mahābhārata, he had also incurred some amount of sin. To gain atonement for those sins, it is said that Bhīma performed tapas here. Thus, the Lord appeared before him and blessed him, granting him atonement for his sins of killing his guru and a hundred brothers.
The legend has it that the Saptarshis worshipped the Lord, proclaiming that He is the Paratatvam, and the Lord took the name Mayapiran at this kshethram.


One can see this iconic mace outside the temple, showing that Bhīma established it.

fields.name: azhwarPasuram
fields.text:
Nam Āzhwār 10 Pāsurams

*** This is one of the Panch-Pāṇḍava Kshethrams. This kshethram is said to have been established by Bhīma.

fields.name: moolavar

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is located near Rameswaram, on the seashore.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend has it that Ādi Jagannatha Perumāl is said to have been present at this kshetram even before Dasharatha came with Kaikeyi to conquer South India. It is noted that Dasharatha performed tapas to this Lord to have children.
Legend tells that Lord Rāma reached the seashore where Vibhīshaṇa performed sharanagathi. As the army contemplated how to cross the ocean, Vibhīshaṇa advised Lord Rāma to pray to Samudraraja by performing praayopavesham (fast for three days and nights) to allow their passage over his waters to reach Lanka. Thus, Lord Rāma is said to have sat in Padmasanam on a bed made of darbha grass with the Anjali mudra for three days. When Samudraraja did not show himself, in a rage, Lord Rāma told Lakshmaṇa to hand Him His bow and an arrow. The Lord mounts the arrow and tells Samudraraja that He would make all the water in the ocean evaporate if he did not show himself. As the Lord was about to fire His deadly weapon, Samudraraja appears and falls at Lord Rāma's feet and tells the army that Nal and Neel were phenomenal architects and that they could build a bridge that would float on the oceanic waters, granting Lord Rāma and His army passage over the ocean to Shri Lanka. As Lord Rāma sat on a bed made of darbha, this kshethram is called Pullaranya Kshethram.
*** The water at this kshethram is considered very holy, as it was the starting point of the Ramasethu. Thus, taking a bath here or sethu-snanam is considered to absolve all sins. Along with sethu-snanam, performing tarpanam here at this kshetram is considered highly auspicious.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is located 11 km from Kāñchipuram on Katapadi road.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
During the Rāmāyaṇa period, when Rāvaṇa abducted Devī Sītā and started to fly away in the Pushpaka Vimānam, a vulture by the name of Jaṭāyu stood in his way and put up a valiant battle against Rāvaṇa until Rāvaṇa cut off Jaṭāyu's wings, causing him to fall in the Panchavati forest. Jaṭāyu held on to his life till he could see Lord Rāma and tell him what had transpired so far. After relaying the information of Devī Sītā's kidnapping to Lord Rāma, Jaṭāyu lost his life. Lord Rāma is then supposed to have cremated Jaṭāyu, offering him salvation(moksham). The Lord here is holding Jaṭāyu on His lap to cremate him.

***A peculiarity of this kshethram is that Shrīdevī Thāyār and Bhūdevi Thāyār have interchanged places, i.e., Bhūdevi Thāyār is on the right, and Shrīdevī Thāyār is on the left. When one sees Shrīdevī Thāyār here, one can observe that she is standing about two feet behind the Lord, as She was unable to handle the heat of the pyre.
On new moon day (Amāvāsyā), pilgrims congregate here at this kshethram to perform tharpanam(rites to the departed souls). In this temple, barren women receive the prasadam, which consists of roasted lentils soaked in water. While taken home, it is believed that if the lentils sprout, they will beget children.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is located 8 km from Sīrkāzhi

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
It is said that Lord Rāma was responsible for establishing this temple at this kshethram. After defeating Rāvaṇa, Lord Rāma was faced with Brahmanhatyadosham, as he had killed Rāvaṇa, who was born a Brāhmiṇ. To engage in pariharam for the dosha, the Lord was seeking solutions. It was then that Dridanetramuni suggested to the Lord that he make an idol of a cow out of pure gold, large enough for the Lord to remain seated within it. Dridanetramuni then asked the Lord to remain seated within the gold edifice for four days, following which he requested that the Lord engage in charitable activities. The Lord did as he was instructed. After the four days had passed, Lord Rāma donated the gold idol to Dridanetramuni. When Dridanetramuni returned to his ashram near Sīrkāzhi, he sold the gold statue to raise money for the temple's construction. Hence, the temple is called Semponsei (Sempon-gold, Sei-made of) Kovil.
*** Lord Rāma is said to have performed daily rituals for the Lord here.

fields.name: travelNote
fields.text: This kshethram is one of the Nava Tirupati temples and is located around 3 km from Shrīvaikuṇṭham.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend has it that Kubera cursed a couple to assume the forms of a weight-measure (tulai) and a bow (Villu). When Athreya Suprapa Muni was performing a yajña at this kshethram, he found the scale and the bow in the yagashala. When he touched them, they transformed into a man and a woman and were relieved of the curse. Thus, the kshethram obtained the name Tulaivillimangalam. It is also believed that the Ashwini Devatas worshipped Lord Vishṇu at this kshetram with red lotus flowers (Senthamarai Kaṇṇan – Aravindalochanan). Lord Devapiran is said to have given darshanam to all the devas after the yajña attained its completion.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
It is said that Devī Sarasvatī, in one of her attempts to stop the yajña from reaching completion, took away all the light from the areas in and around Kāñchipuram, resulting in pitch-black darkness. Thus, the Lord is said to have first appeared as a small kindling light, after which He grew and eliminated the darkness, once again assisting Lord Brahmā in completing the yajña.


***
Svāmi Vedānta Deshikan:
Svāmi Deshikan is considered to be an incarnation of the divine bell of Shri Venkateshwara Svāmi of Tirumalai. Svāmi Deshikan was born here in Tooppul to Shri Anantha Suri and Devī Totaramba. By birth, Svāmi Deshikan was named Venkatanatha. When Svāmi Deshikan was just five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Kidambi Appular, to attend a discourse by Nadadhoor Ammal, a revered Shri Vaishṇava Scholar at the time. As soon as Nadadhoor Ammal saw Venkatanatha, he saw a divine radiance in the child and stopped his lecture to hug the child affectionately. After this, when Nadadhoor Ammal said that he had forgotten where he had stopped his lecture, Venkatanatha reminded him of where he had stopped. This act astonished the crowd, as they had never seen a five-year-old boy comprehend the deep intricacies of philosophical knowledge being discussed. It was then that Nadadhoor Ammal predicted and blessed Venkatanatha, stating that he would become the torch-bearer to spread Shri Vaishṇavism everywhere in the future.
At each place, he composed numerous works in languages such as Tamil, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Manipravalam (a blend of Sanskrit and Tamil), which revealed his ingenuity, creativity, logic, linguistic expertise, devotional fervor, and erudite scholarship.
Some of his greatest works include:
1) Hayagrīva Stotram
2) Sudarshana Ashtakam
3) Paduka Sahasram
4) Abheetistavam
5) Achyuta Shatakam
6) Daya Shatakam
7) Hamsa Sandesham
8) Shri Stuti
9) Yadavabyudayam
10) Kamasikashatakam

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: After completing the churning process of the Samudra, Mathanam appeared Danavantri with a golden chalice containing Amrutham (The elixir of longevity). Both the Devas as well as the Danavas desired the elixir, and hence the Lord took the form of Mohinī and gave the elixir only to the gods. It was during this that Rāhu, a demon, disguised himself as a deva and tried to consume the elixir when he was caught in the act by Sūryan and Chandran. The Lord releases his Chakram and cuts him in such a way that the upper part of the body and the lower part of the body became separate entities. Rāhu swore that he would have his revenge against Sūryan and Chandran. To exact his revenge, it is said that he eclipses the Sun and the Moon. It is said that Sūryan and Chandran went into hiding at the Sūrya Pushkariṇī, and Chandra Pushkariṇī was present at Tiruttetriambalam and Tirumanikoodam. The Lords are said to have come to the rescue of Sūryan and Chandran and assured them of their safety.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The Lord here is standing along with His four consorts, namely, Shrīdevī, Bhūdevi, Neeladevi, and Jambhavathi.
Jambhavathi is the daughter of Jambavan, who is seen in the Rāmāyaṇa. The story of how the Lord married Jambhavathi is as follows. Lord Krishna's royal treasurer Satrajit, used to house the Syamantaka Mani ( a divine gem that is said to give an unlimited amount of treasure ). Once, Lord Krishna is said to have asked to see this gem, but Satrajit refused. Soon, one day, Satrajit's brother is said to have worn the gem and gone out into the forest to hunt and did not return. When Satrajit noticed that the gem was missing, he blamed it on Krishna, saying He had stolen it. Lord Krishna is said to have gone into the forest to prove his innocence. When the Lord was deep in the forest, He found Satrajit's brother's body covered in the mauling of a lion. He decided to check around the area further and soon saw a glimmering twinkle emanating from a nearby cave. When He went to probe the source of the twinkle, He noticed the gem in the hands of a female bear and approached her to claim the gem and clear His name when another male bear attacked Him. Lord Krishna fought a long-drawn battle with the bear, with neither side giving in. Soon, Lord Krishna realized that the bear was none other than Jambavan, one of His generals in the time of the Rāmāyaṇa. Lord Krishna reveals Himself as Lord Rāma to Jambavan, and their fight comes to an end. Jambavan returns the gem to Lord Krishna, and along with the gem, he gives his daughter's hand in marriage to Lord Krishna. The female bear is transformed into a beautiful maiden, who is Jambhavathi.
This kshethram is where Aniruddha was married to Bāṇāsura's daughter, Ushā. The story is as follows.
Bāṇāsura was the king of Sonitpur (a modern-day district in Assam). Bāṇa was an ardent devotee of Lord Shiva. By the grace of Lord Shiva, Bāṇa had received a thousand hands with which he used to play the mridangam for the Lord. One day, when Lord Shiva was dancing, he granted Bāṇāsura a boon that he would personally protect him no matter the circumstance. Bāṇāsura had a daughter named Ushā. Ushā was an ardent devotee of Devī Pārvatī. Devī Pārvatī blesses Ushā, saying a man would appear in her dream,s and he would be the one that she would get married to. After a few days, Ushā had a dream of a man. He had broad shoulders, a slender waist, coral-like lips, a lotus-like face, and eyes that seemed to resemble the sun and the moon. Ushā had a friend named Chitralekhā who could draw an exact copy of any description that was placed before her. Thus, as Ushā described, Chitralekhā drew a picture of the man she dreamed of. When both of them went through to see who the person in the photo was, they discovered that the person in the picture was Aniruddha, the grandson of Shree Krishna. Chitralekhā also possessed another power, enabling her to teleport herself to any place she wished and bring back anyone she willed. Therefore, at night, Ushā asked Chitralekhā to bring Aniruddha to the palace without her father realizing, as her father was a sworn enemy of Shree Krishna.
Chitralekhā did as instructed and brought Aniruddha to Ushā's royal quarters. Soon, news reached Bāṇāsura, saying Ushā was enjoying the company of an unknown man within her personal quarters. Bāṇāsura rushed in a fury and bound Aniruddha with a thousand snakes. The news was then sent to Dvārakā that Bāṇāsura was holding both Ushā and Aniruddha hostage. Krishna, along with Balarāma, immediately left for Sonitpur on Garuḍa. As soon as Krishna and Balarāma reached Sonitpur, they challenged Bāṇāsura to war and demanded that Aniruddha be released and that Ushā be married to Aniruddha. Bāṇāsura refused and commanded his army to attack Krishna and Balarāma. Krishna and Balarāma effortlessly beat Bāṇāsura's army.
Soon, Bāṇāsura was left alone to face Krishna and Balarāma, having prayed to Lord Shiva for protection. Lord Shiva first sent his Gaṇas to face Krishna and Balarāma. When the Gaṇas were defeated, Lord Shiva himself appeared to face Lord Krishna and Balarāma. Lord Shiva and Lord Krishna engaged in a fierce battle, neither side yielding an inch. Lord Shiva was soon left with only his set of divyastras. Lord Shiva released the Pashupatastra, and in response, Lord Krishna released the Nārāyaṇa-Astra. The divine weapons clashed, creating massive explosions. Finally, Lord Shiva executed his final weapon in the form of a plague called Rudra-Jwaram. Lord Krishna replied to this in the form of an antidote called Vaishṇava-Jwaram. Lord Krishna countered Lord Shiva completely, while Lord Balarāma defeated Lord Karthikeya. Bāṇāsura was now bereft of any protection and open to attack. Lord Krishna then sent his Sudarshana Chakra behind Bāṇāsura. Sudarshana chased after Bāṇāsura and cut off 996 of his 1000 arms. Bāṇāsura was left completely humiliated, and he had no other choice but to comply with the wishes of Lord Krishna and Balarāma. Aniruddha and Ushā were released from prison and got married.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
At Tiruvaali, we can see Lakshmī Narasimhar. It is said that after killing Hiraṇyakashipu, the Lord was still furious. To get the Lord to calm down all the devas, Lord Brahmā and Lord Shiva asked Mahālakshmī to isolate the Lord to a different location. Thus, the Lord was taken to Tiruvaali. Usually, we see that Lakshmī is seated on the Lord's left lap, but here, we can see Lakshmī seated on the Lord's right, allowing her to hug and embrace the Lord. Thus, the place got its name Tiruvaali (Tiru meaning Lakshmī and Aali meaning Aalinganam or hug in Sanskrit).

*** Vedupari Utsavam

Tiruvaali is said to be the birthplace of Amritavalli Thāyār, and Tirunagari is said to be the birthplace of Lord Vayalali Māṇavāḷan. It is said that on the night that the Lord got married to Thāyār, they were targeted and looted by Tirumangai Āzhwār. Before becoming a saint, Tirumangai Āzhwār was a dacoit named Kaliyan.

Tirumangai Āzhwār wanted to marry a woman named Kumudhavalli. She placed two conditions, namely, 1) To get Pancha-Samskāram done, and 2) to perform tadhiyararadhanam (annadhanam) for a thousand people for one year. To satisfy the second condition, Tirumangai Āzhwār used to steal gold from anyone he could find, sell the gold to get money to serve people. As fate would have it, Tirumangai Āzhwār ran into the Lord and Thāyār. He pulled out a knife and told them to remove all the jewelry that they were wearing. The Lord and Thāyār gave up all their jewelry. Tirumangai Āzhwār tied up all of the jewelry in a cloth, and as he was about to lift it, the Lord performed an enchantment in such a way that he could no longer lift it. In anger, Tirumangai Āzhwār threatened the Lord to give him the mantra that would allow him to lift the bag. The Lord smiled and told him that he was performing all of this to make sure that Tirumangai Āzhwār would obtain this mantra and propagate it to the world. Thus the Lord gave Tirumangai Āzhwār the ashtakshara mantram. All of this is performed as a drama to date on Pankuni Uttaram day. Find the pictures of the utsavam attached below.
