fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The town of Mathura has been mentioned in all the previous yugams. It is said in Kṛta Yugam that Lord Vāmana's Sidhaashramam was present here. In the Treta Yugam, it is said that Shatrugna beat Lavanasuran and made Mathura his capital for twelve years. In Dvāpara Yugam, Lord Shri Krishna was born here in this kshethram. Although the Lord was born here, the Divyadesam is located in Vrindavan, which is 10 km from Mathura. Mathura is said to be the center of Vraja Bhūmi. Vraja Bhūmi refers to an area of 184 km, which Lord Shri Krishna is said to have roamed with His bare feet.The temple from Āzhwār pāsurams does not stand today but there is a South-Indian style Rangji Mandir in Vrindavan that is very popular.

fields.text:
This kshethram is located at an altitude of 10500 feet on the Himalayan Mountains at Badrināth.
To reach this kshethram, one must start their journey from Haridwar. From Haridwar, one must travel via Rishikesh, reach Devaprayag, stay overnight, preferably at Joshimath, and then reach Badrināth the following morning when the road gates open.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
According to Shrīmad Bhāgavatam, Lord Vishṇu, in His incarnations as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, performed deep tapas for time immemorial for the well-being of all living entities. According to legend, when Nara and Nārāyaṇa were performing tapas in a place where Badri trees were growing. At one point, the sunlight became very intense. Thus, to protect the Lord from the sunlight, Lakshmī Devī is said to have taken the form of a Badri tree and grown in such a way as to provide shade to the Lord.
This fact is reiterated in the Mahābhārata when Lord Krishna tells Arjuna that in their previous lives, Arjuna was the manifestation of Nara, and He was the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa. The Pāṇḍavas are said to have visited this kshethram before embarking on their final journeys to Mana, from where they left their bodies to reach Paramapadam. Mana is 4 km from this kshethram.
This is one of the Swayam-Vyaktha Kshethrams. It is said that there are five Badri kshethrams. Together, they are known as Pancha Badri Kshethram. Vishal Badri (Badrināth Temple installed by Shri Ādi Shankaracharya), Yogadhyan Badri (where the Lord is in a meditative posture), Bhavishya Badri (Badri of the future), Vridha Badri (the original shrine where Vishvakarma carved the idol), Ādi Badri. It is said that the Lord appeared in Shri Ādi Shankaracharya's dream and told him that he would find His idol inside the tapta-kundam ( hot springs ) present outside, where the present-day temple is situated. It is said that Shri Ādi Shankaracharya dipped in the spring multiple times before finding the Lord's idol. To date, the pooja is performed by nambudhri brahmins who follow the Kerala style of pooja.

Badrināth Temple: Raval Ji opening and entering the temple in the early morning.

The only time one can see the true form of the Lord is during the Tirumañjanam/abhishekham, which takes place around 5 am.

fields.text:
Legend has it that a Deva-Asura Yudham once took place, and Lord Vishṇu sided with the Devas, while Lord Shiva was said to have sided with the Asuras. When the battle raged in the dark, Lord Shiva is said to have hurled his Trishūlam at Lord Vishṇu, who responded by stopping the Trishūlam with his Sudarshana Chakram. The Lord then showed Lord Shiva that He, Himself, was Lord Brahmā, Vishṇu, and Shiva. This is said to have humbled Lord Shiva.


***During the Kṛta Yugam, the rakshasas Madhu and Kaiṭabha stole the Vedas from Lord Brahmā, and the Lord took the Matsya Avataram to recover them. The Lord then took the form of Hayagrivar and became the Lord of knowledge. Shrīmān Vedānta Deshikan performed tapas here at Aushadagiri(the divine hill that was brought by Hanumān, containing the divine Sanjeevini), which is adjacent to the temple. Garuḍan is said to have been impressed by his tapas and appeared before Vedānta Deshikan. Garuḍan then initiated the Hayagrīva Stotram(see the picture above). Vedānta Deshikan is then said to have meditated upon Lord Hayagrīva by chanting the stotram. Lord Hayagrīva then presented Vedānta Deshikan with an idol of Himself, which is said to have been passed down through the lineage of various aradhakas, such as Devī Sarasvatī and Bhagavad Rāmānuja, and is currently worshipped at the Parakala Muttam situated in Mysore. One who chants this stotram will attain proper knowledge of education, good concentration in studies, fluency in speech, mastery in debates, vocabulary, and will have outstanding memory power.


The idol of Lakshmī Hayagrīva that was handed to Svāmi Deshikan

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend has it that a local thief, known as Kaladushaka, would donate half of the loot he stole to the deity in the temple. While the King caught him, Vaikunthanathar appeared before the king and expressed that He was also a culprit and thus gained the name Kallapiran. Another sthala purāṇam mentions a demon named Somakan who stole the texts of knowledge from Lord Brahmā. Upon praying to the Lord, Vaikunthanathar killed Somakan, recovered the texts, and presented them to Lord Brahmā.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend of this kshethram tells the tale of a king named Shwetaketu. Shwetaketu was said to have reached the gates of Karya-Vaikuṇṭham(A replica of Shri Vaikuṇṭham and is regarded to be the penultimate stage in one's journey to reach moksham), but is said to have felt hunger. At this point, the king began to question why this was happening, as when one becomes eligible to enter Vaikuṇṭham, they are supposed to be rid of all worldly senses, such as hunger and thirst. To have his problem resolved, the king visited Nārada to find out why he was still feeling hungry. Nārada told the king that during his lifetime, he had not performed the charitable duties of a king. Thus, he was still feeling worldly sensations. Nārada advised the king to perform tapas at Nāgavanam ( Nāga in Sanskrit means elephant. In connection with Tirumanimada Kovil's sthala purāṇam, Airavatha is said to have performed tapas here at Tirunangur to the Lord to redeem himself, as he had insulted Mahālakshmī without knowing that he had done so. Nāgavanam, over time, has become Nangur.) to convince the Lord that he was worthy of attaining moksham. Thus, the king's aathma is said to have descended to Bhūlokam and performed tapas here at this kshethram to gain moksham. The Lord appeared as he would appear at Karya-Vaikuṇṭham and granted moksham to the king. It is said that Utaṅka Maharshi guided the soul to the Lord.

fields.text:
This is the kshethram where Lord Shri Krishna grew up, slew demons, and performed his leelas. In the present day, we can see Shri Nand Yashodha Bhavan, the house where the Lord was brought and grew up. In the present-day scenario, this is the main temple. In the garbha gudi, we can see Lord Balarāma alongside Yashodha and Nanda. Lord Krishna can be seen in a cradle with a rope, which is given to devotees to comfort the Lord. Another important place in this kshethram is the Rāman Reti. This is the place where Lord Krishna played as a child. This is the place where Lord Krishna ate mud and showed Yashodha the entire creation by opening His mouth. It is customary to roll in the sand, as this is the place where the Lord stepped and played. People take the sand from this place asa form of prasadam.

Rāman Reti

According to legend, Mangalathammai used to observe Ekādashī vratham and feed one Brahmachāri on the Dwadasi day. Tolakarana, a demon, was creating hurdles to her vratham. Responding to her prayers, the Lord killed the demon and came for the feast in the form of a Brahmachāri, and later gave darshan to her with Lakshmī adorning His chest and gained the name Tiruvazhmarban. The place Tiruvalla originates from the presiding deity Vallabha.
*** According to legend, Ghantakarnan attained moksha at this kshetram.
The presiding deity is said to have been handmade by Vishvakarma, as instructed by Lord Krishna Himself. Vishvakarma wanted to establish the Lord at this kshetram at the end of the Dvāpara Yuga, but it is said that Garuḍa hid the Lord until Kāli Yuga had taken full effect. Later, Garuḍan established the Lord here.
This kshethram has a separate shrine dedicated to Shri Sudarshana Chakrath Āzhwār.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
As per temple legend, there was once a king named Sumathi. He had once taken a trip to Tirumalai, where he asked to see the Lord in the form of Krishna bearing two hands. Tiruvengadamudayan told the king that it was not possible, as he was in the form of an archa-avataram and not in Shri Vaikuṇṭham. He advised the king to go further south, where he could find Kairavini Pushkariṇī. He asked the king to perform tapas there and told him that his prayers would be heard. At around the same time, Atreya Maharshi, a disciple of Maharshi Vyāsa, brought an idol of Pārthasārathy Perumāl here. When Sumathi Raja's tapas was completed, the Lord appeared to him as Venkata Krishna Perumāl, holding the Pānchajanyam in one hand and displaying the Varada Mudra in the other. Along with the Lord appeared Rukmiṇī Devī, Balarāma(the Lord's older brother), Pradyumna(the Lord's son), Anirudha( the Lord's grandson), and Satyaki(the Lord's charioteer).
*** The utsava murthy, i.e., Pārthasārathy Perumāl, can be seen with scars that are said to have been inflicted on Him by Bheeshma during the Mahābhārata war.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
History:
According to legend, there was once a Nambudhri Priest by the name of Bilwa Mangala Samiyar who used to perform Tiruvaradhanam daily to many Shalagramams. It is said that there was a young boy who accompanied the priest daily during his kanikaryams. The boy was very naughty, but had told the priest not to question anything that he would do. One day, the boy stole some of the Shalagramams from the priest and started to run. The priest pursued the boy. As the chase continued, the boy ran into a dense forest known as Ananthavanam. As the priest ran after the boy, a humungous illupa-maram (Indian Butter Tree) fell in front of him. The height of the tree can be comprehended as follows. It is said that the Lord's tirumukham rested in Tiruvattar, His nabhi rested in Thiruvananthapuram, and his tiruvadi rested in a place known as Tirupaapur.
Similarly, another story states that Diwakara Maharshi chased a boy into the Ananthavanam, and the tree fell; as a result, the Lord appeared in the tree. It is said that Diwakara Maharshi was holding a tridandam, and he asked the Lord to reduce his length to match the tridandam. Thus, the Lord shrank Himself to a length of 18 feet. As the Lord shrank Himself from a humungous length to a more viewable length, He got the name Ananthapadhmanabhan. Anantha, which means immeasurable, and Padmanābhan, as Lord Brahmā emanates from the divine lotus in His navel. Thus, a temple was constructed, and the Lord was present in a wooden form for many years. Even today, one can get a sight of Bilwa Mangala Samiyar as well as Diwakara Maharshi inside the garbha-griha.

Modern Day:
In 1686, a massive fire reportedly broke out in the temple. The then king Marthanda Varman is said to have reconstructed the temple over the course of forty years and performed the samprokshanam for the temple in 1726. It is said that the Lord appeared in the king's dream and told him that He wished to be converted into a shila-vigraham form. It is said that elephants carried 2400 shalagramams on their heads from Nepal and delivered them to the king. The Lord further instructed the king to use 1200 shalagramams to constitute Him in the shila-vigraham form. The remaining shalagramams were to be stored safely till they would be necessary to reconstruct the Lord once more. To this day, that requirement has not arisen. In the year 1750, Marthanda Varman is said to have written down all his wealth in the name of the Lord and the temple and given his family the title of Padmanābha-Dasan, which translates to those who serve Lord Padmanābha. To this day, the Kings of the Travancore family visit the temple in the early hours of the morning and pay their respects to the Lord. Due to being unable to visit the temple on any given day, they pay a fine to the temple. There are two annual festivals during the Tamil months of Pankuni and Aippasi.

The significance of the three doors for viewing the Lord:
Given the length of the Lord being eighteen feet, there are three doors through which one can view the Lord. In the first door, one can see the Lord's tirumukham. This door is said to have been meant for the Nityasooris, such as Garuḍan and Vishvaksenar. In the second door, one can see the Lord's naabhi (navel) from which emanates the divine lotus, inside which is seated Lord Brahmā. This door is said to have been meant for the Devas. In the third door, one can see the Lord's tiruvadi (His holy lotus-feet). This door is said to be meant for all His devotees who seek his refuge as instructed by Him in the Gita, where Lord Krishna says, "Sarva Dharman Parityajya maam ekam sharanam vraja."

*** Other specialties in this temple include Añjanēya Svāmi, who is always adorned in butter. There is a shrine hosting Ugra-Narasimha Svāmi. To keep the Lord's anger under control, Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Parayanam is done daily in front of the shrine.

fields.text: Legend has it that the Lord Brahmā and Vālmīki worshipped the Lord at this kshethram. Another story tells the episode of Mandooka Maharshi. Mandooka Maharshi earned his name as he would perform penance in cold water, holding his breath for extended periods. Once, when he was in deep penance, Maharshi Durvāsa visited the water body. When Mandooka Maharshi did not notice his presence, Maharshi Durvāsa cursed Mandooka Maharshi that he would take the form of a toad. Upon worshipping the Lord at this kshethram, the curse was said to be broken, and he regained his human form. Hence, the pushkariṇī at this kshethram is named Mandooka-Pushkariṇī.

Legend tells the story of the Saptarshis wanting to see the Lord. It is said that they performed tapas at a place called Shuceendram, not too far from this kshethram. When their tapas was completed, Lord Shiva appeared. When the Saptarshis said they wanted to see Lord Vishṇu, Lord Shiva directed them to this kshethram. Here again, the Saptarshis performed tapas, and the Lord appeared as Tiruvazhmarban with thāyār in His heart, granting darshanam for the Saptarshis.

*** There is a shrine for Shri Rāma, Lakshmaṇa, Sītā, Bharatha, and Shatrugna here at this temple. This kshethram is also the avatara-sthalam of Vodaya Nangayar, the mother of Nam Āzhwār.

One day, when Vyagrapadar had gone out in search of flowers, his infant son, Upamanyu, started to cry from hunger. Thus, the Lord sent Purushottama Nayaki Thāyār to feed the infant milk and give him water to prevent dehydration.

fields.text: At the time of creation, Lord Brahmā is said to have summoned his four sons, the Sanathkumaras, for a deliberation session to discuss what had to go into creation. It is said that his four sons refused to attend this session on the advice of Devarishi Nārada, who instructed them to meditate upon Lord Vishṇu rather than waste their time in unwanted deliberation. Thus, Lord Brahmā summoned Devarishi Nārada and cursed him to wander the three worlds, aimlessly preaching about the Lord. When the Devarishi arrived at this kshethram, he is said to have meditated upon the Lord here and requested Him to write a Purana. Thus, this kshethram is the site where Naradeeya Purāṇam was written. Another story recounts the tale of Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi, who sought to see the Lord in His true form. Thus, Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi is said to have meditated upon the Lord here. The Lord is said to have appeared in front of Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi and inhaled him. In the nose of the Lord, Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi is said to have seen the entire process of creation and destruction of the whole universe, along with the Lord's form as a baby(His miracles as a child in His Krishna Avataram) to His Vishwaroopam form.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: The legend tells the story of a brahmin named Vedavit. Vedavit is said to have been looking for the best place to perform dhyanam and tapas, and he is said to have come to this kshethram. When he performed tapas at this kshethram, the Lord is said to have appeared as Vijayaasana Perumāl and performed the ashtaakshara mantra padhesham. Another story tells the tale of Romasa Maharshi and his student Satyavan, who came to this kshethram. It is said that they arrived along the banks of the Tāmraparaṇi river and saw a fisherman dropping his net into the water on the opposite bank. As the fisherman dropped his net into the water, a snake is said to have bitten him, and he passed away on the spot. Satyavan is said to have seen a Swarna-vahanam ( a golden chariot) appear and take the aathma to Vaikuṇṭham. Satyavan is said to have asked his guru why the man was taken to Vaikuṇṭham. Romasa Maharshi is then supposed to have told Satyavan that it's the power of the kshethram that, regardless of what the person was doing when he passed away on this pure land, he achieved moksham.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend tells the tale of the Lord defeating the demon named Adikeshi. After his death, Ādikeshi's wife performs penance and asks the Gaṅgā and Tamraparani rivers to flow in a circular pattern, engulfing the area. The Lord is said to have taken His reclining form and slept atop the demon, using Ādishesha as His bed, at the meeting point of the rivers. Seeing that her efforts to take revenge were in vain, Ādikeshi's wife is said to have surrendered to the Lord.
Another story tells us how the Lord came to take His current form. There was a Maharshi named Hathalekar, who was very short in stature but extremely learned from a young age. One day, the Lord decided to test Hathalekar Maharshi. He approached and began teasing the sage about his height. At one point, when the sage was standing next to a banana tree, the Lord asked if his parents were dwarves too, having given birth to someone of his stature. The sage, in a fit of anger, pointed at the tree and said, "These are my parents."
Not wanting to disappoint His devotee, the Lord caused the parents to emerge from the tree, and then gave him upadesham of the Ashṭākshara mantram, telling the sage that it had all been a test of his faith and devotion. The Lord, pleased with the sage, then instructed him to reconstruct His form as Adikesava Perumāl.
Hathalekar used to perform aaradhanam daily to 16,008 shalagramams. It is said that the Lord was brought into His present form using these 16,008 shalagramams, along with a mixture of karungal (black teak wood) ash, mustard seeds, and jaggery.
As a result, there is no abhishekam performed for the murti at this kshetram. The Lord is preserved through the application of medicinal herbs and oils, as prescribed by the Ayurveda Shāstram.
The Lord here is very similar to Shri Ananthapadmanabha Svāmi at Thiruvananthapuram. The Adikesava Perumāl murti is 22 feet long, compared to 18 feet at Thiruvananthapuram. Another difference lies in the Nabhi Kamalam (navel lotus) of Adikesava Perumāl; Lord Brahmā is not present, as this form of the Lord is said to have appeared before Brahmā was created.
There are three doors through which devotees can have darshan—one to see the Lord's face, one for His navel, and another for His feet.
It is said that Shri Ananthapadmanabha Svāmi reclines in such a direction that He faces Adikesava Perumāl.

Legend has it that Lord Brahmā caused the herds of cattle being grazed by Lord Krishna to disappear, upon which Lord Krishna created another herd. Finding this, Brahmā apologized to Krishna and requested Him to take abode at Tiruvazhandur. In the sanctum, Prahlada is to the right of the mūlavar and Garuḍan to His left. After witnessing Narasimha Avataram of the Lord, Prahlada asks to see the lord in a Shantha-Swaroopam (calm form), to which the Lord gave him darshanam at this kshethram. It is said that the vimānam of this kshethram was given by Garuḍan, hence the name Garuḍa Vimānam.

*** This kshethram is also the birthplace of the great Tamizh poet Kambar, who has given us the magnum opus of Kamba Ramayanam, which rivals and trumps Vālmīki Ramayanam in terms of poetic beauty. One can find a shrine dedicated to Kambar and his wife here at this kshethram.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
According to legend, when all of Sarasvatī Devī's efforts to stop Lord Brahmā's Ashvamedha Yajña failed, she decided to flow like a river(a personification of the speed at which she could deliver any knowledge). Thus, she took the form of Vegavathy and decided to flow over the homa kundam. At this point, Lord Brahmā requested the Lord to stop Devī Sarasvatī. Thus, the Lord took this form and acted as a dam, redirecting the flow of the river. Therefore, this kshethram came to be known as Vegavathy Annai, which later became Vegka.
When Tirumazhisai Āzhwār was living in Kāñchipuram, an old lady who worked as a servant (Daasi) used to clean his house every day. She did this small act of service with full dedication. Pleased by her sincere effort, the Āzhwār blessed her and transformed her into a young and beautiful woman.
Soon, her beauty caught the attention of the king of the region. Surprised by her charm, the king married her, and she became the queen. After some time, the king came to know the story behind the transformation and was curious to meet Tirumazhisai Āzhwār himself.
Now, Kani Kaṇṇan—who was the Āzhwār's close disciple and companion—was called to the palace. The king asked him to request Āzhwār to visit the palace and compose a poem in his praise. But Kani Kaṇṇan respectfully told the king that Tirumazhisai Āzhwār only sings for the Lord Srivaikuntanathan (Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa) and that it was not possible for him to write or sing anything to praise a human being.
Still hoping, the king offered Kani Kaṇṇan gold, silver, diamonds, and all kinds of riches if he himself would sing in the king's praise. But Kani Kaṇṇan firmly refused, saying he would not sing about any human, no matter the reward. This made the king angry. In his fury, he ordered Kani Kaṇṇan to leave Kāñchipuram immediately.
Kani Kaṇṇan returned to Tirumazhisai Āzhwār and explained everything that had happened. Hearing this, the Āzhwār decided that if his devotee was being thrown out of the city, he too would leave along with him.
Before leaving, Tirumazhisai Āzhwār composed a verse addressing the Lord Yathothakari Perumāl (the presiding deity of the Tiruvekka temple). In it, he told the Lord that since Kani Kaṇṇan was leaving the city, and he himself was also leaving, Perumāl too should get up from his serpent-bed (Ādisheshan), roll it up, and leave Kāñchipuram.
To everyone's shock, the Lord actually obeyed. He rose from His resting posture, folded up His bed, and left the temple to follow His devotee.
The king and the people of Kāñchipuram were shaken by this miracle. They ran after them, pleaded for forgiveness, and begged Kani Kaṇṇan and Āzhwār to return. Moved by their repentance, Kani Kaṇṇan agreed to come back.
When they returned, Tirumazhisai Āzhwār once again sang to the Lord, asking Him to return to the temple and rest on Ādisheshan as before. The Lord came back to the Tiruvekka temple and resumed His reclining posture.
Because the Lord acted exactly according to what the Āzhwār said—first leaving, then returning—He came to be known as "Sonna Vannam Seitha Perumāl", which means "The Lord who did exactly as He was told."

*** A peculiarity of this kshethram is that when one sees the Lord reclining here, they can notice that the Lord is laterally inverted, i.e., the Lord's tiruvadi( His lotus feet) are where His head usually rests and vice versa. This is because when Tirumazhisai Āzhwār asked the Lord to return, he did not specify in which direction He must rest.

Dundumaaran is said to have performed tapas for one month when the Lord appeared in front of the king and saved his son from the clutches of death.

*** Annan Perumāl is considered to be elder to Thiruvinnagar (Uppiliappan) and Tirumalai (Shrīnivāsar). Any prayer to be performed to either of the two can be performed here.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text: It is said that Shibi Chakravarthy, the grandson of Yayati, a ruler of Ayodhyā belonging to the Chandravamsham dynasty, once undertook a trip to South India. One night, he decided to stay at the place known as Shwetagiri, which in Sanskrit translates to a hill with white rocks. Shwetagiri in Tamizh may be split as Vella+Arai, which means white hill. One night during his stay, Shibi Chakravarthy's army chieftain complained that a wild white boar was running around and causing trouble to the army. Hearing this, the king ordered its capture. A few days passed, and the army chieftain came back with a complaint, saying the boar would magically disappear as they got close to catching it. Hearing this, Shibi Chakravarthy himself decided to go after the boar. He took his bow and set out in search of the animal. As he was searching, he saw the boar and began pursuing it. As he chased after the boar in the forest, he saw Sage Mārkaṇḍeya in penance. Seeing the sage, Shibi Chakravarthy offered his respects and went to inquire of the great sage if he had seen a wild boar pass by. The sage immediately directed the king to an anthill near the tree where he was meditating. He tells the king that he was in penance, waiting for the day the king would arrive seeking out a boar. He hands the king a pitcher of milk and asks him to pour the milk down the anthill. The king follows the sage's instructions and does as he says. As the king poured the milk down the anthill, it began to melt, revealing a beautiful idol of Lord Pundarikakshan. The king wasted no time in installing the idol of the Lord into a temple. Sage Mārkaṇḍeya then tells the king that he should bring three thousand seven hundred Vaishṇavas from his kingdom and help them to settle down here. The king immediately returned to Ayodhyā and, according to the sage's instructions, found three thousand seven hundred Vaishṇavas and brought them to the temple. As Shibi counted the number of Vaishṇavas that he had brought, he discovered that one of them had mysteriously vanished. The Lord then appeared in the king's dream, saying He was one among the three thousand seven hundred, and told the king that he wanted to experience firsthand what bhakti felt like. In the Garbhagriha, we can see the Lord holding a prayoga chakram, along with His consorts, Shrīdevī and Bhūdevi, as well as Sooryan, Chandhran, Garuḍan, and Aadiseshan.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
This kshethram is associated with the story of Vāmana Avataram. Let us now see the story. It is said that the Lord took this form to defeat the demon king Bali. Bali was a mighty demon king. He was the grandson of Prahlāda. Bali was such a powerful demon that he was individually capable of keeping all the Devas at bay. The Devas then approached Lord Vishṇu to aid in defeating Bali. Bali was a Chiranjeevi, hence he could not be killed. He could merely be pushed down to Pātāla-Lokam. The Lord assured the Devas that he would look into the situation. At the same time, Aditi, the mother of the Devas, wanted to make sure that the Lord would be born to her. To ensure this, Aditi used the means of payovratam (a complete milk-based diet over twelve days). The Lord was born in Aditi's womb to Aditi and Sage Kashyapa. The Lord was born as a dwarf. As soon as he was born, the Lord revealed to Aditi the various stages of his life, and he grew into a young boy. The upanayanam ceremony was performed, and each of the gods presented Vāmana with a gift. Brahmā gave him a kamandalam, and Brihaspati gave him the umbrella. Thus, the Lord set out to fulfill the promise given to the Devas. He reached Bali's palace, where he was giving alms to the brahmins assembled. As the Lord reached the assembly, Shukrāchārya warned Bali that the person responsible for killing his grandfather had come to defeat him. He advised Bali not to give alms to him. Bali was honored that the Lord had come to his assembly. He proceeded with the program and soon reached Vāmana. Bali asked him what he desired as alms. The boy replies, saying all he desires is three paces of land. Bali granted the boy's wish. To prevent Bali from giving alms, Shukrāchārya assumed a tiny form and sat at the mouth of Bali's kamandalam. When water did not come out of the kamandalam, Lord Vāmana took a dharba grass and poked the opening of the kamandalam. In the process of poking the opening, Lord Vāmana poked one of Shukrāchārya's eyes. In pain, Shukrāchārya left the opening of the kamandalam. The boy started to grow. With the first step, he measured the entire earth. With the second step, he took the heavens. By the time he had to take the third step, there was no space left. Bali got onto his knees and, with a posture of namaskaram, bent his head and asked the Lord to place the third step on his head and push him into Pātāla-Lokam. The Lord, now in his Trivikrama form, fulfills Bali's wish and places the third step on his head, sending him to Pātāla-Lokam.
It is said that Shukrāchārya performed tapas here, and the Lord appeared as Kolavilli Rāmar, reclined in the bhujanga shayanam, and granted Shukrāchārya his eye once again.

***This is one of the special kshethrams in which one can find Lord Rāma in a reclining posture.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
This kshethram derives its name from the root words "Vel," meaning "desire," and "Irukkai," meaning "place of stay." Thus, the kshethram became Velukkai. It is said that the Lord came here out of his desire to meditate after killing Hiraṇyakashipu. He also killed all the demons that infested the surrounding land.
Devī Sarasvatī, in her first attempt to send demons, was unsuccessful, as Lord Ashṭabhujar defeated all of them. In her second attempt to spoil the yajña by creating darkness, she was again unsuccessful, as Lord Deepaprakasar provided a source of light. In a third attempt to stop the yajña from taking place, She created a mighty demon named Kapalika and unleashed him upon the land. The Lord is then supposed to have taken the form of Nṛisimha and killed the demon, therefore protecting the yajña.
It is said that the Lord presiding over this kshethram was initially Lord Vishṇu, facing east. However, when Bhṛgu Maharshi asked to see him in the form of Nṛisimha, he took the form of Azhagiyasinga Perumāl.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
"Vina Venkatesham na natho na natha, Sada venkatesham smarami, smarami,
Hare Venkatesha, praseedha praseedha, Priyam Venkatesha, prayacha prayacha."
The meaning of the above shlokam is as follows:
"Without you, Oh Venkateshwara, I would not exist. I keep remembering your name. Please bestow me with your love and grace."
"Venkatādri Samam Sthaanam Brahmande Naasti Kinchanaa…
Venkatesha Samo Devo Na Bhootho Na Bhavishyati.."
The meaning of the above shlokam is as follows:
"Neither in the past nor the future would there be a sacred place in this universe that can equal the sanctity of the Venkatādri hills, nor would there be a God who can equal the Holy Lord Shri Venkateshvara."
This shloka appears in the Bhavishyattottara Purāṇam, written by Maharshi Vyāsa centuries before the Lord ever came to reside at the Venkatādri Hills.
As per legend, after saving the Earth from Hiraṇyāksha, Lord Varāha stayed on this hill on the northern bank of Svāmi Pushkariṇī. Hence, Tirumala Hills is also referred to as Adivarahakshetra. At the beginning of Kaliyuga, Lord Varāha donated land to Lord Venkateshvara at his request. As gratitude, Lord Venkateshvara offered the first bell, puja, and Naivedyam to Varahaswamy before they were offered to him. This tradition is still followed today.

Svāmi Pushkariṇī

Varāha Svāmi

Shri Bhu Varāha
The rishis, headed by Kashyapa, began to perform a sacrifice on the banks of the Gaṅgās. Sage Nārada visited them and asked them why they were performing the sacrifice and who would be pleased by it. Unable to answer the question, the rishis approached Sage Bhṛgu.To solve a direct ascertainment of reality.
Bhṛgu first went to Satyaloka, the abode of Lord Brahmā. At Satyloka, he found Lord Brahmā reciting the four Vedas in praise of Lord Nārāyaṇa, with each of his four heads, and attended upon by Sarasvatī. Lord Brahmā did not take notice of Bhṛgu offering obeisance. Concluding that Lord Brahmā was unfit for worship, Bhṛgu left Satyaloka for Kailāsha, the abode of Lord Shiva.
At Kailāsha, Bhṛgu found Lord Shiva spending his time pleasantly with Pārvatī, unaware of his presence. Pārvatī drew Shiva's attention to the presence of the sage. Lord Shiva was furious at Bhṛgu's intrusion and tried to destroy him. The sage cursed Lord Shiva and left for Vaikuṇṭham. At Vaikuṇṭham, Lord Vishṇu was reposing on Ādishesha with Shri Mahālakshmī in service at His feet. Finding that Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa also did not notice him, the sage became infuriated and kicked the Lord on his chest, the place where Mahālakshmī resides.
At once, Lord Vishṇu hastened to apologize to the angry sage and pressed his feet to allay the pain caused to Bhṛgu's leg. In doing so, the Lord removed the eye in the foot of the sage, which gave Bhṛgu power to defy the Devas. Thereupon, the sage decided that Lord Vishṇu was the most supreme of the Trimūrtis and informed the rishis accordingly. Thereupon, they decided that Lord Vishṇu was the fruit of the yaga. Shri Mahālakshmī was angered by the action of her Lord in apologizing to Bhṛgu, who committed an offense. She, therefore, left Vaikuṇṭham without heeding the entreaties of the Lord. At the commencement of the current Sveta Varāha Kalpa, the whole universe was filled with water, and the Earth was immersed in it. Lord Vishṇu assumed the form of a white boar (Shri Varāha) and dived into the water to lift the Earth. He slew the demon Hiraṇyāksha, who was obstructing Him, and rescued the Earth.
Brahmā and the other Devas praised Shri Varāha for saving the Earth by chanting the Vedas and showering flowers on Him. Lord Vishṇu decided to stay on Earth in the form of Shri Varāha for some time to punish the wicked and protect the virtuous. The place then came to be known as Varāha Kshetra, and the Varāha Kalpa commenced. After the departure of Mahālakshmī, a forlorn Lord Vishṇu left Vaikuṇṭham and took abode in an ant-hill under a tamarind tree beside a pushkariṇī on the Venkata Hill. Taking pity on Lord Vishṇu, Brahmā and Maheshwara decided to assume the forms of a cow and its calf to serve Him.
Sūrya, the Sun God, informed Mahālakshmī of this and requested her to assume the form of a cowherdess and sell the cow and calf to the king of the Chōla country. The king of the Chōla country bought the cow and its calf and sent them to graze on Venkata Hill along with his herd of cattle. Discovering Lord Vishṇu on the ant-hill, the cow provided its milk and thus fed the Lord. Meanwhile, at the palace, the cow was not yielding any milk, for which the Chōla Queen chastised the cowherd severely.
To find out the cause of the lack of milk, the cowherd followed the cow, hid behind a bush, and discovered the cow emptying her udder over the ant-hill.
Incensed over the conduct of the cow, the cowherd aimed a blow with his axe at the head of the cow. However, Lord Vishṇu rose from the ant-hill to receive the blow and save the cow. When the cowherd saw the Lord bleed at the blow of his axe, he fell and died of shock.
On the death of the cowherd, the cow returned, bellowing in fright and with bloodstains all over her body, to the Chōla King. To find out the cause of the cow's terror, the King followed her to the scene of the incident. The King found the cowherd lying dead on the ground near the ant-hill. While he stood wondering how it had happened, Lord Vishṇu rose from the ant-hill and cursed the King, saying that he would become an Asura because of the fault of his servant.
The King pleaded innocence, and the Lord blessed him by saying that the curse would end when the Lord was adorned with a kireetam presented by Akasa Raja at the time of His marriage with Shri Padmāvatī. Thereafter, Lord Vishṇu or Shrīnivāsa decided to stay in Varāha Kshetra and requested Shri Varahaswami to grant Him a site for His stay. His request being readily granted, Shrīnivāsa ordained that a pilgrimage to His shrine would not be complete unless it is preceded by a bath in the Pushkariṇī and darshan of Shri Varahaswami. That puja and naivedyam should be offered to Shri Varahaswami first.
Yashodā brought up Shri Krishna, the son of Devaki, in his early years. However, Yashodā was not blessed to witness the marriage of Shri Krishna with Rukmiṇī, and she felt very sad. Shri Krishna promised to fulfill her desire in her next birth as Vakulādevī in his next avatara as Shrīnivāsa. In Yashodā's next birth as Vakulādevī, she was serving Lord Varahaswami when He sent her to serve Shrīnivāsa. Sometime later, a King named Ākāsha Raja, who belonged to the Lunar race, was ruling over Thondamandalam.
He had a brother named Tondamān. Ākāsha Raja had no heirs, and therefore, he wanted to perform a sacrifice. As part of the sacrifice, he was ploughing the fields when his plough turned up a lotus in the ground. On examining the lotus, the King found a female child in it. Ākāsha Raja was happy to find the child. He carried it to his palace and gave it to his Queen. At that time, he heard a voice from above which said, "Oh! King, tend to it as your child, and fortune will befall you." As the child was found in a lotus, the king named her Padmāvatī.
Over time, Princess Padmāvatī grew up into a beautiful maiden and was attended to by a host of maids. One day, while she was spending her time in a garden picking flowers with her maids, Sage Nārada approached her. Assuring her that he was her well-wisher, he asked her to show him her palm to read her future. He foretold that she was destined to be the spouse of Lord Vishṇu himself. At this time, Lord Shrīnivāsa, who was hunting, chased a wild elephant in the forests surrounding the hills. In the elephant's pursuit, the Lord was led into a garden, where Princess Padmāvatī and her maids were picking flowers.
The sight of the elephant frightened the Princess and her maids. But the elephant immediately turned around, saluted the Lord, and disappeared into the forest. Lord Shrīnivāsa, who was following on horseback, saw the frightened maidens, who accosted Him with queries
When Lord Shrīnivāsa returned, Vakulādevī brought him his usual dinner comprising various delicacies. However, she found him lying on his bed, pining for his love.
When she inquired about the cause, the Lord informed her that unless he married Princess Padmāvatī, he would never recover. Vakulādevī then asked Him to tell her all about the Princess. The Lord then narrated the story of her (Padmāvatī's) previous birth and his promise to wed her.
(The following story is found only in Venkatachala Mahathmiyam and not in Vālmīki Ramayanam.)
In ancient times, Lakshmī, in the form of Vedavatī, resided in an ashram in the forest. At that time, Rāvaṇa, the lord of Lanka, tried to tempt her. In anger, Vedavatī cursed him, saying that she would bring about his death. To demonstrate the truth of her words, Vedavatī walked into the fire, but Agni, the Fire God, rescued her. He took Vedavatī to his house and entrusted her to his wife's care. When Rāvaṇa was about to carry away Sītā from Panchavati, in the absence of Rāma and Lakshmaṇa, Agni appeared and offered Vedavatī to Rāvaṇa as the real Sītā, who was kept with him by Rāma to evade Rāvaṇa. Rāvaṇa was tricked into thinking that Vedavatī was the real Sītā.
Rāvaṇa took Vedavatī to Lanka, thinking she was the real Sītā, while Agni took Sītā to his house and asked his wife, Swahadevi, to look after her. After the destruction of Rāvaṇa, Vedavatī entered the fire when rejected by Rāma. Then, Agni offered the real Sītā to Rāma. Rāma then questioned her as to who the other lady by her side was. Sītā informed Rāma that the lady was Vedavatī, who endured Rāvaṇa's torture for ten months in Lanka for her sake. Sītā requested Rāma to accept Vedavatī as his spouse as well. But Rāma declined her request, saying that he believed in having only one wife during his lifetime. However, He promised to wed her in her next birth as Padmāvatī, born as the daughter of Ākāsha Raja, when Rāma himself would take the form of Shrīnivāsa.
After listening to Shrīnivāsa's story of how he had promised to marry Vedavatī in her next birth as Padmāvatī, Vakulādevī realized that Shrīnivāsa would not be happy unless he married Padmāvatī. She offered to go to Ākāsha Raja and his Queen and arrange for the marriage. On the way, she met the maid-servants of Padmāvatī returning from a Shiva Temple. She learned from them that Padmāvatī was also pining for Shrīnivāsa. Vakulādevī accompanied the maidservants to the Queen. Meanwhile, Ākāsha Raja and his queen Dharaṇīdevī were anxious about the health of their daughter, Padmāvatī. They learned about Padmāvatī's love for Shrīnivāsa of Venkata Hill. Ākāsha Raja consulted Brihaspati about the propriety of the marriage and was informed that the marriage was in the best interest of both parties. After the departure of Vakulādevī, Shrīnivāsa could not rest in peace. He doubted if she would succeed in her mission. He, therefore, assumed the form of a lady fortune-teller and entered the streets of the capital, telling fortunes. Padmāvatī's maids saw her and invited her to the presence of their Queen.
The maid-servants informed Queen Dharaṇīdevī that the fortune-teller was hesitating to enter the palace without the Queen's invitation. The Queen came out herself and invited the fortune-teller into the palace. The fortune-teller was taken to the presence of Princess Padmāvatī. The fortune-teller read the palm of the Princess and told the Queen about the cause of Padmāvatī's indisposition. She advised the Queen to give Padmāvatī in marriage to Lord Shrīnivāsa. She also told the Queen that a lady would approach her shortly on behalf of Lord Shrīnivāsa to formally request Padmāvatī's hand in marriage.
After the departure of the fortune-teller, Vakulādevī arrived at the palace and was taken by the maidservants to the Queen. She informed the Queen that she had come on behalf of Lord Shrīnivāsa to request the hand of Padmāvatī in marriage. Having consulted Brihaspati and heard from his Queen about the prediction of the fortune-teller and the arrival of the messenger from Shrīnivāsa, Ākāsha Raja decided to hand his daughter in marriage to Shrīnivāsa. He asked the palace purohits to fix a muhurtam for the marriage. Ākāsha Raja informed his ministers and other officials of his plans. Immediately, a letter was drafted requesting Shrīnivāsa to come and marry the Princess.
Ākāsha Raja entrusted the delivery of the letter to Sukamahamunin. Shuka went to Venkata Hill with Vakulādevī. He presented the patrika to Lord Shrīnivāsa, who was very happy. The Lord sent his garland for Padmāvatī through Shuka. Kubera lent money to Lord Shrīnivāsa to meet the expenses of the marriage.
About six months after this celestial marriage, Mahālakshmī learns that her husband has remarried and comes to see him in disbelief. It is said that the Lord turns into Stone right when he, Mahālakshmī, and Padmāvatī encounter him. Lord Brahmā and Shiva appear before the confused queens and explain the main purpose behind all this – The Lord's desire to be on the seven hills for the emancipation of mankind from the perpetual troubles of Kāli Yuga. Goddesses Lakshmī and Padmāvatī also turn into stone idols expressing their wish to be with their Lord always. Lakshmī stays with Him on His Chest on the left side while Padmāvatī rests on His Chest's right side.
Raṅgadāsa was a staunch devotee of Vishṇu, and during his pilgrimage, he joined Sage Vaikhānasa Gopinatha, who was ascending the Tirumala Hill for worship of the Lord. This was after the Lord had settled the Adivaraha region. After bathing in the Svāmi Pushkariṇī, Raṅgadāsa viewed Lord Vishṇu beneath a tamarind tree. However, Lord Vishṇu was exposed to the sun, wind, and rain and was only protected by the extended wings of Garuḍa. Raṅgadāsa raised a rough wall of stones around the deity and started supplying flowers to Gopinatha every day for Vishṇu's worship. One day, Raṅgadāsa was distracted by a Gandharva king and his ladies and forgot to supply flowers to Gopinatha for Vishṇu's worship. The Lord then revealed Himself and told Raṅgadāsa that he had not been steadfast and had succumbed to temptation. However, in acceptance of Raṅgadāsa's devoted service to Him till then, the Lord blessed Raṅgadāsa that he would be reborn as an affluent ruler of a province and would enjoy the earthly pleasures. He would continue to serve the Lord, construct a beautiful temple with a vimānam and high surrounding walls, and thereby earn eternal glory. Soon, the site was forgotten, and an ant-hill formed over the temple.


Raṅgadāsa was reborn as Tondaman, the son of the royal couple, Suvira and Nandini. Tondaman enjoyed a pleasurable life as a young man. One day, he set out on a hunting expedition on the Tirumala Hill, and with the help of a cowherd, saw Vishṇu under the tamarind tree. Tondaman returned home, deeply affected by the vision of Vishṇu. Tondaman later inherited his father's kingdom, Tondamandalam. Following the directions given by Ādi Varāha to a forester, Tondaman constructed a prakaram(closed precincts of a temple) and dvara-gopuram and arranged for regular worship of the Lord as per Vaikhānasa Āgama Shāstras.
Lord Venkateshvara appeared in the dream of Tondamān and asked him to build a temple for him, where he turned into stone. Thus, the temple for Venkateshvara on the seventh hill, known as Venkatādri (Venkata Hill), came into being at present-day Tirumala-Tirupati.

Ananada Nilaya Vimānam

Practices established by Shri Rāmānujāchārya:
Making Lord Venkateshvara re-adorn the Sankha and Chakra in a visible manner for devotees, to end the debates over whether the Lord in Tirumala is Lord Vishṇu or someone else.
Renovating Ananda Vimānam.
 Offering and doing pratishtapanam of Vyūha Lakshmī (two-handed Shrīdevī) on the Lord's necklace (kantika).
Changing the schedule of the Lord's Tirumañjanam (Abhishekam) to a weekly occurrence on every Friday, from a daily occurrence.
Recital of Nāchiyār Thirumozhi every Friday during Thirumanjanam when Shrīdevī is taken from the Lord's chest and is offered thirumanjanam.
 Commissioning of the building of wide streets around the temple, and moving back of the Brahmotsavam from Thiruchanur to Tirumala.
Appointing the Vaikhānasa Archaka for the Tirumala temple.
Establishing Yoga Narasimha sannadhi inside the temple.
Installing the moorthys of Rāma, Sītā, Lakshmaṇa, Hanumān, Sugriva, and Angada in the temple at Tirumala and establishing the practice of performing Kalyana Utsavam to Rāma and Sītā on the day after Shri Rāma Navami.
Establishing practices at Varāha Perumāl Sannadhi.
Installation of Azhvar sannadhis in Tirupati.
Consecration of the svayam vyaktha tiruvadi of Lord Shrīnivāsa and Āzhwārs in the foothills.
Code of Conduct as Established by Rāmānujāchārya:
Shri Rāmānuja, upon seeing the flawless service performed by Āchārya Periya Tirumala Nambi and Anantazhvan, and observing the defects in the service provided by many others at Tirumala, sought to establish a code of conduct at Tirumala to prevent any defects in the service to Lord Venkateshvara. He called Periya Tirumala Nambi and Anantazhvan and asked them to implement and maintain the code of conduct as follows.
1. Only those who are responsible for services to the Lord that require a physical presence in Tirumala must live in Tirumala.
2. Any food that is not prasadam of Lord Venkateshvara should not be eaten in Tirumala.
3. Only flowers that have already been offered to Lord Venkateshvara must be offered to the home deities of those who live in Tirumala
4. The last rites (burial or cremation) should not be performed in Tirumala.
5. Animals or birds should not be killed and eaten in Tirumala
6. No one should wear footwear or ride on vehicles in the streets around the temple in Tirumala and in any place in Tirumala where the Lord goes during festival times.
7. Non-believers should not come to Tirumala
8. There should not be any temple for other deities in the region between Svāmi Pushkariṇī and Kapila Theertha
9. The above-mentioned rules should apply to all regions that are within a distance of 1 yojana (around 8 miles) from Svāmi Pushkariṇī.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend tells the tale of Gavala Maharshi, who had 360 daughters. When he was faced with the trouble of getting each of them married, he was directed to perform tapas to the Lord here at Tiruvidandai. Upon completion of his tapas, the Lord came to the Maharshi daily and personally married each of his 360 daughters. On the 360th day, a question arose whether there had to be 360 different households for each daughter. Thus, the Lord took each of the 360 daughters and consolidated them into a single person. This is how Akilavalli Nāchiyār came to be. Here, the Lord can be seen with his right tiruvadi placed on the earth (Bhūmi Devī), and his left tiruvadi can be seen resting on the head of Ādisheshan, with his spouse blessing them eternally.
*** It is said that those who have been unable to get married can visit this kshethram and pray to the Lord and Thāyār here to find a suitable partner for marriage. The couple will be given two garlands and will be advised to revisit the temple after a while for the marriage to take fruit. The philosophy that can be seen at this kshethram is the relationship between the jeevaathma and Paramātma. The 360 daughters here represent the various jeevaathmas, and the Lord is the Paramātma. Each of the individual jeevaathmas longs to reach the Paramātma, who will grant us moksham (Varāha Perumāl, who lifted Bhūmi Devī from the waters of the deluge during pralayam, is the One who will liberate us from the ocean known as Samsara or life).

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
The legend has it that Bhūdevi was reborn as the daughter of Mārkaṇḍeya Maharshi, and one day, Lord Vishṇu, disguised as an old man, sought her hand in marriage. To ward off the marriage, the Maharshi informed the old man that his daughter was not well-versed in household duties, and she would even forget to season the salt in the food she prepared. The old man revealed Himself and took Bhūdevi as his wife. As per the wishes of the Lord, the prasadam is prepared without salt and offered to the presiding deity to date. Thus, the deity is also called Uppiliappan. (Uppillatha appan). It is believed that those who take salt or salted food inside the temple will go to hell. During the festival, Perumāl is always accompanied by Thāyār when He is taken in procession outside the temple.

***Oplliappan Perumāl is treated as the older brother of Shrīnivāsa Perumāl of Tirumala Tirupati. Therefore, all offerings due to Tirupati Perumāl can be made here, and they are considered equivalent to those offered at Tirupati.

fields.name: sthalaPuranam
fields.text:
Legend tells the story of Ambarīsha Maharaja, who was one of the greatest devotees of Lord Vishṇu. It is said that one day, the Lord took the form of Indra, mounted Airāvata, and appeared in front of Ambarīsha Maharaja. The Lord then asked Ambarīsha to ask for any wish. Ambarīsha refused by saying he would not ask anyone but Lord Shrīmān Nārāyaṇa for any sort of wish. The Lord was thus impressed by Ambarīsha and revealed Himself in the form of Uyyavantha Perumāl here at this kshethram. Ambarīsha then asks the Lord to show Himself as His four Vyuhamurthys. Thus, the Lord shows Himself as Vāsudeva, Sankarshaṇa, Anirudha, and Pradyumna. As seen in the picture, there are four vyuhamurthys, which the five Pāṇḍava brothers established. The first Murthy was that of Sankarshaṇa by Yudhishṭhira, followed by Vāsudeva by Arjuna, Anirudha by Bhīma, and Pradyumna by Nakula and Sahadeva.

*** Another story that is connected to the kshethram is as follows. There was once a brahmin who came to South India from the temple of Kashi Vishvanāthar. The brahmin is said to have been carrying an umbrella, which he left near the dwajasthambam and went to bathe in the Bharathapuzha River. When he came back, he noticed that the umbrella had become so heavy that he could not lift it, no matter how hard he tried. It is said that Kashi Vishvanāthar was so attached to his devotee that He had placed Himself inside the umbrella. When the brahmin left the umbrella near the dwajasthambam, the Lord thought it was the ideal place for Him to establish Himself at the kshetram alongside Lord Vishṇu; thus, a Lingam appeared, which is worshipped to this day.

title: Ganapati, the Scribe
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Before the great story could be told, it had to be written down, and the writing of it is itself a story, and a beautiful one, and it is fitting that we begin there, for it holds a lesson we shall need before we are done.
There was a sage named Vyāsa, the son of the sage Parāshara, and he was among the greatest souls the world has known. It was Vyāsa who gathered and arranged the Vedas, the ancient wisdom, into the form in which we have them; and it was Vyāsa who conceived, and would give to the world, the vast epic of the Mahābhārata, the story of a great family and a terrible war, so that the eternal truths of dharma might be kept alive in the hearts of men through all the ages to come.
But when he had conceived the work, whole and complete, in his mind, Vyāsa faced a difficulty, and it was a practical one. The epic was immense, greater than any poem the world had held, and he could not write it down himself and compose it at the same time; he needed a scribe, one who could take down the words as fast as he sang them. And who in all the world could do that? Who could hold a pen swift enough, and a mind vast enough, to receive without pause the whole flooding river of the Mahābhārata as it poured from the sage's lips?
Vyāsa turned in his need to the Creator himself, to Brahmā, and meditated upon him until the great god appeared before him. And Vyāsa bowed, and told him his difficulty: that he had conceived a work of unequalled wisdom, but could find no scribe able to take it down. And Brahmā smiled, and gave him his answer. Call upon Ganapati, he said, the elephant-headed lord, the remover of obstacles; he alone has the swiftness and the wisdom to be your scribe. And having said this, the Creator vanished, leaving the sage to summon the one he had named.
So Vyāsa meditated upon Ganapati, and the elephant-headed god appeared before him in a flash of light, and Vyāsa received him with reverence and made his request: that Ganapati would consent to write down the Mahābhārata as Vyāsa sang it, so that the three worlds might be lit by its truths.
And Ganapati agreed, but he set a condition, and it was a hard one. Very well, he said; I will be your scribe. But my pen, once it begins, must not stop. You must dictate without pause, without hesitation, in an unbroken stream; for if you halt even for a single moment, I will take it that the work is done, and I will lay down the pen and depart. Dictate without ceasing, or not at all.
It was a demand that would have daunted any lesser poet, for who can compose so vast a work without ever once pausing to think? But Vyāsa was wise, and he met the condition with a condition of his own, and in the meeting of the two conditions lies the whole point of the tale. Be it so, Lord, Vyāsa answered. I will not pause. But you, for your part, must not write down a single verse until you have fully understood its meaning. You must comprehend each line, wholly, in your own intellect, before your pen sets it down. And Ganapati, delighted by the cleverness of it, agreed. And so the great work began. Vyāsa sang, and Ganapati wrote, the words flowing between them in an unbroken stream. And whenever Vyāsa needed a moment to compose what came next, he would sing a verse of such difficulty, so knotted and dense and deep in its meaning, that even Ganapati had to stop and think to unravel it before he could write it down; and in the small space of that pause, while the god untangled the hard verse, the sage composed in his mind the verses that were to follow, so that when Ganapati was ready again, Vyāsa was ready too, and the stream never broke.
There is a quiet wisdom folded into this contest of conditions, and it is worth carrying with us into the long story ahead. Consider what Vyāsa's condition truly asked. He did not merely wish to buy himself time; he insisted that the scribe understand every word before writing it, that nothing be set down that was not first comprehended. And is this not the very thing we so often fail to do? We act swiftly, we speak swiftly, we rush from one thing to the next, and how much of it do we truly understand as we do it? Ganapati's swiftness, unchecked, would have written down words without grasping them; Vyāsa's condition forced understanding to keep pace with action, comprehension to walk beside the deed. And that is the marriage the story recommends to us at its very outset: that action without understanding is hollow, that to do a thing swiftly and not to grasp it is no true accomplishment, and that the highest work is done only when the hand and the mind move together, when what we do is lit, at every step, by our understanding of why we do it.
So the Mahābhārata was written, the sage singing and the god comprehending, and it came into the world; and it is that story, conceived by Vyāsa and understood by Ganapati, that we now take up.

title: The Cosmic Origin of the Lunar Dynasty
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Cosmic Origin of the Lunar Dynasty

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The great kings who would one day face each other across the terrible field of Kurukshetra were not men of some ordinary house. They came of an ancient and a sacred line, the Chandravamsha, the Lunar Dynasty, which traced its descent all the way back to Chandra, the god of the moon himself; and there is meaning in that descent, and it is worth pausing on before we follow the line down through the generations.
For there are two great royal lines in the old stories, and they are set against each other like the sun and the moon. There is the Sūryavamsha, the Solar Dynasty, the line of Rāma, and it is like the sun: blazing, steady, unyielding, the line of absolute discipline and public duty, of the dharma that holds firm whatever it costs. And there is the Chandravamsha, the Lunar Dynasty, the line we now follow, and it is like the moon: cool, reflective, changeable, shadowed, the line of deep emotion and deep desire and the tangled struggles of the human heart. If the story of Rāma is a story of duty held fast against every sorrow, the story of the Chandravamsha is a story of the human soul in all its complexity, its passions and its errors and its long slow learning, and the difference is written into the very lineages from which the two epics spring.
From Chandra came Budha, the lord of intellect, who wedded Ilā; and from that union was born Purūravas, the first mortal king of the line. Purūravas was a ruler of great brilliance, honoured by gods and men alike, and it was he who first gave the dynasty its earthly root, coming down into the fertile plains of the north, into the good land that lies between the sacred rivers Gangā and Yamunā, and founding there the ancient capital that would become the seat of the Kuru power, the city of Hastināpura.
And from Purūravas the line came down, generation upon generation: Āyus, and then Nahusha, and then Yayāti, and Kuru, and at last Shantanu, each a king in his turn, and through them all the city of Hastināpura grew from a royal settlement into a great and glorious metropolis, famed for its wealth and its learning and its devotion to dharma. The kings of the Lunar Line ruled, at their best, with a deep understanding of the sacred purpose of a kingdom, holding that the state was not merely an engine of power but a field consecrated to a higher end, a ground upon which the human soul might grow toward the divine, and they built their cities to mirror that order, with broad streets and great temples and halls where the wise debated the deepest questions of the spirit.
And yet, and here is the shadow that lies over the whole line and the whole story we are about to tell, the very richness of the Chandravamsha, its depth of feeling and of desire, was also its danger. For a heart capable of great love is capable also of great longing, and a soul of deep passion is a soul easily pulled by passion into error; and the kings of the Lunar Line carried in their very blood, along with their brilliance and their virtue, a susceptibility to the pull of desire, to the tangling of the heart, that would work itself out, across the generations, in a long chain of passions and curses and tragic choices, until it came at last to its terrible harvest on the field of Kurukshetra. The seeds of both the highest virtue and the deepest ruin lay together in that blood, waiting for the turning of the generations to bring them to their fruit; and the story of the Mahābhārata is, in large part, the story of that ripening.

title: The Ascent and Fall of Nahusha
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Ascent and Fall of Nahusha

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Among the early kings of the Lunar Line was Nahusha, the son of Āyus, and his story is the first of the line's great cautionary tales, a story of a good and righteous man raised to the very throne of heaven and destroyed there by the one enemy that greatness cannot outrun: his own pride.
For Nahusha began as one of the best of kings. He ruled his earthly realm with perfect justice, honoured the gods and his ancestors, performed the sacred rites, followed the scriptures in all things, and through this long discipline of righteousness he built up an immense store of spiritual merit, a punya so great that his own radiance came to rival that of the gods themselves. He was, by every measure, a king deserving of honour.
And it happened, in those days, that the throne of heaven fell empty. For Indra, the king of the gods, had committed a grave sin, the slaying of an enemy by deceit, and to expiate it he had fled his own heaven and hidden himself away, shrinking to the size of an atom and concealing himself within the fibre of a lotus stem in a far northern lake, leaving heaven leaderless and open to its enemies. And the gods and sages, needing a king to hold the celestial throne until Indra should return, searched all the worlds for a mortal of merit great enough to bear that terrible honour, and their eyes fell upon Nahusha, and they raised him up, with great ceremony, to sit upon the throne of heaven and rule the three worlds as Indra in Indra's absence.
And here begins the fall, and it is worth watching closely, for it is one of the oldest and truest patterns of the human soul. For a while, Nahusha ruled heaven well, upheld by the merit he had earned on earth. But sudden and absolute power, poured all at once upon a soul unprepared for it, is among the most dangerous of all spiritual tests, and it is a test that Nahusha failed. Surrounded by the intoxicating pleasures of heaven, lifted to a height beyond any mortal's due, Nahusha began to change. His humility, which had been the root of all his virtue, withered. He forgot the teachings that had raised him. And in their place there grew the thing that destroys the great more surely than any enemy: ahankāra, the swelling of the ego, the intoxication of pride, the poisonous belief that because he had been given power he was therefore owed all that power could seize.
And his pride found its object, as pride so often does, in desire. Walking one day in the gardens of heaven, Nahusha saw Sachī, the wife of the fugitive Indra, and was seized on the instant by a lawless lust for her; and armed now with the arrogance of his stolen office, he did not master the desire but commanded its satisfaction. Why has Indra's wife not come to me, he demanded of the gods; am I not king of heaven now? Send her to my chambers. He would take the wife of the very king whose throne he only borrowed, and he saw in it no wrong, for pride had convinced him that his power made all things his.
Sachī, terrified, fled to the protection of Brihaspati, the preceptor of the gods, who sheltered her; and when the gods and sages came to Nahusha and begged him to master his desire and honour the sacred law of marriage, the infatuated king only mocked them, and pressed his demand the harder. And so Sachī, counselled by the wise Brihaspati, resorted to a stratagem to trap the proud king in his own arrogance. She came to Nahusha and said: I will accept you, Lord; but first you must come to me in greater state than any god before you. Let your palanquin be borne to me upon the shoulders of the seven great sages themselves, the Saptarishi, the masters of the Vedas; carry yourself so, and I am yours.
And Nahusha, so blinded by lust and arrogance that he saw nothing wrong in yoking the holiest sages of the cosmos to his palanquin like beasts of burden, agreed. He summoned the seven great sages, and among them the mighty Agastya, and set them beneath his palanquin, and made them carry him. The three worlds looked on aghast at the sacrilege. And as the sages bore him, slowly, with the gravity of their holiness, toward the waiting Sachī, Nahusha, inflamed and impatient, grew angry at their slow pace, and began to goad them to go faster; and at last, in a moment of utter and crowning madness, he kicked the sage Agastya upon the head with his foot, crying "Sarpa! Sarpa!", which is to say, move faster, move like a snake.
And the word he chose became his doom. For the wrath of a great sage is more terrible than any weapon, and Agastya, his head kicked, his holiness desecrated, turned upon the fallen king with blazing eyes and pronounced a curse that fitted the crime with a terrible justice. Since you have kicked a sage and defiled the sacred order, the sage declared, and since you have called us snakes, become a snake; fall from this heaven you have disgraced, and live as a python in the dust of the earth. And on the instant Nahusha's celestial form withered, all his hard-won merit evaporated in a breath, and he fell headlong from heaven down through the clouds to the earth, to live as a serpent in the forest dust, condemned to crawl there for uncounted ages until, long afterward, the wisdom of a distant descendant should at last release him.
Let us take from Nahusha the lesson his fall was meant to teach, for it is one the whole Lunar Line, and the whole human race, needs to learn and relearn. Here was a man who had earned heaven by a lifetime of genuine righteousness, whose merit was real, whose discipline was real, and all of it was undone, in a breath, by pride. Not by an enemy, not by misfortune, but by the swelling of his own ego once power was given him. No store of merit, no height of learning, no accumulation of good deeds, can save a soul that has surrendered to pride, for pride corrodes the very virtue that raised it, and turns the righteous man into the tyrant, and casts down from heaven, in a single mad moment, the one who spent a lifetime climbing there. The higher we are raised, the more deadly the fall that pride prepares for us; and the only safety is the humility that Nahusha lost, the remembering, at every height, that what we have been given is not owed to us, and can be taken back.

title: Kacha's Devotion and the Curse of Sanjīvinī
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: Kacha's Devotion and the Curse of Sanjīvinī

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
In the ancient days there was an unending war between the gods and the demons, the Devas and the Asuras, for the lordship of the three worlds, and in that long war the demons held one terrible advantage, and the story of how the gods overcame it is a story of devotion, of cunning, and of a curse born from a rejected love.
The advantage was this. Each side had its great preceptor, its spiritual master: Brihaspati guided the gods, and Shukrāchārya guided the demons. But Shukrāchārya alone, of all the beings in the three worlds, knew the secret of Sanjīvinī, a sacred mantra that could call the dead back to life. And so, in the war, whenever a demon warrior fell, Shukrāchārya raised him up again to fight, while the slain gods stayed dead; and no army can win against a foe whose dead will not stay dead. The gods were losing, and losing not for want of courage but for want of that one secret, and they saw that unless they could learn it, the demons would grind them down in the end.
So the gods went to Kacha, the noble son of their own preceptor Brihaspati, and laid before him a hard and dangerous mission. Go to Shukrāchārya, they begged him; become his student; win his trust; and by some means learn from him the secret of Sanjīvinī, so that we too may raise our dead and match the demons. It was a perilous errand, for it meant living among the enemy, in the demon capital, in the very house of the demons' master; but Kacha understood that his duty to the common good outweighed his own safety, and he accepted.
He went to Shukrāchārya and asked, with all humility, to be received as a student, naming his noble lineage; and by the sacred law of the sages, a worthy student who comes seeking knowledge cannot be turned away, and Shukrāchārya, pleased with the young man's bearing and his descent, took him in. And Kacha served him for years, faithfully, flawlessly, the perfect student. Now Shukrāchārya had a daughter, Devayānī, spirited and lovely, whom he cherished; and Kacha, part by design and part by the natural sweetness of his nature, devoted himself to pleasing her, with song and dance and gentle companionship, and won her deep affection, all the while keeping strictly his vows of chastity.
But the demons were not fools, and they grew suspicious. They guessed why Kacha had truly come, that he meant to carry off the secret of Sanjīvinī to the enemy, and they resolved to kill him before he could succeed. And here begins the strange and terrible sequence at the heart of the tale. One day, while Kacha was out grazing his master's cattle, the demons fell upon him, killed him, tore his body to pieces, and fed the pieces to wild dogs. When the cattle came home without him, Devayānī was frantic, and ran to her father weeping that Kacha had not returned and that she could not live without him. And Shukrāchārya, unable to bear his daughter's grief, used the Sanjīvinī art and called Kacha back, and the young man's scattered body reassembled and he returned, alive, smiling, telling how the demons had killed him though he knew not how he had been restored. So the demons killed him a second time, and this time ground his body to paste and mixed it into the sea; and again Devayānī wept, and again Shukrāchārya raised him. And then the demons devised a cleverer murder. They killed Kacha a third time, burned his body to ashes, and mixed the ashes secretly into the wine that Shukrāchārya loved to drink, so that the master himself unknowingly swallowed his own student. And when Kacha did not return, Devayānī, in despair, declared that she would fast to death and follow him into the fire.
Once more, to comfort his daughter, Shukrāchārya used the Sanjīvinī art and called Kacha to appear; and to his astonishment, he heard the young man's voice answering from within his own belly. Kacha explained: that he had been burned, his ashes mixed in the wine, and that he was now trapped inside his master's body. And here Shukrāchārya faced a dreadful dilemma, and it is the pivot of the story. For Kacha to live, he must tear his way out of Shukrāchārya's stomach; but that would kill Shukrāchārya. The student's life could be bought only with the master's death.
And Shukrāchārya found a solution worthy of his wisdom, and it turned upon the very secret at the heart of the whole tale. He spoke to Kacha within him: You have won your goal, son of Brihaspati; I will teach you the Sanjīvinī mantra now, this moment, while you are inside me. Then, when you tear your way out and I fall dead, you must at once use the mantra to raise me, so that my daughter need grieve for neither of us. And so, from inside his own body, the master taught the student the very secret the student had come to steal; and Kacha, having learned it, tore his way out of Shukrāchārya, emerging like the full moon from a dark cloud, while the great preceptor fell dead upon the grass; and Kacha at once chanted the mantra he had just been given, and Shukrāchārya rose, alive and whole. The student had won the secret; the master had been raised by his own art in the hands of another; and the demons' cruel murders had, in the end, only served to place the secret exactly where they most feared it would go.
Shukrāchārya, sobered by the deceit that had been worked through his own cup of wine, made from it a solemn warning for all people ever after: that virtue deserts the man who, through folly, drinks wine and loses his wits, and that such a one becomes an object of scorn; let this, he said, be held as a binding rule. So even the master's humiliation was turned to a teaching.
Kacha stayed on to finish his studies, and when at last his term was complete and he prepared to return to the world of the gods, Devayānī came to him and spoke, with the frank dignity of a noble woman, what was in her heart. You have won my love, she told him; I have loved you long; now marry me and make me happy. And here Kacha had to refuse her, and his refusal, gentle but firm, was rooted in dharma, and it cost him dearly. You are my master's daughter, he told her, ever worthy of my reverence. And more than that: because I was, in a manner, born again out of your father's body, you are as a sister to me, and a brother may not wed his sister. It would be against all law. Forgive me, and let me go.
And Devayānī, wounded in her love and her pride together, answered his refusal with a curse: that the Sanjīvinī mantra he had won from her father should prove fruitless to him in his own hour of need. And Kacha accepted the curse calmly, and answered it with the deepest thing in him. I accept your curse, Devayānī, he said. Though I myself may never use this knowledge, I will teach it to others, and they shall conquer death; the knowledge will not be lost, only my own use of it. For I am bound to the path of dharma, which is greater than my own life and greater than my own gain. And with those words he departed for the heavens, leaving behind him a curse he had accepted without bitterness and a devotion to duty that outweighed even the power over death itself.
There is a lesson in Kacha to carry forward, and it is a quiet one. He had gained the power over death, the very thing he had risked everything to win; and he gave it away, freely, to others, keeping none of its use for himself, because a curse had bound it and because dharma mattered to him more than his own advantage. That is the mark of the truly noble soul, that it holds even its greatest prize with an open hand, and would rather serve the good with a gift it cannot use itself than betray the good to keep the gift. Kacha lost the use of his hard-won knowledge and did not count it a loss, because he had never sought it for himself.

title: The Marriage of Devayānī
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The story of Devayānī does not end with Kacha's departure, for her pride, which we glimpsed in her love, was about to draw her into a quarrel that would reshape the whole line, and the quarrel began, as such things often do, over a small thing: a tangle of clothes by a forest pool.
One warm afternoon Devayānī went to bathe in a woodland pool, and with her went Sharmishṭhā, the daughter of Vrishaparvā, the king of the demons, a princess of royal blood. They left their garments and their garlands on the grassy bank and went into the water; and while they bathed, a sudden wind blew through the forest and tumbled their clothes together into a heap. Coming out in haste, Sharmishṭhā by accident put on Devayānī's garment; and Devayānī, vexed, spoke sharply, half in jest and half in earnest, reminding the princess that it was improper for a disciple's daughter to wear the clothes of the master's daughter, and that the king's house owed its spiritual guidance to her father.
It was a small remark, but it struck the princess's pride, and Sharmishṭhā answered with venom. Your father, she retorted, is only a beggar who stands at our gates singing for his bread; my father is the king, and it is his charity that feeds you; how dare you speak to me of equality? And in her fury she struck Devayānī, and pushed her into a dry, overgrown well, and left her there, believing she would die in the wilderness, and went home.
But Devayānī did not die, for it happened that the emperor Yayāti, hunting in that forest and grown thirsty, came to the well in search of water and heard, instead of water, the cries of a woman. Looking down, he saw the beautiful Devayānī, and she reached up her right hand, and he took it and drew her up out of the well. And when she stood on dry ground, Devayānī spoke to him in a way that bound him: You have taken a maiden by her right hand, she said, and by the sacred law you must now accept me as your wife. But Yayāti drew back, for there was a difficulty of dharma. I am a kshatriya, a man of the warrior caste, he told her, and you are a brāhmaṇa maiden, of the priestly caste; and the law forbids such a union, where the woman is of the higher caste and the man of the lower, for the sake of the purity of the lineage. Return home, and let us both obey the scriptures. And with that the king departed.
Devayānī, however, would not return to the demon capital where she had been so insulted, and she sent word to her father; and Shukrāchārya came and found her weeping beneath a tree, and heard the story of Sharmishṭhā's insults. And the proud preceptor lifted his daughter up with words meant to console her, and they are worth hearing, for through them the sage Vyāsa gives counsel to all of us. You are not the daughter of a beggar, Shukrāchārya told her; your father does not live by flattery; you are the child of one whom the whole world reveres, whose spiritual power upholds this very kingdom. But mark this: no worthy man boasts of his own merits. Be patient. And then he spoke the deeper teaching, on the mastery of anger, which the story sets down as wisdom for the ages.
