He conquers the world, he said, who patiently endures the abuse of his neighbours. He who reins in his rising anger, as a skilled horseman masters an unruly horse, is the true charioteer, not the one who merely holds the reins while the horse runs where it will. He who sheds his anger as a snake sheds its old skin is a true hero. The man who never yields to anger is greater than the one who performs a hundred years of sacrifices. For anger drives away everything a man holds dear: his friends, his family, his wife and children, his virtue, and his truth.
It is among the finest passages of counsel in the whole epic, and we should let it sink in, for anger is the commonest and the most destructive of our failings, and the mastery of it is set here above even a lifetime of ritual devotion. The man who cannot be angered has a strength that no ceremony can give.
Devayānī heard her father's teaching with respect, and yet she answered it with a truth of her own, and her answer too has its wisdom. I understand the greatness of forbearance, father, she said; yet it is not right to go on living among people who have no decency, who insult one's family; the wise do not keep company with the ill-mannered. And she added a thing that is painfully true: that wounds made by weapons heal in time, but wounds made by words stay painful as long as one lives. My mind is still ablaze with what Sharmishṭhā said; I cannot go back to a place where I am so insulted. And in this she and her father were both right, each holding a piece of the truth: he, that anger must be mastered; she, that one need not remain where one is degraded. Wisdom is not always all on one side.
Shukrāchārya then went to King Vrishaparvā, and his word carried the weight of the kingdom's very survival, for without his spiritual power the demon realm was defenceless against the gods. He named the wrongs: the repeated murder of his disciple Kacha, which he had borne; and now the insult to his daughter and her casting into the well. My daughter cannot stay in your kingdom, he said, and without her I cannot stay either; I am leaving. And the king, knowing that his kingdom's whole defence would crumble if the preceptor left, threw himself at Shukrāchārya's feet and cried that if the sage abandoned them he would enter the fire and die.
I care more for my daughter's happiness than for your whole realm, Shukrāchārya answered; appease her, and I stay; otherwise I go. So the king and his ministers hurried to the forest and prostrated themselves before Devayānī, begging her to be reconciled. And Devayānī, still proud, named her price: that Sharmishṭhā, who had called her a beggar's daughter, should become her handmaiden, and attend upon her in the house of whatever husband her father should choose for her. It was a hard demand, that a king's daughter should become a servant; and yet Sharmishṭhā, when it was put to her, showed a nobility that rose above her earlier pride, and accepted it, for her father's sake and her kingdom's. Let it be as Devayānī wishes, she said; my father shall not lose his preceptor for a fault of mine; I will be her attendant. And so, at the cost of a princess's freedom, the quarrel was patched, and they returned to the capital, carrying with them, all unknowing, the seed of the next generation's sorrows.

title: Yayāti's Realisation
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
In time Devayānī married the emperor Yayāti, for Shukrāchārya gave his special sanction and so set aside the scriptural bar to their union; and Sharmishṭhā, as the price of the reconciliation, came with her to Yayāti's palace as her handmaiden. And here the seed that had been planted by the forest pool grew into a bitter fruit.
For Sharmishṭhā, though now a servant, was a princess of royal blood, and one day she met Yayāti in secret and pleaded with him to take her also as his wife, arguing that she too was worthy of his love. And Yayāti yielded, and married her secretly, without Devayānī's knowledge, and she bore him children. And when Devayānī at last discovered the secret marriage and saw the children, she was consumed with fury and went to her father; and Shukrāchārya, enraged that his daughter should be so wronged, cursed Yayāti on the spot with instant old age, so that the emperor, in the very prime of his manhood, was transformed in a moment into a decrepit, wrinkled old man.
Yayāti was devastated, and begged the sage for mercy, pleading that his desires were still unfulfilled, that he was not ready to be old. And Shukrāchārya relented a little, for the curse could not be recalled, but it could be shifted. If you can persuade one of your sons, the sage told him, to take on your old age and give you his youth in exchange, then the exchange will hold, and you shall have your strength again. So Yayāti went to his sons.
He called his five sons and appealed to their love, begging one of them to bear his old age and lend him their youth. And here the story tests each of them, and four of them fail the test. The eldest refused: the women and servants will mock me, he said, if I take on an old man's decrepitude; I cannot. The second refused: old age destroys not only strength and beauty but wisdom too; I am not strong enough to bear it. The third and fourth also refused, shrinking from the pitiable state of an old man who cannot even keep his own body clean. Each had his reason, and each reason was the reason of self, of a young man unwilling to give up his own youth even for his father's sake.
But there was a fifth son, the youngest, Pūru; and Pūru did not refuse. He knelt before his father and spoke the words that set him apart. Father, what is this body of mine compared to your happiness? I gladly take your old age and give you my youth; let your desire be satisfied. And the moment Yayāti touched him, the exchange was made: the father was restored to the glory of youth, and the young Pūru was turned into a wrinkled, frail old man, who nonetheless ruled in his father's stead with wisdom and care.
And now Yayāti, young again, went out to do the thing the whole exchange had been for: to satisfy his desire at last. And here the story delivers its great teaching, and it is one of the deepest in the whole book, so let us follow it closely. For a thousand years Yayāti enjoyed the pleasures of the world. He roamed the earth; he gathered untold riches; he spent long years even in the pleasure-gardens of the gods, in the company of celestial nymphs; he denied himself nothing, and pursued every delight without limit for ten centuries. And at the end of it, his desire was not satisfied. It was not even lessened. Every pleasure he seized had left him hungrier than before, for that is the nature of desire fed by indulgence: it does not cool, but burns hotter, as a fire flares higher the more you pour upon it.
Have you noticed this in your own small wantings? That the having of a thing we craved so rarely quiets the craving, but only teaches it a new shape to want in? Yayāti learned it on the grandest scale a soul has ever learned it: a thousand years of unlimited indulgence, and desire at the end of it as fierce as at the beginning, and himself no nearer peace than when he started. And at last, worn out with the endless futile chase, the great truth broke upon him, and he understood.
He went back to his son Pūru, and bowed before him, and made the declaration that is the crown of his whole story. Dear son, he said, sensual desire is never quenched by indulgence, any more than a fire is put out by pouring butter upon it. I had heard this said, and read it in the scriptures, but only now, after a thousand years of chasing, have I learned it in my own life. There is no object of desire on this earth, no gold, no wealth, no pleasure, no beauty, that can ever satisfy the endless hunger of the human mind. Peace comes only when the mind grows still, when it rises beyond its likes and its dislikes, and rests in the silent contemplation of the eternal. Take back your youth, my noble son, and rule the kingdom well.
And Pūru received his youth again, and was crowned emperor of Hastināpura; and Yayāti, having learned at last the lesson of his whole long life, retired to the forest to spend his remaining days in meditation and detachment, and in the end attained liberation, mokṣha, the freedom he had never found in a thousand years of pleasure.
This is the great threshold of the Lunar Line, and the story sets it here at the beginning as a warning over the whole tale to come. For the Chandravamsha was a line of deep desire, and here, in Yayāti, that desire is followed to its very end and shown for what it is: a fire that indulgence only feeds, a hunger that no having can fill. All the sorrows that are coming in this long story, the passions and the graspings and the ruinous choices of the generations, are in some sense the working-out of the truth that Yayāti learned and that his descendants would have to learn again, each in their turn, the hard way: that worldly conquest is hollow if it is not joined to the conquest of oneself, and that the only desire that can ever be satisfied is the desire that has learned, at last, to be still.

title: Shantanu and Gangā
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
King Shantanu was a mighty and righteous king of the Lunar Line, ruling Hastināpura in devotion to dharma; and it was to him that there came, one day on the banks of the river Gangā, a love that was also a mystery, and that would give the dynasty its greatest son.
Walking by the river, Shantanu saw a maiden of such loveliness that his senses were overwhelmed, a beauty beyond anything of this world; and drawn irresistibly, he asked her to be his wife. And she accepted, but she bound her acceptance with a strict and binding condition. I will be your wife, she told him, but only on these terms: that you never ask me who I am or where I come from; that you never stand in the way of anything I do, whether it seems to you good or evil; that you never grow angry with me for any cause, and never say to me a single word that displeases me. Break any of these, and I will leave you on the instant. Do you agree? And Shantanu, mastered by his passion, agreed to all of it, and they were married.
And then came the horror. Within a few months Gangā bore a beautiful son, and the moment he was born she carried him to the river and drowned him. Shantanu, devastated, could not say a word, for his promise bound him. And this happened again, and again: one after another she bore seven sons, and one after another, with the same cold, unyielding silence, she drowned all seven in the river. And through it all Shantanu held his tongue, tormented, grieving, but bound by the vow he had made in his passion, watching his children die and unable even to ask why.
But when the eighth child was born, and Gangā moved once more toward the river to drown him, Shantanu could bear it no longer. He broke. He confronted her, crying that he had endured the drowning of seven sons in silence but would endure it no more, and he pleaded for the life of the eighth. And Gangā, at his broken silence, smiled sadly, and revealed at last who she was and what she had been doing.
She was the goddess Gangā herself. And these eight children were the eight Vasus, celestial beings, who had been cursed by the sage Vasishṭha to be born as mortal men, a punishment for the theft of the sage's sacred cow by one of their number, Prabhāsa, the eighth. And her drownings, which had looked like monstrous cruelty, had in truth been mercy: for by drowning each of the first seven the instant he was born, she had freed him at once from the curse of a mortal life, releasing him back to his celestial nature. Only the eighth, Prabhāsa, who had been the instigator of the theft, was fated to live out a long life in the mortal world. And since Shantanu had broken his vow and questioned her, she would keep her word and leave him; but she would take the eighth child with her, to raise him and train him for the great destiny that awaited him.
We should pause on this strange and terrible tale, for it teaches something hard about the difference between how a thing looks and what it is. To Shantanu, watching, Gangā's acts were pure horror, a mother murdering her own children one by one. And they were, in truth, acts of deliverance, each drowning a release from a curse, each death a mercy. He could not see it, because he did not know what she knew; he saw only the surface, the drowning, and it broke his heart. And so it often is with the workings of a providence we cannot fully see: what looks to us like cruelty, like meaningless loss, may be, in a design we cannot grasp, a mercy and a release. This is not to say our griefs are not real; Shantanu's grief was real, and his breaking was human and forgivable. But the story sets beside his limited sight the larger truth he could not see, and asks us to consider that the losses that break our hearts may have a meaning hidden from us, as the drownings had a meaning hidden from Shantanu.
Gangā raised the eighth child to youth, and gave him the finest of all educations: the Vedas and Vedānta from Vasishṭha himself, the arts and sciences from Shukrāchārya, and the supreme mastery of arms from the great Parashurāma. This child was Devavrata; and when his training was complete, Gangā brought the resplendent prince back to his father Shantanu, and placed him in his care, and vanished once more. The son of the river had come home, and he would become the greatest and the most tragic figure of his age.

title: Satyavatī
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The next thread of the story begins in mystery, with a fish drawn from the Yamunā, and it leads to the birth of the very sage who would one day compose this whole epic.
In the kingdom of Uparichara, a fisherman caught a great fish in the Yamunā, and when it was cut open, there were found inside it twin children, a boy and a girl. They were brought to the king, who kept the boy to raise in his own household, and this boy grew up to found the kingdom of Matsya, which means fish. The girl, who carried about her the smell of fish, was given to the chief of the fishermen to be raised, and she was named Satyavatī. And as a young woman she helped her foster-father by working the ferry across the Yamunā.
One day the great sage Parāshara wished to cross the river, and Satyavatī ferried him; and midway across, the sage was seized with a sudden longing for the beautiful girl, and made his desire known. And Satyavatī was both flattered and afraid, and raised her objections: the smell of fish that clung to her, her unwed state, the open daylight in which the sages on the banks might see them. And Parāshara, by his yogic power, answered each: he wrapped the boat in a dense mist that hid them from all eyes; and he granted her two boons, that her virginity would be restored after their union, and that the fishy odour that had marked her all her life would be replaced by a divine fragrance that would carry for miles through the forest.
From this union, upon a misty island in the Yamunā, Satyavatī bore a child; and this child was Vyāsa, the great compiler of the Vedas and the author of the Mahābhārata, the very sage whose story we followed at the opening of this book. And Vyāsa, born already destined for greatness, grew at once to maturity, bowed to his mother, and departed to his life of penance, but he left her with a solemn promise: that whenever she should call upon him in difficulty or need, he would return to help her. Remember that promise; the story will call it in.
Years passed, and King Shantanu, who had kept his senses under strict discipline since Gangā left him, was one day wandering on the banks of the Yamunā, when the air was suddenly filled with a fragrance so divinely sweet that he sought its source; and he traced it to Satyavatī, whose divine perfume, the sage's boon, now pervaded the whole forest. And the sight of this beautiful maiden burst the bonds of the king's long restraint, and he was filled with an overmastering desire to make her his wife. And so the two great threads, the widowed king and the fragrant ferry-girl who had already borne the author of the epic, were drawn toward one another, and toward the fateful bargain that their marriage would require.

title: Bhīshma's Terrible Vow
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
When Shantanu went to the chief of the fishermen to ask for Satyavatī's hand, the shrewd old chief named a heavy condition. The child born of Satyavatī, he said, must be the one to be crowned king after you. And at this Shantanu, mad with desire as he was, could not agree; for it would mean setting aside his eldest son, the godlike Devavrata, the rightful heir, the greatest young prince of the age. And so the king, unable to make such a promise and unable to master his longing, returned to Hastināpura in silence, and there he pined, sick with a desire he would not name, wasting away with a secret sorrow.
His son Devavrata saw his father's decline, and could not understand it, and came to him and asked: Father, you have everything a heart could wish; why are you so unhappy, like a man pining with some secret grief? And Shantanu, ashamed to confess a lustful longing, would not tell him the truth, but spoke vaguely of anxiety for the family's future, saying that Devavrata was his only son and life uncertain. But Devavrata was not satisfied, and determined to find the true cause, and he questioned his father's charioteer, and so learned the whole matter: the fisher-chief, Satyavatī, the condition about the throne.
And then Devavrata did a thing that would define his whole life, and give him his name. He went himself, with a delegation of elders, to the chief of the fishermen, and there, before them all, he made his first great renunciation. I give you my word, he declared, that the son born of Satyavatī shall be king; and I renounce, in his favour, my own right as heir to the throne. He gave up the kingdom, freely, for his father's happiness.
But the fisher-chief, cunning still, raised a further objection, and it was a shrewd one. I do not doubt that you will keep your word, best of the Bharata race, he said; but how can I be sure of your children? Your sons will be mighty heroes like yourself, and if they should one day seek to seize the throne by force from Satyavatī's line, who could resist them? That is the doubt that torments me. And to answer this doubt, Devavrata took his second vow, and it was the terrible one, the one that would cost him everything a man can lose. Raising his arm to the heavens, he declared: Then I shall never marry. I dedicate myself to a life of unbroken chastity, and I shall have no children who could ever claim the throne.
It was a vow of absolute and total renunciation, the giving-up not only of a kingdom but of marriage, of children, of a whole ordinary human life, all for his father's passing desire; and as he spoke it, the gods themselves showered flowers upon his head, and from the heavens came the cry, Bhīshma! Bhīshma!, which means, the one who takes a terrible vow and keeps it. And from that day Devavrata was called Bhīshma, and he escorted Satyavatī to his father, and she was married to Shantanu, and the price of the marriage was paid, in full, by the son who had everything and gave it all away. Let us not pass too quickly over the enormity of what Bhīshma did, for the story means us to feel it, and to feel too the shadow that lies over it. Here was the greatest prince of his age, the rightful heir, godlike in his gifts, and he renounced his throne, his marriage, his children, his whole future, in a single afternoon, for no fault of his own, to satisfy an old man's infatuation. There is a terrible grandeur in it, the grandeur of a total sacrifice freely made out of love for a father. And yet the story does not present it as simply admirable, for we will see, across the long tragedy to come, that Bhīshma's vow, magnificent as it was, bound him also to terrible things: it chained him to the throne of Hastināpura through all its later corruption, made him the servant of whoever held that throne, and set him at last, this best of men, on the wrong side of the great war, fighting for a cause he knew to be unjust, because his vow bound him to it. A sacrifice can be noble and can also be a chain; a vow can be heroic and can also imprison; and Bhīshma's terrible vow, which made him the wonder of the gods, made him also the prisoner of a lifetime, and that is a truth about renunciation that the story will unfold, slowly and sorrowfully, all the way to Kurukshetra.

title: Ambā's Retribution
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Satyavatī bore Shantanu two sons, Chitrāngada and Vichitravīrya. The elder, Chitrāngada, a proud and powerful warrior, was killed in a long combat with a Gandharva; and so the younger, Vichitravīrya, still only a youth, came to the throne. And when the time came for Vichitravīrya to marry, Bhīshma, acting as ever for the house he had bound himself to serve, heard of the svayamvara, the bride-choosing, of the three princesses of Kāshī: Ambā, Ambikā, and Ambālikā. And Bhīshma went to Kāshī, challenged all the assembled princes, defeated them, and carried the three sisters away in his chariot to Hastināpura, to be wed to Vichitravīrya. And from this forceful carrying-off came a tragedy, and a hatred that would reach all the way to the great war.
For the eldest sister, Ambā, had already given her heart to another: to King Sālva, whom she loved, and who she had hoped would win her at the svayamvara. And as they journeyed, Sālva had opposed Bhīshma to try to reclaim her, and Bhīshma had defeated him but spared his life. And now, arriving at Hastināpura, as the wedding was being prepared, Ambā came to Bhīshma and told him the truth: that she had already chosen Sālva in her heart, that Bhīshma had carried her off by force in ignorance of this, and that he should now do what was righteous. And Bhīshma, acknowledging the justice of her plea, sent her with an honourable escort back to Sālva.
But Sālva rejected her. Bhīshma defeated me before all and carried you away, he said; I have been disgraced; I cannot now take you as my wife; go back to him. And so Ambā, sent back to Hastināpura, found that Vichitravīrya too would not have her, for her heart had been given to another; and she was refused by both, wanted by neither, ruined, as she saw it, through no fault of her own. And her grief hardened into a burning hatred, and she fixed upon the one she held responsible for her whole ruin: Bhīshma, who had carried her off in the first place and set the whole disaster in motion.
She sought vengeance. She went first to Parashurāma, Bhīshma's own teacher, and moved by her anguish he took up her cause and fought Bhīshma, his own pupil, in a long and terrible combat; but the two were so equally matched that in the end even Parashurāma had to acknowledge that he could not defeat Bhīshma, and he advised Ambā to give up and throw herself on Bhīshma's mercy. But Ambā would not. Her hatred had become the whole purpose of her existence, and she retired to the forest and undertook the most extreme austerities to win a boon from Lord Shiva, that she might herself become the instrument of Bhīshma's death. And Shiva granted it, giving her a garland of ever-fresh lotuses, and promising that whoever wore that garland would be the cause of Bhīshma's fall. She hung the garland on the palace gate of King Drupada, and then, unwilling to wait a whole lifetime, she threw herself into a sacrificial fire, and was reborn as Drupada's child, Shikhaṇḍī, who would in time become a warrior and stand, at Kurukshetra, as the shield behind which Arjuna would at last bring down the mighty Bhīshma.
There is a sobering lesson threaded through Ambā's terrible story, and it is a warning about what a wholly justified grievance can become when it is nursed into hatred. Ambā was genuinely wronged; no one denies it; she was carried off, then rejected, then rejected again, her life ruined through the pride and the rigidity of men, and her anger was just. And yet she let that just anger consume her so entirely that it became the single purpose not only of her life but of her death and her very rebirth; she gave herself wholly, across the boundary of death itself, to the one aim of vengeance. And the story lets us feel both the justice of her wrong and the terrible waste of a soul poured out entirely into hatred, so that a woman who deserved our pity becomes, in the end, an instrument of destruction, her whole being narrowed to a single vengeful point. A wrong suffered is one thing; a life surrendered to avenging it is another; and Ambā's fate stands as a warning of what even a righteous grievance can make of us, if we let it become the whole of who we are.

title: The Law of karma and the Birth of Vidura
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Law of karma and the Birth of Vidura

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The world of Hastināpura was governed, beneath all its politics and its passions, by the deep and unyielding law of karma, that every action bears its fruit; and this law is shown plainly in the strange story of the sage Māṇḍavya and the birth of the wise Vidura.
Māṇḍavya was a sage of great spiritual power, won through long penance and the practice of truth, living in a forest hermitage. One day a band of robbers, fleeing the king's soldiers, hid their stolen goods in his ashram while the sage sat immersed in deep meditation, unaware. The soldiers, tracking the robbers, found the stolen goods there and arrested Māṇḍavya along with the thieves, taking him for their accomplice. And the king, without proper inquiry, sentenced them all to be impaled upon spears. And Māṇḍavya, though impaled, did not die, but survived upon the stake through his yogic power, chanting his sacred texts. When at last the king discovered his terrible error, he released the sage and begged his forgiveness.
But Māṇḍavya was not content merely to be released; he wanted to understand the justice of what had befallen him, and he went to Lord Dharma himself, the god of justice, and demanded an answer. Why was I subjected to this torture? he asked. What sin did I ever commit, to deserve impalement? And Lord Dharma replied: As a child, you tortured small birds and insects, piercing them with sharp blades of grass; and every action, however small, bears its fruit; this was the fruit of that. And Māṇḍavya was outraged at the answer, and it is worth understanding why, for his objection carries a real moral weight. A punishment so terrible, he said, for a thoughtless cruelty committed as a child, in ignorance, is far in excess of any justice. A child does not know; to visit so dreadful a penalty upon an act of childish ignorance is itself unjust. And in his anger he cursed Lord Dharma: for this injustice, you shall yourself be born as a mortal in the world, born of a low-caste servant.
Now this curse is the hinge of the story, for it explains the birth of one of the noblest figures of the epic. It happened that Vichitravīrya died young and childless, leaving the royal line of Hastināpura in danger of ending. And to preserve the line, Satyavatī called upon her firstborn son, the sage Vyāsa, keeping the promise he had made her long ago that he would come whenever she called; and she asked him to father children upon the widowed queens of Vichitravīrya, Ambikā and Ambālikā, by the ancient custom of niyoga. And here the fear of the queens shaped their children. Ambikā, frightened by the austere and terrifying appearance of the great sage, closed her eyes throughout their union; and so her son, Dhritarāshtra, was born blind. Ambālikā turned pale with fear; and so her son, Pāṇḍu, was born pale and sickly.
And when Satyavatī asked Vyāsa to come once more, to father a healthier heir, Ambikā, unwilling to face the sage again herself, secretly sent her humble servant-maid in her place. And the servant-maid, unlike the frightened queens, received the great sage with reverence and joy and calm; and from that union, free of fear, was born Vidura, who was the incarnation of Lord Dharma himself, come to be born of a low-caste servant exactly as Māṇḍavya's curse had decreed. And Vidura grew to be a man of unmatched wisdom and virtue and knowledge of the scriptures, the wise and righteous counsellor of Hastināpura, the one clear moral voice that would speak truth through all the long tragedy to come.
There is a beautiful justice folded into the manner of these three births, and it rewards a moment's thought. The two queens, born to their high station, met the sacred moment with fear, one shutting her eyes, one turning pale, and their fear marked their sons with blindness and sickness. But the humble servant-maid, of no rank at all, met the same moment with reverence and joy and an untroubled heart, and from her calm devotion was born the wisest and most righteous soul of the age, the very incarnation of dharma. The high-born, in their fear, bore the flawed; the low-born, in her devotion, bore the divine. And the story sets this before us quietly, as it set Shabari and the squirrel before us in the other epic: that it is not rank or birth that determines the worth of what we bring forth, but the spirit in which we meet the sacred; and that a servant's reverence may bring into the world a greater soul than a queen's frightened heart, for the divine attends not to our station but to the quality of our devotion.

title: Pāṇḍu and Dhritarāshtra
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Because Dhritarāshtra had been born blind, he was barred by the royal law from inheriting the crown, for a blind man could not perform all the duties of a king; and so it was the younger brother, Pāṇḍu, who ascended the throne of Hastināpura, while Dhritarāshtra remained in the palace, sightless, brooding, and nursing within him a deep and unspoken attachment to the power he had been denied and the world he could not see. That thwarted attachment, quiet now, would grow across the years into the fatal weakness of his later life: his inability to deny his sons anything, his blindness of heart to match the blindness of his eyes.
Pāṇḍu was a capable and victorious king, who extended the borders of the realm, and he married two wives, Kuntī and Mādrī. But his glorious reign was cut short by a single tragic error, and it was an error of exactly the careless kind that we saw destroy Dasharatha in the other epic. Hunting in the forest, Pāṇḍu shot a pair of deer as they mated, not knowing that they were in truth a sage, Kindama, and his wife, who had taken the form of deer. And the dying sage, in his agony, pronounced a curse upon the king: that if ever Pāṇḍu should seek intimacy with either of his wives, he would die on that very instant.
It was a curse that struck at the root of a king's life, for it denied him the children who must carry on his line. And Pāṇḍu, stricken with remorse for the careless killing and unable to bear the burden of kingship under such a shadow, abdicated his throne, and retired to the forest with his two wives to live in penance. In his absence, Dhritarāshtra was made caretaker king, ruling Hastināpura under the watchful guidance of Bhīshma and the wise Vidura. And in the forest, Pāṇḍu grieved over his childlessness, the curse that denied him heirs, until Kuntī revealed to him that she possessed a secret and a power that might yet give them sons: a divine mantra, granted to her long ago, whose story must now be told.

title: Kuntī
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Kuntī was born Prithā, a princess of the Yādava clan, daughter of Shūrasena and sister of Vāsudeva, who would be the father of Lord Krishna; so that Kuntī was Krishna's own aunt, a thread that binds her to the divine heart of the whole story. Because her father's cousin Kuntibhoja was childless, Prithā was given to him in adoption, and took from him the name Kuntī.
When she was still a girl, the formidable sage Durvāsā, famous for his terrible temper, stayed as a guest in Kuntibhoja's palace; and the young Kuntī served him with such unwavering patience, devotion, and care, never once giving him cause for his notorious anger, that the sage was deeply pleased, and granted her a divine boon: a mantra, by which, if she called upon any god, that god would appear to her and bless her with a son equal to himself in glory.
And here the young Kuntī made the error of the innocent and the impatient, and it would shadow her whole life. Out of simple girlish curiosity, wishing to see whether so wonderful a power could truly be real, she tested the mantra then and there. Looking up at the sky, she invoked Sūrya, the Sun God. And at once the heavens darkened, and Sūrya himself stood before her, radiant and undeniable. Terrified now of the scandal, Kuntī begged him to depart; but the mantra's power could not be recalled, and Sūrya, bound by it, blessed her with a child, though he restored her virginity afterward as the boon allowed.
So Kuntī, unmarried and afraid of public ruin, bore a son in secret; and he was a radiant child, born wearing golden armour and golden earrings, fused to his very body. And Kuntī, in her fear and her desperation, did a thing that would break her heart for the rest of her life: she placed the baby in a sealed basket and set it afloat upon the river, casting away her firstborn son to save herself from disgrace. The basket was found downstream by Adhiratha, a charioteer, who was childless; and he and his wife Rādhā raised the boy as their own, and named him Karṇa. And so Karṇa, born of the Sun and of a princess, was raised as the son of a charioteer, not knowing his true birth; and the secret of his origin, and Kuntī's abandonment of him, would become one of the deepest tragedies of the whole epic, for he would grow up to stand against his own unknown brothers, and Kuntī would carry, through all the years, the unbearable knowledge of the son she had cast away.
Later, in the proper course of her life, Kuntibhoja held a svayamvara for Kuntī, and there she placed the marriage garland upon King Pāṇḍu, and became his queen. But she carried her secret and her divine mantra with her; and now, in the forest, hearing her husband grieve over his childlessness under the sage's curse, she revealed to Pāṇḍu that she held the power to call down the gods themselves for sons, and so opened the way for the birth of the heroes who would be the heart of the story to come.

title: Gāndhāra's Relationship with Hastināpura
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
To strengthen the alliances of Hastināpura, Bhīshma arranged the marriage of the blind Dhritarāshtra to Gāndhārī, the princess of Gāndhāra; and Gāndhārī, when she learned that the husband chosen for her had been born blind, made a vow of extraordinary devotion. She would not enjoy a sight that her husband was denied; and so she bound a cloth over her own eyes, blindfolding herself for life, choosing to share her husband's darkness rather than to see what he could not. It was an act of remarkable dedication, and the story honours it; and yet there is a shadow in it too, for a queen who blindfolds herself cannot watch over her children, cannot see them going astray, cannot use a mother's sight to check their course; and Gāndhārī's chosen blindness, noble as it was, would leave her as unable as her blind husband to see and restrain the sons who would ruin them all.
But this marriage carried within it a deeper and more dangerous seed, a seed of hatred that would grow into the poison of the whole tragedy. For Gāndhārī had a brother, Shakuni, and Shakuni nursed a silent, unyielding hatred toward Bhīshma and the whole Kuru house. The reason lay in an old cruelty. The Kurus, it was said, had conquered Gāndhāra, and imprisoned its king, Subala, and all his sons, and set out to destroy them by slow starvation, giving the whole family only a single grain of rice each day. Understanding that they were all meant to die, Subala chose his youngest and cleverest son, Shakuni, to survive and to carry out the family's revenge; and he made all his other sons give up their single grains to Shakuni, so that they starved the faster and Shakuni lived. And before he died, the old king broke Shakuni's ankle, crippling him for life, so that with every step he took, every day, Shakuni would feel the pain and remember the cruelty of Hastināpura and never let his hatred cool.
And from the bones of his dead father, the story says, Shakuni made a set of dice that obeyed his every command, always falling as he willed; and carrying these dice and his lifelong limp and his undying hatred, he came to the court of Hastināpura, where his sister was queen, and made himself the closest companion and the evil genius of her eldest son, Duryodhana, dedicating his whole cunning life to a single secret purpose: the absolute destruction, from within, of the Bharata race that had destroyed his own. So the alliance that Bhīshma made to strengthen Hastināpura brought into its very heart the instrument of its ruin, a crippled schemer with a grievance that would never die, waiting patiently for the generation through whom he could work the vengeance of Gāndhāra.

title: The Kauravas
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Impressed by Gāndhārī's devotion to her husband, the sage Vyāsa granted her a boon: that she should have a hundred sons. And she conceived; but her pregnancy went on far beyond its natural term, two whole years, and no child came. And when at last she heard the news that Kuntī had given birth to her first son, Yudhishthira, Gāndhārī was seized with frustration and grief that Kuntī's line should have the firstborn ahead of hers, and in her anguish she struck her own womb.
And at that blow there fell from her not a child but a cold, lifeless, grey mass of tissue. Horror-stricken, she called for Vyāsa; and the sage came, and did not despair, but took the lifeless mass and divided it, with great care, into exactly one hundred parts, and placed each part in an earthen pot filled with ghee, to be incubated; and when Gāndhārī asked also for a daughter, he made one part more, and set it in an extra pot. And after two years of this strange incubation, the pots began to be opened.
But when the first pot was opened, and the firstborn son emerged, the omens were terrible. The dogs of the palace began to howl; thunder rolled from a clear sky; jackals cried; every sign of ill portent appeared at once. And Bhīshma, Vidura, and Vyāsa, reading these omens, understood that this child was born to be the destroyer of his race, and they pleaded with Dhritarāshtra and Gāndhārī to do the terrible but necessary thing, to abandon this one child, to prevent the ruin of the whole family and the whole world that he would otherwise bring. Let this one go, they begged, to save all the rest.
And Gāndhārī refused. She would not abandon her firstborn; no mother's heart, she felt, could do it; and Dhritarāshtra, doting already on the son he could not see, would not force her. And so the child was kept. This child was Duryodhana. And after him the other pots were opened, and there came forth his ninety-nine brothers, and their one sister, Duhshalā; and together these hundred sons of Dhritarāshtra were the Kauravas.
Let us mark this moment, for it is one of the great tragic hinges of the whole epic, the road not taken that would have saved the world. The wisest men of the age, reading the omens truly, told the parents plainly that this one child would destroy them all, and begged them to give him up. And the parents, out of love, out of a mother's natural refusal to abandon her child and a father's doting blindness, would not. Who can blame them? What mother could cast away her newborn on the strength of an omen? And yet the omen was true, and the refusal, however human, however understandable, was the choice that doomed them; for Duryodhana, kept and cherished, would grow to be exactly the destroyer the omens had foretold, and the hundred sons would perish, and the race would fall, and all the rivers of blood at Kurukshetra would flow from this one moment when love could not do the terrible thing that wisdom advised. The story does not tell us the parents were wicked to keep him; it shows us, rather, the terrible truth that love itself, unwilling to face a dreadful necessity, can be the very thing that opens the door to ruin, and that the hardest choices are precisely those where the heart and the deeper good are set against each other, as they were set here, over a newborn child in whom the whole doom of an age lay sleeping.

title: Droṇa and Drupada
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
In the hermitage of the sage Bharadvāja, two boys studied side by side: Droṇa, the son of a poor brāhmaṇa, and Drupada, prince of Pānchāla. They were close as boys are close, and Drupada, in the warmth of that friendship, promised his companion that when he came to his throne he would share his royal wealth with him. Boys make such promises easily; time keeps them rarely.
Drupada became king, inheriting fortresses and treasuries and vast armies. Droṇa took the harder road, of scriptural austerity and poverty; he married Kripī, sister of Kripāchārya, and had a son, Ashvatthāmā. And poverty fell heavy on his house. When his little son cried for milk and had never tasted it, and cruel neighbours mocked the child with flour stirred in water in its place, Droṇa was stung to the heart, and remembered his friend's old promise, and went to Drupada expecting to be received in love.
But Drupada, seated in his royal state, looked upon the thin, dust-covered brāhmaṇa with contempt. A king can be a friend only to a king, he declared; friendship is only between equals; a poor beggar cannot claim the companionship of a monarch. And he dismissed his old friend with a cold offering of charity. Droṇa refused the coins and walked away in silence, his heart burning with a quiet and terrible resolve.
Here is the whole poison of pride born of possession, and the story lays it bare. Drupada had not changed in worth, nor Droṇa; only Drupada's fortune had changed, and it had changed his heart, and taught him to measure a man by his wealth rather than his soul. To build our sense of another's worth upon so passing a thing as riches is to live inside an illusion, for wealth comes and goes and the soul it wraps is the same soul whether it is clothed in gold or in dust. Drupada looked at his friend and saw only poverty, and so lost the friend and gained an enemy; and Droṇa carried away from that hall a wound that would one day split Pānchāla in two. He went toward Hastināpura, keeping his purpose hidden, waiting.

title: The Master of Arms
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Droṇa came quietly to Hastināpura and lodged in the house of his kinsman Kripāchārya. And one day the young Kuru princes, the sons of Dhritarāshtra and the sons of Pāṇḍu together, were at play with a ball on the city's edge, when the ball rolled into a deep well; and worse, as they peered down, Yudhishthira's ring slipped from his finger and fell in too. They stood helpless around the well, seeing ball and ring shining far below and no way to reach them.
A dark-skinned brāhmaṇa stood watching with a gentle smile. Princes of the Bharata line, he said, trained in the royal arts, and you cannot lift a ball from a well? Watch. He took a blade of grass, and speaking words of power over it, cast it like an arrow into the well, and it pierced the ball; and he cast another that joined to the first, and another, building a chain of grass blades, and by that chain drew the ball up. Then he borrowed a bow and shot an arrow that struck through the ring and rebounded, carrying the ring back into Yudhishthira's astonished hand.
The princes bowed and asked who he was. Describe these deeds to Bhīshma, said Droṇa; he will tell you. And Bhīshma, hearing of the chain of grass, knew at once that the son of Bharadvāja had come, and brought Droṇa to the palace with honour, and made him the supreme teacher of arms to all the princes. So the wound of Drupada's hall became the great preceptor of Hastināpura, and the poor brāhmaṇa who had been turned from a king's door now held the training of a whole royal generation in his hands.

title: Karṇa
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The training of the princes ended in a great public exhibition of arms. There Arjuna displayed such archery, wielding the celestial weapons, that the crowd was lost in wonder. And then a sound like thunder came from the gate, and the crowd parted, and there stood a youth of godlike bearing, radiant, armoured. It was Karṇa, the abandoned firstborn of Kuntī, wearing still the golden armour and earrings he had been born with, though none there, and least of all he, knew his true birth. And Karṇa strode to Arjuna and matched, with careless ease, every feat Arjuna had performed.
Duryodhana, thrilled to see at last a rival to Arjuna, embraced Karṇa as a brother. But when Karṇa challenged Arjuna to single combat, Kripāchārya invoked the law of the arena: only a prince may fight a prince; let this youth name his lineage. And Karṇa bowed his head, for he could name none. Then Duryodhana stepped forward: if the bar is only that he is no king, then I make him a king; I crown Karṇa King of Anga, here and now. And he consecrated him on the spot with royal waters and gave him a crown.
Just then old Adhiratha the charioteer tottered into the arena, and Karṇa, newly crowned, at once knelt and touched the old man's feet in a son's reverence; and Bhīma laughed cruelly: he is only a charioteer's son, a suta; take up the whip, you are not fit to die by Arjuna's arrows. But Duryodhana cut through the mockery: valour is the mark of a warrior, not birth; can a tiger be born of an antelope? Look at his bearing, his armour, his skill; I hold him fit to rule the earth. And in that defence, Karṇa's loyalty to Duryodhana was sealed forever, a gratitude that would bind him, to the end, to the wrong side of every quarrel.
And here is the tragedy of Karṇa, which runs through the whole epic. He was noble by birth and nobler by nature, born of the Sun, generous beyond any man of his age; and all of it was chained to Duryodhana by the debt of that one public rescue, so that his gratitude, itself a virtue, bound him to serve injustice. His gifts were real and his loyalty was real, and both were spent in a bad cause; and that is his sorrow, that so great a soul, wronged from birth by his own mother's abandonment, gave his whole magnificent strength to the side of adharma out of love for the one man who had honoured him. Even his learning came at a price: he studied under Parashurāma by falsely claiming to be a brāhmaṇa, and when his endurance, a warrior's endurance, betrayed the lie, his teacher cursed him that his greatest weapon would fail him at his fated hour. The curses gathered on him through his life like his armour, and he bore them all, and went on, loyal and doomed.

title: The Wax Palace
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The strength and the goodness and the rising fame of the young Pāṇḍavas filled Duryodhana with a jealousy that would not let him sleep. Urged on by his uncle Shakuni and his friend Karṇa, he pressed the blind king Dhritarāshtra to permit a plot to destroy them; and Dhritarāshtra, caught as always in his doting love for his eldest son, yielded, as he would go on yielding until it destroyed them all.
The plan was laid with care. The court began to praise the beauty of the forest-town of Vāraṇāvata and a great festival to be held there, until the unsuspecting Pāṇḍavas, wishing to please Dhritarāshtra, agreed to go as royal guests. But Duryodhana's man Purochana had gone ahead to build a palace for them, and he built it of the most combustible things: jute and lac and hemp, resin and fat and oil, the walls plastered with clay mixed with butter, the beds set where the fire would catch quickest. The plot was simple: let the Pāṇḍavas settle in, and one night while they slept set the whole thing ablaze, and let the world call it a tragic accident.
This is the nature of envy, which the story shows us in the very fabric of that house: a silent, waiting thing, harmless-seeming, like the lac in the walls, that needs only a single spark to consume everything. Duryodhana's jealousy had been building since childhood, quiet and combustible, and now it had built a whole palace to burn his cousins in. But the wise Vidura had seen it coming, and was already at work to save the righteous sons of Pāṇḍu.

title: The Escape of the Pāṇḍavas
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
As the Pāṇḍavas left Hastināpura, Vidura drew Yudhishthira aside and warned him in a hidden speech that only he could follow: that the enemy's fire cannot harm the one who prepares against it, that the forest blaze cannot reach the rat in its burrow or the porcupine in the earth, that a wise man finds his way by the stars. Yudhishthira understood, and at Vāraṇāvata he kept his brothers watchful, and confirmed that the palace reeked of lac and fat and butter. Soon a miner came secretly from Vidura, with the passcode Vidura had used, and worked for weeks in secret to dig a tunnel running beneath the walls and the moat, out into the forest.
On the night Purochana meant to strike, the Pāṇḍavas struck first. They set fire to Purochana's own quarters and the palace's inflammable corners, and went down into the tunnel, and escaped into the dark just as the wax palace erupted into a tower of flame. They came out into the wild forest; and when Kuntī and the younger sons collapsed with exhaustion and terror, the mighty Bhīma carried them, his mother on his shoulders, the twins on his hips, Yudhishthira and Arjuna on his arms, and forced his way through the tangled woods. They crossed the Ganges in a boat Vidura's boatman had ready, and went on disguised as humble brāhmaṇas toward Ekachakra. On the way they met the sage Vyāsa, who comforted the grieving Kuntī with a hard truth: that life is woven of good and evil together, that no good man is wholly free of sorrow nor any wrongdoer free of consequence; put on the garb of brāhmaṇas, he told them, and wait in Ekachakra for your time.

title: Ekachakra and Bakāsura
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Disguised as begging brāhmaṇas, the Pāṇḍavas settled in the quiet town of Ekachakra, in the house of a poor brāhmaṇa who sheltered them, going out each day for alms and sharing them with their mother. But one day loud weeping came from their host's inner rooms, and Kuntī went in to find the family in despair: the father unable to give up wife or daughter or baby son, the wife insisting she must go, the daughter bravely offering herself, even the baby lisping that he would kill the monster with a stick of firewood.
For the town was terrorized by a cannibal demon, Bakāsura, and by an old agreement each household in turn must send him a cartload of food, two buffaloes, and a human being, whom he ate along with the rest; and now it was this family's turn. And Kuntī, without hesitation, declared: do not weep; I have five sons; one of them shall carry the food to the demon and save your family. When Yudhishthira heard, he was alarmed, for it was on Bhīma's strength that all their hopes rested; why risk him? But Kuntī's answer stood on the highest ground. We have lived in this good man's house and eaten his bread, she said; gratitude is the highest of virtues, and to repay kindness with kindness is a sacred duty; and I know Bhīma's strength; he who carried us out of the flames will crush this demon. And so Bhīma went, and calmly ate the demon's food before his eyes, and in the great combat that followed tore Bakāsura apart, and freed the town.
Mark Kuntī's reasoning, for it is the heart of the chapter. She did not weigh her own son's safety against a stranger's; she felt the host's suffering as her own, and held that a kindness received creates a debt that must be honestly repaid, whatever the cost. The suffering of the one who shelters us must be felt as our own; and true worship is not ceremony but exactly this, the active repaying of kindness with kindness, the treating of another's peril as a claim upon our own strength.

title: Draupadī
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
In Ekachakra the Pāṇḍavas heard of the great svayamvara of Draupadī, daughter of King Drupada of Pānchāla; and Kuntī, reading her sons' silent wish and seeing the alms grow thin, suggested they move on to Drupada's kingdom. There they lodged in a humble potter's cottage and went to the royal assembly disguised as young brāhmaṇas. Drupada had set an extraordinary test: a great stiff bow, and high above a rotating fish target behind a spinning wheel, and the archer must string the bow and send five arrows through the wheel into the fish's eye, aiming only by its reflection in a vessel of oil below.
Mighty kings and warriors tried and failed and were humbled, the stiff bow flinging them off; even Karṇa tried and failed by a hair. Then Arjuna, in his plain brāhmaṇa's deerskin, stepped out from among the priests; and meditating on the Lord, he lifted the great bow with ease, strung it without a tremor, and looking down at the reflection in the oil, sent five arrows through the spinning wheel into the target's eye, and it fell amid a rain of flowers. Draupadī set the garland of victory on Arjuna's neck.
But when the brothers brought her home and called out to their mother that they had brought the most precious alms won that day, Kuntī, speaking from within without looking, gave the command that could not be recalled: share the alms equally among yourselves. And so, by a mother's unwitting word, held sacred because it could not be unsaid, Draupadī became the wife of all five brothers. Unusual as this union was, it served a deep purpose: it bound the five Pāṇḍavas into a single unbreakable unit, one household, one shared devotion, welded together to stand as a single instrument of dharma against the storms that were gathering out of Hastināpura.

title: Indraprastha and the Reclaimed Desert
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
When it became known that the Pāṇḍavas had survived the burning of the wax palace, and they returned to Hastināpura alive, a crisis of succession arose, for now there were two sets of heirs, and Dhritarāshtra, torn as ever between his love for Duryodhana and his duty, resolved it by dividing the kingdom. And the division was itself an insult, for to the Pāṇḍavas he gave Khāṇḍavaprastha, a barren stretch of desert and ancient wasteland, desolate and unwanted, while Duryodhana kept the rich and settled heart of the realm.
To the eye of the world it was a cruel bargain, the best of the princes fobbed off with a wilderness. But the Pāṇḍavas did not complain, and here the story shows its first great turn from misfortune to triumph, for with the guidance of Lord Krishna and the labour of celestial architects they took that wasteland and transformed it, clearing and building and raising, until where there had been only desert there stood a magnificent city, Indraprastha, one of the wonders of the age.
There is a quiet teaching in this reclaiming, and it is worth pausing on before the splendours overtake it. The Pāṇḍavas were given a desert and made of it a paradise; they did not curse the poverty of their portion but poured their strength into it and made it flower. And is this not the very task of a life? Each of us is given some barren ground, some portion we did not choose and would not have chosen, some wilderness of circumstance; and the measure of a soul is not the richness of the ground it is given but what it makes of the ground it has. The Pāṇḍavas took the worst land in the kingdom and made it the most beautiful, and in doing so they showed that the desolate places, met with the right spirit and the right help, can be made to bloom.
And the city held one marvel above the rest. Mayāsura, the great architect of the demons, whose life the Pāṇḍavas had spared, built for them a hall of assembly of such refined art that it confounded the senses: floors of polished crystal that looked like water, and pools of clear water that looked like solid floor, so that the eye could not tell the solid from the seeming. It was a wonder; and it was also, though none yet knew it, a snare, for the confusion it worked upon the senses would one day work upon a proud guest and kindle the quarrel that would burn down the world. But that lay ahead. For now there was only the reclaimed desert turned to a shining city, and the Pāṇḍavas at the height of their fortune, and the hall of illusions gleaming at its heart, beautiful and treacherous, a fit emblem of the whole material glory that looks so solid and is built, at bottom, of deception.

title: The Fall of Jarāsandha
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
As Indraprastha rose to its glory, the brothers and counsellors of Yudhishthira urged him to perform the Rājasūya, the great imperial sacrifice by which a king declares himself emperor over all other kings. But there stood in the way a mighty obstacle: Jarāsandha, the powerful king of Magadha, who could not be left unconquered while any man claimed to be emperor. And Jarāsandha was no ordinary tyrant. He held eighty-six captive kings in his dungeons, and he meant to sacrifice them all, to slaughter these eighty-six men to feed his own ego under the cloak of ritual piety. He was raw material power at its most monstrous, strength wholly divorced from righteousness.
Krishna counselled Yudhishthira that Jarāsandha could not be beaten by armies, for his hosts were too vast; he must be reached another way, through the very code of honour he lived by. And so Krishna, Bhīma, and Arjuna disguised themselves as ascetics under vows of silence, and came to Magadha, and by coming at midnight, when a king of honour must receive holy guests whatever the hour, they gained entry to Jarāsandha's presence. And Jarāsandha, noting the warrior's calluses that the bowstring leaves, and knowing these were no true ascetics, challenged them; and they threw off their disguises and demanded a duel to the death. And Jarāsandha, honourable even in his tyranny, accepted, and chose Bhīma as his match in wrestling.
The duel raged for fourteen days, a titanic struggle of two mighty bodies, and Bhīma could not prevail, for Jarāsandha, however he was broken, seemed always to knit himself whole again. And here Krishna gave the wordless clue that won the fight. For Jarāsandha had been born in two halves, joined together by a demoness, and the two halves could always rejoin; and Krishna took up a blade of grass and split it in two and threw the halves in opposite directions. And Bhīma understood, and when next he broke Jarāsandha he tore him clean in two and cast the halves far apart, so that they could not find each other and rejoin, and the tyrant died. So fell Jarāsandha, and his eighty-six captive kings went free; and the lesson of his fall is plain, that raw strength without the light of wisdom to guide it is finally self-destroying, mighty enough to hold whole kingdoms captive and yet undone in the end by a single blade of split grass in the hand of the wise.

title: The Rājasūya and the First Honour
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Rājasūya and the First Honour

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
With Jarāsandha slain and the captive kings freed, the Rājasūya of Yudhishthira went forward in unmatched splendour, drawing sages and kings and teachers from across the whole land. And it came to the height of the ceremony, the moment of the arghya, the offering of the first and highest honour of the whole assembly to the one worthiest soul present; and on the recommendation of Bhīshma himself, that honour was offered by Sahadeva to Lord Krishna, acknowledging him as the supreme refuge of all beings.
And this choice enraged one man: Shishupāla, the king of Chedi, who bore Krishna a long and bitter hatred. Blinded by envy and by pride, Shishupāla rose and poured out a torrent of insult, mocking the aged Bhīshma as a senile fool and Yudhishthira as an ignorant boy, and above all deriding Krishna as a mere cowherd of no royal blood, unfit to be honoured above venerable teachers like Droṇa and sages like Vyāsa. It was the very voice of spiritual blindness, that could look upon the Supreme Lord himself and see only a low-born herdsman bound by the rankings of the world.
But Krishna sat in serene silence and let the insults come, counting them; for he had made a promise long ago to Shishupāla's mother, that he would forgive his cousin a hundred offences. And so he waited, and let Shishupāla heap up his insults, patiently, until they reached a hundred. And when the hundred and first insult left Shishupāla's lips, the promise was fulfilled and the patience was complete; and Krishna released his discus, the Sudarshana Chakra, and struck off the head of the king of Chedi in the midst of the whole assembly. And from the fallen body there rose a light, which passed into the feet of the Lord; for even this, the story tells us, is a mystery of grace: that Shishupāla, who had fixed his whole mind upon Krishna, even in hatred, even in the intensity of his enmity, was in the end drawn back into the very source he had opposed, so complete had his attention been, though its form was loathing rather than love.

title: The Gamble
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The splendour of Indraprastha and the imperial glory of Yudhishthira were more than Duryodhana's envious heart could bear. And a particular humiliation had sharpened his envy to a blade: for in the hall of illusions, that hall of crystal floors and watery-seeming stone, Duryodhana had been deceived by the cunning surfaces, mistaking solid crystal for water and lifting his robes to cross where there was no water, and falling into a real pool where he had thought there was floor; and Draupadī, it was said, had laughed at his confusion. That laughter festered in him. And so, when he pined with jealousy of his cousins' glory, Shakuni offered him the means to destroy them without an army: a game of dice, playing upon Yudhishthira's known weakness for the game and upon Shakuni's own absolute mastery of loaded, obedient dice.
Dhritarāshtra gave his consent, overriding the grave warnings of Vidura, as he always overrode wisdom when his son desired otherwise. And when Vidura carried the formal invitation to Indraprastha, he warned Yudhishthira openly that the game was a trap laid to ruin their house. And yet Yudhishthira accepted; for by the warrior's code a formal challenge could not be refused without shame, and beneath the code there was in him too an inner, unmastered pull toward the game itself, a weakness he could not deny. And so, against all warning, he went.
In the great hall of Hastināpura, before Bhīshma and Droṇa and Kripa and Vidura, the tragic game began. Shakuni cast the dice for Duryodhana, the bone dice that answered to his will. And Yudhishthira lost, and lost, and could not stop. He staked and lost his gold and his silver; his herds and his stables; his armies; his servants; and still, gripped by the fever of the game, refusing to rise, he staked more. He staked and lost his brothers, one by one, Nakula, Sahadeva, Arjuna, Bhīma. And at last, with everything else gone, he staked his own self, and lost that too, and fell into bondage, while Shakuni shouted his triumph.
Let us understand what the story is showing us in this terrible descent, for it is one of its deepest warnings, and the shloka the tradition sets beside it names the whole mechanism: that from dwelling on the objects of the senses comes attachment, and from attachment desire, and from desire, when it is thwarted, anger, and from anger the ruin of the mind. Yudhishthira, the most righteous of men, the very son of Dharma, was undone here not by any villainy of his own but by a single unmastered attachment, the pull of the game, which he would not or could not set down. He was warned; he knew the trap; and still the fever held him, and drove him from stake to stake down into total ruin, dragging his brothers and his wife and his kingdom down with him. That is the terror of an unmastered attachment: that it can take even the best of men, in a single evening, and strip him of everything, because the one weakness he would not govern became the door through which all his enemies entered. The dice were loaded; but the deeper loading was in Yudhishthira's own heart, in the one desire he had never learned to still.

title: Draupadī's Grief and the Miracle of the Robes
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: Draupadī's Grief and the Miracle of the Robes

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
With all five brothers reduced to slaves, Shakuni set before Yudhishthira one last stake: Draupadī herself, the empress, the wife of all five. And Yudhishthira, sunk now in a bewilderment of the mind past all reason, staked her, and lost. And Duryodhana, exulting, ordered that Draupadī be dragged into the assembly to sweep its floors as a slave.
But Draupadī, receiving this monstrous command, did not collapse; she met it with the clear mind that even in her extremity did not desert her, and sent back a question, a piercing question of law: did the king stake me after he had already lost himself and become a slave, or while he was still a free man? For a slave owns nothing, not even the right to wager; and if Yudhishthira had already lost his own freedom before he staked her, then he had no more right to stake her than any other slave, and the wager was void. It was a question that laid bare the whole injustice, and the assembly had no honest answer to it.
Enraged by her resistance, Duryodhana sent his brother Duhshāsana to drag Draupadī by her hair into the open court; and there she stood, weeping, her single garment disordered, a queen shamed before the whole assembly, and the elder statesmen of the Kurus, Bhīshma and Droṇa and the rest, sat in paralyzed silence, hiding behind the rigid technicalities of duty, unable or unwilling to stop the outrage. Only one young prince, Vikarṇa, rose to declare the wager illegal, on the very grounds Draupadī had named: that Yudhishthira, already a slave, had no right to stake her, and that in any case she belonged to all five brothers and could not be staked by one. But Karṇa harshly silenced him, and worse, commanded Duhshāsana to strip the garments from the Pāṇḍavas and the robe from Draupadī herself.
And now came the deepest moment of the whole scene, and it is the moment that gives it its meaning. As Duhshāsana laid his hands on her garment and began to pull, Draupadī understood that no human protection would come, that the elders would not save her, that her husbands, enslaved, could not save her, that every earthly help had failed. And in that instant she let go. She let go of her own grip on her robe, of her own struggle, of her reliance on any power of this world; and she raised both her arms above her head in total surrender, and cried out to Krishna alone, calling on Govinda to be her only refuge. And in that surrender the miracle came. For as Duhshāsana pulled, the cloth did not end; an endless stream of silk flowed around her, robe upon robe without limit, so that pull as he might he could not strip her, and the fabric piled in mountains upon the floor, until Duhshāsana himself sank down in exhaustion, defeated, unable to disrobe the woman whom the Lord himself had clothed.
This is the great teaching of sharaṇāgati, of surrender, set here at the very pit of the story's darkness, and it is the same truth we met in the other epic, on the shore before Lankā: that there is a moment when every human help fails, when our own strength is spent and no earthly power can save us, and that in that moment the one thing left is to let go and cast ourselves wholly upon the Divine; and that this letting-go is not defeat but the opening of the only door that cannot be shut. Draupadī was saved not while she gripped her own robe and fought, but the instant she released it and raised her empty hands and cried out for refuge. Her helplessness, fully accepted, became the very condition of her rescue; for grace comes most surely to the one who has given up all other hope and turned, with empty hands, to the source of all protection.

title: Dhritarāshtra's Anxiety
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The miracle of the endless robes shook the hall, and after it came the omens: jackals howling in the streets, donkeys braying, every sign of a coming retribution, as though the cosmos itself recoiled from what had been done. And Gāndhārī, hearing of these portents, came to her husband and warned him plainly to undo his sons' evil before it consumed the whole line. And Dhritarāshtra, frightened at last, roused himself, and soothed the wronged Draupadī, and granted her boons; and she, with a nobility that shames the whole assembly that had failed her, asked only for the freedom of her husbands and the return of their weapons, and refused a further boon, saying that greed did not become her. So the Pāṇḍavas were freed, and set out again for Indraprastha, their honour wounded but their lives and their liberty restored.
But it was not to last, for Duryodhana and Shakuni and Duhshāsana would not let their prey escape. They upbraided the blind king for releasing the Pāṇḍavas on the very threshold of victory, arguing that no self-respecting warrior would ever forgive such humiliation, that the Pāṇḍavas would surely return with an army to destroy them, that the only safety now lay in finishing what had been begun. And Dhritarāshtra yielded once more, as he always yielded, and sent a messenger to recall Yudhishthira for one final game.
The terms of this last game were fixed in advance: the losers would go into exile for twelve years in the forest, and a thirteenth year in hiding, unrecognized; and if they were discovered during that thirteenth year, the whole cycle would begin again. And Yudhishthira, though his family begged him not to go, accepted once more, declaring that destiny cannot be escaped and a challenge to dice cannot in honour be refused. And once more Shakuni's loaded dice defeated him. And so the Pāṇḍavas put on the deerskins of forest exiles and prepared to leave, while the citizens of Hastināpura lamented aloud and openly accused Dhritarāshtra and his sons of treachery. And the sage Nārada appeared in the court and spoke with the authority of prophecy: that fourteen years from that day, the whole Kaurava race would be destroyed, as the fruit of the crime that Duryodhana had committed. The sentence was passed; the doom was named; and the exile began.

title: The Teaching of Exile and the Warning of Nala
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Teaching of Exile and the Warning of Nala

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The Pāṇḍavas settled in the Kāmyaka forest, and there Yudhishthira was seized with remorse, blaming himself without cease for the ruin of his brothers and the humiliation of Draupadī, all of which his own weakness at the dice had brought upon them. And to comfort the grieving king there came the sage Brihadashva, who listened to his laments and then told him a story to set his own sorrow in its place: the long and famous story of King Nala.
For Nala too, the sage said, had lost everything at a rigged game of dice, his kingdom and his wealth and even the clothes off his back, defeated by his own brother Pushkara, and driven into the forest in utter desolation. And Nala's suffering had been sharper than Yudhishthira's, for he had been separated from his beloved wife Damayantī, and had wandered for years in disguise, disfigured, serving as a horse-trainer under another king, sunk to the very bottom of fortune. And yet, through it all, Nala had held fast to dharma and to patience; and in the end he had regained his kingdom, his form, and his family, and all had come right. Take comfort, the sage told Yudhishthira; adversity is the common lot even of the greatest, and it is a refiner, not a destroyer. You have your brave brothers, your devoted wife, the company of holy men; do not sink into self-pity, for even the greatest kings have been tried by sorrows and have come out of them like gold from the fire.
And this is the teaching that the whole exile exists to work into the souls of the Pāṇḍavas, and the sage names it plainly: that suffering is not an end in itself but a schooling, a stripping-away of the soul's false attachment to its outer fortunes, to kingship and wealth and comfort and status, all of which are but garments, temporary and removable, worn over the eternal self. The body and the crown are outer robes; the soul is what wears them; and the task, in suffering as in prosperity, is to keep the soul steady in its devotion, neither puffed up by the pleasant nor broken by the painful, holding to dharma through both. Yudhishthira's exile was to teach him what Yayāti had learned at the end of a thousand years, what the whole Lunar Line had to learn again and again: that the outer fortunes are not the self, and that peace lies not in holding them but in the steadiness that can lose them and remain whole.

title: The Quest for the Pāshupata
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
While Yudhishthira kept his calm and his patience, Bhīma and Draupadī chafed, and pressed him again and again to abandon this passive endurance and make war on Hastināpura at once. Bhīma argued that the thirteen years were only a trap to let Duryodhana entrench his power, and even proposed that by certain sacred incantations they might compress the thirteen years into thirteen days and so fulfil the letter of the oath while escaping its cost. But Yudhishthira refused it utterly, holding that truth is higher than power and must be kept whatever it costs, that a vow honoured only in its letter and cheated in its spirit is no honoured vow at all.
But if he would not make war before the time, he would prepare for the war that must come at the end of it; and on the counsel of Vyāsa, he sent Arjuna to the Himālayas to win divine weapons from the gods against the day of battle. And Arjuna climbed the rugged heights of Indrakīla and performed severe austerities. There Indra came to him first, disguised as an old ascetic, and tested him by offering him celestial pleasures in place of weapons; and Arjuna refused, saying his only desire was to protect dharma upon the earth. And then Arjuna turned his penance toward Lord Shiva.
And Shiva came to test him in a stranger way. A wild boar charged at Arjuna, and Arjuna shot it, and at the very same instant a hunter, a Kirāta, also pierced it with a shaft; and a fierce dispute arose over whose kill it was, and it grew into open combat between Arjuna and the hunter. And Arjuna, for all his supreme skill, could not prevail: his arrows were swallowed up, his mighty bow Gāṇḍīva was wrenched from him, and he was overpowered. And then, at last, he understood, and recognized that the hunter was none other than Shiva himself, come to test him; and he fell down in total surrender at the god's feet. And Shiva, well pleased with Arjuna's courage and his humility both, raised him up, restored his bow, and gave him the greatest of gifts, the infallible Pāshupata weapon, the ultimate astra, against the day of the war. So Arjuna, who had first shown his valour and then his humility, was found worthy, for the highest gifts are given not to valour alone nor to humility alone, but to the soul in which the two are joined.

title: Agastya and the Humbling of Vindhya
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: Agastya and the Humbling of Vindhya

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
While Arjuna was away in the celestial regions winning his weapons, the sage Lomasha came to the other Pāṇḍavas and led them on a pilgrimage to the sacred places, and along the way he told them the old stories that clung to those places, and among them the story of the sage Agastya and his wife Lopāmudrā.
Agastya, the story went, once saw his own ancestors hanging head-downward in a void, suffering because he had begotten no children to continue their line and secure their peace; and so, to fulfil his duty to them, he resolved to marry, and wedded the beautiful princess Lopāmudrā of Vidarbha. But Lopāmudrā, raised in a palace, found the bare poverty of his forest hermitage hard, and asked that before they had children they might live for a time in royal comfort, in the manner she was used to.
