And Agastya, unwilling to spend his hard-won spiritual merit on mere temporary wealth, set out instead as a humble beggar to ask riches of the wealthy kings of the earth.
And here the story folds in a quiet lesson in governance. For as Agastya examined the treasuries of king after king, he found in each that the state's expenditure exactly equalled its revenue, that there was no true surplus anywhere, and that to take a gift from any of these kings would only mean laying a heavier tax on their common people to make up the loss. And so he would not take from them, for he would not enrich himself at the cost of the poor; a lesson, the tellers note, in what righteous rule requires, that a king's wealth is his people's wealth, and not to be given away to enrich one man at the expense of the many.
Agastya then came to a demon named Ilvala, who had a cruel custom of murdering brāhmaṇas: he would turn his brother Vātāpi into a goat, cook and serve the meat to his guest, and then call Vātāpi to come forth, and the demon would tear his way out of the guest's belly and kill him. And Agastya knew the trick, and ate the meal calmly, and then, before Ilvala could call his brother, rubbed his own stomach and said: Vātāpi, be digested. And so Vātāpi was digested and could not return, and Ilvala's murderous magic failed, and the demon, overcome, surrendered his great riches to the sage. This story, the tellers say, shows the power of a true sage to digest and neutralize even the most poisonous things the material world can offer him, to take in what would destroy a lesser soul and render it harmless, so complete is the mastery that genuine spiritual power confers.

title: Rishyashringa's Innocence
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The pilgrimage carried the Pāṇḍavas through the valleys of Anga, and there Lomasha told them the tale of the sage Rishyashringa, the story of an innocence so complete that it had never known the world at all, the same story, in another telling, that opens the tale of Rāma, and it carries here the same tender and difficult lesson.
Rishyashringa had been born and raised in absolute isolation by his father, Vibhāṇḍaka, deep in the forest, and had never in his life seen a woman, nor indeed any human being but his own father. His heart was a clean and untouched slate, wholly ignorant of the desires and the divisions of the world, pure with the purity of one who has never been tempted because he has never met temptation.
And when a terrible famine struck the kingdom of Anga, its king, Romapāda, was told that the rains would return only if the pure and innocent Rishyashringa set foot in the land. So the king sent a company of beautiful courtesans, who built a lovely floating garden upon a boat and moored it near Vibhāṇḍaka's hermitage; and in the father's absence they approached the young sage, and embraced him, and fed him sweet things, all under the guise of the hospitality of one hermitage to another. And Rishyashringa, in his complete innocence, took these soft and lovely visitors for a new kind of hermit, wonderful shining ascetics with strange soft features, and was captivated, and eagerly boarded their floating garden to visit their hermitage; and the moment he was drawn into the kingdom of Anga, the rains came pouring down and saved the land.
And here the story draws a lesson about innocence that is worth weighing, for it is not the simple lesson we might expect. Innocence, it tells us, beautiful as it is, is not the same as virtue, and is not enough by itself; for an innocence that has never been tested, that owes its purity only to never having met temptation, is a fragile thing, easily led, as Rishyashringa was led, by the first cunning that comes to it. True spiritual stability is not the innocence of the one who has been kept from the world, but the mature and conscious detachment of the one who has met the world, its temptations and its snares, and has learned to stand steady within it. Isolation from temptation is not mastery of temptation; and the goal is not to be kept forever in a sheltered grove, untested and therefore untried, but to develop the inner strength that can meet the world and not be swept away by it. Rishyashringa's innocence was lovely, and it served the kingdom's need; but the story gently marks that it was innocence still untempered into virtue, and that the tempering can only come through the very friction with the world that the sheltered grove had spared him.

title: Yavakrīda's Fruitless Penance
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
At the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, Lomasha told a darker story, the story of Yavakrīda, and it is a warning about the wrong way to seek knowledge, and about the emptiness of learning that is won by pride rather than by patience.
Yavakrīda was the son of the sage Bharadvāja, and he was consumed by envy of the great scholarly fame of another sage, Raibhya, and Raibhya's learned sons. And rather than earn such learning as it must be earned, by the long, humble, patient road of study under a teacher, Yavakrīda resolved to seize it by force: he undertook fierce, flesh-mortifying penances to compel Lord Indra to grant him mastery of the Vedas directly, all at once, bypassing the slow discipline of study.
And Indra came, and warned him, again and again, that his whole path was mistaken. Austerity is not the road to learning, the god told him; the road is study, patient study, and study alone. And to show him his folly, Indra took the form of a gaunt old man and began, day after day, to throw handfuls of sand into the rushing Gangā, as though to build a dam across it. And Yavakrīda laughed at the old man's foolishness, to dam a great river with sand; and Indra answered: is my sand dam across this mighty river any more foolish than your attempt to master the Vedas by raw penance instead of by study? The two are the same folly.
But Yavakrīda would not hear, and so at last Indra granted him the boon he demanded, the learning he had not earned; and it destroyed him, exactly as the warning had foretold. For the knowledge sat in a mind that had never been refined by the discipline of earning it, a mind still full of vanity and unmastered desire; and lacking all self-control, Yavakrīda was swept away one spring morning by lust, and violated Raibhya's pure daughter-in-law; and that crime brought his swift and terrible ruin. This is the lesson the story presses: that knowledge or power seized through pride, taken as a shortcut, without the long inner discipline by which it is properly earned, is hollow and even dangerous, for it gives the mind a power its character has not grown fit to hold. Learning is not merely information poured into the head; it is a thing that must be digested slowly into the whole character, and knowledge that has not been so digested, that sits in an unrefined and prideful soul, becomes not wisdom but a weapon that destroys its own bearer.

title: Yavakrīda's End and Raibhya's Wrath
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
When Raibhya discovered the outrage done to his daughter-in-law, he was seized with a terrible and righteous anger, and in his wrath he plucked a hair from his matted locks and offered it into the sacrificial fire with mantras of power; and from the flames there rose a beautiful maiden in the likeness of the violated woman, and behind her a fearful, weapon-wielding demon; and Raibhya commanded them to hunt down and destroy Yavakrīda.
And Yavakrīda, pursued by the terrible demon, fled toward his father's hermitage for protection; but his father Bharadvāja was blind and helpless and could not turn aside the working of the law of retribution his son had brought upon himself. Yavakrīda tried then to take shelter in a nearby temple, but the gatekeeper barred him, for his recent crime had made him ritually impure, unfit to enter the holy place; and so, shut out from the sanctuary he had defiled himself out of the right to enter, he was overtaken by the demon and slain.
There is a stern justice in the manner of his death, and the story means us to see it: that the refuge of dharma is closed to the one who has himself violated dharma's foundations, that a man cannot flee for shelter to the very sanctity he has just trampled. Yavakrīda sought the temple's protection with the stain of his crime still on him, and the temple could not receive him; his own act had shut its door against him.
And the chain of sorrow did not end there, for such chains of anger and vengeance rarely do. When Bharadvāja learned of his son's death, he was plunged into grief, and in his grief he cursed Raibhya, that Raibhya should be killed by his own eldest son; and then, unable to bear his loss, Bharadvāja gave up his own life upon his son's funeral pyre. So the anger of one sage and the crime of another had now set a curse upon a third and killed a fourth, the sorrow spreading outward from soul to soul. And the tellers draw from this dark chain a vital truth: that even the most advanced ascetics, men of great penance and great power, are undone in an instant the moment they let their minds be swept away by anger and the thirst for vengeance; that all the spiritual attainment in the world is no protection against the ruin that unmastered anger brings, but rather makes that ruin the greater, for the more power a soul holds, the more destruction its anger can loose upon the world.

title: Mere Learning is Not Enough
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The curse that Bharadvāja had laid upon Raibhya now worked itself out, and its working carries the story's judgment on the difference between learning and virtue.
Raibhya had two sons, Parāvasu and Arvāvasu, both deeply learned scholars of the Vedas. One night, as Parāvasu walked through the dark forest to attend a great sacrifice being held by King Brihadyumna, he saw a shape moving in the bushes, and took it for a wild beast, and shot it; and found that he had killed his own father, Raibhya, who was walking there wrapped in a deerskin. So the curse was fulfilled, the father slain by the eldest son exactly as Bharadvāja had decreed.
And now the true test came, the test not of learning but of character, and it exposed the two brothers utterly. Parāvasu, terrified of the guilt of having killed his father, begged his younger brother Arvāvasu to take upon himself the long penances of expiation for the crime, while Parāvasu himself completed the king's sacrifice; and Arvāvasu, out of pure brotherly love, agreed, and spent years in the rigorous rites of purification for a sin that was not his. But when Arvāvasu returned at last to the sacrificial hall to rejoin his brother, Parāvasu, corrupted by jealousy and by the wish to be rid of him, loudly proclaimed before all that Arvāvasu was a sinner, a man guilty of killing his own father, unfit to enter the holy ground. And the guards, believing him, drove the innocent Arvāvasu away.
But Arvāvasu retired to the forest and performed intense penances to the Sun God, who in time appeared and vindicated him and declared his innocence before all. And the story sets the two brothers side by side and draws its plain lesson: that scriptural learning is only an outer garment unless it has been digested into lived and active virtue. Both brothers knew the Vedas equally; but Parāvasu, for all his learning, lacked the basic purity of heart, and used his knowledge to shield his own guilt and to slander his innocent brother; while the humble Arvāvasu lived the true spirit of dharma, taking his brother's guilt upon himself in love and bearing slander without bitterness. Learning had made Parāvasu clever and left him corrupt; virtue had made Arvāvasu great. And so the story reminds us that what finally matters is not how much we know but what we have become, that a head full of scripture in a heart empty of goodness is worth nothing, and that the whole purpose of learning is to be lived, not merely to be held.

title: Ashtāvakra's Triumph
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
In the forest of Mithilā, Lomasha told the Pāṇḍavas the story of the young sage Ashtāvakra, and it is a story that overturns the world's way of judging a soul by its outward form.
Ashtāvakra had been born with eight deformities twisting his body, the fruit of a curse his own scholarly father Kahoḍa had laid upon him when, still in the womb, the unborn child had presumed to correct his father's faulty recitation of the Vedas. So Ashtāvakra came into the world bent and broken in body; but within that broken frame lived an intellect of peerless clarity, a mind that was a perfect mirror of the highest wisdom.
At the age of twelve, Ashtāvakra journeyed to the court of King Janaka to challenge the proud court scholar Vandin, who had defeated many learned men in debate and drowned the losers in the ocean, and among them Ashtāvakra's own father. And as the boy approached, the king's men commanded the deformed child to make way; and Ashtāvakra rebuked them with a dignity beyond his years: even a king must make way for the deformed, the blind, for women, and for those who carry the light of the Vedas. And when the assembled scholars of the court laughed at his twisted limbs, Ashtāvakra answered them with words that cut to the very heart of the matter: I thought this was an assembly of scholars, but I see it is a gathering of cobblers, who judge a man by his skin rather than by his soul.
And then, in a profound debate on the nature of the One and the Many, Ashtāvakra silenced the mighty Vandin, proving his absolute mastery of the deepest philosophy; and Vandin, defeated, revealed himself as the son of the god Varuṇa, and restored to life all the scholars he had drowned. So the boy triumphed, and won back his father, and the whole story stands as a rebuke to the shallow judgment of the world. For the world saw a broken and deformed body and assumed a lesser soul; and the soul within was greater than any straight-limbed scholar in that hall. The eternal self, the story tells us, is wholly unaffected by the shape or the soundness of the body it wears; the body is a vehicle, and a deformed vehicle may carry a perfect soul, as a plain vessel may hold the finest wine. To judge a man by his skin, as Ashtāvakra said, is the trade of cobblers; the wise look through the outer form to the soul within, which no deformity can touch and no beauty can improve.

title: The Wind-Sons: Bhīma and Hanumān
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
High in the Himalayan heights, a fragrant and beautiful flower was carried on the north-east breeze to Draupadī, and she was captivated by its celestial scent and begged Bhīma to find the plant it came from, that they might have it in their forest home. And Bhīma, eager as always to please his beloved, strode off to the north-east, following the fragrance, giving no thought to the wild beasts that crossed his path, for his strength feared nothing.
Deep in a grove of banana trees, Bhīma found a huge old monkey lying directly across his path, and shouted at it to move; and the monkey drawled that it was old and unwell, and asked why it had been woken, and said that if Bhīma had scruples about jumping over it, he might simply push its tail aside and pass. And Bhīma, proud of his immense strength, the strength that had torn demons apart, reached down to fling the old monkey's tail out of his way.
And he could not move it. He could not shift the tail a hair's breadth. He set his jaws and strained every muscle in his mighty body until the sweat poured off him, and the tail lay as immovable as a mountain root. And Bhīma, his pride broken, understood that this was no ordinary monkey, and bowed down in humility and asked who this being was, and begged forgiveness for his arrogance. And the monkey smiled and revealed himself: he was Hanumān, the great devotee of Rāma from the elder age, and he was Bhīma's own brother, for both were sons of the Wind God, Vāyu. And Hanumān blessed his younger brother, and promised that in the great war to come he would sit upon the flag atop Arjuna's chariot, to strike terror into the enemy.
The meeting of the two wind-sons carries a plain and useful lesson, and it is a lesson in humility for the strong. Bhīma was perhaps the mightiest man of his age, and his strength had never met its match, and that unbroken strength had made him proud. And here, in a single old monkey's immovable tail, his whole pride was humbled, and he was taught that however great his strength, there was strength beyond it, and that the truly great, like Hanumān, wear their power not with arrogance but with a gentle, drawling ease. It is good for the strong to meet, now and then, a strength they cannot move; for strength without humility is only arrogance waiting to fall, and Bhīma was the better, and the wiser, for having strained with all his might against a tail he could not lift.

title: I Am No Crane
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The sage Mārkaṇḍeya comforted the Pāṇḍavas with the story of Kaushika, and it is one of the most quietly revolutionary stories in the whole epic, for it locates true holiness not in the forest or the temple but in the faithful doing of ordinary duty.
Kaushika was a proud ascetic who had won great yogic power through his penances. One day, as he sat in meditation beneath a tree, a crane perched above befouled his head with its droppings; and Kaushika looked up in anger, and the mere burning glance of his wrath struck the bird dead on the instant. And seeing the power of his own anger, Kaushika was not chastened but made vain, proud that his glance could kill.
Later, going to a house to beg for alms, Kaushika stood at the door and waited; and the housewife within, busy at that moment dutifully serving her sick husband, kept him waiting a long while. And when at last she came, Kaushika rebuked her harshly for keeping a holy brāhmaṇa waiting. But the housewife only smiled and said: be not angry, O sage; I am no crane, to be killed by your violent thoughts; your rage can do no harm to a woman who is devoted to her duty. And Kaushika was stunned, for how could she know of the crane, which no human eye had seen?
And the housewife told him: go to Mithilā, and be instructed in the secret of duty by Dharmavyādha, a butcher. And Kaushika went, astonished, and was more astonished still to find that the wise teacher he had been sent to was a common butcher, selling meat in a busy shop in the marketplace. And this butcher taught the proud ascetic the deepest lesson: that the highest spiritual perfection is not won by outward austerity, nor by the pride of penance, nor by fleeing the world to a forest, but by the sincere, humble, ego-free performance of one's own duty in the place where one is set, whatever that place may be. The butcher at his trade, honestly and without ego, doing the duty of his birth and serving those around him; the housewife serving her husband and her household; these had reached a holiness that the proud forest-ascetic with his death-dealing glance had not, for all his power. And Kaushika, humbled, went home to serve his own aged parents, and so turned his raw penance at last into true and living virtue.
This is one of the great teachings of the whole tradition, and the story frames it in the shloka the tradition sets beside it: that we have a right to our action but not to its fruits, that we must do our duty for its own sake without grasping at its rewards. The housewife and the butcher had learned exactly this: to do the duty before them, faithfully, without ego, without grasping, and in that faithful doing they had found a holiness that the ambitious ascetic, hungry for spiritual power and proud of what he had won, had entirely missed. Holiness, the story tells us, is not somewhere else, in the forest or the temple or the height of penance; it is here, in the faithful doing of the ordinary duty that lies before us, done without pride and without greed for its fruits.

title: Krishna's Hunger
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Back in Hastināpura, Duryodhana performed a great sacrifice, and hosted the fearsome sage Durvāsā, famous for his terrible temper, together with his ten thousand disciples; and Durvāsā, pleased with Duryodhana's lavish hospitality, offered him a boon. And Duryodhana, ever plotting the ruin of his cousins, asked a cruel thing: that Durvāsā should go and visit the Pāṇḍavas in the forest, and go at a time Duryodhana carefully chose, late in the day, after Draupadī would have finished serving the day's meals, so that there would be no food left to offer the sage and his ten thousand, and the irritable Durvāsā, finding no hospitality, would curse the Pāṇḍavas in his wrath.
And it fell out as Duryodhana had planned. Durvāsā arrived with his host just after Draupadī had eaten and cleaned the Akshayapātra, the miraculous vessel given by the Sun God, which supplied food each day until she took her own meal, whereupon its power ceased until the next day. Now the vessel was empty and spent for the day, and here were ten thousand hungry ascetics and their terrible master, and no food, and the certainty of a devastating curse. And Draupadī, in her helplessness, did the one thing left to her: she prayed, fervently, to Krishna.
And Krishna appeared at once, and said: I am very hungry; bring me something to eat first. And Draupadī cried out in confusion, pointing to the empty vessel. But Krishna took up the pot and looked into it, and found clinging to its rim a single grain of rice and a scrap of vegetable, and he ate that one grain, with satisfaction, saying: may the Lord of the universe be pleased with this. And in that instant, Durvāsā and his ten thousand disciples, bathing in the river before their meal, felt their stomachs grow full, wholly satisfied, as though they had eaten a great feast; and, unable to swallow another bite, and ashamed now to demand a meal they could not eat, they quietly departed, and the curse never came.
The meaning of this lovely episode is set in its heart: that when the Supreme Soul is satisfied, the whole universe is satisfied; for all beings are, at the deepest level, one in him, and to feed him is to feed all. Krishna ate one grain of rice, and ten thousand men were filled; because the many are joined in the One, and what satisfies the source satisfies all that flows from it. It is a teaching of the deep unity of all things, that we are not the separate islands we seem, but branches of a single life; and Draupadī's simple, desperate turning to Krishna, when every other resource had failed, once again brought the grace that human effort could not.

title: The Dialogue of the Pool
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Near the end of the long exile came its final and greatest test, and it fell, fittingly, upon Yudhishthira, the son of Dharma, and it took the form of a series of questions beside a forest pool.
A magic deer had run off with a brāhmaṇa's fire-sticks, and the Pāṇḍavas pursued it deep into the forest but lost it, and found themselves exhausted and burning with thirst. Yudhishthira sent Nakula to find water, and Nakula came to a beautiful clear pool; but as he bent to drink, a bodiless voice warned him that the pool belonged to it, and that he must answer its questions before he drank, or die. And Nakula, maddened by thirst, ignored the warning and drank, and fell dead. And one after another Sahadeva, then Arjuna, then Bhīma came seeking him, and each ignored the same warning, and each drank and fell dead beside the pool.
At last Yudhishthira came, and found his four brothers lying dead by the water, and mastered his grief, and when the voice, the voice of a Yaksha, gave its warning once more, Yudhishthira bowed and said: ask your questions; I shall answer to the limit of my understanding. And the Yaksha put to him a swift series of deep questions, and Yudhishthira answered them, and his answers are among the treasures of the epic. What makes the sun shine? The power of the Eternal. What rescues a man in danger? Courage. What is higher than the sky? The father. What is more sustaining than the earth? The mother. What is the greatest wonder in all the world? And Yudhishthira answered: that every day men see other creatures die and depart to the abode of Death, and yet those who remain behind live as though they themselves will live forever; this is the greatest wonder. And what accompanies a man in death? Not his wealth, not his kin, not his fame, but dharma alone; that alone goes with the soul.
And the Yaksha, pleased with his wisdom, offered to restore one of the four dead brothers to life, and told Yudhishthira to choose which. And Yudhishthira chose Nakula. And the Yaksha, surprised, asked why he chose Nakula, a son of Mādrī, over his own full brothers, the mighty Bhīma or the great Arjuna. And Yudhishthira answered: I am the son of Kuntī, and one son of Kuntī, myself, still lives; but Mādrī, my father's other wife, has no living son; and justice between my two mothers requires that a son of Mādrī should live as well as a son of Kuntī. Let Nakula live, that both my mothers may have a son. And the Yaksha was delighted beyond measure with this answer, for it showed a perfect and impartial justice, a fairness that held even between his own blood and his stepmother's, even in the extremity of grief; and he revealed himself as Lord Dharma, Yudhishthira's own divine father, come to test his son; and he restored all four brothers to life, and blessed them, and gave them a boon that they should pass their coming thirteenth year unrecognized. So the long exile drew toward its end, and Yudhishthira, tested to the last, was found true.

title: Virāṭa Nagari
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The thirteenth year had come, the hardest of all, for in this final year the Pāṇḍavas had to live in the midst of a peopled kingdom, in disguise, unrecognized, and if they were discovered before the year was out, the whole cycle of exile would begin again. So they came out of the wild forest and into the civilized court of King Virāṭa of the Matsya country, and there they had to lay down every mark of their royalty, their armour and their weapons and their very names, and take on the humble garments of servants. And this disguise, the tellers note, was itself a spiritual discipline: the shedding of the outer, temporary self, the surrender of pride and rank and identity, while the inner and eternal soul held steady to its purpose beneath the servant's dress.
They hid their celestial weapons in a leather bag high in a Shamī tree near the cremation grounds, where no common traveller would dare to touch it; and then each took on a disguise. Yudhishthira, the king, became Kanka, a learned brāhmaṇa who could entertain the king with dice and astrology and scriptural talk. The mighty Bhīma, who could slay demons, became Valala, a humble cook. Arjuna, master of the celestial weapons, turned a curse he had received from the nymph Urvashī into a shelter, and became Brihannalā, a teacher of dance to the princess Uttarā, living as a eunuch. Nakula became the keeper of the king's horses, and Sahadeva the keeper of his cattle. And Draupadī, the empress, became Sairandhrī, a serving-woman to Queen Sudeshṇā, dressing her hair and doing light domestic tasks.
There is a deep lesson in this year of disguise, and it is worth pausing on, for it completes the teaching of the whole exile. The greatest souls of their age, a king, warriors whose strength shook the earth, an empress, laid down every outward token of their greatness and served in humble stations, and did it without complaint, holding their true selves steady and hidden beneath the servant's garb. And they were not diminished by it; the king was a king still, in the cook's kitchen and the serving-woman's chamber, for their greatness was in their souls and not in their robes. It is the final proof of the truth the exile had been teaching them: that the outer fortunes, rank and title and finery, are only garments, and that the soul beneath is untouched by their putting-on or their putting-off; and that one who knows this can wear a crown or a servant's dress with equal steadiness, being neither exalted by the one nor humbled by the other.
But the year did not pass in peace, for the queen's brother Kīchaka, the powerful commander of Virāṭa's armies, saw Sairandhrī and was seized with a violent lust for her. She warned him that she was guarded by unseen and terrible husbands, but he would not be deterred, and pursued her relentlessly, even scheming with the queen to trap her; and when at last he laid hands on her, she wrenched free and fled to the royal assembly, where Kīchaka, before the very eyes of King Virāṭa, kicked her to the ground, and the whole assembly sat silent in fear of his power. And Draupadī, weeping in her helpless agony, went in the dead of night to Bhīma, and Bhīma's rage flared up, and he swore to end Kīchaka's life. And by a careful plan, Sairandhrī pretended to yield, and invited Kīchaka to a secret midnight meeting in the darkened dancing hall; and when Kīchaka came there expecting the woman, he found instead Bhīma waiting in the dark, and in a brutal silent struggle Bhīma crushed him into a shapeless mass, and so avenged Draupadī and proved once more that those who abuse the helpless are consumed, in the end, by the swift reaction of their own sins.

title: Matsya Defended and Prince Uttara
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The strange and violent death of Kīchaka struck terror into the people of Matsya, who guessed that Sairandhrī was guarded by fearful powers; and word of it reached the searchers of Duryodhana, who had been hunting the Pāṇḍavas in vain for nearly the whole year. And they began to suspect that the mysterious slayer of Kīchaka was Bhīma, and Sairandhrī was Draupadī, and that the Pāṇḍavas were hidden in Matsya. And so Duryodhana, together with King Susharmā of Trigarta, devised a double invasion of Matsya, hoping to force the Pāṇḍavas into the open before the thirteenth year should end and so trap them into another twelve years of exile.
Susharmā struck first, from the south, seizing the royal cattle and ravaging the southern lands; and King Virāṭa marched out to meet him, and with him went his four humble servants, Kanka and Valala and the two keepers of horse and cattle, who volunteered to ride to their king's defence. And in the battle Susharmā captured Virāṭa and threw the Matsya army into panic; but at Yudhishthira's command Bhīma charged the enemy, broke their ranks, and rescued the captured king. And here again the story marks the virtue of gratitude, for these disguised princes risked their lives and their secret to save the king who had unknowingly sheltered them, repaying his shelter with their protection.
But this southern attack was only a feint, for the moment Virāṭa and his army had marched south, the main Kaurava host swept down from the north, led by Bhīshma and Droṇa and Kripa and Karṇa and Duryodhana himself, seizing the royal herds; and with the king and the army away in the south, the city lay undefended. And there remained only the young prince Uttara, boastful and untried, who declared loudly before the ladies of the court that he would rout the whole Kaurava army single-handed, if only he could find a charioteer to drive him. And Sairandhrī suggested that Brihannalā, the dance-teacher, had once served as Arjuna's own charioteer; and so, reluctantly, the prince took the disguised Arjuna to drive him against the Kauravas.
But when they came within sight of the great Kaurava host, and Uttara beheld the terrible standards of Bhīshma and Droṇa and the radiant armour of Karṇa, his boasting collapsed into terror, and he flung down his bow and leapt from the chariot and fled toward the city in panic. And Arjuna ran after the fleeing prince, and caught him, and dragged him back to the chariot, and made him a promise: that Arjuna himself would fight the whole Kaurava army, if only Uttara would hold the reins and guide the horses. So the boaster who could not fight became the charioteer, and the servant who had seemed nothing became the warrior; and the true worth beneath the outward show was about to be revealed.

title: The Promise Fulfilled
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Arjuna had Uttara drive to the Shamī tree by the cremation grounds, and there, over the prince's fear of touching what hung in a tree by a burning-ground, he had him climb up and bring down the leather bag; and when it was opened, Uttara beheld weapons that blazed like the sun, and among them the legendary Gāṇḍīva. And Arjuna revealed to the trembling prince who he truly was: that he was Arjuna, and that the five servants of Virāṭa's court, and Sairandhrī, were the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī themselves, come out of their hiding at last.
The very touch of the Gāṇḍīva sent a surge of courage through Uttara's heart, and he took up the reins gladly now, while Arjuna drew on his gauntlets and twanged the great bow, and its sound rolled like thunder across the plains of Matsya. And on the other side, Droṇa heard that sound and knew it, and turned to Bhīshma and said: the great archer Arjuna has come. And Duryodhana was elated, for if Arjuna had truly been discovered before the thirteenth year was out, the Pāṇḍavas would be bound to return to the forest for twelve years more.
And here a sharp dispute broke out among the Kuru leaders, and it revealed their souls. Karṇa boasted that he would slay Arjuna single-handed; and Ashvatthāmā, Droṇa's son, rebuked him sternly, reminding the whole assembly that the kingdom had been won not by heroism but by the fraud of loaded dice, and that Arjuna's Gāṇḍīva would answer them now with sharp arrows, not with numbers thrown on a gaming board. But it was Bhīshma, the wise patriarch, who settled the matter, for he made a precise reckoning of the movements of the stars and the planets, and declared that the thirteen years of exile and hiding had in fact ended the day before, that the term was fully and honourably complete, and that the Pāṇḍavas' vow had been kept to the letter. So even the enemy's own patriarch confirmed that the Pāṇḍavas had fulfilled their pledge exactly.
Then Arjuna charged the Kaurava host; but before he fought, he did a thing that reveals him, for as he passed his revered teachers Bhīshma and Droṇa, he saluted them, shooting arrows that fell gently at their feet in reverence rather than in war. And then he routed the Kaurava army, recovered the royal cattle, and returned in triumph, and, to guard the disguise a little longer until the formal unmasking, he let the young prince Uttara take the public credit for the victory. So the exile ended, the vow fulfilled to the day, and the Pāṇḍavas stood ready at last to reclaim what was theirs.

title: Taking Counsel
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The thirteen years complete, the Pāṇḍavas shed their disguises and settled openly in the city of Upaplavya in the Matsya land, and sent word to their friends and kinsmen; and they came. Krishna and his brother Balarāma came from Dvārakā, with Subhadrā and the young hero Abhimanyu; Drupada of Pānchāla came with his forces, and Shikhaṇḍī, and Draupadī's sons. And the wedding of Abhimanyu to Virāṭa's daughter Uttarā was celebrated, binding the houses of Matsya and Pānchāla and the Yādavas into a single alliance.
Then the kings met in council to decide their course, and Krishna rose and set the matter fairly before them. He reminded them that Yudhishthira had been cheated at the dice and robbed of his rightful kingdom, and that justice was wholly on the Pāṇḍavas' side; and yet, he said, Yudhishthira had no desire for bloodshed, and the right course was to send an able envoy to Hastināpura to seek a peaceful settlement, the return of half the kingdom, without war.
But the council was divided, and the division is worth marking. Balarāma supported peace, but in doing so he faulted Yudhishthira, saying that he had gambled obstinately against all warning and so should now go humbly and beg for his rights. And this stung Sātyaki, who rose in indignation and declared that Yudhishthira was no beggar and need beg from no one; that to let the Kauravas keep the stolen kingdom would be like confirming a thief in his theft; and that they should prepare for war at once. And Drupada took Sātyaki's side, saying that soft words would never move Duryodhana, and that while they might send an envoy to fulfil the forms of diplomacy, they must at the same time prepare for war with all their strength. And Krishna agreed with this course, and, having ties of affection with both sides, returned to Dvārakā, leaving Drupada's envoy to carry the formal terms of peace to Hastināpura, while both sides made ready for war.

title: Arjuna's Charioteer
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
As the drums of war began to sound, both sides understood that the alliance of Krishna would weigh more than any army; and so both Duryodhana and Arjuna set out in haste to Dvārakā to win his support, and by chance they arrived on the very same day. Duryodhana came first, and finding Krishna asleep, seated himself proudly at the head of the bed; Arjuna came shortly after, and stood humbly at the foot, his hands folded in reverence.
When Krishna woke, his eyes fell first upon Arjuna standing at his feet; then, turning, he saw Duryodhana at his head. Duryodhana at once claimed precedence, arguing that he had arrived first. But Krishna answered that though Duryodhana had come first, he himself had seen Arjuna first on waking, and so his help was owed equally to both. And he offered them a choice between two forms of aid: on one side his vast and undefeated army, the Nārāyaṇī Sena, thousands of veteran warriors; and on the other side Krishna himself, alone, unarmed, pledged never to lift a weapon or take part in the fighting. And because custom gave the younger man the first choice, he offered it to Arjuna.
And Arjuna, without a moment's hesitation, bowed and chose Krishna, unarmed though he would be. And Duryodhana could scarcely hide his delight at what he took for Arjuna's folly, and gladly claimed the mighty army for himself. And when Duryodhana had gone, Krishna asked Arjuna why he had chosen a weaponless non-combatant over an invincible host. And Arjuna answered: I do not doubt my own power to defeat the enemy; but I long for your presence, to guide my chariot and to light my path. And in that choice lies the whole heart of the matter, and the whole difference between the two cousins: Duryodhana chose the army, the outward power, the countable strength; Arjuna chose the Lord, unarmed, wanting not his weapons but his presence and his guidance. The one grasped at force; the other sought the Divine itself, and asked for nothing but that it be near him; and in that difference the war was, in a sense, already decided, for the side that has the Lord's presence, even unarmed, has more than the side that has all the armies of the earth.

title: Shalya against His Nephews
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
King Shalya of Madra, the maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva, heard that his nephews the Pāṇḍavas were preparing for war, and he mustered a great army and marched to join them. But Duryodhana learned of his coming, and devised a cunning trick to steal him away. Along the whole route of Shalya's march, Duryodhana had beautiful rest-houses built, and lavished upon Shalya and his soldiers such splendid feasts and hospitality that Shalya, assuming all this bounty came from his nephew Yudhishthira, was deeply moved, and called for the host to be brought so that he might reward him. And at that moment Duryodhana stepped forward and revealed that he himself was the host.
And Shalya, a man of honour, was stunned, but bound by his own gratitude, and asked how he might repay such hospitality. And Duryodhana at once demanded that Shalya fight on the Kaurava side. And Shalya, held fast by the ancient code that one who has eaten a host's food is indebted to grant his request, agreed, though he bitterly regretted that he had been tricked into betraying his own nephews.
Then Shalya went on to Upaplavya to confess his mistake to Yudhishthira. And Yudhishthira, hiding his disappointment, acknowledged that the promise was binding and must be kept. But he made a request, for he knew that Shalya was the equal of Krishna in the driving of a chariot, and that Duryodhana would surely make Shalya the charioteer of Karṇa in his final duel with Arjuna. When that hour comes, Yudhishthira asked, use your place to dishearten Karṇa, to deflate his pride, to weaken his spirit, and so protect Arjuna's life. And Shalya agreed: he would fight honourably on the Kaurava side, as his vow required, but he would use his tongue, as Karṇa's charioteer, to undermine Karṇa's confidence and so shield Arjuna. So even among the enemy's forced allies, the Pāṇḍavas had a hidden friend.

title: Krishna's Mission
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Despite all the vast preparations for war, Krishna resolved to make one last solemn attempt to prevent the catastrophe that would consume the whole warrior race, and he went himself to Hastināpura as an envoy of peace. The citizens thronged the streets to see the Lord; and Duryodhana, hoping to buy his favour, prepared lavish gifts and a grand feast. But Krishna passed by Duryodhana's palace and chose instead to lodge in the humble house of Vidura, and spent the night in quiet talk and in comforting Kuntī, who wept over the coming tragedy.
The next day Krishna entered the royal court, and declined Duryodhana's feast, saying famously that an envoy eats only after his mission is accomplished. And addressing the blind king Dhritarāshtra, he made a moving plea for peace, asking now not for half the kingdom, but for only five villages, one for each of the five brothers, that the whole quarrel might be settled honourably and the war averted. And Dhritarāshtra agreed with the plea, but confessed his utter helplessness over his own sons. Then Krishna turned to Duryodhana and urged him to cast off his envy and save his race from destruction; and Bhīshma and Droṇa and Vidura all joined in pressing him to yield. But Duryodhana, furious at being rebuked before the court, declared that the Pāṇḍavas had lost their kingdom fairly at play and that he would never yield to threats, that he would not give them even so much land as could be balanced on the point of a needle.
And more than refuse, Duryodhana and his associates plotted to seize Krishna himself and bind him prisoner. And Krishna, knowing their plan, laughed, and revealed in that hall his cosmic form, the Vishvarūpa, his single body containing the whole universe, all the worlds and all beings within him, a vision of overwhelming divinity. And the blind Dhritarāshtra, by the Lord's grace, was given sight for a moment to behold it; and having seen the Supreme thus, he begged to be made blind again, for he wished never after to look upon any lesser, worldly thing. And Krishna withdrew the vision and departed from the court, his mission of peace refused; and with its failure, the great war became a certainty that nothing could now prevent.

title: Attachment and Duty
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
With the peace mission failed, Kuntī was overwhelmed with grief, for now the war of total destruction was unavoidable; and worst of all to her was the thought that her firstborn son, Karṇa, the child she had abandoned, would stand on the enemy's side against his own brothers, who did not even know he was their kin. And so she resolved to seek him out and reveal to him the secret of his birth, hoping to save him, and to save her other sons from having to kill him.
She went to the banks of the Yamunā, where Karṇa performed his daily worship of the Sun, and stood silently behind him, and shielded his back from the burning sun with the hem of her garment as she waited. And when Karṇa finished and turned and saw the queen of Hastināpura standing there, he bowed in respect and wondered at her coming. And Kuntī told him the truth: that he was the firstborn son of the Sun God, born of her own womb before her marriage; that he was no charioteer's son but a prince, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas; and she begged him to join his true brothers and be crowned emperor as the eldest, and so end the war.
And Karṇa felt a quiet warmth in his heart, and sensed that the Sun himself endorsed his mother's plea; and yet, with a great effort of will, he mastered his feeling and refused her. And his refusal is one of the most moving speeches in the epic, for it is spoken without bitterness and with a terrible dignity. You abandoned me, he said, as a helpless newborn, and cast me on the river, and robbed me of my birthright and my mother's love; and it was Duryodhana who took me up when all the world rejected me, who gave me honour and trust and a kingdom when I was scorned as a low-born. To desert him now, on the eve of battle, for the sake of a birth I never knew, would be the blackest treachery and the basest ingratitude, unworthy of a true warrior. I cannot do it. I will stand with the one who stood by me.
And yet, Karṇa said, your plea shall not be wholly in vain. And he made her a promise, a promise of heartbreaking generosity: that he would spare the lives of four of her sons, Yudhishthira, Bhīma, Nakula, and Sahadeva, whatever they did to him; that he would raise his hand against Arjuna alone. So that whether Karṇa fell to Arjuna or Arjuna to Karṇa, Kuntī would still have five living sons at the end; either her four spared ones and Arjuna, or her four spared ones and Karṇa himself. Either way, she would have five. And Kuntī, overwhelmed by the nobility of this doomed and generous soul, this son she had wronged so deeply and who yet gave her so much, embraced him in silence, and went away, resigning herself to the workings of a destiny that not even a mother's love could now turn aside.
Here is the whole tragedy of Karṇa gathered into a single scene, and it is worth holding in the heart. Everything noble in him is on display: his loyalty, his gratitude, his refusal to betray the friend who had honoured him, his generosity even toward the mother who had abandoned him and the brothers who would fight him. And all of it is bent, by the wound of his abandonment and the debt of his gratitude, toward a doomed and wrongful cause, so that his very virtues chain him to the side of adharma and to his own death. He is the great tragic figure of the epic, the good and generous soul ruined by a wrong done to him at his very birth, holding fast to his loyalty and his honour even as they carry him to his doom; and the story asks us not to condemn him but to grieve for him, for there is no one in all the tale more sinned against, and few who bear their sinning with a nobler heart.

title: An Introduction to the Bhagavad Gītā
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: An Introduction to the Bhagavad Gītā

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
On the holy plain of Kurukshetra the two vast armies stood arrayed, sheathed in steel, bearing weapons of terrible power. In all, eighteen akshauhinis stood gathered upon that field: eleven under the standard of the aged patriarch Bhīshma for the Kauravas, and seven under Dhrishtadyumna for the Pāṇḍavas; and the field was a great pageant of banners, the palm tree of Bhīshma, the ascetic's bowl of Droṇa, the bull of Kripa, the boar of Jayadratha, the outspread cobra-hood of Duryodhana. The air was torn with the blowing of conches, the trumpeting of war-elephants, the thunder of the royal drums.

An akshauhini was reckoned by a fixed and ancient arithmetic. One elephant, one chariot, three horses, and five foot-soldiers made a patti; three pattis a sena-mukha; three sena-mukhas a gulma; three gulmas a gana; three ganas a vahini; three vahinis a pruthana; three pruthanas a chamu; three chamus an anikini; and ten anikinis, at last, one akshauhini -- 21,870 chariots, as many elephants, 65,610 horses, and 109,350 foot-soldiers. Eighteen such hosts stood that day at Kurukshetra: the greatest army the earth had ever borne to war.
And at this supreme moment, as the great conches sounded and the Gāṇḍīva was raised, Arjuna asked Krishna to drive his chariot into the space between the two armies, that he might look upon those he was about to fight. And Krishna drove him there, into the middle of the field, between the arrayed hosts.
And Arjuna looked, and what he saw undid him. For he did not see faceless enemies. He saw his own teachers, Bhīshma who had held him on his knee, Droṇa who had taught him the bow; he saw his uncles, his cousins, the companions of his childhood, standing there ready to be killed and to kill. And in an instant his whole resolve collapsed. His hands trembled; his mouth went dry; the mighty Gāṇḍīva slipped from his grasp; and he sank down in his chariot in an anguish of despair. What victory could be worth this? he cried. What joy, what righteousness, could there be in a kingdom won by the slaughter of my own kinsmen, my elders, my teachers, my blood? Better to be killed myself than to win such a victory. And he cast down his bow and would not fight.
Let us understand what has happened here, for it is the doorway to the whole great teaching that follows, and it is not what it first appears. Arjuna's collapse is not cowardice; the greatest warrior of his age does not suddenly lose his physical courage. It is something deeper and more terrible: a crisis of the whole understanding, the moment when a soul, standing at the point of its hardest duty, is overwhelmed by the weight of it and by the tangle of its own attachments, and cannot see its way. Arjuna is paralyzed not by fear but by grief and confusion, by the collision of his duty as a warrior with his love for those he must fight, by the sudden horror of the thing he was born and trained to do. And it is precisely here, at the bottom of this despair, when all his human resources have failed him and he turns at last, helpless, to Krishna and asks to be taught, that the greatest of all dialogues begins. For it is only when we have come to the end of our own understanding, and know that we have, and turn for guidance to something higher, that the deepest teaching can reach us; and Arjuna, broken on the field between the armies, casting down his bow and turning to the Lord, becomes the pupil to whom the eternal wisdom can at last be given.

title: The Field and the Knower
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
To lift Arjuna from his despair, Krishna did not begin with strategy or with exhortation, but with the deepest metaphysics, with the truth about the soul; for Arjuna's grief rested on a false belief, that in killing the body one destroys the person, and the whole despair could be dissolved only by uprooting that false belief at its source.
The wise, Krishna told him, grieve neither for the living nor for the dead:
अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे।
गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः॥

ashochyān anvashochas tvaṁ prajñāvādāṁsh cha bhāṣase
gatāsūn agatāsūṁsh cha nānushochanti paṇḍitāḥ
You grieve, Krishna said, for that which is not worthy of grief, while speaking words of wisdom; but the wise do not mourn for the living or the dead. For there was never a time when I was not, nor you, nor any of these kings, nor shall we ever cease to be. The soul does not die when the body dies. And he gave the great image, which the whole book has been circling since Yayāti's day:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही॥

vāsāṁsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya navāni gṛhṇāti naro 'parāṇi
tathā sharīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇāny anyāni saṁyāti navāni dehī
As a person casts off worn-out garments and puts on new ones, so the soul casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones. The soul is not born and does not die; it is unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient; it is not slain when the body is slain:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे॥

na jāyate mriyate vā kadāchin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ
ajo nityaḥ shāshvato 'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne sharīre
The soul, Krishna taught, cannot be cut by any weapon, nor burned by fire, nor wetted by water, nor dried by wind; it is unbreakable, unburnable, eternal, present everywhere, unchanging, immovable, everlasting. And knowing this, Arjuna, you should not grieve; for the body is perishable and was always going to perish, but the dweller in the body is beyond all harm.
This is the foundation of the whole teaching, and it is worth resting on before we go further, for it changes everything. Arjuna grieved because he believed that in this battle he would destroy the very being of his kinsmen; and Krishna's first answer is that no one can destroy the being of anyone, that the soul is untouchable, that what falls in battle is only the outer garment while the wearer passes on. This is not offered as a cold comfort or an excuse for slaughter; it is offered as the deep truth about what we are, that we are not these perishable bodies but the eternal souls that wear them, infinitesimal fragments of the Supreme, indestructible and everlasting. And from this truth flows a great freedom: the freedom from the terror of death, both our own and others', the understanding that the deepest self is beyond all that can be done to the body, and that our grief, real as it is, mourns the garment and not the soul. All the rest of the Gītā's teaching rests on this ground: that the self is eternal, and that to know this is to be freed from the fear that paralyzes us.

title: God, Nature, and Right Action
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Having shown Arjuna the eternal nature of the soul, Krishna turned to the nature of the world and of action, to the great question that Arjuna's paralysis had raised: what should a soul do, and how, and in what spirit?
The whole physical universe, Krishna taught, with all its changing forms, is the lower energy of the Divine, called Prakriti, material nature; and behind it and within it stands the Supreme, Paramātma, whose will upholds all its changes. And the individual soul, the jīvātma, is an eternal fragment of the Supreme, which, bound in material nature, struggles with the mind and the senses, and passes from body to body carrying its accumulated tendencies as the wind carries fragrance from place to place. And the soul is bound to this wheel of birth and death by one thing above all: by its clinging to the fruits of its actions, by its desire to be the doer and to seize the rewards of what it does.
And now Krishna gave the great practical teaching, the one that answers Arjuna's despair directly, the doctrine of nishkāma karma, action without desire for its fruits:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि॥

karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadāchana
mā karmaphalahetur bhūr mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi
You have a right to your action, Krishna said, but never to its fruits. Do not act for the sake of the reward; but do not, on that account, fall into inaction either. Here is the resolution of Arjuna's whole crisis. He must not abandon his duty and flee the battle; that would be a failure of his dharma. But neither must he fight for the sake of the kingdom, the victory, the fruits; that grasping is the very thing that binds the soul. He must fight because it is his duty, his dharma as a warrior and as the defender of the right, and he must fight with his whole strength, but with complete detachment from what the fighting will win him, offering the action itself as a consecrated thing and leaving its fruits to the Divine.
This is one of the deepest and most liberating teachings the world has been given, and it is worth dwelling on, for it applies not to Arjuna alone but to every one of us in every duty we face. We are torn, so often, between two errors: between grasping so hard at the fruits of our action that we are enslaved by hope and fear and are corrupted into doing wrong to gain our ends; and, on the other side, between despairing and abandoning our duty altogether because its fruits seem too painful or too uncertain. And the Gītā's answer cuts between them: do your duty, fully, with all your strength, because it is your duty; but release your grip on its fruits, do not act for the reward, offer the action itself and let the outcome be what it will be. To act so is to be free: free from the anxiety of the grasping, free from the paralysis of the despairing, free to do the right thing wholly for its own sake. The action continues, for the world's order must be upheld and our duties must be done; but the selfish desire behind it is surrendered, and in that surrender the soul is freed from the very bondage that action would otherwise create. The doer becomes a witness; the modes of nature do the work; and the self, offering all to the Divine, remains untouched and free.

title: Mind Control and Devotion
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
To act without desire for the fruits, Krishna taught, a soul must master its own mind and senses, and this is the hardest of all conquests; and Krishna named plainly the enemies that must be overcome and the way to overcome them.
The senses, he warned, are so strong and turbulent that they can carry away by force even the mind of a wise man who is striving to control them. And he traced the whole descent into ruin, step by step, in one of the most famous passages of the Gītā:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते।
सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते॥

dhyāyato viṣayān puṁsaḥ saṅgas teṣūpajāyate
saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho 'bhijāyate
Dwelling on the objects of the senses, Krishna said, a man forms attachment to them; from attachment springs desire; from desire, when it is thwarted, springs anger; from anger comes delusion; from delusion, the loss of memory and understanding; and from the loss of understanding, the man is utterly ruined. This is the whole mechanism of our destruction, traced from its small beginning in a wandering thought to its end in total ruin; and we have watched it work itself out through the whole epic, in Yayāti's endless desire, in Duryodhana's envy, in the anger that undid sage after sage. And Krishna names, as the three gates of self-destruction, lust, anger, and greed, and bids us abandon all three.
The story sets beside this teaching a lovely image of what mastery looks like: a duck swims in the lake, moving through the water all day, and yet when it steps onto the land it gives a single vigorous shake and every drop rolls off, and it is perfectly dry. So must the seeker live in the world, moving through all its affairs, and yet be able to shake off its clinging temptations and remain, in the soul, spotless and detached. To be in the world and not soaked by it, to act and not be stained by the action, this is the mastery the Gītā teaches.
But Krishna knew, and said, that to subdue the mind by one's own effort alone is fearfully hard, almost beyond human power; and so he revealed the deepest secret of all, the highest teaching of the whole Gītā: bhakti, loving devotion, and sharaṇāgati, complete and unconditional surrender to the Divine. For those who cannot master the mind by their own strength, there is a surer way, which is to give the whole self, mind and action and all, to the Lord, in love and in surrender, and to let him carry the burden. And the Lord makes a promise to such souls, the most comforting promise in all the scripture:
अनन्याश्चिन्तयन्तो मां ये जनाः पर्युपासते।
तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां योगक्षेमं वहाम्यहम्॥

ananyāsh chintayanto māṁ ye janāḥ paryupāsate
teṣāṁ nityābhiyuktānāṁ yogakṣemaṁ vahāmy aham
Those who worship me with undivided devotion, always thinking of me, Krishna promised, to them I myself carry what they lack and preserve what they have; I take up their burden as my own. And he asked for no grand offering, but only love:
पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति।
तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः॥

patraṁ puṣpaṁ phalaṁ toyaṁ yo me bhaktyā prayachchhati
tad ahaṁ bhaktyupahṛtam ashnāmi prayatātmanaḥ
Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, Krishna said, that offering of love, made by a pure heart, I accept and delight in. And this, the tellers note, is the very truth we saw in Shabari's half-eaten berries and the squirrel's grains of sand in the other epic: that the Divine looks not at the greatness of the offering but at the love with which it is given, and that the humblest gift, given with a whole heart, is received and cherished. The leaf, the flower, the fruit, the water, the simplest things, offered in love, are enough; for it is the love, and not the gift, that the Lord receives. And in this surrender, this loving offering of the whole self, lies the way that is open to everyone, the high and the low, the learned and the simple, who cannot conquer the mind alone but can give their hearts.

title: The Vision of the Universal Form
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Vision of the Universal Form

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
To dispel the last of Arjuna's doubt, and to give him not merely the teaching but the direct sight of the truth, Krishna granted him divine vision, and revealed his cosmic form, the Vishvarūpa, the Universal Form; and Sanjaya, given divine sight by Vyāsa, described the terrifying and magnificent vision to the blind king Dhritarāshtra far away in his palace.
For in the single body of Krishna, Arjuna beheld the whole universe: all the worlds and all the galaxies, the sun and the moon and the stars, the gods and the sages and all beings, all the elements of nature, the whole of creation gathered into one boundless cosmic form, without beginning or middle or end, blazing with the light of a thousand suns. It was a vision of overwhelming majesty, beautiful beyond bearing. And it was also terrible, for within that form Arjuna saw the face of Time itself, Kāla, with its blazing devouring mouths, and into those mouths he saw the warriors of both armies rushing to their destruction, Bhīshma and Droṇa and Karṇa and all the hosts of Kurukshetra pouring into the jaws of Time and being ground to nothing. And he understood that their destruction was already ordained, that Time itself had already consumed them, that he was but the instrument through which a doom already decreed would be accomplished.
And Arjuna, overwhelmed, terrified, humbled to the depths, bowed down before the vision and poured out his praise and his fear together, saluting the Lord again and again, from every side, acknowledging him as the source and the end of all, as father and creator and refuge of the worlds. And he begged forgiveness, in words of great tenderness, for all the times he had treated Krishna carelessly as a mere friend and companion, not knowing his true greatness: as a father forgives his son, he prayed, as a friend forgives his friend, as a lover forgives the beloved, so forgive me, Lord, my familiarity, my thoughtless words. And, unable to bear the terror of the cosmic form, he begged Krishna to withdraw it and to return to his familiar, gentle, human shape. And Krishna, in his grace, resumed his beautiful human form, and comforted his frightened friend.
And with that the great dialogue drew to its close, its purpose accomplished; for Arjuna's doubt was gone, his understanding restored, his heart anchored now in devotion, and he rose up ready to take up his bow and do his duty, no longer as a grasping man seeking a kingdom, but as a willing instrument of the Divine will, acting without attachment to the fruits, surrendered to the Lord. And here we may gather the whole teaching of the Gītā into a single thread, for all its many paths converge in the end upon one thing. The path of knowledge, which knows the eternal soul; the path of action, which does its duty without grasping at the fruits; the path of meditation, which stills and masters the mind: all of these are true, and all are taught, and all lead upward. But they find their ultimate perfection and their surest fulfillment in the path of loving devotion and surrender, in the giving of the whole self to the Divine; for this is the way that is open to all, that carries even those who cannot master the rest, and that lifts the soul above the bondage of material nature toward its final liberation. This is the heart of the Gītā, spoken on the field of battle at the hour of the world's greatest crisis: that we must do our duty, fully and without grasping, and surrender the whole of ourselves, in love, to the Lord who upholds all and receives all and carries the burden of all who turn to him. And having heard it, Arjuna took up his bow; and the great and terrible war began.

title: The Battle Begins
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The great war of Kurukshetra erupted with the blare of a thousand conches and the thunder of eighteen divisions, and the plain became a terrifying arena where the strength of men clashed against the unbending laws of cosmic justice. For ten days the aged Bhīshma led the Kaurava host as its supreme commander, and he raged across the field like a consuming fire, so swift in his movements that to the bewildered Pāṇḍava soldiers he seemed to multiply into a hundred Bhīshmas, laying waste their ranks.
The first days went hard for the Pāṇḍavas. Young Prince Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, was impaled by Shalya's javelin and fell lifeless; his brother Shveta, avenging him, broke Bhīshma's standard before Bhīshma pierced him too with a fatal shaft. And the unchecked onslaught of the patriarch threw Yudhishthira into despair, until Krishna comforted him and steadied him. Stung by Duryodhana's bitter charge that he was sparing the Pāṇḍavas out of love, Bhīshma fought with terrible heroism; and when Arjuna, paralyzed by reverence and love for the grandfather who had raised him, held back his hand and shot weak, hesitant arrows, Krishna's righteous anger flamed up. To defend the cause of dharma, Krishna flung down the reins, leapt from the chariot, and caught up a broken chariot wheel, brandishing it like his discus, vowing to slay Bhīshma himself; and Arjuna threw himself at the Lord's feet, weeping, begging him not to break his sacred vow never to fight, and pledging to cast off his hesitation and do his warrior's duty.
But Bhīshma could not be beaten while he chose to fight, and the Pāṇḍavas at last resorted to a solemn stratagem to release him. For Bhīshma had vowed never to raise a weapon against one who had been born a woman; and so they placed Shikhaṇḍī, who had been born the woman Ambā and reborn to be Bhīshma's death, at the front of Arjuna's chariot. And when Bhīshma saw Shikhaṇḍī, he recognized the reincarnation of the woman he had wronged so long ago, and he understood that his hour had come; and he laid down his weapons and stood peaceful amid the storm of battle. And Arjuna, screened behind Shikhaṇḍī, steeled his heart and loosed a torrent of arrows that pierced the patriarch at every joint.
Bhīshma fell headlong from his chariot; but so densely was his body transfixed with arrows that it did not touch the earth, and he lay instead upon a bed of arrows, a bed of honour formed by Arjuna's own shafts. And as the great veteran lay there, waiting, for he had the power to choose the hour of his death and would not die until the auspicious northern turning of the sun, Arjuna, to quench his grandfather's thirst, drove an arrow into the earth and brought up a cool stream of water to his lips. And both armies stood in silent reverence around the fallen patriarch, the grandsire of them all, who lay dying by inches on his bed of arrows, keeping the war waiting upon his own chosen hour of death.
There is a deep sorrow at the heart of Bhīshma's fall, and it is the sorrow of his whole life come to its harvest. That terrible vow of his youth, the renunciation of throne and marriage and children for his father's sake, had bound him ever after to the throne of Hastināpura, whoever held it and however they used it; and so this best of men, this soul of honour, had been chained by his own vow to fight, at the last, for Duryodhana's unjust cause, against the very Pāṇḍavas whom he loved and knew to be in the right. His greatness and his tragedy were one: the vow that made him the wonder of the world made him also the prisoner of a lifetime, and set him at the end on the wrong side of the great war, to fall by the hand of a wrong he himself had done long ago. He fell released, at last, from the long bondage of his own magnificent renunciation.

title: Abhimanyu
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
After Bhīshma's fall, Droṇa was made supreme commander of the Kauravas, and he fought with the fury of a storm despite his years. On the thirteenth day he arrayed his forces in the Chakravyūha, the great wheel-formation, a maze of concentric circles designed to trap and hold; and he drew Arjuna far away to the south with a suicide-squad sworn to victory or death, so that with Arjuna gone, none among the Pāṇḍavas knew the secret of piercing the formation and coming safely out again, save Krishna alone.
None but one. For the young Abhimanyu, the sixteen-year-old son of Arjuna and Subhadrā, still almost a child, stepped forward to save his family's honour. He had learned the secret of entering the Chakravyūha, he said, while still in his mother's womb, overhearing his father tell it; but he had never learned the secret of coming out, for his mother had fallen asleep before the telling was done. And on the promise of Yudhishthira and Bhīma to follow close behind and guard his back, the boy broke through the outer circle of the formation like a bolt of lightning, scattering the veteran warriors before him.
But Jayadratha, king of the Sindhus, by a boon from Shiva, stood in the breach behind him and held back Yudhishthira and Bhīma and the twins, closing the gap, so that Abhimanyu was cut off, alone, deep in the hostile heart of the formation. And there the boy fought with a fury that was godlike. Alone, surrounded by the whole Kaurava vanguard, he defeated Karṇa, disarmed Droṇa, and struck down Duryodhana's own son. And Duryodhana, mad with grief and rage, commanded six of his greatest veterans, Droṇa, Kripa, Karṇa, Ashvatthāmā, and two others, to abandon every law of chivalry and fall upon the single isolated child together.
From behind, Karṇa cut his bowstring and killed his horses; others shattered his chariot; and the dauntless boy, stripped of chariot and weapons, stood on the bare earth and fought on with a chariot wheel held up like a discus, the very image of Vishṇu with the Sudarshana; and when that was smashed, he fought with a mace, until at last a blow to the head struck him down, and the child lay dead, six great warriors having combined against one boy to kill him. And the Kaurava warriors danced around his body in savage celebration, blowing their conches over a victory that would stand forever as the blackest stain on their honour.
When Arjuna returned at twilight and found his brothers silent and downcast, and learned how his firstborn had been surrounded and murdered by six veterans against every law of war, he twanged the Gāṇḍīva in a paroxysm of grief and swore a terrible oath: that before the sun set on the next day, he would slay Jayadratha, who had sealed the breach and doomed his son, or else enter the fire himself. The murder of Abhimanyu is the story's clearest picture of what happens when the banks of dharma are broken in war: that once the code of honour is abandoned, even by the noble, there is no floor to the descent, and grown men of great name will combine to butcher a lone child and dance over his corpse, and call it victory.

title: Somadatta's End
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The fourteenth day was the day of Arjuna's terrible oath, and Droṇa, knowing that Arjuna's failure to reach Jayadratha would mean Arjuna's own death by fire and so an effortless Kaurava victory, hid Jayadratha far in the rear, twelve miles back, behind layer upon layer of formation and the heavy guard of his greatest warriors. And Arjuna advanced like the Destroyer, his hands loosing an unending cloud of arrows, cutting his way through whole divisions toward the hidden king, racing the sun.
In the midst of this a deadly old feud flared between Sātyaki and Bhūrishravas, whose families had been enemies for generations. Bhūrishravas, a peerless swordsman, overpowered the wearied Sātyaki, dragged him across the ground, and raised his sword for the killing blow. And Krishna urged Arjuna to save his devoted disciple; and Arjuna, though it troubled his conscience to strike a warrior not engaged with him, loosed a shaft that severed Bhūrishravas's upraised arm. And the old warrior, bitterly reproaching Arjuna for striking him from the side unseen, cast down his weapons and sat in a posture of yoga to release his soul; but the impetuous Sātyaki, mad with wrath, rushed forward and struck off the head of the meditating warrior, an act of raw ungoverned passion that the whole field condemned. And here again the story sounds its warning: that once the banks of dharma are breached, the flood of adharma spares no one, and even the wronged and the righteous are swept into cruelty.
As the sun sank fast toward the west and Jayadratha remained out of reach, the Kauravas began to exult, certain now that Arjuna must fail and burn. And then Krishna, master of all appearances, veiled the sun, and made a false and premature dusk; and the Kaurava warriors, believing the day was done and themselves victorious, dropped their guard, and Jayadratha himself came forward, laughing, to watch Arjuna enter the flames. And in that instant Krishna withdrew the shadow, and the true sun blazed out still above the horizon, and Krishna cried to Arjuna to strike now. And Krishna warned him of one thing more: that Jayadratha's father had long ago pronounced a curse, that whoever made his son's head fall to the ground would have his own head burst into a hundred pieces. And so Arjuna, with supreme skill, loosed a shaft that struck off Jayadratha's head and kept it aloft on a stream of following arrows, carrying it twelve miles through the air to drop it into the very lap of Jayadratha's father, who sat at his evening prayers in a distant hermitage. And the startled father rose, and the head rolled from his lap to the ground, and his own head burst into fragments, and so the circle of the old curse closed upon its own author, and Arjuna's oath was fulfilled before the setting of the sun.

title: Droṇa Passes Away
parentTitle: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: JAYA: A Journey of the Mahabharata

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The fourteenth night brought no ceasefire, and the battle raged on by torchlight through the dark. And in that midnight fighting Ghatotkacha, Bhīma's mighty demon son, unleashed a terrifying campaign from the air, destroying whole divisions with his magic, until Karṇa, desperate to save his collapsing army, was forced to hurl at him the infallible Shakti spear, the one divine weapon Karṇa had hoarded all these years for his final duel with Arjuna. Ghatotkacha fell dead, but his vast body crushed a whole division as it fell; and so, even in dying, he served the cosmic design, for he drew from Karṇa the one weapon that would surely have killed Arjuna, spending it on himself and leaving Arjuna safe. This too is part of the deep pattern of the war, that the deaths of the Pāṇḍava side, terrible as they were, again and again drew out and exhausted the enemy's deadliest weapons, so that the losses served, in the hidden reckoning, the final victory.
On the fifteenth morning Droṇa fought with unchecked fury, and Krishna saw that while the preceptor held his weapons no force in the three worlds could defeat him, and that his one vulnerability was his love for his son Ashvatthāmā; if he believed his son dead, he would lay down his arms. So Bhīma killed a war-elephant that happened to be named Ashvatthāmā, and shouted across the field that Ashvatthāmā was dead. And Droṇa, doubting, turned to Yudhishthira, whose truthfulness was famed across the whole earth, and asked him if it was so. And here Yudhishthira faced the hardest moment of his life, pressed by Krishna to speak, for the good of dharma, a word that was not wholly true. And Yudhishthira said aloud: Ashvatthāmā is dead; and added, in a whisper the grieving father could not hear, the elephant, not the man.
