And now, too late, the demons began to see it, to understand that the man they had despised was the God they could not defeat, that their contempt for the human form had blinded them to the divine that wore it, and that they had warred, all unknowing, against the very Lord of the worlds. This recognition, dawning among the demons even as they fought and fell, gives the last phase of the war its peculiar character, for it is a war fought now by the doomed against a foe they have begun to know is divine, a hopeless resistance continued out of pride and loyalty and desperation against an enemy recognized, too late, as God himself. The demons who now came out to fight came out, many of them, knowing in their hearts that they could not win, that they fought the Supreme Lord, that their cause was doomed; and they came out anyway, out of loyalty to Rāvaṇa, out of the momentum of a war too far advanced to stop, out of the demon’s pride that would not surrender even to God; and they fell, one after another, into the doom they had begun to foresee.

And the recognition points forward, too, to the great confrontations still to come, to the death of Indrajit and the final duel with Rāvaṇa, in which the divine nature of Rāma, dawning now as a suspicion, would be made manifest in full, as the champion of dharma accomplished the doom for which he had descended into the world. The demons had begun to ask, Is this Nārāyaṇa himself? and the answer, which the whole story has known from the beginning, was yes; and the last chapters of the war would be the working-out of that answer, the Supreme Lord in human form bringing to its appointed end the evil that he had come into the world to destroy.

title: The Death of Indrajit
parentTitle: Sri Rama Charithram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The Death of Indrajit

Of all Rāvaṇa’s champions, the greatest and the most dangerous still remained: Indrajit, the conqueror of Indra, the master of sorcery, the one who had bound Rāma and Lakshmaṇa with the serpent-darts and would have slain them but for Garuḍa. And the death of Indrajit is the breaking of the backbone of Lankā’s defence, the fall of its mightiest warrior, and it came about through a combination of cunning matched against cunning, of Lakshmaṇa’s valour and Vibhīshaṇa’s knowledge, and it turned upon one of the cruelest of all Indrajit’s deceptions.

For Indrajit, seeing the war going against Lankā, resorted to his deepest sorceries, and among them he worked a deception aimed, like Rāvaṇa’s illusion of Rāma’s head, at breaking the enemy’s spirit through a counterfeit of grief. Indrajit conjured, by his magic, an illusion of Sītā, a perfect phantom of the captive queen, and he brought this phantom out where the vānara host could see it, and then, before their horrified eyes, he slew it, struck off the head of the false Sītā, murdered the phantom of Rāma’s wife in full view of the army, so that the vānaras should believe that Sītā herself was dead, that the whole purpose of the war was lost, that the queen they had come to rescue was slain, and should despair.

And the deception worked its horror, for the vānaras, seeing what they took to be Sītā murdered before them, were plunged into grief and despair, and the news reached Rāma, and even Rāma was stricken, believing for a terrible moment that Sītā was dead and all his labour come to nothing. The illusion spread its poison of despair through the host, exactly as Indrajit had intended, threatening to break the army’s spirit at the very moment when victory was near.

But Vibhīshaṇa knew better, and here again the righteous brother’s knowledge proved decisive. Vibhīshaṇa understood Indrajit’s sorceries, understood the workings of Lankā, and he saw through the deception at once. It is an illusion, he told Rāma and the grieving host; it is a phantom, a trick of Indrajit’s magic; Rāvaṇa would never permit Sītā to be killed, for he desires her still and holds her as his prize; the Sītā you saw slain was a conjured phantom, not the true queen, who lives yet in the Ashokavana. Do not despair; do not believe the illusion; it is a stratagem meant to break your spirit, and you must not let it. And more than that, Vibhīshaṇa understood the true purpose behind the illusion, and it was this understanding that turned the deception against its maker. Indrajit, Vibhīshaṇa explained, has worked this illusion not merely to grieve you but to buy himself time and cover, for he intends now to perform a secret sacrifice, a rite at the shrine of Nikumbhilā, by which he will gain a boon that will make him invincible, unbeatable by any foe. If he completes that sacrifice, he cannot be defeated; but the rite has a weakness, for while he performs it he is vulnerable, and if he is attacked and the sacrifice is interrupted before it is complete, then the boon is lost and he can be slain. The illusion of Sītā’s death was meant to occupy us with grief while he slips away to complete the rite; we must not be occupied; we must strike at the sacrifice before it is finished.

And so Lakshmaṇa was sent, guided by Vibhīshaṇa, to the secret shrine of Nikumbhilā, to find Indrajit at his sacrifice and to interrupt it and to slay him before the rite could make him invincible. It was a desperate and a crucial errand, for on it hung the whole war: if Indrajit completed his rite, he would be unbeatable and Lankā might yet prevail; if Lakshmaṇa could reach him and stop him and kill him, the greatest of the demon champions would fall and the war would be all but won. Lakshmaṇa went, with Vibhīshaṇa to guide him and a force of vānaras, to the hidden shrine, and there they found Indrajit at his dark sacrifice, and they fell upon him and interrupted the rite before it could be completed.

And then followed the greatest single combat of Lakshmaṇa’s life, for Indrajit, his sacrifice broken, his invincibility lost, turned in fury upon those who had interrupted him, and he and Lakshmaṇa fought a duel of tremendous and prolonged ferocity, the master of sorcery against the devoted brother, and it was a combat worthy of both, long and terrible and closely matched, the two of them contending with every weapon and every art, neither able for a long while to master the other. Indrajit was the mightier in sorcery, and he was fighting for his life and for Lankā’s last hope; Lakshmaṇa was fighting for Rāma and for Sītā and for the whole cause of dharma, sustained by his devotion and guided by Vibhīshaṇa’s knowledge; and the two of them fought until the shrine and the field around it shook with the fury of their contention.

And at the last, Lakshmaṇa prevailed. Summoning all his power, invoking a mighty weapon, sustained by the righteousness of his cause and the devotion that was his whole strength, Lakshmaṇa loosed the fatal shaft, and it struck Indrajit, and the conqueror of Indra, the master of sorcery, the mightiest of Rāvaṇa’s champions, fell dead upon the field, his head struck off, his terrible power ended at last. The greatest warrior of Lankā was slain, the backbone of its defence broken, its last real hope of victory destroyed, and Lakshmaṇa had accomplished the deed on which the whole war had turned. The fall of Indrajit was the decisive blow, and the tellers mark it as such, for with his death the outcome of the war was no longer in doubt. Lankā’s mightiest was gone; its sorceries were spent; its champions were fallen; only Rāvaṇa himself remained, and Rāvaṇa, for all his might, was one, and had already been defeated once and spared. The death of Indrajit meant the death of Lankā’s hope, and everyone on both sides knew it.

And it broke Rāvaṇa utterly, for Indrajit was his greatest son, his mightiest warrior, the last real bulwark of his kingdom, and to lose him was to lose everything but his own person and his pride. The tellers give us Rāvaṇa’s grief and rage at the death of Indrajit as the most terrible of all his griefs, for now he had lost his brother Kumbhakarṇa and his son Indrajit and champion after champion, his whole house emptied, his whole strength spent, and nothing left between him and the doom but himself. And out of that grief and rage, that final desperation, Rāvaṇa resolved at last to go out himself, in his full and final power, to meet Rāma in the last combat, to stake everything on his own might in a last duel with the champion of dharma, having nothing left to send and no one left to fight for him, the last demon standing against the doom that had consumed all the rest.

title: End of Rāvaṇa
parentTitle: Sri Rama Charithram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
End of Rāvaṇa

Rāvaṇa came out for the last time, in his full and final power, in the uttermost of his might and his despair, to meet Rāma in the last combat, and the death of Rāvaṇa is the climax of the whole war and of the whole story’s long movement toward the destruction of evil, and the tellers give it all the weight and splendour it deserves.

He came in a fury and a grandeur that surpassed anything he had shown before, for now he had nothing left to lose and everything to avenge, his brother and his sons and his champions all fallen, his kingdom crumbling, his doom upon him, and he poured into this last battle the whole of his terrible strength and his whole armoury of celestial weapons, resolved to destroy Rāma or to die. The final combat between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was a thing beyond all the combats that had gone before, a battle of such magnitude that the tellers say the gods themselves gathered to watch it, the very cosmos holding its breath as the champion of dharma and the lord of the demons met at last in the combat that would decide everything.

And it was long, and it was terrible, and it was not easily won, for Rāvaṇa in his final desperation was a foe of tremendous power, and the two of them contended with a fury that shook the worlds, hurling their celestial weapons against one another, the whole sky ablaze with the terrible astras they loosed, the earth trembling beneath the violence of their contention. And Rāma, though the mightier, found the demon king hard to bring down, for Rāvaṇa fought with the strength of despair and the whole accumulated power of his boons and his sorceries, and the combat raged on and on without decision, the two of them matched in a struggle that seemed as if it might never end.

And there was a wonder in the fighting that made Rāvaṇa seem almost undefeatable, for when Rāma struck off one of Rāvaṇa’s ten heads, another grew in its place; and when he struck off another, it too regrew; so that however many of the demon’s heads Rāma severed, they grew back as fast as they were cut, and Rāvaṇa could not be killed by the striking-off of his heads, for they were endlessly renewed. This was the fruit of an old boon or an old power, and it made the demon king seem proof against death, for the very means of killing him, the severing of his heads, availed nothing against their endless regrowth, and Rāma, cutting off head after head only to see them regrow, could not by that means bring his enemy down.

And there came a point in the long combat when even Rāma grew weary, when the endless struggle against the seemingly undefeatable demon wore upon him, when the battle seemed as if it might exhaust even the champion of dharma. And in that hour of weariness, help came, and it came in the form of wisdom and of a sacred hymn, for the sage Agastya, who was present among the watchers, came to Rāma and taught him a great and sacred prayer, the Āditya Hṛdayam, the Hymn to the Heart of the Sun, a hymn of praise to Sūrya the sun-god, the source of all light and life and strength. Recite this hymn, Agastya counselled Rāma, and worship the sun, the source of all energy, and your strength will be renewed and your victory assured, for in this hymn is the power to overcome even the mightiest foe. And Rāma, receiving the hymn, recited it, and worshipped the sun, and his weariness fell away and his strength was renewed and his whole being was filled with a fresh and radiant power, and he turned back to the combat renewed, ready now to accomplish the doom that his weariness had delayed.

Renewed by the Āditya Hṛdayam, Rāma understood now, too, the secret of Rāvaṇa’s seeming invincibility, for the endless regrowth of the heads meant that Rāvaṇa could not be killed by the severing of his heads, and another means was needed. The secret was this: that within Rāvaṇa, in his body, there was a vessel or a store of amrita, the nectar of immortality, and it was this that renewed his heads and sustained his life, and while it remained he could not be slain; but if it could be destroyed, if the shaft could be aimed not at his heads but at the seat of the nectar in his body, then the source of his renewal would be destroyed and the demon king could die. And Vibhīshaṇa, or the counsel Rāma had received, made this known, and Rāma fitted to his bow the mightiest of all weapons, the Brahmāstra, the supreme celestial shaft, and he aimed it not at Rāvaṇa’s heads but at his heart, at the seat of the nectar of immortality within him.

And Rāma loosed the Brahmāstra, and it flew true, and it struck Rāvaṇa in the heart, and it pierced the vessel of the nectar and destroyed it, and dried up the source of the demon king’s renewal, and with the nectar destroyed the heads no longer regrew and the life could no longer be sustained, and Rāvaṇa, the ten-headed lord of the demons, the conqueror of the gods, the terror of the three worlds, was slain at last, brought down by the supreme weapon in the hand of the champion of dharma, falling in his full might and his full pride to the earth, dead, his long reign of terror ended, the evil he embodied destroyed, the doom that the wise had foretold and the demons had come to dread accomplished at the last.

And the tellers give us a moment at the demon king’s death that lifts it above mere triumph into something graver and more just, for as Rāvaṇa lay dying, his chief queen Mandodarī came and lamented over him, and in her lament she spoke the truth of his fall, that Rāma was no mere man but the Supreme Lord himself, Vishṇu descended into the world, and that Rāvaṇa had brought about his own destruction through his own sinful desire, that the whole doom had been the fruit of his own lust and pride, that he had warred against God and destroyed himself in the warring. It was the final confirmation of the suspicion that had been dawning among the demons: that they had fought Nārāyaṇa himself, and that Rāvaṇa’s ruin was self-inflicted, the harvest of his own crime. And there is a strange grace even here, for the tellers note that Rāvaṇa, mighty and learned and in many ways great, fallen through his one ungoverned passion, was granted in his death by Rāma’s hand a kind of liberation, released from his evil existence by the very Lord he had opposed, so that even the destruction of the great enemy was, at its deepest level, a deliverance.

So Rāvaṇa fell, and the war was won, and the evil that had darkened the three worlds was destroyed, and the long labour of the road and the alliance and the crossing and the war was accomplished at last. And the tellers pause to draw the meaning of Rāvaṇa’s whole tragic greatness and terrible fall, for he was not a small villain but a mighty one, gifted and learned and powerful beyond almost any being of his age, and all of it was poured down the drain of a single ungoverned appetite, a single refusal to master his own desire, a single crime that he would not undo. His fall is the story’s deepest warning about the ruin that lies in wait for the great, that the mightiest strength avails nothing against the enemy within, that a being who conquers gods may be destroyed by his own lust, that the failure to govern the self is the failure that undoes all other greatness. Rāvaṇa had everything, and lost everything, for the sake of a woman he could not have and would not release, and his end is the end of all who set their ungoverned wanting above the law of dharma and their own pride above the counsel of wisdom.

title: The End of the War
parentTitle: Sri Rama Charithram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The End of the War

Rāvaṇa was dead, and the war was won, and now came the aftermath, and it held both the fulfillment of a promise, the recovery of Sītā, and a moment so painful and so troubling that it has been debated for as long as the story has been told, the Agni Parīkshā, the ordeal of fire. This chapter holds the joy of victory and the shadow that fell across it, and the tellers render both without flinching.

First there was justice to be done and order to be restored, and Rāma did it. Vibhīshaṇa, the righteous brother who had left Lankā for the sake of dharma and served Rāma’s cause so faithfully, was crowned king of Lankā, exactly as Rāma had promised on the shore before the war began. The evil reign of Rāvaṇa was replaced with the righteous reign of Vibhīshaṇa; the throne that had been held in lust and pride passed to one who would hold it in dharma; and the war’s true purpose, not the destruction of the demons but the replacement of evil rule with good, was fulfilled in the crowning of the righteous brother over the golden city. Lankā, which had been the seat of terror, would now be the seat of justice, and the demon race, no longer led into evil by a tyrant’s crimes, might live henceforth in peace under a righteous king.

And then Sītā was sent for, brought from the Ashokavana where she had endured her long captivity, bathed and adorned and arrayed once more as a queen, and brought before Rāma at last, after all the long separation, the abduction and the search and the war, the husband and wife who had been torn apart in the forest so long ago now to be reunited in the hour of victory. And Sītā came to Rāma with a joy beyond words, her long ordeal ended, her faith vindicated, her husband victorious, the rescue she had defiantly promised Rāvaṇa and faithfully awaited now accomplished, coming to Rāma with her whole heart, expecting the reunion that all her endurance had earned.

And Rāma received her coldly.

This is the moment that has troubled every reader and every teller of this story, and the tellers do not soften it, for it is one of the hardest things in the whole epic. Rāma, instead of embracing the wife he had crossed a sea and fought a war to recover, looked upon her coldly, and would not take her simply back, and spoke to her harsh words that fell upon her and upon the whole assembly like a blow. I have done what honour required, he said in effect; I have avenged the insult to my house and destroyed the demon who took you; but you have dwelt for a long time in the house of another man, in Rāvaṇa’s Lankā, and I cannot simply take you back as though nothing had happened, for the world would question your purity and mine, and I cannot take back a wife who has lived so long in another’s power without the world’s doubt falling upon us both. He spoke as though he doubted her, as though her long captivity had stained her, as though he could not receive her without proof of the purity she had guarded so fiercely through all her ordeal; and the coldness and the cruelty of it, after all she had endured, after all her faithfulness, struck the whole assembly with shock and struck Sītā to the heart.

And Sītā, wounded beyond anything the demons had been able to do to her, wounded now by the very husband for whom she had endured everything, responded not with pleading but with a terrible dignity, and her response is the true greatness of the scene. If Rāma doubted her, if the world doubted her, then she would prove her purity in the only way that could not be questioned, by the ordeal of fire. She turned to Lakshmaṇa and asked him to build a pyre, a great fire, and Lakshmaṇa, grief-stricken, unwilling, obeyed, for Sītā commanded it with a dignity that would not be refused. And when the pyre was built and blazing, Sītā spoke, calling upon Agni, the god of fire, to be her witness: if she had been faithful, if her heart had never wavered from Rāma through all her captivity, if she was pure in thought and word and deed, then let the fire not harm her; and if she was not, let it consume her. And with these words, before the whole horrified assembly, Sītā walked into the blazing fire.

And the fire did not harm her. For Sītā was pure, her fidelity absolute, her purity perfect, and the fire-god himself, Agni, would not touch her, could not harm so faithful a soul; and out of the flames Agni himself rose, bearing Sītā unharmed, presenting her back to Rāma, attesting before the whole assembly and the whole world to her absolute purity, declaring that she was faultless, faithful, unstained, that the fire had found in her nothing to burn, that her virtue was perfect and proven beyond any possibility of doubt. Sītā came forth from the fire unharmed, vindicated, her purity established by the god of fire himself before all the worlds.

And now Rāma received her, and embraced her, and his coldness fell away, and he explained himself, and his explanation is the key to the whole troubling scene, though it has never entirely satisfied those who love Sītā and grieve at what she was made to endure. I never doubted you, Rāma told her; I never doubted your purity for a single moment; I know your faithfulness as I know my own heart. But I am not merely a husband; I am to be a king, and a king’s wife must be above not only fault but even the suspicion of fault, for the whole moral order of the kingdom rests upon the king’s household being beyond reproach. The world would have doubted you, having dwelt so long in Rāvaṇa’s power; the whisper would have spread; and that whisper would have stained not only you but the throne and the kingdom and the very order of dharma that I must uphold. I subjected you to this ordeal not because I doubted you but so that the whole world should see your purity proven beyond any possibility of doubt, so that no whisper could ever touch you, so that you should be received and honoured by all as the faultless queen you are. It was not my doubt but the world’s that required this proof, and now it is given, and you are vindicated before all, and no one can ever question you again.

The tellers give us this explanation, and they give us also the deep unease that surrounds it, for it is one of the places where the story confronts the hardest tensions of dharma and does not pretend they are easily resolved. Was it just, what Rāma did? To subject the faithful Sītā, who had endured so much, to so cruel a public ordeal, for the sake of the world’s opinion? The explanation, that it was the demands of kingship and public order rather than personal doubt, eases the scene but does not entirely dissolve its pain, and the story seems to intend that it should not, for here, as in the killing of Vāli, we are shown that the path of dharma, especially the dharma of a king, can require things that trouble the conscience even as they serve a larger order, that the demands of public duty and private love can come into a terrible conflict, and that even Rāma, the very measure of righteousness, is caught in tensions that admit no clean resolution. The Agni Parīkshā is not presented as a simple triumph but as a painful necessity, or a painful choice, that reveals the hard cost of the kingly dharma and the terrible weight that falls, again and again in this story, upon Sītā, who must prove and prove again a purity that was never truly in doubt.

But for now, in the hour of victory, the ordeal was passed and the vindication complete, and Rāma and Sītā were reunited, and the long separation was ended, and the joy of it filled the whole host. The exile was nearly over; the fourteen years were nearly accomplished; and it was time to go home. They boarded the Pushpaka Vimāna, the divine flying chariot that had been Rāvaṇa’s and was now Rāma’s by conquest, and they rose into the sky and turned north, toward home, toward Ayodhyā, and as they flew Rāma pointed out to Sītā the landmarks of their long ordeal passing below, the bridge over the sea, the shores where they had camped, Kishkindhā, the lake Pampā, Panchavaṭī where she had been taken, Chitrakūṭa where they had been happy, the whole long geography of their exile unrolling beneath them as they flew home, transforming the places of their suffering into a shared memory of a journey completed, a trial endured together and survived. And they came to Ayodhyā, and the fourteen years were accomplished to the day, and Bharata, who had waited all that time at Nandigrāma with Rāma’s sandals upon the throne, ready to enter the fire if Rāma did not come on the appointed day, saw his brother return at last, and was saved from his vow, and the reunion of the brothers was a joy beyond telling. And the whole city, which had mourned Rāma’s exile with such grief, now welcomed his return with a joy as great as its grief had been, and Ayodhyā was illuminated with countless lamps to celebrate the homecoming of its beloved prince, the city ablaze with light in welcome, and Rāma was crowned king at last, the coronation that had been prepared and prevented fourteen years before now accomplished, Rāma seated upon the throne of Ayodhyā with Sītā beside him, the rightful king come at last into his kingdom.

And so began Rāmarājya, the reign of Rāma, which the tellers hold up as the very ideal of righteous rule, an age of perfect justice and perfect peace and perfect prosperity, when the kingdom flourished under a king who was the measure of dharma, when there was no injustice and no suffering and no want, when the whole land lived in harmony under the rule of the perfect king. The long story of exile and abduction and war had come, it seemed, to its perfect ending: the evil destroyed, the queen recovered, the king enthroned, the golden age begun. And here, in a simpler telling, the story might end, in the triumph and the joy of Rāmarājya. But there was a further sorrow still to come, a last and bitter testing, for the story does not end in simple triumph but goes on, into the Uttara Kāṇḍa, to show that even in the golden age, even for the perfect king, the path of dharma held one more terrible price to pay.

title: The Agony of the Throne
parentTitle: Sri Rama Charithram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The Agony of the Throne

Rāmarājya was a golden age, and for a time all was well, and Rāma and Sītā reigned in joy and the kingdom flourished; but the crown is a heavy burden, and a king’s life is not his own, and this chapter tells of the terrible price that the kingly dharma exacted from Rāma at the height of his reign, the banishment of Sītā, which is among the most painful and most debated episodes in the whole of the story.

For the golden age held within it, unseen at first, a shadow, and the shadow was this: that among the people of the kingdom there began to spread a whisper, a doubt, concerning Sītā. She had dwelt, after all, for a long time in the house of Rāvaṇa, in the power of the demon king; and though she had passed through the fire and been vindicated by Agni himself, the memory of that vindication faded, and the whisper grew, among the common people, that the queen had lived in another man’s house and that her purity was therefore in question, that a king who took back a wife who had dwelt so long in a demon’s power set a poor example, that the royal household was not, in the people’s eyes, above the suspicion that a royal household must be above.

The whisper came to a head, the tellers say, in the words of a common man, a washerman, who in a quarrel with his own wife rejected her for having stayed in another man’s house, and declared that he was not like the king Rāma, who took back a wife who had lived in the house of Rāvaṇa. And this saying, the harsh judgment of a common washerman upon his queen, came to Rāma’s ears through his spies and informers, who reported to the king what the people were saying, that the citizens doubted the queen’s purity, that the king’s example in taking her back was questioned, that the whisper had spread through the kingdom and touched the honour of the throne.

And Rāma was faced now with the most agonizing conflict of his whole life, and the tellers render it as an agony, not a simple decision, for it set against each other the two things he held most sacred, and allowed no way to honour both. On the one side was his love for Sītā, his knowledge of her absolute purity, his tenderness for the wife who had endured so much for him and with him, the wife he loved more than his own life. On the other side was his dharma as a king, the duty he held to be above even his own happiness, the duty to a moral order that required the king’s household to be beyond not only fault but even the suspicion of fault, so that the whole moral authority of the throne, on which the order of the kingdom rested, should not be undermined by the people’s doubt. If the king’s own wife were subject to public doubt, then the king’s moral authority was compromised, and if that authority was compromised, then the whole order of dharma that the king upheld was weakened, and the good of the whole kingdom was put at risk. And Rāma held, as the deepest principle of his life, that the king’s private happiness must always yield to the public good, that a king does not own his own life but holds it in trust for his people, that the ruler must sacrifice his own desire whenever the good of the ruled requires it.

And so Rāma made the terrible decision, and it broke his heart to make it: he would banish Sītā. For the sake of the people’s doubt, for the sake of the throne’s moral authority, for the sake of the dharma that required the king’s household to be above suspicion, he would send away the wife he loved and knew to be pure, sacrificing his own happiness and hers to the demands of his kingly duty. It was a decision that cost him everything of his personal joy, that he made in an agony of grief, weeping in the privacy of his chambers, and that he made nonetheless, because his whole life was built on the principle that duty comes before desire, that the king’s own happiness is the first thing he must be willing to sacrifice, and that he would hold to that principle now though it broke his heart and though it fell, cruelly, upon the innocent Sītā who had already suffered so much.

Let us confront the terrible difficulty of this, for the story means us to, and it is perhaps the hardest thing in the whole epic, harder even than the Agni Parīkshā, and it has troubled and even angered readers for as long as the story has been told. For here Rāma sacrifices not himself but Sītā; he banishes an innocent and faithful wife, whom he knows to be pure, whose purity was proven by fire, for the sake of the people’s unjust doubt; and no explanation of the kingly dharma entirely eases the injustice of what is done to Sītā, who is made, again, to pay the price of others’ suspicion, who is punished for a fault she never committed, who is cast out despite her proven innocence for the sake of a whisper. The story does not hide this injustice; it presents Rāma’s decision as an agony precisely because it is not a clean or a satisfying choice but a genuine and terrible conflict between two goods, love and duty, in which the honouring of the one requires the wounding of the other, and in which the innocent Sītā bears the cost of a duty that is not even her own.

And the tellers, in rendering it, invite us into the deepest questions the story raises, questions it does not finally answer, for it is honest enough to leave them open. Was Rāma right? Was the kingly dharma truly worth so cruel a price, paid by so innocent a victim? Is a duty that requires the sacrifice of the innocent truly a duty, or is it a kind of tyranny of principle over love? The story presents Rāma’s choice as the choice of the perfect king, holding to his terrible duty at the cost of his own heart; and it presents also, unmistakably, the injustice and the grief of it, the wrong done to Sītā, the agony of a love sacrificed to a principle. It does not resolve the tension; it holds it open, as one of the places where the path of dharma runs through darkness that no light entirely dispels, where doing one’s duty and doing right seem to come apart, where the very perfection of Rāma’s fidelity to his kingly duty produces a result that the heart cannot help but call a wrong. This is the agony of the throne, that it can require the perfect king to break his own heart and wound the innocent for the sake of an order he holds sacred, and the story lets us feel the full weight and the full darkness of that agony.

So the decision was made, and it fell to Lakshmaṇa, once again, to be the instrument of a grief he could not prevent, for Rāma charged Lakshmaṇa with the terrible task of carrying it out: to take Sītā, who was now with child, expecting, away from the palace, out to the forest, and to leave her there, near the hermitage of the sage Vālmīki, banished, without even, in some tellings, being told directly by Rāma of the banishment until it was done. Lakshmaṇa, weeping, unable to refuse his brother and king, unable to bear what he was commanded to do, took Sītā out on the pretext of a journey, and carried her to the forest, to the region near Vālmīki’s ashram, and there, at last, broken with grief, he told her the truth: that she was banished, that Rāma had sent her away for the sake of the people’s doubt, that she was to be left here in the forest, cast out from the palace and the kingdom and her husband’s side, alone and with child, for a fault she had never committed. And then, having delivered his cruel message and left the innocent queen alone in the wilderness, Lakshmaṇa returned, weeping, to Ayodhyā, and Sītā was left, banished and alone and pregnant, near the hermitage of the sage who would shelter her, to bear the last and bitterest of all her long sufferings.

title: The Return to the Earth
parentTitle: Sri Rama Charithram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The Return to the Earth

Sītā, banished and alone in the forest, was not left wholly without shelter, for the sage Vālmīki, the great seer, found her, and took her into his hermitage, and gave her refuge, and there, in the peace of the ashram, cared for and honoured by the sage and his people, Sītā made her home in her exile, and there she gave birth to her children, twin sons, whom she named Lava and Kusha.

And so, in the quiet of Vālmīki’s hermitage, far from the palace and the throne and the husband who had banished her, Sītā raised her two sons, and the years passed, and the boys grew, and it was a gentler exile than it might have been, for the hermitage was a place of peace and holiness, and Sītā was honoured there, and her sons grew up strong and good under the care of the great sage. And Vālmīki himself took the boys as his pupils, and taught them, and among the things he taught them was a wonderful thing: for Vālmīki, the tellers say, was the very sage who composed the Rāmāyaṇa, the great poem of Rāma’s whole life and deeds, and he taught this poem to Lava and Kusha, and trained them to sing it, so that the two boys, all unknowing, learned to sing the epic of their own father, the whole story of Rāma, in the hermitage where their banished mother had raised them.

The years turned, and the boys grew to youth, and there came an occasion that brought the long-separated family, at last, toward its final reckoning. For Rāma, reigning in Ayodhyā, undertook to perform a great sacrifice, the Ashvamedha, the horse-sacrifice, the grandest of royal rites; and the celebration of it drew people from all the kingdom and beyond; and to this great gathering came, among the many, the sage Vālmīki, and with him the two boys, Lava and Kusha. And the boys, trained by Vālmīki, sang the Rāmāyaṇa, the poem of Rāma’s life, in the assembly, before the king and the whole court, singing the beautiful story of Rāma’s deeds in their pure young voices, all unaware that they sang before the very hero of the tale, their own father.

And Rāma, listening, was moved beyond words, for he heard his own life sung back to him in the voices of these two beautiful youths, heard the whole story of his exile and his loss and his war and his triumph, sung with such beauty and such truth that it pierced his heart; and as he listened, and looked upon the two singers, he perceived a likeness, and a wonder grew in him, and he understood, or came to suspect, that these two boys who sang his story so were his own sons, the children of Sītā, born in the exile to which he had banished her. And the recognition broke over him with all the force of the grief and the love that he had held down through all the years since the banishment, the grief for the wife he had sent away and never ceased to love, the sudden knowledge of the sons he had never known.

And Rāma sent for Sītā, for the recognition of his sons brought the whole matter to its crisis, and he summoned Sītā to come to the assembly, to be reunited, but on a condition that reveals that even now, even after all the years, the terrible logic of the kingly dharma still held him: he summoned her to come and to prove her purity once more, publicly, before the assembled people, so that the old doubt might be finally laid to rest and she might be received back with the world’s acceptance. Once more, after everything, after the fire, after the years of unjust banishment, Sītā was to be asked to prove the purity that had never truly been in doubt, to satisfy the demand of the people and the throne with a public vindication.

And Sītā came, brought by Vālmīki to the great assembly, and she stood before Rāma and the court and the people, and she was asked once more to prove herself. And Sītā, who had endured so much, who had been taken and imprisoned and threatened and tormented and vindicated by fire and then banished despite that vindication and left to raise her sons alone in the forest for all these years, Sītā had reached at last the end of what even her great endurance could bear, not in the sense of breaking, but in the sense that she would prove herself no more; she would not submit again to the endless demand for proof of a purity that was perfect and that she should never have been made to prove even once; and she made instead a final, sacred, and terrible declaration, a proof that would end all proofs.

If I have been faithful, she declared, calling now not upon fire but upon the earth itself, her own mother, from whom she had come; if I have never in thought or word or deed been untrue to Rāma, if my heart has been pure through all my life and all my suffering, then let my mother, the Earth, from whose furrow I came, open and receive me back, and take me home. It was a calling-upon of her own origin, her own mother, the Earth from which she had been born in the furrow so long ago; and it was a declaration that she would return to that source rather than endure any longer the demands of a world that would not cease to doubt her; and it was her final and unanswerable proof, for she staked her vindication on the Earth’s own response.

And the Earth answered. As Sītā spoke, the ground opened, and Mother Earth herself rose up, or a great throne rose from the opening earth, and the Earth took Sītā into her arms, received her daughter back, and drew her down, and the earth closed over her, and Sītā was gone, returned to the source from which she had come, vindicated absolutely by the Earth’s own reception of her, and gone forever from the world of Rāma and Ayodhyā and the endless demands of the throne.

And Rāma was left, stricken, crying out in grief, reaching for the wife who had been received back into the earth, gone now beyond any recovery, taken from him not by any enemy but by the Earth herself, who had judged, as it were, that the world was no longer worthy to hold so faithful a soul, so tried and so doubted and so wronged a queen. The Earth had received Sītā, and Sītā was gone, and Rāma understood at last, in the fullness of his grief, that his divine companion, who had come with him into the world and shared his whole long journey of exile and war and sorrow, had returned to her source, that the goddess who had taken human form to walk beside him had laid that form down at last and gone home, leaving him alone in the world she had departed.

Let us mark the terrible dignity of Sītā’s end, for the tellers give it to her as the final vindication of her whole long-suffering greatness. Through the whole story she had been the one who endured, who held fast, who bore the sufferings that were laid upon her, taking and imprisonment and doubt and banishment, always faithful, always wronged, always enduring; and at the last, she reached the point where endurance became refusal, where the faithful soul, having proven itself again and again and been doubted again and again, would prove itself no more, but would rather return to its source than submit to a world that would not cease to demand what it had no right to demand. Her return to the Earth is not a defeat but a final and absolute vindication, the Earth itself receiving her as proof of a purity beyond all further question, and it is also a judgment upon the world and the throne that had wronged her, a declaration that the demands laid upon her had at last exceeded what any faithfulness should be asked to bear, and that she would go home rather than endure them further. Sītā, who had been born from the earth in a furrow and had come into the world as a gift, returned to the earth at the end, her work done, her faithfulness perfect and proven, her long suffering ended, gone home to the mother from whom she came, leaving behind her a grief in Rāma that nothing in the world could console, and a story of endurance and fidelity that has been honoured and wept over for as long as the tale has been told.

title: The Return of the Avatar
parentTitle: Sri Rama Charithram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The Return of the Avatar

Sītā was gone, returned to the earth, and Rāma reigned on, but the joy had gone out of his reign, and he lived now in a deepening detachment from the world, for the departure of Sītā had loosened the last of his ties to the life he had lived, and he understood, in the quiet of his grief, that his own time in the world was drawing toward its close.

He reigned still, and reigned well, for the dharma of the king held him to his duty as long as the duty remained; and Rāmarājya continued, the golden age of justice and peace, under a king who governed now with a heart turned increasingly away from the world and toward the source from which he too had come. But the tellers show us a Rāma grown quiet and detached, his great work accomplished, his divine companion departed, his purpose in the world all but fulfilled, waiting, as it were, for the time when he too might lay down the human form he had taken up so long ago and return to his eternal nature.

He established his legacy, for that remained to be done. His sons, Lava and Kusha, the twins born in the forest and raised by Vālmīki, were brought to him and acknowledged and given their place, the heirs of his line, and to them, and to the sons of his brothers, Rāma in time entrusted the kingdoms, dividing the rule among the next generation, settling the succession, ensuring that the order he had established would continue after him. He gave his final instructions to his brothers, to Bharata and the others who had shared his whole long story, arranging all the affairs of the kingdom and the family, setting everything in order, as one who prepares to depart and wishes to leave nothing unfinished behind him.

And when all was arranged, when his sons were established and his legacy secured and the kingdom set in order, Rāma understood that his time had come, that his avatar was complete, that the purpose for which the Supreme Lord had taken human form and entered the world was accomplished, and that it was time to return. For he had come into the world, the story has told us from the beginning, to destroy the evil of Rāvaṇa, to restore dharma, to walk the human path and show what the perfect life of dharma looked like in a human being; and all of this was now done. The evil was destroyed; dharma was restored; the perfect example was given; the golden age was established. There remained nothing more for the avatar to accomplish, and so it was time for the Lord to lay down the human form and return to his eternal nature.

And so Rāma made his final departure from the world, and the tellers render it with a great and solemn beauty. He went, in the fullness of time, to the river Sarayū, the river that flowed past Ayodhyā, the river that had witnessed his whole life, from his birth to this last hour; and there, attended by his people and his kin, in a solemn and sacred passing, Rāma walked into the waters of the Sarayū, entering the river, and in that entering he laid down the human form he had worn for so long, and returned to his eternal and divine nature, to his true being as Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme, from whom he had descended into the world and to whom he now returned. The avatar was complete; the human life was ended; and the Lord who had walked the earth as Rāma, who had been born and had grown and had loved and had suffered and had triumphed and had grieved, all as truly and as fully as any man, now returned to the source, his work accomplished, his purpose fulfilled, leaving behind him in the world he departed a legacy that would guide humanity for as long as the world endured.

And here the great story ends, and the tellers, before they lay it down, pause to draw its final meaning, and it is fitting that we pause with them, for the whole long tale has been building toward this final reflection.

The journey of Rāma, they tell us, is not a simple fairy tale of good defeating evil, though it contains that; it is something deeper and truer and more useful to us than that. It is a profound exploration of the human condition, of what it means to live a life of dharma in a world that is not simple, where the right path is often hard and dark and costly, where duty and love come into conflict, where the innocent suffer and the faithful are doubted and the good is bought at a terrible price. Rāma’s life was not an easy triumph but a long ordeal of sacrifice and sorrow: he lost his kingdom, his father, his wife, again and again, and bore each loss with a fidelity to duty that never wavered but never spared him pain. Sītā’s life was a long endurance of suffering unjustly laid upon a faithful soul, borne with a dignity that never broke. And the story does not pretend that all of this was easy, or that the path of dharma is a smooth road to happiness; it shows us, with unflinching honesty, that the path of dharma is filled with sacrifice and sorrow, that doing one’s duty can cost everything, that the world is not arranged to reward the good with ease.

And yet, the tellers say, this is precisely the story’s gift to us, and its consolation. For it shows us that the path of dharma, hard as it is, costly as it is, filled with sorrow as it is, is nonetheless the highest and the truest path, the one worth walking whatever it costs; that to carry out our duty with grace and devotion, even through suffering, even at the price of our own happiness, is the highest purpose a human life can serve; that faithfulness held through sorrow, duty done through loss, love kept through separation, are not defeated by the sufferings that attend them but are precisely what give a human life its greatness and its meaning. Rāma and Sītā suffered greatly, and were faithful greatly, and their greatness lies not in escaping suffering but in the fidelity with which they bore it; and this is the example the story holds up for us, the light it offers for our own walking of the path of truth: that we too will meet suffering and loss and hard choices and unjust burdens, and that our task is not to escape them, which we cannot, but to bear them with grace and devotion and fidelity to what is right, and that in so bearing them we fulfill the highest purpose of a human life.

May this telling, the tellers conclude, bring you closer to the wisdom of the ancient sages who first sang this song, and offer you light for your own walking of the path of dharma; for the story of Rāma is not merely a tale of long ago but a mirror and a guide for every soul that seeks to live rightly in a world where living rightly is hard, and its light, kindled so long ago on the banks of the Sarayū, still burns, and still shows the way, for all who have eyes to see it and hearts to follow where it leads.

Here ends the Sri Rāma Charithram, the story of Rāma, the descent of the Lord, who walked the earth in the form of a man, and bore all that a man can bear, and was faithful to the last, and returned at the end to the source from which he came, leaving behind him the light of dharma to guide the world.

title: Invocation
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body

title: Parikshith
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Parikshith

The great war of Kurukshetra had ended, yet its echoes still haunted the land. Within the royal halls of Hastināpura, the last hope of the Pāṇḍava lineage awaited birth, for Uttara, the young widow of Abhimanyu, carried in her womb the sole heir who would one day continue the dynasty. But even as life prepared to enter the world, death cast its shadow over it.
Ashwatthāmā, the son of Droṇāchārya and the last surviving warrior of the Kaurava side, had pledged to Duryodhana that he would wipe out the Pāṇḍavas and their line. In the dead of night he crept into the sleeping camp and slew the sons of the Pāṇḍavas born of Draupadī, unarmed and defenseless. When Arjuna discovered the massacre he pursued Ashwatthāmā across the land, and the two came face to face. Knowing he could not match Arjuna in open battle, Ashwatthāmā invoked the Brahmashiras-Astra, the most destructive of celestial weapons, and Arjuna answered by invoking his own. The heavens braced for annihilation.
Before the two weapons could collide, Maharishi Vyāsa appeared between the warriors and warned them that the impact of such a clash would consume the heavens above, the earth in the middle, and the netherworlds below. He asked them both to withdraw their weapons. Arjuna, honoring dharma, at once drew his back; but Ashwatthāmā confessed that he possessed the knowledge to launch his weapon and not to recall it — he could only redirect it. Vyāsa instructed him to send it toward some place where there were no living beings, where it could cause no harm. In one final act of spite, Ashwatthāmā turned the weapon instead upon the unborn child in Uttara's womb.
Arjuna pleaded with Krishna to save the child. It is said that the Lord took upon Himself a miniscule form and entered Uttara's womb, where He moved in a protective circle around the infant, absorbing the searing energy of the weapon into Himself. Within the darkness of the womb the child watched the luminous form that circled him, following its motion with wonder, and so, even before his birth, he beheld the Supreme. When he was born, his gaze was unlike that of other infants — steady and searching, as though looking for someone he had already met. For this the sages named him Parikshith, "the one who examines," for all his days he would seek the divine presence he had once seen encircling him.
Parikshith grew into a ruler unmatched in wisdom and strength, a king whose very righteousness held the age of Kali at bay. Kali Yuga had arrived, yet it could find no entry into his kingdom, for justice still sat upon the throne. Taking human form, Kali sought a way in, but each time he was turned aside — he could not corrupt the courts, could not taint the people, and could not touch the mind of the king, whose devotion burned too brightly. At last he resorted to deception, slipping unseen into the golden crown upon Parikshith's head, where he whispered slow poison into the king's thoughts.
One day, after a long hunt, Parikshith was overcome by a thirst like none he had known. Searching for water, he came upon the hermitage of the sage Shamika, who sat in deep meditation and did not stir at the king's approach. Under the influence of Kali within his crown, Parikshith took the silence for an insult; seeing the freshly shed skin of a snake nearby, he lifted it and draped it around the sage's neck. The sage's son, Shringi, learning of the offense, burned with anger and pronounced a curse — that within seven days the serpent Takshaka would strike, and the king would die.
When Parikshith heard of the curse he neither panicked nor sought vengeance. He saw in it not a punishment but an invitation, and resolved that the question was no longer how he would die but how he would spend the days that remained. Handing his throne to his son Janamejaya, he went to the banks of the sacred Gangā. There, as though summoned by destiny, came Shuka Maharishi, the son of Vyāsa, a sage untouched by the burdens of the world. Parikshith bowed before him and asked how one might cross beyond death. In answer, over the seven days and nights that followed, Shuka Maharishi narrated to him the Shrīmad Bhāgavatam — not for a king alone, but for all who seek to understand the eternal beyond the fleeting.

title: Mapping of Space and Time
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Mapping of Space and Time

Shuka Maharishi began his discourse in an orderly fashion. He first set out the forms of yoga and dharma one must follow in life, and then explained the concepts of the jeevatma, the individual soul, and the paramatma, the Supreme. In the language of the Vedas, the Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇa is described as the one who pervades everything inside and outside of creation; He is Brahmā, He is Shiva, He is Indra, He resides in every atom that has been made, and He is supreme over all. Having established this, the sage turned to describe how space and time are arranged. It is a vast and intricate picture, and the listener is asked to build it up patiently in the mind.
Consider first how a place is located. A city sits within a region, the region within a land, the land within a subcontinent, the subcontinent within a continent, and the continent upon the Earth. The Earth, as the texts name it, is Boohu. Above it lie six ascending worlds — Buvaha, Suvaha, Mahaha, Janaha, Tapaha, and finally Satyam, where Brahmā himself dwells. Below Boohu lie seven descending worlds — Athala, Vithala, Suthala, Rasaatala, Thalaathala, Mahathala, and the deepest, Pathala. Imagine these fourteen worlds as the layers of a single vast form, Boohu at the middle, seven above and seven below.
This entire fourteen-layered structure is contained within a great egg, and because it was fashioned by Brahmā it is called the Brahmandam. The egg is protected by a shell, the Aavaranam, and above and below Boohu flows a cosmic fluid, the Aavarana-Jalam. Beyond the egg lie further realms in ascending order — the world of Vayu, then of Agni, of Sūrya, of Chandra, of the stars, of lightning, and beyond them the circle of the Saptarishis, the seven great sages. This whole formation is held to rest within the eye of an inverted celestial dolphin, the Simshumara, which revolves like a great wheel — hence it is called the Simshumara-Chakram. At its heart lies the Dhruva-Mandalam, the fixed abode of the pole star, around which all else turns. And this immense revolving form is itself borne upon the lotus that emanates from the navel of the Lord. So the mapping of space comes to a close.
Time, seen from the creator's vantage, is no less vast. Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes an hour, twenty-four hours a day, and so on through months and years in the familiar way. Four hundred and thirty-two thousand years constitute one Kali Yuga. Twice that span is the Dvāpara Yuga, thrice it the Tretā Yuga, and four times it the Kṛta Yuga. Taken together, these four ages form one Chaturyuga. A thousand Chaturyugas pass in what is, for Brahmā, the span of a single day, and as many again in his night. Three hundred and sixty such days make one of his years, and the office of a single Brahmā lasts a hundred such years, after which the next Brahmā succeeds him.
A thousand Chaturyugas make one Kalpa. To oversee each Kalpa, Brahmā appoints fourteen presiding demigods called Manus, each ruling seventy-one Chaturyugas. We currently fall under the seventh Manu, Lord Sūrya, who bears the title Vivasvān; within his tenure we are in the twenty-eighth of his seventy-one Chaturyugas, and within that Chaturyuga, in the age of Kali.
It is this precise reckoning of space and time that is drawn together in the Saṅkalpam, the ancient declaration of intent recited at the start of every sacred act. A sankalpam is, in essence, a statement of where and when the worshipper stands. Before beginning any rite, one first announces one's exact place within the whole of creation — descending from the vastest cosmic cycles all the way down to the present hour — and only then states the purpose for which the rite is being performed. The effect is to root the smallest human act firmly within the largest possible frame, so that the worshipper acts not in isolation but as a conscious point within the ordered breath of the creator. It moves, as it were, from the greatest to the smallest: first the age of the presiding Brahmā, then the Kalpa, the Manvantara, the Chaturyuga, and the yuga; then the continent, the land, the region, and the sacred river; and finally the year, the season, the month, the fortnight, the lunar day, the weekday, and the star under which the moment falls.
To see how this works, consider the sankalpam as it would be recited on this very day. One would declare that it is now the second half of the reigning Brahmā's lifetime, in the Shvetavarāha Kalpa, in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, in the twenty-eighth Chaturyuga, in the first quarter of Kali Yuga, upon the Jambu Dvīpam, in the land of Bharata — and then, narrowing to the immediate present, that it is the year Parābhava; the Dakshiṇāyana, the sun's southward course; the Varsha season of the rains; the month of Siṃha; the bright fortnight, the Shukla Paksha, of the waxing moon; the sixth lunar day, the Shashṭhi; the day of Bhauma, which is Tuesday; and the hour falling under the star Svātī. Only after all of this is named — the entire cosmos funnelled down to a single blessed moment between one sunrise and the next — does the worshipper finally state the purpose of the rite. In this way even the briefest observance is understood as taking place at a precise coordinate in space and time, held within the boundless order of creation.
Parikshith listened in wonder, for he had been shown the shape of the universe, and now stood ready to hear of the One who lies beyond it.

title: Jaya-Vijaya
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Jaya-Vijaya

Parikshith, having grasped the vastness of space and the endless cycles of time, asked the sage a deeper question: if all things move according to dharma, how is it that even those closest to the Lord may be cast into the world of birth and death? Shuka Maharishi answered that the ways of the divine cannot be understood by reason alone, for even the Lord's dearest may play their part in the unfolding of creation. To illustrate, he told the story of Jaya and Vijaya, the gatekeepers of Vaikuṇṭham.
Here it should be understood that there are, in truth, two Vaikunthams, each an exact replica of the other. One is Sri Vaikuṇṭham, the abode from which there is no return; the other is Karya Vaikuṇṭham, to which gods and revered sages come in their times of need and from which they return once their purpose is served. It was at the gates of this Karya Vaikuṇṭham, where the Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇa rested upon His serpent recliner Ādishesha, that Jaya and Vijaya stood guard — warriors unmatched and devotees unwavering.
One day the Four Kumaras — Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, and Sanatkumāra, the mindborn sons of Brahmā — approached the gates seeking an audience with the Lord. Though ancient beyond measure, they bore the appearance of small children, for they had conquered time through their wisdom. Bound by their duty, Jaya and Vijaya barred the path, saying the Lord was in yoga-nidra and could not be disturbed. The sages, who had been welcomed even by the humblest of devotees, felt the weight of the refusal, and in their indignation they cursed the two guardians: for failing to see that the Lord belongs to all, they would be cast down from this realm of purity and made to walk the path of birth and death.
The words struck like thunder, for fear had never before existed in Vaikuṇṭham. Jaya and Vijaya fell at the feet of the sages and begged forgiveness, but the curse could not be recalled. When the Lord Himself appeared, adorned in yellow silk and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, He confirmed that the words of the great sages could not be undone. He offered His devoted gatekeepers a choice: they might be born seven times as His devotees and return to Him thereafter, or they might be born only three times as His adversaries, dying at His own hands each time before returning. Unwilling to bear so long a separation, Jaya and Vijaya chose the shorter path — three births as enemies of the Lord.
And so they fell. In their first birth they became Hiraṇyāksha and Hiraṇyakashipu, and the Lord descended as Varāha, the boar who lifted the Earth, and as Narasimha, who tore the tyrant apart to protect Prahlāda. In their second birth they became Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, and the Lord descended as Rāma of Ayodhyā to end their arrogance. In their final birth they became Shishupāla and Dantavakra, and the Lord, now as Krishna, struck them down with the whirling Sudarshana Chakra. With that last blow the cycle was complete, and Jaya and Vijaya returned at last to their place at the gates of Vaikuṇṭham. Thus, Shuka observed, even in opposition they were never truly apart from the Lord — for even the fiercest storm is but a whisper in the presence of the eternal.

title: Varāha Avataram
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Varāha Avataram

The order of the universe rests upon dharma, and whenever dharma is disturbed the tremor is felt across all creation. In one such age a great asura rose to power. His name was Hiraṇyāksha, born to the sage Kāshyapa and his wife Diti, and with him was born his twin, Hiraṇyakashipu. From the moment of their birth the heavens sensed that these two would bring great turbulence to the world.
Hiraṇyāksha's thirst for dominance knew no bounds. He waged war upon the Devas, scattered even Indra from his throne, and silenced the heavens with his power. Not content with conquering the celestial realms, he set his gaze upon Bhoomi Devī, the Earth herself. Seizing her, he cast her down into the depths of the Garbhodaka Ocean, drowning her beneath the cosmic waters. With the Earth lost, the very axis of existence was thrown into disorder — the rishis could no longer perform their yagnas, and all beings suffered under his tyranny.
Stripped of their power, the Devas turned to Brahmā for refuge and pleaded with him to summon the one who alone could restore balance. Brahmā closed his eyes and meditated upon the Supreme, and as he meditated a movement stirred within him. From his own nostril there emerged a tiny boar, no larger than a thumb. Even as Brahmā watched in wonder, the boar began to grow, expanding beyond all measure until its golden form stretched radiant across the heavens. Looking upon its lotus-like eyes, Brahmā knew at once that this was none other than Sriman Nārāyaṇa, come to lift the Earth, and he bowed before the Supreme Boar in reverence.
The Lord in His form as Varāha turned toward the vast ocean where Bhoomi Devī lay submerged and plunged into the cosmic waters. Through the limitless depths He searched for her, and when He found her He cradled her gently and lifted the Earth upon His tusks, carrying her upward through the darkness. As He rose, the celestial beings showered Him with flowers and the rishis chanted His praise.
But Hiraṇyāksha, learning that a boar bearing tusks had rescued the Earth, rushed in fury to recapture her and came face to face with the Lord. Blinded by arrogance, he charged, his weapons gleaming. Varāha met him with effortless grace, and their clash sent tremors across the universe. The battle is said to have raged for a great span of time, until at last, with a single mighty strike, the Lord shattered the pride of the asura and cast an end to him. The universe fell silent, balance was restored, and the Lord set Bhoomi Devī once more upon the cosmic plane. Afterward, the Lord was wedded to Bhoomi Devī.
Among the many places associated with this avatara, Shrimushnam in Tamil Nadu holds a special significance. It is counted among the eight Swayambhu Kshetras — sites where the deity is said to have manifested of its own accord — and its temple enshrines Lord Bhuvaraha, the very form of Varāha who lifted Bhoomi Devī from the cosmic ocean. Revered by Vaishṇavas and Shaivas alike, it stands as a symbol of the all-encompassing grace of the Lord.

title: Kapila Charitram
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Kapila Charitram

Kapila was no ordinary child, for He was Bhagavān Himself, descending into the world to reveal the highest knowledge and to guide those who sought liberation. His father was Kardama Muni, a great sage who had spent countless years in deep penance in solitude. Pleased with his devotion, Sriman Nārāyaṇa appeared before him and granted him a rare boon — that the Lord Himself would be born as his son.
Kardama, however, had another duty to fulfill first. Svāyambhuva Manu, the ruler of the world and son of Brahmā, approached him seeking a suitable groom for his daughter Devahūti — a princess of great beauty, humility, and devotion. Though Kardama had lived detached from worldly affairs, he accepted the proposal, understanding it to be part of a greater design, and assured Devahūti that once his duties as a householder were complete he would renounce the world, and that she too should prepare herself for the path of liberation. It is said that when the Lord had descended to grant this boon, He arrived seated upon Garuḍa, and as Garuḍa beat his wings the sound of the Sama Veda mantras was heard — a sign that the essence of the Vedas rests upon the Vedas themselves, and that the Lord who rides upon them is the Purushottama celebrated in the Upanishads.
For years Devahūti served her husband with unwavering devotion, embracing the austere life of an ascetic's wife though she had once known only royal comfort. In time nine daughters were born to them, and then a son — Kapila, the Supreme Lord in human form. Even as a child His presence filled the hermitage with an indescribable peace, His lotuslike eyes shining with the brilliance of eternity. His duties as a householder now complete, Kardama bowed before his own divine son, sought his blessings, and departed for the forests to spend his remaining years in meditation.
Devahūti, left in the presence of her divine child, had one final request. She turned to Kapila not as a mother to her son but as a seeker to her teacher, and asked how one might gain mastery over the senses and be freed from the endless cycle of birth and death. In answer, Kapila revealed to her the knowledge of Sāṅkhya — the eternal truth of the soul and the path to liberation. He taught that this body and this world are but a play of prakriti, material nature, formed from twenty-four elements: the five great elements, the five senses, the mind, intelligence, ego, and the unmanifest material energy. The soul, the twenty-fifth principle, stands distinct from all of these; it is bound only by its false identification with the body, and the one who truly understands this is no longer moved by joy or sorrow, gain or loss.
Devahūti then asked how the soul comes to take shape within a mortal body, and Kapila explained to her the making of a human life. He described how the fertilized seed forms into a small mass within ten days; how the head takes shape by the end of the first month and the limbs by the second; how the nails, hair, skin, and organs form by the third month, and the blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, and vital fluids by the fourth. By the fifth month the child feels hunger and thirst; by the sixth it settles within the enveloping membrane and, tasting the food the mother eats, begins to develop taste. By the seventh month it turns its head downward and, feeling the confinement of the space, becomes aware of the sounds around it. In the eighth month, it is said, the child remembers all its previous births and even catches a glimpse of the Lord, and is filled with joy. By the ninth month it is ready to be born, delivered head first, its head still soft. And as it emerges into the air, a certain force acts upon it and causes it to forget all that it once knew of its former lives, so that the newborn cries in sorrow at all it has lost.
Kapila counseled his mother to place her whole faith in Sriman Nārāyaṇa, for devotion alone is the path to liberation — the one who chants His name with love and serves Him without expectation is already free, even while living in this world. As Devahūti absorbed this wisdom her mind grew free of ignorance; she saw herself no longer as queen, wife, or mother, but only as the soul, and in time she attained liberation, her being merging into the divine. Kapila, having fulfilled His purpose, left the hermitage and traveled across the lands, sharing the knowledge of Sāṅkhya and devotion for the awakening of countless souls.

title: Dhruva Charitram
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Dhruva Charitram

Dhruva was still a child when he left the comforts of a palace in search of something far greater than a kingdom. He was the son of King Uttanapada and Queen Sunīti, yet in his father's court he was made to feel that he did not belong, for the king's other wife, Suruchi, was the favored queen, and it was her son Uttama whom the king openly cherished.
One day Dhruva saw Uttama seated upon his father's lap and ran toward the throne, longing for the same affection. But before he could climb up, Suruchi drew him away and set her own son in his place. She told the boy that he had no right to that seat, that he was born of Sunīti and so was destined for no greatness, and that if he wished for such a place he would have to be born again from her own womb. She warned him never to approach his father in this way again, and the king sat silent, unwilling to oppose her.
Wounded but not weeping, Dhruva went to his mother Sunīti and told her what had passed. She did not fill his heart with bitterness, nor urge him to fight for what was his; instead she spoke the one truth that would change his destiny. She told him not to seek love where it was not given, and not to ask of men what only the Supreme could grant — for if he desired something truly great, he should seek it from Sriman Nārāyaṇa, who never turns away those who come to Him.
Her words kindled a fire in the boy. He left the palace and walked alone into the dense forest, not knowing where the Lord might be found, but certain that he would find Him. As he wandered, the sage Nārada appeared before him and, to test his resolve, told him that even the greatest sages meditate for lifetimes without beholding the Lord, and that he, a mere child, should return home. But Dhruva would not be turned aside. Seeing in the boy a heart that burned with true longing, Nārada relented, and taught him how to meditate. He told Dhruva to hold in his heart the image of a dark-complexioned Lord, His form like a monsoon cloud, His neck shaped like a conch, His shoulders broad and His waist slender, His lips like coral and His feet like lotuses, bearing in His four hands the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. He sent the boy to the sacred forest of Madhuvana, and gave him the mantra to chant.
There Dhruva began a penance of extraordinary severity. In the first month he ate only fruit, in the second only water, in the third he lived on air alone, his mind fixed unwaveringly upon the Lord. So powerful did his meditation grow that the very balance of the cosmos was disturbed, and the Devas, alarmed, rushed to Sriman Nārāyaṇa, who told them only that the boy sought Him. And so the Lord appeared. As Dhruva opened his eyes there stood before him Sriman Nārāyaṇa, clad in golden silk, smiling with infinite grace. Overwhelmed, the boy could find no words, until the Lord gently touched His conch to the child's throat and blessed him with speech.
Dhruva, his eyes filled with tears, confessed that he had come seeking a mere throne but now desired nothing but the Lord Himself. Moved by such innocence and devotion, the Lord granted him far more than he had ever asked. He promised the boy that he would rule the earth in righteousness for many years, and that when his time was done he would ascend beyond the Brahmandam itself, to shine forever as the Dhruva Mandala, an eternal realm untouched by destruction; and his mother Sunīti, who had earned it through her own devotion, would join him there. So the child who had once been denied a place on his father's lap was granted a place beyond the universe — for the one who seeks the Supreme, even beginning with a worldly wish, receives in the end His eternal refuge.

title: Daksha Yagnam
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Daksha Yajñam

Daksha was a Prajāpati, one of the chief progenitors of creation, born to Svāyambhuva Manu and Shatarūpā. Entrusted with the continuation of life in the universe, he had many children, among them twenty-seven daughters who became the Nakshatras and were wedded to Chandra, the moon god. Another of his daughters was Satī, also called Dākshāyaṇī, the embodiment of Shakti herself, who in a later birth would return as Pārvatī.
Satī had chosen for her husband Lord Shiva, the great renunciant who smeared His body with ash, adorned Himself with serpents, and dwelt among ascetics in the snow-clad Himālayas. To Daksha, who prized worldly grandeur and status, Shiva seemed an unworthy outsider, and he never forgave what he took to be an affront in his daughter's marriage. He failed to understand that Shiva was no mere recluse but the Supreme Yogi and the greatest among the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa.
His resentment found its opening at a grand yajna dedicated to Lord Vishṇu, where all the celestial beings had gathered, Brahmā and Shiva among them. When Daksha arrived, he offered his respects to the others but pointedly ignored Shiva. Shiva, who neither sought honor nor feared insult, remained unmoved; but Daksha mistook his silence for weakness and unleashed the anger he had long held within, declaring before the assembly that Shiva was unfit to sit among the righteous and cursing him to have no share in any yajna performed thereafter. At this, Shiva's devoted attendant Nandi could not stay silent. He cursed Daksha in turn, saying his pride would be shattered and he would bear the face of a goat, and he cursed the assembled brahmins who had sat silent while dharma was mocked, that they would wander the earth in torn clothing, cut off from the true essence of the Vedas. The sage Bhrigu, angered by Nandi's words, cursed those who disregarded Vedic ritual, that they would become the ash-smeared devotees of Shiva who dwell in cremation grounds. It is from this that the practice of smearing sacred ash, or bhasma, upon the body came to be associated with Shiva's devotees — not as a mark of impurity, but as a symbol of detachment from worldly illusion, even though the Vedas ordinarily regard anything connected with death as inauspicious.
Daksha's arrogance only grew, and he resolved to perform another great rite, the Brihaspati-sava Yajña, to which he invited all the celestials save Shiva and Satī. When Satī learned that she and her husband had been excluded, she was torn between her duty as a daughter and her devotion to her husband. Shiva, ever detached, told her she was free to go, but warned that where reverence is absent even the most sacred place becomes impure. Satī went to the yajna and demanded to know why her husband had been slighted; when Daksha answered only with fresh insults against Shiva, her heart burned — not for herself, but for the offense against the greatest devotee of the Lord. Declaring that she would return the body her father had given her, she sat in a yogic posture, drew forth a fire from within herself, and was consumed by the flames.
When the Ganas carried word of Satī's fate to Shiva, He who had borne every insult in silence now acted. In His fury He tore a lock from His matted hair and struck it upon the ground, and from it arose Veerabhadra, a being of terrible wrath. Veerabhadra stormed into the yajna, scattered the fleeing celestials, severed Daksha's head, and plucked the moustache from Bhrigu's face. When the sages and Devas at last pacified him, the yajna lay in ruins. But the Lord does not destroy to punish; He destroys to transform. At the pleading of the assembled beings, Shiva's wrath subsided, and Daksha was restored to life — but with the head of a goat, a mark of the folly of his pride, while a goat's beard was fixed upon Bhrigu's face. Only then, in true surrender, was the yajna completed. The lesson of this tale is that Shiva, the foremost devotee of Vishṇu, was insulted, and that to insult the Lord's devotee is, knowingly or not, to insult the Lord Himself, and to bear the consequences. And though Satī was gone, she was destined to return as Pārvatī, daughter of the Himālayas, and once more find her way to Shiva.

title: Gajendra Moksham
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Gajendra Moksham

To understand the liberation of Gajendra, one must first know the histories of the two beings whose fates were bound together in it. In the land that would one day become Puri in Odisha, there ruled a noble and devoted king named Indradyumna, whose heart overflowed with devotion to Sriman Nārāyaṇa and who, it is said, built the great Jagannath Temple. So absorbed was he in his worship that when the sage Agastya once came to his court seeking hospitality, the king, lost in meditation, did not notice his arrival. Agastya, known for his fiery temper, mistook the silence for arrogance and cursed the king to be reborn as an elephant, that through such a form he might truly learn the meaning of devotion.
Elsewhere, a Gandharva named Huhu, proud of his beauty and celestial voice, once mocked the sage Devala and disturbed his penance; the angered sage cursed him to be reborn as a crocodile, to dwell in the waters until the Lord Himself should grant him release. And so two souls — a king turned elephant, a Gandharva turned crocodile — were set upon a course to meet.
Reborn as Gajendra, Indradyumna became the mighty ruler of an elephant herd upon the Mountain of Trikuta. Yet even in this new form his soul remembered, and each day he would go to a sacred lake upon the mountain, pluck a lotus from its waters with his trunk, and raise it to the sky in offering to the Lord.
