Seeing his plight, Arjuna stepped forward and vowed upon his kshatriya dharma that he would retrieve the child, and that if he failed he would enter fire and end his life. When the brahmana's wife conceived for the tenth time, Arjuna stood guard with his celestial weapons, raising an impenetrable barrier of divine arrows around their home so that no force, earthly or celestial, could breach it. Yet at the moment of birth the child vanished just as before. Stunned and humiliated, Arjuna searched the heavens and the netherworld with his divine vision, and finding nothing, prepared to honor his vow and enter the fire.
Before he could, Krishna intervened, smiling, and bade Arjuna come with Him to search for the missing children together. Mounting His celestial chariot, Krishna bore Arjuna beyond the earthly realms into a vast and terrifying expanse of absolute darkness, a void where neither sun nor moon nor star could penetrate, where time itself seemed to dissolve. Sensing Arjuna's unease, Krishna summoned His Sudarshana Chakra, and the divine discus, radiant like a thousand suns, cut through the darkness and illuminated the path ahead, revealing a cosmic ocean of swirling energies and celestial pathways unknown to mortals. Guided by its light, the chariot advanced unhindered, and Arjuna understood that without Krishna's presence no being, however mighty, could cross that realm.
Their journey led them to Karya Vaikuṇṭham, where Lord Maha-Vishṇu Himself resided in all His glory, surrounded by celestial beings — and there before Him sat the missing children, unharmed, their faces glowing with divine radiance. Maha-Vishṇu revealed that it was He who had brought the children there, for He had desired to behold Krishna's divine form; now that His wish was fulfilled, they would be returned. With reverence Krishna and Arjuna gathered the children and descended to Dwārakā, where the griefstricken parents wept with joy to embrace their long-lost sons. Arjuna, humbled by all he had witnessed, understood at last that Krishna, whom he had known as his dear friend, charioteer, and guide, was none other than the Supreme Lord, beyond time and space and comprehension.
According to tradition, along with returning the children Krishna gifted the brahmana a divine idol of Maha-Vishṇu, the very form He and Arjuna had beheld in Karya Vaikuṇṭham, as a blessing for uninterrupted progeny and prosperity. This idol is believed to be the one now worshipped as Poornathrayeesa in the Poornathrayeesha Temple at Tripunithura in Kerala, a revered site where devotees seek the Lord's blessings for children and the well-being of their families.

title: Rukmiṇī Kalyanam
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Rukmiṇī Kalyanam

Rukmiṇī, princess of Vidarbha, was the very embodiment of beauty, virtue, and devotion. Though she had never seen Krishna, her heart belonged to Him, for from childhood she had heard of His divine pastimes — the slaying of Kaṃsa, the lifting of Govardhan, His boundless compassion for His devotees. From the words of sages, travelers, and poets she had gathered a picture of a Lord whose every action was rooted in dharma and love, and the more she heard, the deeper her love grew, until she resolved to accept no one but Sri Krishna as her husband.
But fate seemed to work against her. Her elder brother Rukmi was a staunch adversary of Krishna, and disregarding his sister's wishes he arranged her marriage to his close friend Shishupāla, king of Chedi and Krishna's sworn enemy, determined that she should never be united with Krishna. As the wedding preparations went forward Rukmiṇī found herself trapped in despair, but she was not one to surrender. On the night before the wedding she summoned Sunanda, a trusted brahmana messenger, and entrusted him with a letter to be carried with all haste to Dwārakā and placed in Krishna's own hands.
In the letter she poured out her heart, telling Krishna that she had heard of His glories and His kindness toward those who take refuge in Him, that she had surrendered her heart and soul to Him alone, and that cruel fate now sought to bind her to a man she did not love. She wrote that on the morning of the wedding she would visit the temple of Goddess Pārvatī at dawn, and that she would await Him there; if He did not come, she would surrender her life, for a life without Him was a fate worse than death. She begged Him to come swiftly and claim her as His own, just as Lord Vishṇu had rescued the Earth from the depths of the ocean.
Deeply moved by her devotion and urgency, Krishna wasted no time. Summoning His charioteer Daruka, He set out for Vidarbha with the speed of the wind. As dawn broke, Rukmiṇī walked gracefully to the temple of Pārvatī, performed her prayers, and deliberately lingered, buying time for Krishna to arrive. Just as she stepped out of the temple, Krishna appeared like a streak of lightning; before anyone could react He lifted her into His chariot and rode away.
News of the abduction spread swiftly, and Rukmi, enraged and humiliated, set out with his army and several allied kings to pursue Krishna and reclaim his sister. Catching up, Rukmi ordered his forces to attack, and a fierce battle erupted, arrows raining down upon Krishna. But Krishna countered every assault with effortless grace, His bow Sharṅga cutting through the enemy ranks, while Balarāma joined the fray and scattered the army with sheer force, until Rukmi's forces lay in ruins. Rukmi himself then stood before Krishna, defiant yet outmatched; Krishna broke his bow with a single shot and struck aside his sword, leaving him defenseless. As Krishna raised His weapon to deliver the final blow, Rukmiṇī rushed forward and fell at His feet, pleading that He spare her brother, for though he had wronged her, she could not bear to see his life taken. Honoring her request, Krishna spared Rukmi's life, but as a mark of humiliation cut off half of his moustache and hair, leaving him disgraced.
With Rukmi defeated, Krishna and Rukmiṇī proceeded to Dwārakā, where their wedding was celebrated with unparalleled joy, the Devas themselves showering flowers from the heavens. Thus Rukmiṇī became the chief queen of Dwārakā and the beloved of Sri Krishna, the very embodiment of devotion and surrender — proof that true love, joined with devotion and determination, always triumphs.

title: The Narayaneeyam and Melpathur Nārāyaṇa Bhattathiri
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Narayaneeyam and Melpathur Nārāyaṇa Bhattathiri

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The Nārāyaṇīyam and Melpathur Nārāyaṇa Bhattathiri

The Shrīmad Bhāgavatam has inspired countless devotees across the ages, and among the most beloved of the works it gave rise to is the Nārāyaṇīyam, a condensed retelling of the Bhāgavatam in Sanskrit verse, composed in Kerala toward the close of the sixteenth century by Melpathur Nārāyaṇa Bhattathiri. Where the Bhāgavatam runs to some eighteen thousand verses, the Nārāyaṇīyam distills its essence into roughly a thousand and thirty-six shlokas, arranged in a hundred cantos called dasakas, each of about ten verses. To this day it is sung at the Guruvayur temple in Kerala, where its story began.
Bhattathiri was born around 1560 into a Namboothiri Brāhmaṇa family near the temple town of Tirunavaya, on the banks of the Bharathapuzha river. He was a prodigy, and it is said that he had mastered the Vedas, the Vedangas, and the disciplines of Mimamsa, Vyakarana, and Tarka by the age of sixteen, learning first from his own father, Mathrudatta, himself a great scholar, and later from the celebrated grammarian and astronomer Achyuta Pishārati. Beyond his devotional fame, Bhattathiri was a formidable grammarian in his own right; his treatise on Sanskrit grammar, the Prakriya-sarvasvam, elaborated upon the classical system of Panini and secured his reputation among scholars.
The composition of the Nārāyaṇīyam is bound up with a moving legend. It is said that when Bhattathiri's teacher, Achyuta Pishārati, was afflicted with paralysis, Bhattathiri, out of devotion to his guru, prayed that the disease be transferred to his own body, and so took the ailment upon himself to relieve his teacher. Now himself afflicted and suffering, he had himself carried to the temple of Lord Krishna at Guruvayur, and lay prostrate before the Lord seeking refuge. He sought counsel from Tuñchath Ezhuthachan, revered as the father of the Malayalam language, who gave him the cryptic advice to "begin with the fish." Bhattathiri understood at once that he was being told to compose a hymn to the incarnations of Vishṇu beginning with Matsya, the fish — that is, to retell the Bhāgavatam itself.
And so, seated before the Lord at Guruvayur, Bhattathiri composed one dasaka each day, ten verses at a time, each canto ending with a heartfelt prayer for relief from his affliction. Over a hundred days he summarized the whole of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, moving through the philosophy of the Supreme, the avataras, the deeds of Krishna, and the teachings of devotion. Tradition holds that on the hundredth day, as he lifted his head to begin the final canto, he was granted the vision of Guruvayurappan himself standing before him, and was at last cured of his illness; the hundredth dasaka, the celebrated Kesadi-pada Varnanam, is his rapturous description of that vision, tracing the Lord's form from the crown of His head down to His feet. Because the work is about Nārāyaṇa and was composed by one who himself bore the name Nārāyaṇa, the Lord is said to have named it the Nārāyaṇīyam.
The opening of the poem is not narrative but philosophical, establishing at once that the charming cowherd of Guruvayur is none other than the supreme Brahman. Its very first verse describes the Lord as sāndrānanda — the embodiment of dense, unbroken bliss and pure awareness, beyond compare, free of the limits of time and space, eternally liberated, illumined by countless scriptures — and marvels that this very Brahman shines forth directly and visibly in Guruvayur, calling it the great good fortune of all people:

sāndrānandāvabodhātmakam anupamitaṃ kāladeshāvadhibhyāṃ
nirmuktaṃ nityamuktaṃ nigamashatasahasreṇa nirbhāsyamānam;
aspashṭaṃ dṛshṭamātre punar uru purushārthātmakaṃ brahmatattvaṃ
tat tāvad bhāti sākshād gurupavanapure hanta bhāgyaṃ janānām.

In this way the Nārāyaṇīyam holds together two great currents of thought — the vision of the formless, non-dual Supreme, and the loving worship of the Lord in His beautiful, accessible form — and throughout, it lifts up the chanting of the divine name and complete self-surrender, prapatti, as the surest paths to liberation. Its final canto describes the Lord in intimate detail from head to foot, and the work closes with the celebrated prayer āyurārogya-saukhyam — a plea for long life, health, and happiness — words that devotees have repeated ever since in the faith that the careful recitation of the Nārāyaṇīyam is itself a balm for both body and spirit. The day on which Bhattathiri dedicated his work to the Lord is still observed each year at Guruvayur as Nārāyaṇīyam Dinam.

title: The Benefits of Reading or Listening to Srimad Bhagavatam
parentTitle: Srimad Bhagavata Kathasagaram

fields.name: title
fields.text: The Benefits of Reading or Listening to Srimad Bhagavatam

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The Benefits of Reading or Listening to Shrīmad Bhāgavatam

The Bhāgavatam itself describes the fruits that come to one who reads or hears it with sincerity. Such a person attains merit equal to the charity of a thousand cows, and gains the benefit of studying all eighteen Purāṇas. One who reads or listens with full concentration need not fear Yama after death, for they are assured of moksha, and the act is as meritorious as a pilgrimage to all the sacred teertha-kshetras. It grants a long life free from disease and the burden of past sins, and the purity it bestows surpasses even the blessings of visiting Badrikashramam or bathing at Prayāga. Most importantly, the Lord never forsakes one who sincerely reads or listens to the Shrīmad Bhāgavatam, remaining ever present by their side.
And so this retelling closes with the traditional benediction of auspiciousness to the Lord who is the beloved of Sri and the treasury of all that is good:

shriyaḥ kāntāya kalyāṇa-nidhaye nidhaye'rthinām;
shrī-veṅkaṭa-nivāsāya shrīnivāsāya maṅgalam.

Sarvam Sri Krishnarpanamastu.

title: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

title: Foreword
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Foreword

Human life is marked by a perennial quest: Who am I? Why am I here? What lies beyond this life? These timeless questions form the foundation of all philosophical inquiry. In the sacred traditions of India, particularly in the teachings of Bhagavad Rāmānujar and the lineage of acharyas before and after him, we find profound answers to these questions—answers that are both intellectually satisfying and spiritually liberating.
This book seeks to offer a gateway into the rich and nuanced worldview of Vishishṭādvaita Vedānta, the philosophy of qualified non-dualism. At its heart lies the understanding of the jeevaathma—the individual soul—as a conscious, eternal entity distinct from the body, ever longing to reach Sriman Nārāyaṇa, the Paramātma. The journey of the soul through various embodiments, and its eventual goal of attaining moksham—liberation from the cycle of birth and death—is central to this tradition.
In the pages that follow, I have endeavoured to present the essential concepts of Vishishṭādvaita in a manner that is accessible yet faithful to scriptural and traditional authority. From the foundational tattvas—Chith, Achith, and Īshvara—to the paths of Bhakti and Prapatti, and the ultimate goal of divine service in Sri Vaikuṇṭham, this work aims to illuminate the path for spiritual aspirants who seek both knowledge and devotion.
This book is not merely an academic exposition, but a heartfelt offering—a tribute to the great acharyas and to the grace that flows through the guru-parampara. May it serve as a humble companion for those who wish to deepen their understanding of the jeevaathma's divine destiny and the compassionate philosophy that guides it.
May the blessings of Sri Rāmānujar, Swami Deshikan, and all our Poorvaacharyas guide every reader on their journey toward the eternal feet of the Divine Couple, Sriman Nārāyaṇa and Sri Mahālakshmī.

title: Tattvas
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Tattvas

The Vishishṭādvaita Philosophy speaks of three tattvas or three ways one can interpret creation. Those three tattvas are:
Chith or the Jīvātmā
Achith or the Prakriti
Īshvara or the Paramātma
Chith or the Jīvātmā refers to the souls of any living being in creation.
Achith, or the Prakriti, refers to nature or surroundings in which the soul would reside.
Īshvara or the Paramātma refers to the Lord, who is the Almighty Supreme Ruler of the universe.
In nature, we observe hundreds of thousands of living creatures, each of which possesses a soul. Therefore, Achith acts as a residence for all that is Chith. From this, we can draw the inference that Chith and Achith are inseparable from one another.
As for Īshvara, He dwells in both Chith and Achith. Thus, Chith and Achith are inseparable from Īshvara.
From this, we establish what is known as Sharīra-Sharīri Bhāva, i.e., the relationship between the dweller and that which dwells. We see that Īshvara lives within Chith and Achith, bringing them together. Hence, Īshvara Tattva is treated as the Ultimate, which controls everything in creation.

title: Aathma
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Ātma

The soul that is otherwise known as Chith, Ātma, or Jīva, is an independent entity that should not be confused with the functions of the body or its brain. It is free of thought, emotion, will, or intelligence. It is not situated in any particular part of the body. It pervades the entirety of space, throughout every atom in every living being. When an organism dies and is burnt or buried, the soul does not die. The aathma is incapable of death. It is eternal. The aathma is not visible, is incomprehensible, and is unchangeable. The aathma is constituted by knowledge and bliss and is self-luminous.
The knowledge that constitutes the aathma is of two types, namely

 i)Dharmi Jnānam
 ii)Dharmabhuta Jnānam
Dharmi Jnānam helps the aathma be aware of itself at all times, whereas the Dharmabhuta Jnānam helps it know its body, the body's surroundings, all the people in the body's lifetime, and the objects beyond the body. Thus, when the body expires, the aathma loses its Dharmabhuta Jnānam. The best comparison to understand this concept is that of a luminous lantern. The aathma can be interpreted as a bright flame. The body is the fuel of the fire. Even if the body expires, the aathma can find refuge in another vessel, which will act as fuel to the eternal flame. For the fire to be genuinely immortal, it must merge with the Paramātma. Upon merging with the Paramātma, the aathma would not require any new body and would know eternal bliss as it reached its final destination.

title: Eternal bliss in Shri Vaikuṇṭham
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Eternal bliss in Sri Vaikuṇṭham

On attaining moksham, the aathma gains unrestricted access to Paramapadam or Sri Vaikuṇṭham, which is the highest realm attainable, according to Vishishṭādvaita Philosophy. It is said that upon reaching Paramapadam, the aathma enjoys four experiences eternally. These four experiences are called:
Sālokya: Being able to live in the same world as the Lord.
Sārūpya: Having the same appearance as the Lord with Chaturbhujam, Shanku, Chakram, Gadha, and Padmam.
Samipa: Always being near the Lord.
Sāyujya: Being able to partake in the Lord's bliss and enjoy it just the same as Him.
The Dharmabhuta Jnānam achieved in Paramapadam is eternal and complete. The Lord restores to the new muktha-aathma eight qualities, i.e.;
 i) Being free from any sin
 ii) Being free of any aging
 iii) Being free of death
 iv)Being free of sorrow
 v)Being free of hunger
 vi) Being free of thirst
 vii)Being endowed with all that the muktha-aathma desires
 viii) Finally, offering the muktha-aathma no return to samsaaram or bhu-lokam.
Therefore, the ultimate goal for any jeevaathma is to attain moksham or liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
Moksham or mukti provides what is known as Paripurna Brahmā-Anubhavam, which is a complete understanding of the Paramātma. We can understand the Lord's nature ( swarupa ), His delightful nature ( vigraha ), His auspicious qualities ( kalyana gunam ), His ability to put time on hold or let it run according to His will ( Leela Vibuti and Nithya Vibhuti ). The aathma's enjoyment is eternal and will always result in service to the Paramātma at all times under any given situation.

title: The aathma, as mentioned and described by the Bhagavad Gītā
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: The aathma, as mentioned and described by the Bhagavad Gītā

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The aathma, as mentioned and described by the Bhagavad Gītā

The main takeaways that one can take from the Gītā when talking about the aathma are as follows:
i) The number of births that are taken by a jeevaathma is innumerable:
 The Lord tells Arjuna that both of them have taken numerous incarnations together in this world. But only the Lord remembers all of them, whereas Arjuna does not. The Lord elucidates that He can remember everything as He is eternal and pure.


ii) Nature of the aathma:
The Lord tells Arjuna that just as birth, childhood, youth, and old age are inevitable stages of a human's growth in life, similarly, it is unavoidable for the soul to find a new body after its current vessel expires. The Lord says the soul is unborn, indestructible, and never dies. It is eternal. Fire cannot burn it, water cannot moisten it, and wind cannot dry it. Just as a man casts off old, worn-out garments, the soul casts off old, worn-out bodies and enters a new one.

iii) Effect of the three Guṇas on the manifested aathma:
Grossly speaking, the three Guṇas quickly bind to the body, which in turn impacts the aathma. The three Guṇas are:
iii.i) Sattva Gunam: This Gunam is associated with individuals who engage in activities that are pure and focused on seeking genuine knowledge of the Supreme.
iii. ii) Rajas Gunam: This Gunam links to those who engage in activities that are driven by passion, thirst, and action.
iii. iii) Tāmasa Gunam: This Gunam links to those who engage in ignorance, negligence, and lethargy.
 The three Guṇas bind to the body at the time of death, granting different realms to the aathma upon bondage. If Sattva Gunam predominantly occupies the body, then the aathma attains Brahmalokam, a realm of knowledge. If Rajas Gunam predominantly occupies the body, then the person is reborn as a radical or a person of action. Finally, if Tāmasa Gunam mainly occupies the body, then the person is reborn as an irrational being.


iv) Attaining Liberation
 The one who declares that their devotion to the Lord transcends the three Guṇas becomes qualified to attain moksham. The Lord tells Arjuna to relinquish all dharma and take refuge solely in Him. He will liberate you from your sins and grant you moksham.

v) What sort of person can reach Paramapadam?
Lord Krishna declares that a person who is free from pride, delusion, evil, attachment, self-obsession, desire, pleasure, and pain can attain Paramapadam.

title: Artha Panchakam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Artha Panchakam

Swami Deshikan is considered to be an incarnation of the divine bell of Sri Venkateshwara Swami of Tirumalai. Swami Deshikan was born here in Tooppul to Sri Anantha Suri and Devī Totaramba. By birth, Swami Deshikan was named Veṅkaṭanātha. When Swami Deshikan was just five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Kidambi Appular, to attend a discourse by Nadadhoor Ammal, a revered Sri Vaishṇava Scholar at the time. As soon as Nadadhoor Ammal saw Veṅkaṭanātha, he saw a divine radiance in the child and stopped the lecture that he was delivering to hug the child affectionately. After this, when Nadadhoor Ammal said that he had forgotten where he had finished his discourse, Veṅkaṭanātha reminded him as to where he had stopped his lecture. This act astonished the crowd as they had never seen a five-year-old boy comprehend the deep intricacies of philosophical knowledge that was being discussed. It was then that Nadadhoor Ammal predicted and blessed Veṅkaṭanātha that he, in the future, would become the torch-bearer to spread Sri Vaishṇavism everywhere.

At each place, he composed many different works in languages such as Tamil, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Manipravala (a mixture of Sanskrit and Tamil) that revealed his ingenuity creativity, logic, linguistic expertise, devotional fervor, and erudite scholarship.

Some of his greatest works include:
 1) Hayagrīva Stotram
2) Sudarshana Ashtakam
3) Pādukā Sahasram
4) Abhītistavam
5) Achyuta Shatakam
6) Dayā Shatakam
7) Haṃsa Sandesham
8) Sri Stuti
9) Yādavābhyudayam
10) Kamasikashatakam

The Artha Panchakam, composed by Swami Deshikan, is a set of 11 Pāsurams dedicated to Sri Varadaraja Perumāl of Kanchipuram. The 11 Pāsurams are assigned to two of each of the five doctrines or truths of the Artha Panchakam.
The five doctrines discussed are as follows:
The Svarūpam of Parabrahman.
The Svarūpam of the jeevaathma.
The obstacles that prevent us from reaching Paramapadam
The means to moksham: Bhakti and Prapatti
The supreme goal of Bhagavat Anubhavam

Now, we will examine each of the 11 Pāsurams and understand their meaning.


Amalan aviyAtha-sudar aLavillaa-AarAmudham
amala uru guNangaL aNi aayudhangal adiyavarkaL
amala azhiyAtha nahar azhinthu yezhum kaavudan yellAm
Kamalayudan arasALum Karigiri mERk-KaavalanaE … 1
Meaning:
Svarūpam of Parabramham
This samsaaram is a karma bhumi. The Lord plays a sport of distributing karma-phalam to the aathma as per what it had accumulated through the course of its janmam. There are no limits to the Lord's auspicious gunas. He has "Svarūpa-Niroopaka Viseshanam and Niroopita-Svarūpa Viseshanam" among his gunas. Viseshanam is a distinctive characteristic that sets Him apart from others.
The Svarūpa Niroopaka Guṇas are five in number:
Satyatvam: He is invariant at all times.
Jnatatvam: His knowledge is eternal.
Anantatvam: He is present everywhere at all times.
Anandatvam: His presence brings out eternal bliss.
Amalatvam: He is the only one who is blemishless.

uLLa poruL anaitthukkum uruva nilai karumangaL
teLLisaivin vasamAkkit-thihazhnthu uyirAi uRaihinRAn
naLL iruL theertthu adiyavarkku nalam kodukkum ThiruvudanE
VaLLal AruLALar yenum VaaraNa veRppu IRayavanE … 2

Meaning:
Everything in creation is under the control of the Lord's Saṅkalpam.
Attigiri Nathan and Perundevi Tāyār pervade in all objects of creation and control them by their will. The Lord will sever all the bonds of samsaram for those who perform sharanagati and will grant them moksham.


BhUtha vudal pulankaL manam pul aavi punthi yenum
yAthum alanAi ilahi yaann yenum inn nuNN aRivAi
chEthananAi adimaiyumAmm yuirkellAm tiNNuyirAi
theethal inRi thihazhum Seer Athtigiri Thirumaal … 3

Meaning:
Svarūpam of jeevaathma.
The Pancha-bhutas, the senses, the mind, prana, and jnana constitute the body. This is distinctly different from the jeevaathma. The jeevaathma is of a diminutive size, and it differs from one body to another. The only aspect that is common to all jeevaathmas is the property of being a servant to the Lord.

taan adaittha guNam karuvi tamm girisai vazhi ozhukki
oon yedutthu uNDu umizhnthu uzhalum yuirkku yellAm uyirAhi
kaan nadatthi Kamalayudan kaNDuhanthu viLayAdym
tEn yeduttha solaihaL soozh Thiru AtthiyUrAnE … 4

Meaning:
The Lord witnesses how the jeevaathma enjoys the karma-phalam that was provided.
As seen in the first Pāsuram, the Lord distributes the karma-phalam to every jeevaathma. As the jeevaathma begins to experience the karma-phalam, it begins to detest it, and desires start to occupy the body. Due to this desire, the jeevaathma is sent continuously back into the ocean, known as samsara, to fulfill its desires. Perarulalan, along with Perundevi Tāyār, enters the jeevaathmas and bears witness to how the jeevaathma enjoys its karma-phalam.

uyyum uRavu isayAthE otthavarkkE adimayumAi
poy uruvai tamakku yERRip-pulan koNDa payanE koNDu
iyuRavum aar iruLum al-vazhiyum adainthavarkkE
meyyaruL seythidum ThirumAl vEzha malai MEyavanE … 5

Meaning:
The Moksha Virodhi
The jeevaathma does not remember its inherent, inescapable links to the Lord and unfortunately, gets associated with another bonded jeevaathma. The jeevaathma starts to engage itself in trivial pleasures because it cannot recall the difference between itself and the body in which it is temporarily stationed. Such a jeevaathma fails to find the right Āchārya and is therefore full of arrogance and ignorance. The jeevaathma feels agony and engages itself in inauspicious activities. The Lord feels pity for such jeevaathmas and opens up a path to find the right Āchārya and re-engage in bhakti so that it may qualify for sharanagati and prapatti, thus allowing the Lord to liberate it from its cycle of birth and death.
vidhai muLayin nyAyatthAl adi illA vinai adaivE
sathai udala nAlvahaikkum saraNamaLIppAn yenat-thihazndhu
padhavi aRiyAthu pazham pAzhil uzhalhinRArkku
sithaivu ill aruL tarum Thiru AtthinaharAnE … 6

 Meaning:
The bondages of Samsaaram and Karma
The Lord protects and blesses all jeevaathmas, showing them ways of redemption, leading them to moksham and freedom from being reborn as either Deva, Manushya, Thiyak, and Sthavara. He showers his grace eternally, leading it to moksham. vidhai muLayin nyAyam refers to an age-old debate/question. What came first, the seed or the plant? This is hard to tell.
Similarly, our Āchāryas raised the question of what came first, the body or the karma-phalam? The answer that was decided was that both karma and the body are intertwined, as whatever karma the previous vessel of the aathma performed, so that it would reap the karma-phalam leading into the next vessel. Thus, both karma and body are timeless and ancient. This was the conclusion that our Āchāryas arrived at.


yama niyama aasanangaL iyal aavi pulanadakkam
tamathu aRiyum dhAraNaikaL tArai aRA ninaivu ozhukkam
samam udaya samAdhi nalam sAthippArkku ilakku aahum
amarar thozhum Atthigiri ambhyutthAL AaramudhE … 7

Meaning:
Bhakti and Prapatti Upayam
The Lord severs all the bonds of Samsaram for those who practice bhakti-yogam in its totality along with its eight angams. The eight angams of bhakti-yogam are mentioned as follows:
(1) Yamam ( ahimsa, Sathyam, non-stealing, control of Kaamam et al.)
(2) Niyamam ( Parisuddhi, Satisfaction with what one has, the performance of
vratham/tapas, efforts at Vedantha Paricchayam, Saathvika Thyagam )
(3) Aasanam ( Yogic postures like Padhmasanam)
(4) Pranayamam ( Control of Breath)
(5) PrathyAhAram ( Control of senses & Turning them away
from the worldly sukhams and temptations)
(6) Dharanai( Imprint of Bhagavān's Tirumeni in one's mind)
(7) Dhyanam ( uninterrupted meditation of the Lord)
(8) Samadhi ( reaching a state of anubhavam through dhyAnam,
wherein the performer feels that he is seeing the Lord directly).
One can attain moksham by opting for either bhakti-yoga or by performing sharanagati at the feet of an Āchārya.



puhal ulahil illAthu ponnaruL kaNDu uRRavaRkkum
ahalahilA anbarkkum anRE TannaruL kodutthup-
pahalathanAl pazham kangul vidivikkum PankayatthAL
ahalahilEn yenRu uRayum Atthigiri aruL muhilE … 8

Meaning:
Elaboration on Prapatti
Attigiri Nathan is compared to a dark cloud in the rainy season, full of water, ready to shower at any time. Similarly, the Lord is a cloud of daya and karunai. Those who perform prapatti to the Lord shall forever feel the grace of the Lord showering over them. Before performing prapatti at the feet of the Lord, it is necessary first to seek permission at the feet of Mahālakshmī to help us successfully perform prapatti at the Lord's feet.

iru vilangu vidutthu iruntha siRai vidutthOr naadiyinAl
karu nilankaL kadakkum vazhi kAvalarAl kadatthuvitthup-
perunilam kaNDu uyir uNarnthu piriyAmal aruL seyyum
uru nalam koNDu uRum ThiruvOdu uyar AtthigiriyAnE … 9




Meaning:
Elaboration on Moksha Svarūpam
Mahālakshmī has roopam and kalyana gunams. These allow Her to stay eternally with the Lord. When one performs sharanagathi to the Lord, the jeevaathma becomes capable of entering Sri Vaikuṇṭham and forgetting the burdens of the Achiraadi Margam. Paapam and Punyam bind to the jeevaathma before performing sharanagathi. Once Sharanagathi is completed, neither paapam nor punyam can link with the aathma, as the Lord offers a permanent place by His holy feet for all eternity.

Tamm ThirumAthudanE thAmm tani arasAy uRaihinRa
antham ilA pEr inbatthil adiyavarOdu yemai sErtthu
munthi izhanthana yellAm muhizhhikka tanthu aatkoLLum
antham ilA aruLAzhi Atthigirit-ThirumAlE … 10

Meaning:
Gaining of Sarva Kainkaryam during Moksham
The Lord and Mahālakshmī eternally rule over Sri Vaikuṇṭham. When the Lord grants moksham to any jeevaathma, He turns the jeevaathma into a mukthaathma, giving them a place alongside the Nitya-Sooris and other fellow mukthaathmas, allowing the mukthaathma to perform kainkaryam to the Lord eternally.


Ayan paNiyum Atthigiri AruLALar adiyiNai mEl
nayankaL seRi Kacchi nagar nAnnmaRayOr nallaruLAl
payankaL ivai anaitthum yenap-paNDuraitthAr padi uraittha
viyan kalaikaL yeerainthum vEdhiyarkku iniyanavE …11
Meaning:
Phala Stuti
This prabhandham was created in tune with the upadesams of Poorva Āchāryas and has been realized with the anugraham of Parama Bhagavathas, who have the good fortune of enjoying the dhivya soundharyam and Kalyana gunams of Lord Varadarajan, who presides over Atthigiri . Only Mahans with the familiarity of the meanings of Vedams can relate to them and enjoy the sweetness of the implications of these Paasurams.

title: The vital, crucial role of an Āchārya
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: The vital, crucial role of an Āchārya

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The vital, crucial role of an Āchārya

A person who understands that he lacks the prescribed qualifications or ability to follow Karma, Jnāna, and Bhakti but has the conviction and a longing desire to reach the Lord has a smooth and sure path laid out for him. All one must do is seek out an Āchārya who will act as the spiritual guide. One must remain devoted and steadfast, with absolute faith that the Āchārya will see them through in their spiritual journey to attain the Supreme. The only requirements are total desire, devotion, and faith in the Āchārya. If a disciple follows the teachings of their Āchārya, they will obtain all the benefits of dharma, artha, kama, and moksha.

title: Sriman Nārāyaṇa is the first Āchārya
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: Sriman Nārāyaṇa is the first Āchārya

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Sriman Nārāyaṇa is the first Āchārya

There are many reasons why the Lord is attributed to our first Āchārya. The following can be considered the most significant reasons:
a) The Lord taught the Vedas to Lord Brahmā.
b) The Lord revealed the Dwaya Mantram to a scared Mahālakshmī when Madhu-Kaithaba stole the Vedas.
c) Through the teachings propagated to Lord Brahmā, He made sure that man reaps the benefit of the Vedas.
d) The Lord graced the four sons of Lord Brahmā- Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanatsujata, and through them, He propagated Hita.
e) He is present as the Antharyami (the one who governs from inside) of great souls like Devarishi Nārada, Parāshara, and Parankusha.
f) The Lord incarnated as Hamsa, Hayagriva, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Sri Krishna, and propagated Tattva-Hita-Purushārtha.
g) He made a great soul, such as Bhīshma, give the world great teachings such as the Neeti Shāstra.
h) At the end of Dwapara Yugam, when the teachings of the Pancharatra Agamas were lost, the Lord reincarnated as Sankarshana to re-establish them.
i) To establish the Āchārya-Sishya relationship, He incarnated as Nara-Nārāyaṇa and taught Nara the Tirumantram to Nara at Badrinath.
j) As access to the Vedas became restricted, the Lord, through the Āzhwārs, gave the world the Nalayira Divya Prabandhaṅgaḷ or the Tamil Veda, which propagated the message of the Vedas in a local language.
k) When the Buddhists tried to preach their teachings, which went against the Vedas, the Lord, through Āchārya's teachings, re-established the Vedantic Philosophy.

title: The need for an Āchārya in one's spiritual life
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: The need for an Āchārya in one's spiritual life

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The need for an Āchārya in one's spiritual life

One who desires moksham must seek out an Āchārya. When one seeks out an Āchārya and surrenders at their feet, any sin will not pose any hindrance to moksham. Without an Āchārya, regardless of how many good deeds we may commit in our lifetime, we will not be eligible for moksham.
Here are a few anecdotes that elucidate the role of an Āchārya in our lives.

Vishṇu Dharmam tells the story of Kshethrabandhu, who retorted to evil ways but was reformed by a sage. The sage was pleased by Kshethrabandhu's attention span and advised him to chant the name of Govinda, and that one day, the Lord would show him the path of righteousness, reforming him. Kshethrabandhu followed the sage's advice and gained Paramapadam.

Padmottara Purāṇam tells the story of Pundarika, who relentlessly practiced bhakti-yoga but could not get a glimpse of the Lord and hence became dejected. One day, Pundarika encountered Devarishi Nārada and explained to him what plight he was facing. Devarishi Nārada told Pundarika not to worry and gave him the Ashtaakshara Mantram, instructing him to chant and meditate upon it. Pundarika earnestly followed Devarishi Nārada's advice and attained Paramapadam.

title: The duties of an Āchārya
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
The duties of an Āchārya

The Āchārya must first master the three divine secrets and their meaning in their entirety. Only after learning it in its entirety is he supposed to pass it on to his pupils. The Āchārya must perform Pañcha-Saṃskāram, which includes initiation to the three divine mantras, namely the Tirumantram, Dwaya Mantram, and Charama Shloka.
The Āchārya must impart in privacy to the disciple seeking moksham the inner meanings of the three Rahasyams. The disciple, in turn, must reflect with utmost concentration the implications of the mantras and how they can conduct themselves accordingly to attain moksham. Living per the Āchārya's instruction will relieve one from all sin and grant them a state free from fear about anything.
We must understand that the Lord and Mahālakshmī are the controllers of creation, sustenance, and destruction of all Chith and Achith. We must also recognize that the Lord is present as Antharyami within each of us, and that He will grant the karma-phalam to all our actions. Knowing the Lord's unique position, we must try only to seek Him out and nobody else. From time immemorial, we see the importance of an Āchārya through the course of our history in the form of Swetaketu-Uddalaka, Brighu-Varuna, Maithreyi-Yagnavalka, Sanatkumāra-Nārada, Yama-Nachiketa, Prajāpati-Indra, Vasishṭha-Rāma, Sandipani-Krishna.

title: Performance of Panchasamskaram
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Performance of Pañcha-Saṃskāram

By resorting to an Āchārya and gaining his acceptance, the person will soon realize, by the grace of the Āchārya, true knowledge, non-attachment to worldly pleasures, and devotion to the Lord starts to bloom like a flower. In Srivaishṇava Sampradāyam, the panchasamskaram is the most crucial ceremony performed by the Āchārya. The Āchārya, out of compassion, without any expectations, accepts the disciple regardless of their caste or creed. The Āchārya then performs panchasamskaram, and then the disciple becomes a Sri Vaishṇava. Being a Sri Vaishṇava is not determined by birth. This is the reason why one can see men and women from all communities and all walks of life as a Srivaishṇava.
The panchasamskaram, as the name suggests, consists of five samskarams, namely,

i) Tapa Samaskaram: The Āchārya embosses the impressions of the Panchajanya Shankam and the Sudharshana Chakram on the left and right arms of the disciple.

ii) Pundra Samskaram: The Āchārya makes the disciple aware of the places in the body where the upavyuha forms of the Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇa are to be worshipped. Each upavyuha-sthanam is represented by one of the twelve thiruman-kapu adorned by the disciple. The tiruman represents the Lord, whereas the Sricharnam represents Mahālakshmī. The worship of the Lord is performed by holding the hands in Anjali-mudra and reciting "Keshavaya Namaha" prefixed by the Pranava. Similarly, Devī Mahālakshmī is worshipped, reciting "Sriyai Namaha" prefixed by the Pranava.

iii) Nama Samskaram: The Āchārya adds the suffix of dasan to the disciple's name, indicating the disciple is now an eternal servant to the Lord and Swami Rāmānujar.

iv) Mantra Samskaram: Of all the five samskarams performed, this is the most important without an iota of doubt. The mantras received when this samskaram is being delivered are together known as the Rahasya Trayam or the three divine secrets.

v)Yajña Samskaram: The Āchārya teaches the disciple the ways of Bhagavadh Ārādhana and the methods to perform Salagrama pooja.

title: Nam Āzhwār
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Nam Āzhwār

Forty-Three days had passed since Lord Sri Krishna had ascended to Sri Vaikuṇṭham. A childless couple, Kari and Udayanangai, visited Tirukkuṟuṅkuṭi to pray for the birth of a child. It is said that they requested the Lord for a child who would be just like Him. As none in this universe is comparable to Him, it is noted that Nambi Himself reincarnated as Nammāzhvār. Thus, in the Vaikasi month under Visaka Nakshathram, Nammāzhvār was born. As soon as he was born, he exhibited very peculiar behavior in the form of not crying or suckling. The couple, out of concern, is said to have taken the baby to the Adinatha Perumāl Temple to pray to the Lord for the baby's well-being. Nammāzhvār is also said to be an amshavataram of Sri Vishwakshenar, who is said to be third in line in the Āchārya Paramparā after the Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇa and Mahālakshmī Tāyār. The couple is said to have tied a cradle near the Tamarind tree that was present in the temple courtyard.

Divine Tamarind Tree

The baby is said to have crawled out of the cradle and into a small crater-like space within the tree, where it started a deep meditation. The baby is said to have stayed in this meditative state for sixteen years. At this time, Madurakavi Āzhwār is said to have been at Ayodhyā and offering argyam as per his Nityakarmam when he saw a blinding light at the edge of the horizon. Recognizing the meditative nature of the divine light is said to have started to follow the light. In pursuit of the light, Madurakavi Āzhwār is said to have traveled south, crossing Tiruveṅkaṭam, then Tiruvallikēṇi, then Sri Rangam, then Madurai, and finally, he reached Kurugur. When Madurakavi Āzhwār reached the divine tree, he saw a child in a deep meditative state and was worried whether the child was still alive or not. Madurakavi Āzhwār is said to have thrown a rock near the boy to test his consciousness. When the boy opened his eyes, Madurakavi Āzhwār was said to have asked a question, "Sethathin Vayatrill Siriyadhu Pirandhaal Yeththai Thindru Enge Kiddakum?" Madurakavi Āzhwār was referring to the Jīvātmā. Madurakavi Āzhwār asked When the jeevaathma enters a lifeless body, how would it survive? What would it feed on, and how would it survive? This is when Nam Āzhwār is said to have first spoken by saying, "Aththaith Thindru Ange Kidakkum.". Nam Āzhwār's reply said that the lifeless body would experience the pleasures and pains of life before attaining paramapadam or moksham. Madurakavi Āzhwār was so stunned by the boy's response that he begged to be his disciple. Madurakavi Āzhwār composed 11 pasurams in praise of his Āchārya, Swami Nam Āzhwār, known as Kanninun Shiruthambu, which are included among the 4000 Nālāyira Divya Prabandham.

When Nam Āzhwār was ready to attain paramapadam, Madurakavi Āzhwār asked Nam Āzhwār, full of tears, what to do next. Nam Āzhwār advised Madurakavi Āzhwār to boil the waters of Tamraparni, and he said that an idol would form during the boiling of the water. Madurakavi Āzhwār did as per Nam Āzhwār's advice. After boiling the waters of Tamraparni, he obtained an idol of Bhagavad Rāmānuja. He was surprised to see that the idol was different from what he had expected. He went to Nam Āzhwār with the idol, and the latter told him that this idol was that of a Bhavishyadhacharya (Future Guru) and that he would be born 4000 years from then. He again advised boiling the waters of Tamraparni. Madurakavi Āzhwār once again boiled the waters of Tamraparni and finally got the idol of Nam Āzhwār.

title: Nathamunigal
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Nāthamunigaḷ

Nāthamunigaḷ is considered to be the second guru of the Sri Vaishṇava Guru Paramparā. He is believed to have been born near Viranarayanapuram, near modern-day Mannargudi, in what is believed to be 823 AD. He is credited with the resurgence and the compilation of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhaṅgaḷ.

At one point, all of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhaṅgaḷ were lost except for ten pashurams that were being sung at this temple. Here, Nāthamunigaḷ heard this, and the verses told ten out of a thousand pashurams. This had Nāthamunigaḷ intrigued as to where the other nine hundred and ninety pashurams had disappeared. These ten pashurams also spoke of Kurugur (present-day Āzhwār Tirunāgari), Sadagopan (Nam Āzhwār). Thus Nāthamunigaḷ went in search of Nam Āzhwār. Upon reaching Kurugur and enquiring about these ten pashurams, the locals denied knowing of the ten pashurams that he asked for, but they knew of eleven other pashurams. Nāthamunigaḷ recited these eleven pashurams twelve thousand times in front of the divine tamarind tree where Nam Āzhwār had once resided. Upon completion of the recitation, Nam Āzhwār is said to have appeared in front of Nāthamunigaḷ and blessed him with the thousand pashurams sung by him, as well as the three thousand other pashurams which were sung by the nine other azhwars. Nāthamunigaḷ is said to have taught the Naalayira Divyaprabandhaṅgaḷ to his two nephews at Shrīraṅgam and introduced them at the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple, where he served as the temple administrator.
The ritual of worship, as followed in Vishṇu Temples, is based on two early standard works. The first is the Vaikhanasa Sūtra, which probably belongs to the Krishna Yajurveda school. The other is the Panchratra Agama, which belongs to the extensive Tantra literature, believed to have been composed by Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇa himself. The Agama has a peculiar philosophy of its own, the Bhāgavata Cult, which is very old and is referred to in the Mahābhārata and Bādarāyaṇa Sūtras. Nāthamunigaḷ made a provision for the recitation of Tamil Vedas on appropriate occasions during the main festivals of the Lord.
Nāthamunigaḷ is said to have attained Paramapadam at Gangaikona Cholapuram.
Nāthamunigaḷ's grandson, Yamunacharya, became the torch-bearer of Sri Vaishṇava Philosophy.

title: Manakkaal Nambigal
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Manakkaal Nambigaḷ

Manakkaal Nambi was born as Rāma Misrar in Manakkaal near Trichy. He was the disciple of Uyyakondar, who was the prime disciple of Nāthamunigaḷ. Manakkaal Nambi served his Āchārya for 12 years, during which his Āchārya's wife attained Paramapadam. After his Āchārya's wife attained Paramapadam, Manakkaal Nambi took care of his Āchārya, his house, and his children. One day, Uyyakondar's children were crossing the Kaveri River when they came across a puddle, which they were hesitant to cross. Seeing this scene, Manakkaal Nambi fell face-first and asked the girls to use his body as a bridge to cross over to the other side. When Uyyakondar came to know of this incident, he was very impressed with his disciple and immediately performed the dwayamantropadesham. Before attaining Paramapadam, Uyyakondar instructs Manakkaal Nambi that he would become the Āchārya to Yāmunāchāryar(Āḷavandār), who was Nāthamunigaḷ's grandson. He also instructed Manakkaal Nambi to perform panchasamskaram to Yāmunāchāryar and groom him to become the torch-bearer of the Sri Vaishṇava Philosophy.

title: Yamunacharyar
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Yāmunāchāryar

Yāmunāchāryar was born as the son of Īshvara Muni and as a grandson of Nāthamunigaḷ. He was born on the banks of the Yamunā River; hence, he got the name of Yāmunāchāryar. He studied under Manakkaal Nambi, who was an expert in Mimamsa. After mastering Sanskrit and Tamizh grammar, he had composed a shloka which loosely translates to "he would destroy the poets who were looking cheaply for publicity instead of performing their duties of studying various literature." This news reached the ears of Aakiaazhwaan, who was the royal poet to the Pallava kings, whose capital was situated in Gangai Kondapuram near Shrīraṅgam. The Pallava king was a staunch Shaivite, whereas his wife was a staunch Vaishnavite. The queen asked the king to hold an open debate in the court between Aakiaazhwaan and Yāmunāchāryar to decide who was a better poet. Thus, the king sent a royal palanquin to receive Yāmunāchāryar to hold an open debate in the royal court. Before the discussion began, the king announced that whoever would win the debate would receive half of his kingdom as a prize. The king was confident that Aakiaazhwaan would win the contest. Aakiaazhwaan let Yāmunāchāryar open the discussion, as he was younger and said he would refute any statement that Yāmunāchāryar would place in front of him. Thus, Yāmunāchāryar began the debate with three remarks.

1) Aakiaazhwaan's mother is not childless.
2) The king is all capable.
3) The queen is a true pathivratha naari.
Aakiaazhwaan started to think hard about how he would refute the three statements that were placed before him. As hard as he tried to think, there was no way he could refute the statements placed before him without insulting his mother, the king, and the queen. Aakiaazhwaan was dumbfounded and asked Yāmunāchāryar to refute his arguments. Yāmunāchāryar quickly refuted the three statements as follows:
1) Aakiaazhwaan's mother is childless, as, according to shastras, if a parent has only one child who does not care for the parent, it's as good as being childless.
2) The king was not all capable as he was only capable of ruling his stipulated piece of land.
3) The queen could not be considered as a true pathivratha naari as, according to shastras, when a woman is getting married, she is first married to Gandharva, Agni, and Soma before being married to the groom. Thus, she is not a true pathivratha naari.
Aakiaazhwaan understands Yāmunāchāryar's mastery and asks to become his disciple. Even the queen was so impressed by Yāmunāchāryar's responses that she gave him the title of Āḷavandār. As promised, the king gave Āḷavandār half of his kingdom. Thus, Āḷavandār, who was born as a brahmin, became a king and became busy with administrative activities. To remind him of his actual duties, Manakkaal Nambi tries to meet his disciple, but his efforts are in vain as the royal guards stop him from meeting Yāmunāchāryar. Thus, Manakkaal Nambi, in a scheme to reform his disciple, befriends a cook in the royal kitchen and secretly starts to feed the king thoothuvalai keerai (a green leafy vegetable), which is a type of sattvic food. Āḷavandār starts to like this vegetable, and one day, the cook was instructed not to serve it. Thus, one day, when he was not served thoothuvalai keerai, Āḷavandār approached the cook and asked why he had not served it that day. The cook said he was following the instructions of an elderly Sri Vaishṇava Āchārya. Āḷavandār went out seeking this Āchārya and realized that it was none other than Manakkaal Nambi. He invites Manakkaal Nambi to his royal court, gives him a royal seat, and performs all the stipulated athithi sathkaaram to Manakkaal Nambi. Manakkaal Nambi reminds Yāmunāchāryar of his duties and starts to teach him the Bhagavad Gītā and its meaning. Āḷavandār became immersed in Bhagavath-Dyaanam and decided to give up his life as a king to become an aesthetic at the feet of Sri Ranganathar.
His famous works include:
1) Chathusloki
2) Stotraratnam - a prayer in praise of Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇa
3) Siddhitrayam - consisting of (i) Atmasiddhi. (ii) Samvitsiddhi and (iii) Iswarasiddhi, which describe the Vishishṭādvaita school of thought, illustrating a relation between the soul, god, and the universe
4) Agama Pramanya - stating the authority of the Pancharatra agama
5) Maha Purusha Nirnayam - describing that the ultimate reality is the god-goddess pair Sri and Nārāyaṇa
6) Gitartha Sangraha - a commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā
7) Nityam
8) Mayavada Khandanam

title: Birth of Swami Ramanujar
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Birth of Swami Rāmānujar

Rāmānujar is regarded as the greatest theologian of the Srivaishṇava Lineage Sampradāyam, which is one of the two theistic Schools of Vedānta following the philosophy of Vishishṭādvaita — the other being the Dvaita system. The Srivaishṇava Sampradāyam arose in the Tamizh region of South India, and as a tradition, had its origin with twelve mystics known as the Āzhwārs. These Āzhwārs composed hymns in Tamizh expressing their love and devotion to God, particularly in the form of Sri Krishna. According to modern scholarship, they lived from about the 2nd to the 8th century CE, but ancient tradition ascribes to them a period from 430 BCE downwards. Their lives and compositions encompassed all forms of intense love for the Lord. This devotional approach has been categorized in later times by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu with attitudes known as Dasya, Apatya, Sakhya, Vatsalya, and Madhurya.
Swami Rāmānujar was the only child of a learned Yajur Vedi Brāhmaṇa named Asuri Kesava Dikshitar and his wife, Kantimati. Kesava Dikshitar was known by the title of Sarvakratu, meaning the performer of all Vedic sacrifices, by way of recognition of his expertise in Vedic rituals. He lived in the village of Sriperumbudur, which is situated about 30 miles to the southwest of the modern city of Chennai. This village is famous for its magnificent temple of Sri Adikeshava Perumāl. Keshava Dikshitar had no children even after several years of marriage. Finally, he decided to seek the grace of Lord Parthasarathy, residing at Tiruvallikēṇi. Lord Sri Krishna appeared to him in a dream and said he was impressed with the devotion and steadfast observance of dharma that Keshava Dikshitar followed. He then told Keshava Dikshitar that He would reincarnate as his son to establish order in the times of Kali Yugam, which was dominated by adharma. He said that the son who would be born would become a great Āchārya whom all would revere for time immemorial.

Accordingly, a year later, in 1017, in the Chaitra month under the Tiruaadra nakshatram.
Kantimati gave birth to a son with the auspicious marks of Vishṇu on his body; he was named Rāmānuja, which was the name of Lakshmaṇa, the younger brother of Sri Rāma. Lakshmaṇa was considered to be the incarnation of a part of Vishṇu called Ādishesha, who is the foremost servant of the Lord in Sri Vaikuṇṭham.

title: Education under Yādava Prakashar
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Education under Yādava Prakashar

When Swami Rāmānujar was very young, he had his upanayanam done. His father, Keshava Dikshitar, attained paramapadam; thus, Swami Rāmānujar had to perform his last rites at a very young age. He had not received any formal education and wanted to understand the meaning of the mantras that were being recited. After all the ceremonies were completed, Swami Rāmānujar started to receive education from Yādava Prakashar, who was the foremost Advaita guru at the time. Yādava Prakashar's gurukulam was situated in Tirupputkuḻi, which lies outside Kanchipuram.

Swami Rāmānujar used to walk 40 km every day from Sri Perembudur to Kanchipuram to receive an education. One day, in one of the lectures on the Upanishads, the Upanishad Vaakyam stating " Satyam, Jnānam, Anantham Brahmā" is said to have been uttered by Yādava Prakashar. It was at this point that one of Swami Rāmānujar's classmates asked Yadav Prakashar to give further clarity on the Upanishad Vaakyam. Thus, Yādava Prakashar tells the class that "Satyatvam, Jnanatvam, Ananthatvam are individual characteristics similar to that of the horns of a cow. The horns of a cow can be categorized as Khandatva, Mundatva, and Poornashringatvam.

According to Advaita philosophy, a man can see that a cow has no horns, half a horn, or has a complete horn. But all three conditions cannot exist at the same time. Similarly, the Lord cannot possess all three qualities at the same time. Thus, the Lord is termed as Nirguna Brahmā ." It is then that Swami Rāmānujar poses a question to Yādava Prakashar, saying if I, a student, can sit, can breathe, can listen and question you all at once, why cannot the Lord possess Satyatvam, Jnanatvam, and Anathatvam all at once? Yādava Prakashar was silenced by the question and felt very insulted. Thus, he called off the rest of the lesson for the day.

The following day, Swami Rāmānujar did not attend classes as his mother was not keeping well. The following day, when Swami Rāmānujar went to the gurukulam, the students were talking amongst themselves that they had to perform kainkaryam to their Āchārya in the form of massaging their Āchārya's head. Swami Rāmānujar volunteered to apply oil and massage his Āchārya's head. As Swami Rāmānujar was massaging his Āchārya's head, a student asked the Āchārya a question. The student asked the Āchārya to repeat the previous day's lesson, which was another Upanishad Vaakyam from the Chandogya Upanishad that says " tasya yatha kapyasam pundarikam evam akshini. " This verse describes how the Lord's divine eyes appear.

Yādava Prakashar begins his explanation by giving an exact translation of the verse by saying His eyes are like those of a monkey's posterior. Swami Rāmānujar felt so insulted that he started weeping when he heard this type of comparison being made. Swami Rāmānujar then said that this comparison being made is very wrong.


The word kapyasam in Sanskrit grammar has many meanings. One can be interpreted as the posterior of a monkey. Another interpretation is that of the thin disk of light that envelopes the sun during sunrise. Another interpretation is something that is blown up and out of proportion. When Swami Rāmānujar gives these three explanations, he says none of these explanations can be used to describe the eyes of the Lord. Yādava Prakashar gets furious and tells Rāmānujar to come to the point and give a so-called befitting explanation that would be better than Adi Shankaracharya's commentary, which says the Lord's eyes look like the posterior of a monkey.

Swami Rāmānujar describes that the word kapi, in Sanskrit, refers to the sun. The word kapyasam refers to kapya: aayasam, which can be described in the following scenario. Imagine a pond with still freshwater, which has lotus flowers blooming in it. When the rays of the sun fall on the surface of the pond, the water evaporates, causing the lotus to bloom with all its resplendence. Thus, the eyes of the Lord can be described as equivalent to those of the sun and possess a gaze that is as soft as the petals of the lotus.
All the students started to praise Swami Rāmānujar, and this insulted Yādava Prakashar for the second time. Yādava Prakashar felt so insulted that he decided to kill Swami Rāmānujar as he realized that he would become an outstanding personality in the future if nothing were done.

Thus, Yādava Prakashar planned a field trip to Kāshī. On the way somewhere in the vicinity of the Vindya Hills, he told the rest of the students that the next morning, when they would bathe in the river, one student should push Rāmānujar's head, and one must push Rāmānujar's back so that he would drown. Among the students who were present was Swami Rāmānujar's cousin, Govindan. Govindan could not bear to let his cousin die. Thus, in the middle of the night, he woke Rāmānujar from his sleep and told him Yādava Prakashar's plans. He then asked him to run away, or he would lose his life.

Thus, Rāmānujar is said to have started running and reached some forests in modern-day Maharashtra. Swami Rāmānujar began to look around and realized he was lost beyond any possible help. It was then that he thought that he had to reach Kanchipuram somehow, as he knew the way home from there.

Then a hunter-huntress couple is said to have come and told Swami Rāmānujar that they were coming from Sidhashramam, which is situated in Uttar Pradesh, and said they were traveling towards South India. They decided to travel together in the morning and then sleep. In the morning, when Swami Rāmānujar awoke from his sleep, he saw the couple had fled and a group of Vaishṇavas, and asked them how he could get to Kanchipuram.

The Vaishṇavas laughed at him and asked him to look ahead, and he would see the gopuram of Varadaraja Perumāl Kōvil. Swami Rāmānujar went to the temple and had darshanam of Sri Varadaraja Perumāl and Sri Perundevi Tāyār. When Swami Rāmānujar saw Varadaraja Perumāl, he saw a close resemblance to the hunter, and when he saw Perundevi Tāyār, he saw a close resemblance to the huntress. Thus, he concluded that the hunter and huntress were none other than Varadaraja Perumāl and Perundevi Tāyār, who had come to rescue him from the forest during the night.

title: Swami Ramanujar in Kanchipuram
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Rāmānujar in Kanchipuram

After being saved by Sri Varadaraja Perumāl and Perundevi, Tāyār Rāmānujar stayed back in Kanchipuram, performing kainkaryam to Varadaraja Perumāl. In a few months, Yādava Prakashar started the journey back to Kanchipuram. On the way back, he and his entourage made a stop at Kalahasti. Here, Yādava Prakashar was impressed with Govindan and told him that he should no longer be a Vaishṇava and applied vibuthi on his forehead. Yādava Prakashar then placed a rudrāksha-mala on Govindan's neck and renamed him Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar. He left Govindan there to perform puja and kainkaryam to Lord Shiva.


Upon reaching Kanchipuram, Yādava Prakashar realized that Swami Rāmānujar was still alive and well. He also noticed that he seemed oblivious to his plan to kill Swami Rāmānujar. Yādava Prakashar then went to Swami Rāmānujar and invited him to be his student again. Swami Rāmānujar obliged and went back to Yādava Prakashar's gurukulam. The daily routine continued for Swami Rāmānujar, who fell under the tutelage of Yādava Prakashar. At around this time, Āḷavandār was visiting Kanchipuram in search of a future propagator for the Sri Vaishṇava philosophy.


One day, when Yādava Prakashar and his students were taking a trip to Kanchipuram, Āḷavandār caught a glimpse of Swami Rāmānujar. He asked his pupils who that person was. They told Āḷavandār of all the exploits they had heard of Swami Rāmānujar and how he had dared to give a new commentary to the various Upanishad Vaakyams. It was then that Āḷavandār decided that Swami Rāmānujar would become the future torchbearer to propagate the Sri Vaishṇava Philosophy.


Soon, in another Upanishad lecture, there arose a controversy between Swami Rāmānujar and Yādava Prakashar. It was at this time that a royal guard from the king's court approached Yādava Prakashar. The imperial guard brought news that the local princess had become the victim of a Brahmā-rakshas and that the king had requested Yādava Prakashar to appear before the royal court to break Brahmā-rakshas' hold over the princess. Yādava Prakashar thought it was a waste of his time and told the guard to inform the brahma-rakshas that Yādava Prakashar had commanded the brahma-rakshas to release the princess at once. When the guard approached the brahma-rakshas, it mocked Yādava Prakashar, saying it would not leave until the old fool came in person and tried to release it from the princess.


The next day, Yādava Prakashar, along with his student group, went to the royal palace to assess the situation and release the brahma-rakshas. Yādava Prakashar was placed face-to-face with the possessed princess and was asked to help her. Yādava Prakashar, in pride, spoke to the brahma-rakshas. He told the brahma-rakshas that he was the great Advaita Sanyāsī Yādava Prakashar, and he commanded the brahma-rakshas to release the princess. The brahma-rakshas started cackling and told Yādava Prakashar that it remembered everything about its previous life and also knew everything about Yādava Prakashar's past life.


It said to Yādava Prakashar that in his earlier life, he was a peasant who would eat out of others' leftover plates. It then said that once, when he was living in Maduranthakam, he had the opportunity to eat a single grain of rice out of a Vaishanva's plate, which gave him the punyam to be reborn as an Advaita Sanyāsī in this life. It further said that in its previous life, it was a brahmin who was well-versed in the Vedas. It was brought into this form after an error was made in the shruthi while chanting the Vedas.


It then stated that Yādava Prakashar was not qualified to be a teacher and would not leave the princess under his instruction. Yādava Prakashar felt brutally insulted. He asked a final question to the brahma-rakshsas. He wondered whose command it would free the princess. The brahma-rakshsas laughed and asked him to look behind him to his pupil, who would dare to defy him.


There was only one student who had ever challenged his saying. In complete embarrassment, Yādava Prakashar called Rāmānujar to release the brahma-rakshsas. Swami Rāmānujar approached the princess and gently told the brahma-rakshas to leave the princess's body, pointing to a tree from the window.


He instructed the brahma-rakshasas to break a branch of that tree, thereby relieving them of their current state. The brahma-rakshsas immediately left as commanded, and Swami Rāmānujar's fame started to grow once again.

title: Ramanujar's Journey to Shri Rangam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Rāmānujar's Journey to Sri Rangam

After the miracle performed by Swami Rāmānujar at the king's court, he gained an unbelievable amount of fame among the masses. This caused Yādava Prakashar's jealousy to stir up even further. This caused Swami Rāmānujar's mother to get worried. She told Swami Rāmānujar that his guru was not showing the ideal characteristics of a teacher as he was getting jealous of his students' achievements, and that Swami Rāmānujar should withdraw from Yādava Prakashar's gurukulam.


Thus, Swami Rāmānujar stopped attending his lessons at the gurukulam. At this same time, Āḷavandār, who was residing in Sri Rangam, wished to see Swami Rāmānujar so that he could take him under his wing as a disciple. To make this a certainty, Periyanambi, who was one of Āḷavandār's foremost disciples, was sent to receive Swami Rāmānujar from Kanchipuram. Thus, Periyanambi rushed to Kanchipuram and found Swami Rāmānujar performing kainkaryam to Sri Varadaraja Perumāl in the form of getting water from a well for the Lord. Periyanambi went to Swami Rāmānujar and told him the wish of his Āchārya, who wished to take Swami Rāmānujar under his tutelage.


Swami Rāmānujar was elated by the news and chose to travel to Sri Rangam to become Āḷavandār's disciple. Upon reaching Sri Rangam, sad news reaches the ears of Swami Rāmānujar, saying Āḷavandār had attained Paramapadam. According to Guru Paramparā, we cannot treat Paramapadam here as death but as a state of coma, the reason for which we will discuss further.


When Swami Rāmānujar went to see Āḷavandār's mortal remains, he noticed that Āḷavandār's right hand was holding up three fingers. When Swami Rāmānujar asked the fellow disciples why he was holding out three fingers, they said those three fingers represent Āḷavandār's final wishes that he wished Swami Rāmānujar to carry out. The three requests are as follows:
1) To write a commentary on the Vedānta Sūtras that were written by Maharishi Vedavyasa, revealing its knowledge to the commoner.
2) To honor Maharishi Vedavyasa, who wrote the Mahābhārata, and Maharishi Parāshara, who wrote the Vishṇu Purāṇam, by naming two capable people after their names.
3) To propagate the Vishishṭādvaita Philosophy, name a person after Nam Āzhwār and get them to write a commentary for the Tiruvāymoḻi.


As Swami Rāmānujar vowed to satisfy each of these three wishes, Āḷavandār's three fingers closed into his palm, and a sense of satisfaction was visible on his face. Thus, we can infer that Āḷavandār was in a state of coma and had not yet attained Paramapadam. After Swami Rāmānujar took these three vows, Āḷavandār truly attained Paramapadam.

title: Encounter with Tirukacchi Nambigal
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Encounter with Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ

We have seen the three vows taken by Swami Rāmānujar at the mortal remains of Āḷavandār at Sri Rangam. After returning to Kanchipuram, Swami Rāmānujar got married to a woman named Rakshambal. At the age of 28, Swami Rāmānujar's mother attained Paramapadam. After his mother attained Paramapadam, Swami Rāmānujar continued his education under the disciples of Āḷavandār and continued performing kainkaryam to Sri Varadaraja Perumāl at Kanchipuram.


At Kanchipuram, Swami Rāmānujar first met Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ, who was another disciple of Āḷavandār. Although Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ was not a brahmin, he was treated with immense respect because of his simple-minded and broad-minded approach. Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ was allowed to perform chamara seva to Sri Varadaraja Perumāl. It is said that Varadaraja Perumāl used to converse with Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ during the time in which he used to perform chamara seva. Swami Rāmānujar was anxious to meet Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ.



When Swami Rāmānujar first met Tirukacchi Nambi, he invited Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ to come over to his house for a meal. Swami Rāmānujar's house was situated in the periphery of the Varadaraja Perumāl Temple, which is humongous. Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ accepted the invite and told Swami Rāmānujar that he would love to come to his place for a meal. He said he would enter the following day for lunch. The next day, near lunchtime, Swami Rāmānujar was anxiously awaiting the arrival of Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ. As he was very anxious, he told his wife Rakshambal that he would go and check on where their guest was situated and left the house. Soon Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ arrived at Swami Rāmānujar's house. Rakashambal was a very narrow-minded woman. She knew that Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ was not a brahmin. Hence, she asked him to sit outside the house's central courtyard. She then asked him if he had anything to eat. He replied that he had come to their home as Swami Rāmānujar had invited him for lunch. She then spread out a banana leaf in the outer courtyard and served his meal very scantily.


Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ thanked her for the meal and left. As soon as Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ had left the house, Rakshambal pushed the banana leaf with a stick, cleaned the area with cow dung, broke the earthen vessels in which she had prepared meals for Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ, and took a bath to cleanse herself. When Swami Rāmānujar returned, he noticed that Rakshambal's hair was untied and was wet. He asked if Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ had come to the house. Rakshambal, with a disgusted face, tells Swami Rāmānujar that the vaishya had come and she had served him food. She was disgusted by the fact that her husband wanted to engage himself with the likes of a lower caste man.


Swami Rāmānujar felt insulted by her behavior but did not speak up as he did not wish to incite violence inside the household. A few days passed by, and Swami Rāmānujar ran into Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ inside the temple, and with folded hands, he pleaded for forgiveness for his wife's actions. He told Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ that he had some questions about his dharmam that he would like to talk about with him. Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ said he was on his way to perform chamara seva to Varadaraja Perumāl and told Swami Rāmānujar he would ask the Lord, as He is all-knowing.


As Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ waved the chamaram to the Lord, the Lord sensed a longing emanating from Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ and asked him if he had any questions to ask Him. Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ told the Lord that the questions were not his but those of Swami Rāmānujar. Varadaraja Perumāl is then supposed to have said Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ's six statements as follows:
Ahameva Paramtatvam
Darshanam bedameva cha
Upayeshu Prapatti syaath
Anthima Smrithi Varjanam
Dehaa Vasaane Mukti Syaath
Purnacharya Samashrayaha
These six statements can be interpreted in the following way:

Ahameva Paratattvam: The Lord is the ultimate truth, and He is all-knowing.
Darshanam Bedameva cha: This statement is interpreted by the statement of " Tat Tvam Asi. " The jeevaathma is always independent of the Paramātma but longs to reach the Paramātma.

Upayeshu Prapatti Syaath: To be truly free from the cycle of life and death, one must perform Prapatti to the Lord at the hands of an Āchārya.

Anthima Smrithi Varjanam: According to shastras, one will genuinely attain moksham when they remember the Lord at the time before the jeevaathma leaves the mortal body. As it is difficult for everyone to remember the Lord during Kaliyugam, the Lord tells Tirukacchi Nambi that He would remember those on their deathbed if they had performed Prapatti during their lifetime.

Dehaa Vasaane Mukti Syaath: After death, the soul is weighed to see if it is fit to attain moksham. If the jeevaathma in its lifetime had performed Prapatti, it would gain direct access into Vaikuṇṭham to thrive in the presence of the Lord eternally.

Purnacharya Samashrayaha: Taking refuge at the feet of an Āchārya and getting panchasamskaaram done by his hands is the means to Prapatti.


After his conversation with Varadaraja Perumāl, Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ informs Swami Rāmānujar about his conversation with the Lord, sharing the six statements the Lord made. Swami Rāmānujar immediately rushes to meet Periya Nambi at Sri Rangam. At the same time, Ranganatha Perumāl instructs Periya Nambi to perform panchasamskaaram to Swami Rāmānujar. The two meet at Maduranthankam's Yeri Kaatha Raamar Perumāl temple, where Periya Nambi performed panchasamskaaram to Swami Rāmānujar and initiated him into Sri Vaishṇava Paramparā.

title: Swami Ramanujar takes up Sanyasam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Rāmānujar takes up Sanyasam

After getting panchasamskaaram done at the hands of Periya Nambi, Swami Rāmānujar invites Periya Nambi to his house. Swami Rāmānujar feels he could gain and learn a lot from an Āchārya living under the same roof. Swami Rāmānujar tells Periya Nambi that his home was partitioned into the ground and first floors. Swami Rāmānujar tells Periya Nambi that he and his wife would occupy the ground floor, and Periya Nambi could move into the first floor. Periya Nambi agreed to Swami Rāmānujar's arrangement and moved into Swami Rāmānujar's house in Kanchipuram. Under Periya Nambi's tutelage, Swami Rāmānujar learned about the Naalayira Divyaprabandhaṅgaḷ, except for the part of Tiruvāymoḻi, he learned the various Brahmasutrams with their meaning to become capable of writing a commentary for them. He also learned about the contributions of all the Purvaacharyas.
One day, a poor Vaishṇava came to Swami Rāmānujar's doorstep seeking alms. The poor man called out from the door, and Rakshambal came out to answer before Swami Rāmānujar. When the elderly man asked for some food, Rakshambal immediately said there was no food left in the kitchen. The poor man left the house hungry and empty-handed. Swami Rāmānujar immediately rushed into the kitchen and saw that there was still food left in the pots. He questioned Rakshambal as to why she sent the poor man away empty-handed. She told Swami Rāmānujar that the man might have been a Vaishṇava, but he had been roaming the streets in search of food. He might have come in contact with other caste men. Hence, she refused to feed him. Swami Rāmānujar again felt insulted but stayed silent for the second time.
In a few days, Swami Rāmānujar had gone to the Varadaraja Perumāl Temple as he usually would and performed kainkaryam to Varadaraja Perumāl. During the time Swami Rāmānujar was at the temple, Periya Nambi and his wife packed all their belongings and left to return to Sri Rangam. They thanked Rakshambal and told her that they were returning to Sri Rangam. When Swami Rāmānujar returned home, he noticed that his Āchārya and his Āchārya-Patni were not at home. He immediately enquired with Rakshambal as to where they had gone. Rakshambal told Swami Rāmānujar that they had left the house and gone back to Sri Rangam. Swami Rāmānujar asked why they did that. Rakshambal tells Swami Rāmānujar that she had gotten into a big argument with Periya Nambi's wife in the morning. She told Swami Rāmānujar that as they were drawing water from the well in the morning, a few drops of water from Periya Nambi's wife's pot had accidentally dripped into her own pot. Getting angry, Rakshambal had called Periya Nambi's wife a blind hag who did not know the difference in caste between their families. After saying this, Rakshambal casually mentioned that she was glad that they had left the household. This last incident was more than Swami Rāmānujar could handle. He wrote out all of his wealth in her name and told her that he had received a message from her father, stating that they wanted Rakshambal to come home, as her younger sister's marriage was soon approaching. As soon as Rakshambal had left for her parents' house, Swami Rāmānujar immediately changed out of his current attire and took on kaashaayam, the saffron-colored wear of a sanyasi. He then went to Sri Varadaraja Perumāl, held the tridhandam, and asked the Lord to grant him sanyasaashramam. Through the guidance of Tirukacchi Nambi, Varadaraja Perumāl gave Swami Rāmānujar the title of Yathiraja.

title: Gaining of Disciples
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
