fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Gaining Disciples

After taking up sanyasaashramam, Swami Rāmānujar's fame and popularity further grew. Swami Rāmānujar started to gain many followers and disciples. Among the first disciples were Swami Rāmānujar's first cousin, Dasharathi, from Purvaasharama, and another young man named Kuresha (Kūrattāzhvān). Kūrattāzhvān came from a very wealthy household. Hundreds of people would throng to Kūrattāzhvān's doorstep seeking alms, clothing, and vessels that Kūrattāzhvān would give without any second thought. When Kūrattāzhvān met Swami Rāmānujar, he decided to give up all his wealth and stay by the side of his acharyan to perform kainkaryam. Kūrattāzhvān and his wife, Andal-amma, gave away all their wealth and, by sunset, left their house for Sri Rangam to be by the side of Swami Rāmānujar. As they were going through the forest, Andal-amma started to show signs of fear. Kūrattāzhvān sensed that his wife was still holding on to some wealth and asked her what she had brought along with her. Andal-amma tells Kūrattāzhvān that she had kept one golden cup in her possession just in case Kūrattāzhvān wanted to drink water along the way. Kūrattāzhvān immediately took the golden cup and flung it away, telling her the only wealth they were to possess was the wealth of knowledge that Swami Rāmānujar would preach to them. Thus, Kūrattāzhvān and his wife reached Sri Rangam to be under the guidance of Swami Rāmānujar. In the meantime, Yādava Prakashar's gurukulam had closed due to the lack of students. Yādava Prakashar spent his days in remorse and torment, thinking of how he felt he was superior. It was then that Yādava Prakashar's mother told him to go and seek refuge at the feet of Swami Rāmānujar. Thus, Yādava Prakashar leaves for Sri Rangam and falls at the feet of Swami Rāmānujar, asking him for the opportunity to become a changed individual. Swami Rāmānujar wholeheartedly obliges and performs the panchasamskara ritual to Yādava Prakashar, thereby converting him into a Vaishṇava and giving him the name Govinda Yati.

title: Meeting with Tirukkotiyur Nambigal
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Meeting with Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ

After reforming his former teacher, Yādava Prakashar, to Vaishṇavism and giving him the name of Govinda Yati, Swami Rāmānujar remembered his cousin Govindan, who had saved his life years ago. Govinda Yati informs Swami Rāmānujar that his cousin, now known as Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar, is serving Lord Shiva as an Advaiti at Kalahasti. Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar used to serve Lord Shiva, who was in the form of Bana Lingam. He used to apply sandalwood paste to the lingam, perform pushpa kainkaryam, and offer aaradhanam to Lord Shiva. At Swami Rāmānujar's request, Sri Saila Purna, Swami Rāmānujar's uncle, reformed Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar and introduced him to Vaishṇavism, giving him the name Embaar. Embaar took his formal leave from Lord Shiva and went to Sri Rangam to stay by the side of Swami Rāmānujar.
Soon, a time came when Swami Rāmānujar wished to learn the three rahasyams or secrets of Sri Vaishṇava Philosophy, which are :
Tirumantram or the Asthaaksharam.
The Dwaya Mantram.
The Charama Shlokam.
Swami Rāmānujar traveled to Tirukkoṭiyūr to meet Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ to learn the rahasyams. When Swami Rāmānujar arrived in Tirukkoṭiyūr, he first met Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ, who asked Swami Rāmānujar to return the following day. Swami Rāmānujar went back to Sri Rangam and returned the next day. When Swami Rāmānujar met Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ the next morning, he again requested Swami Rāmānujar to return the next day. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ repeated the same exercise seventeen times.
Each of the seventeen times Swami Rāmānujar was sent back was an indication of a real student to return after he had gained or overcome the following to gain knowledge of the rahasyams :
1. Samsara Bijam Tholaindha Pin Varum: A student must be free from worldly desires.
2. Ahaṅkāram, Mamakaram Tholaindha pin Varum: A student must not possess any arrogance, ego, or self-centered attitude.
3. Ātma Jñānam Kidaitha pin Varum: A student must possess the knowledge of the behavior and nature of the aathma.
4. Dehaathmabhimanan Tholaindha pin Varum: Lose the impression that the body and asthma are the same.
5. Aishwarya, Aamushmiga, Kaivalyathigalil Moham Vittu Varum: Lose the attitude of wanting to cheat anyone for money.
6. Vishayantaratil Patru vitta pin Varum: Lose the attitude of seeking a second opinion concerning the Lord and His Bhagvath Vishayam.
7. Bhagavadh Vishayatil ruchi pirantha pin Varum: Find a sense of love in the Lord and His Bhagavth Vishayam.
8. Raga-Dveshathikal Tholaindha pin Varum: Realize the actions committed in anger and desire have repercussions and act accordingly.
9. Para thantriya unarva pirandha pin Varum: Realize that we are dependent on the Lord to live.
10. Sri Vaishnavatvam kai kudiya pin Varum: Realize the meaning of compassion( Sri Vaishnavathvam).
11. Sathvika parikgraham kidaitha pin Varum: Learn to realize and enjoy the nature of Sattva Gunam.
12. Bhagavatha parikgraham kidaitha pin Varum: Learn to converse with a Bhagavatha at the first meeting.
13. Bhagavath parikgraham kidaitha pin Varum: Learn upon seeing the Lord that our thoughts must not waver, and our thoughts must solely be focused on Him through immense bhakti.
14. Ananya-Seshatvam-Upayatvam kidaitha pin Varum: Learn that we as human beings are all equals, and if there is anyone that we cannot equate ourselves to, that is the Lord.
15. Ananya Prayojanatvam kidaitha pin Varum: Learn that the most tremendous boon that the Lord offers us is moksham, and we must accept it with open arms without the desire for anything else.
16. Ananya Bhogyatvam kidaitha pin Varum: Learn that performing sharanagathi beyond all the difficulties of our life will see us through to safety and ensure the Lord's grace upon us.
17. Āchāryan Kidaitha Pin Varum: A student must find a capable Āchārya who can guide and teach him all of the above.
18. Tirumantra Artham kai koodum: When one satisfies all of the above, the Tirumantram, Dwayam, and Charama Shlokams come into effect in one's life.

When Swami Rāmānujar returned to Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ for the eighteenth time, he shared the eighteen reasons with Swami Rāmānujar. He said to him that he did not doubt in his mind that Swami Rāmānujar possessed the above qualities. Still, he conducted this exercise because it was how Swami Rāmānujar was to test his disciples before imparting to them the knowledge of the three great secrets. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ agrees to give Swami Rāmānujar the insight of the rahasyams and calls him to enter a room. As Swami Rāmānujar arrived, Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ noticed that Swami Rāmānujar was accompanied by Nadathoor Azhvān, Embaar, and Modhali Aandaan, who were Swami Rāmānujar's foremost disciples. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ questions Swami Rāmānujar about how his disciples entered the room with him. Swami Rāmānujar then tells Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ that the three of them are like the tridandam he holds and the pavithram he wears. They are inseparable for a sanyasi.
Similarly, his three disciples are inseparable from him. They had made the same journey as Swami Rāmānujar had made over the past seventeen days, and they were worthy of receiving the rahasyams. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ agreed with Swami Rāmānujar and provided them with the three rahasyams and their meanings. The meanings of the three rahasyams are as follows:
Ashtaaksharam: This mantram consists of the Pranavam, followed by Namo Narayanaya. The mantra and meaning for which can be found in the Vedas and interpreted in the following way :

The meaning of the mantram can be understood in the following way. Pranavam is split into a-u-m. Where a-kaaram represents Bhagavān Mahā Vishṇu, m-kaaram represents the jeevaathma, and u-kaaram represents Mahālakshmī. Thus, after uttering the Pranavam, when Namaha is said, one must have the feeling of no self-centeredness and a sense of total unconditional surrender. Finally, when speaking the Lord's name, Nārāyaṇa, the person must wholeheartedly think of the path to reach Him. Thus, the Tirumantram can be understood as the way to Sharaṇāgati.
Dwaya Mantram: This mantram consists of two halves—the first half acts as a means to ask the Lord and Mahālakshmī to accept our Sharaṇāgati. The second half serves as a means to ask the Lord and Mahālakshmī to shower their grace upon us constantly.
Charama Shlokam: This shloka is the means to Prapatti as given by Lord Krishna to Arjuna, wherein Lord Krishna tells Arjuna that He is the Ultimate Truth. He tells Arjuna to surrender and put all of his faith solely in Him, and he would relieve him from the cycle of birth and death and offer moksham.

Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ explains the rahasyams and their meanings to Swami Rāmānujar, informing him that he is to propagate this knowledge only to disciples who possess the eighteen qualities that he had previously mentioned to Swami Rāmānujar. Swami Rāmānujar steps out of the closed quarters of Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ and briefly thinks for a while, and decides that he must do something before leaving Tirukkoṭiyūr. Swami Rāmānujar races up to the top of the Ashtanga Vimanam of the Sowmya Nārāyaṇa Perumāl Temple. He tells everyone who wishes to listen that if they want to be relieved from the cycle of life and death, they must perform Sharaṇāgati under the guidance of an Āchārya. A few people who heard Swami Rāmānujar asked him what the means of obtaining this divine gift was. Swami Rāmānujar instructed them to seek his refuge, and he would perform the panchasamskaaram and reveal the heavenly secrets to achieve moksha. After saying this, he started to descend from the Vimanam. In this brief moment, as Swami Rāmānujar descended from the Vimanam, word reached Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ of what Swami Rāmānujar had done in revealing the divine secrets to the general public. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ, in a fury, rushed to the temple and confronted Swami Rāmānujar, saying he had betrayed his guru by revealing the divine secrets. As punishment, he would undoubtedly go to hell for treason. Swami Rāmānujar prostrated himself before his guru and told Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambigaḷ that he was more than ready to go to hell if he could provide the means for so many people to go to Vaikuṇṭham.

title: Swami Ramanujar in Shri Rangam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Rāmānujar in Sri Rangam

After learning the three divine rahasyams from Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi, Swami Rāmānujar, along with his disciples, returned to Sri Rangam. Upon returning to Sri Rangam, Swami Rāmānujar starts to preach and propagate all that he has learned thus far. In the meantime, he leaves Kūrattāzhvān and Modhali Aandaan with Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi to grasp the meaning of the Charama Shlokam and asks them to come back and teach. Soon, he started work on a magnum opus known as Sri Bhashyam. During the compilation of Sri Bhashyam, Swami Rāmānujar would dictate the shlokas and their commentary, while Kūrattāzhvān would sit and write down whatever Swami Rāmānujar said. Once while compiling the Sri Bhashyam, a question arose as to which character of a given jeevaathma would be its prime characteristic? Would it be Jnatritvam or Seshatvam? Jnatritvam refers to the aathma expressing dharma jnanam, whereas Seshatvam refers to the aathma expressing that it is below the Lord and is dependent on Him for its existence. Swami Rāmānujar claimed that Jantritvam should be the character mentioned, whereas Kūrattāzhvān claims that Seshatvam should be the quality specified. Swami Rāmānujar says this argument could only be solved by Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi and sends Kūrattāzhvān to ask him which character should be mentioned. Kūrattāzhvān went to Tirukkoṭiyūr to ask Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi the question of debate. According to the shastras, one must not request an Āchārya a question until they give the student the authority to do so. Thus, Kūrattāzhvān went to Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi's house and began performing kainkaryam to the Āchārya. Soon, two days passed. Five days passed. A fortnight passed. Fortnight became a month. One month became three months, and this finally became six months. Kūrattāzhvān could not bear being separated from Swami Rāmānujar any further. Kūrattāzhvān tells Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi that he will take his leave. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi senses that Kūrattāzhvān had come with a question and tells him, as he is about to leave, "Adiyan Ullana Pāsuram Marandhadho?". Hearing this, Kūrattāzhvān understands what Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi was trying to convey and, satisfied, goes to Swami Rāmānujar's side at Sri Rangam. Upon arriving at Sri Rangam, Kūrattāzhvān tells Swami Rāmānujar that Seshatvam should be the character that should be mentioned. To substantiate, Kūrattāzhvān tells Swami Rāmānujar that the Āzhwārs stated in their Pāsurams that the Lord lives within us, and we are nothing but a mere vessel to Him. Hence, Seshatvam should be the character mentioned.

As time passed, Swami Rāmānujar sensed that changes needed to be made in the temple administration at Sri Rangam. Uttama Nambi, the temple administrator at the time, was opposed to any type of change. He planned to kill Swami Rāmānujar. One day, when Swami Rāmānujar was going around for alms, he came to the doorstep of Uttama Nambi, who called Swami Rāmānujar inside and seated him. Before serving Swami Rāmānujar food, Uttama Nambi laced the rice with poison. Uttama Nambi's wife sees what her husband does and tells him that it's wrong. Uttama Nambi threatens that he would slit her throat if she opened her mouth. Thus, to prevent Swami Rāmānujar from eating the rice, she prostrates before him and performs pradakshinam, placing the leaf with the food in front of Swami Rāmānujar. When anyone conducts themselves in this manner before a sanyasi, it is the sanyasi's duty to reject the food and leave. Swami Rāmānujar takes the leaf and throws it into the Kaveri River. Swami Rāmānujar notices the fish in the river that ate the rice start plopping up and die a painful death. Swami Rāmānujar understood that the rice was poisoned and that Uttama Nambi's wife conducted herself as she did to save him. Soon, the news that Uttama Nambi tried to kill Swami Rāmānujar started to spread like wildfire.

Soon, the news reached the ears of Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi, who rushed to Sri Rangam to see Swami Rāmānujar. When Swami Rāmānujar found out that his Āchārya was coming to Sri Rangam, he ran to receive him. When Swami Rāmānujar saw Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi, he immediately began prostrating himself before his Āchārya. The sand on the banks of the river was scorching hot, and Swami Rāmānujar continued to prostrate his Āchārya. Soon, a crowd gathered around the two great acharyas. The crowd noticed that, due to the heat, Swami Rāmānujar was getting burned and was almost cooked to a crisp. A man in the crowd speaks up and asks Swami Rāmānujar to stop prostrating, as the sight was unbearable. Once the man spoke up, Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi asked Swami Rāmānujar to stop prostrating and assigned that man to perform kitchen duties for Swami Rāmānujar. He asks the man his name. The man replies that his name is Kidambi Achan. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi tells Kidambi Achan that his devotion was genuinely exceptional, as he could not even bear to see Swami Rāmānujar in pain. Tirukkoṭiyūr Nambi said that he would be one of Swami Rāmānujar's most trusted aides. Swami Deshikan comes in the lineage of Kidambi Achan on his maternal side.

title: Reforming Periya Kovil Nambi
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Reforming Periya Kōvil Nambi

Swami Rāmānujar continued his stay in Sri Rangam. He continued to attempt to gain access to the Ranganatha Perumāl temple keys to reform the way the temple was being administered. The temple keys were being held by a person named Periya Kōvil Nambi. Periya Kōvil Nambi was a man with a harsh temperament and was very stubborn. However much Swami Rāmānujar tried to get the temple keys, Periya Kōvil Nambi would avoid Swami Rāmānujar. Before Periya Kōvil Nambi became a respected person in charge of temple administration, he was a gambler. Periya Kōvil Nambi's mother came to Swami Rāmānujar for help to reform her son's behavior. Swami Rāmānujar went to the gambling house to observe Periya Kōvil Nambi. After observing Periya Kōvil Nambi's behavior, Swami Rāmānujar sends Kūrattāzhvān to retrieve Periya Kōvil Nambi from the gambling house to initiate reform.

Kūrattāzhvān taught Periya Kōvil Nambi the shastras and various vyakyanams, transforming the gambler into a respectable man who earned the right to control the temple administration. Over time, Periya Kōvil Nambi began to develop a superiority complex, as he had the sole right to control the temple and oversee its operation. In his opinion, he was above everyone except Ranganatha Perumāl. Swami Rāmānujar noticed that there were errors in the way he was conducting the temple rituals and hence deemed it necessary to gain access to the temple keys to change the way the temple was being administered.

One day, Periya Kōvil Nambi was conducting a homam for which he required a learned acharya to be present for a position known as Ekaham. At the time, it was customary to visit Swami Rāmānujar to bless such occasions. Thus, Periya Kōvil Nambi came to Swami Rāmānujar to grace the event. Swami Rāmānujar said he would send his guru, Kūrattāzhvān, to grace the occasion. Periya Kōvil Nambi was delighted to hear that his guru would be gracing the event. After the conduction of the homam, it was customary to give daanam to the person taking the position of Ekaham. The custom of providing daanam was to continue giving until the person receiving the daanam said they were satisfied. Thus, Periya Kōvil Nambi began to offer daanam to his guru, and after the daanam, he would ask if his guru was satisfied. Kūrattāzhvān would reply that he was not happy. Soon, it came to a point where Periya Kōvil Nambi asked his guru what it would take to earn his satisfaction. When this question was asked, Kūrattāzhvān asked for the keys to the temple. Periya Kōvil Nambi handed over the keys of the temple to Kūrattāzhvān, who, in turn, handed them to Swami Rāmānujar.

Swami Rāmānujar immediately took charge of all the temple activities. He established all the rituals that are practiced at the temple to date. When Periya Kōvil Nambi noticed the changes, he realized that he was at fault. Swami Rāmānujar then handed the keys back to Periya Kōvil Nambi. Periya Kōvil Nambi promises to uphold the traditions established by Swami Rāmānujar.

title: Ananthazhwan
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Ananthazhwan

After Swami Rāmānujar brought about reform in the Sri Rangam temple, he was getting ready to take leave for Kanchipuram. He visited the lotus feet of Ranganatha Perumāl to inform Him that he would be taking his leave. Ranganatha Perumāl then instructed Swami Rāmānujar to reside in Sri Rangam and establish it as his headquarters. Swami Rāmānujar thus made Sri Rangam his headquarters.
At around the same time, a Hoysala king named Bittideva, who was a Jain, was ruling in Karnataka. His wife, Shantala, was a Vaishṇava. She came to Sri Rangam to see Swami Rāmānujar and asked him to reform her husband into Sri Vaishṇavism. Thus, Swami Rāmānujar went to see Bittideva and converted him to Sri Vaishṇavism. Bittideva then adopted the name Vishnuvardhan and constructed the renowned Channakeshava Temple at Belur.
Time passed, and Swami Rāmānujar was looking for a troupe he could take along with him to Tirumala. Tirumala at the time was densely forested, inhabited by many varieties of poisonous snakes and many wild animals. It was considered a journey once made that would send the person straight to Sri Vaikuṇṭham, as few would return from making the journey up the hill. In such a situation, Swami Rāmānujar held an open forum meeting with anyone who wished to listen to him. Swami Rāmānujar asked in the forum who would accompany him on the journey to Tirumala. Only one person volunteered from the entire forum. This man was Ananthazhwan.

Ananthazhwan

Ananthazhwan used to perform puspha-kanikaryam and theertha-kainkaryam to Sri Tiru-veṅkaṭamuṭaiyān sincerely. Ananthazhwan had constructed a pushpa-brindavanam and named it after Swami Rāmānujar. One day, he was building a tank for the temple with the help of his wife, who was expecting at the time. Ananthazhwan used to till the soil with the help of a crowbar, place the mud into a mud tray, and give it to his wife, who would put it on her head and dispose of the mud at a distance. One day, when the same routine was running, a small boy approached Ananthazhwan's wife and told her that he would help her dispose of the mud without her husband noticing what was happening. Ananthazhwan's wife accepted the help. Soon, Ananthazhwan saw the boy and chased after him, saying the work was being done in the name of the Lord, and he wanted nobody to help him. The boy seemed to run away, but soon came back to assist Ananthazhwan's wife. When Ananthazhwan saw the boy again, he started to chase him. The boy started running and ran into the temple, soon entering the garbha griha. Seeing the boy run inside the garbha griha, Ananthazhwan threw his crowbar in the boy's direction and soon noticed blood flowing out of the garbha griha. When he went to check on the boy, he saw a scar on Lord Tiru-veṅkaṭamuṭaiyān's chin. He immediately realized that the boy was none other than the Lord Himself, who had come to assist Ananthazhwan in his work. Ananthazhwan is said to have cleaned the wound and applied camphor on the Lord's chin to give a soothing and cooling effect. The crowbar can still be seen in the temple to this day.

Ananthazhwan's Crowbar

title: Swami Ramanujar Reaches Tirupati
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Rāmānujar Reaches Tirupati

After Swami Rāmānujar finished reforming the Ranganathar Temple at Sri Rangam, he decided to take a trip to Tirupati. When news of Swami Rāmānujar's arrival at Tirupati reached the ears of Periya Tirumalai Nambi (Swami Rāmānujar's maternal uncle and Āchārya) in Tirumala, he sent Ananthazhwan to go and bring Swami Rāmānujar uphill.

Ananthazhwan immediately went down to where Swami Rāmānujar was staying in Tirupati and expressed Periya Tirumalai Nambi's wish and message. At first, Swami Rāmānujar refused, saying he could not reside on the hill, as it was a personification of the Lord Himself. Ananthazhwan went back and told Periya Tirumalai Nambi that Swami Rāmānujar had refused.

The next morning, news reached Swami Rāmānujar that Periya Tirumalai Nambi himself was on his way to meet him. Swami Rāmānujar ran to meet Periya Tirumalai Nambi. As soon as Swami Rāmānujar saw Periya Tirumalai Nambi, he immediately started to prostrate to him. Periya Tirumalai Nambi asked Swami Rāmānujar to stop prostrating to him and gave him the ladoo prasadam of Sri Tiru-veṅkaṭamuṭaiyān. He then requested Swami Rāmānujar to come and stay with him on top of the hill.

Swami Rāmānujar agreed and went and stayed with Periya Tirumalai Nambi. During his first stay for three days, Swami Rāmānujar neither ate nor drank water, as that was the means not to excrete and impurify the hill. For the next year that followed, Swami Rāmānujar stayed in Tirupati and learned the entirety of the Rāmāyaṇam from Periya Tirumalai Nambi.

At the same time, he completed a magnum opus, which was a commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, which expresses the essence of all the Upanishads. He traveled to the top of the hill and presented this magnum opus at the holy lotus feet of Lord Tiru-veṅkaṭamuṭaiyān. This magnum opus is known as Vedaartha Sangraha.

After writing and giving Vedaartha Sangraha, Swami Rāmānujar wrote another magnum opus, known as Gītā Bhashyam, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā. He also placed this at the holy feet of Lord Tiru-veṅkaṭamuṭaiyān.

title: Swami Ramanujar's Digvijaya Yātrā
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Rāmānujar's Digvijaya Yātrā

After returning from Tirupati, Swami Rāmānujar announced a Digvijaya Yātrā in which he would tour the entire country on foot, visiting multiple kshethrams. Accompanying Swami Rāmānujar on the journey were a few disciples, of whom the most prominent was Kūrattāzhvān. Swami Rāmānujar's first destination was Tirukkuṭantai. Here, he first visited the Sarangapani Perumāl Kōvil. After visiting the temple, he engaged in an intense philosophical debate with the Advaita scholars at Kumbakonam and convinced them to become Sri Vaishṇavas. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tirumāliruñchōlai, where he visited the Kallazhagar Perumāl Kōvil. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tiruppuḷḷāṇi, where he visited the Kalyana Jagannatha Perumāl Kōvil and the Darbhashayana Rāmar Kōvil and performed the Setu Snānam.

 The next destination in his yatra led him to Āzhwār Tirunāgari. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tirukkuṟuṅkuṭi. Here, Swami Rāmānujar had a conversation with Tirukkuṟuṅkuṭi Nambi. The Lord tells Bhagawad Rāmānujāchārya that he has accomplished what He could not achieve in all His births. The Lord asks to be initiated into Sri Vaishṇavism by Bhagawad Rāmānujāchārya. Bhagawad Rāmānujāchārya is said to have performed the Pancha-Samskara ceremony for the Lord here, giving Him the name Sri Vaishṇava Nambi. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tiruvaṇparisāram, Tiruvaṭṭāṟu, and then Tiruvanantapuram. Then, traveling north, Swami Rāmānujar reached Dwārakā, where he went to see Lord Dwarkadeesh. Moving further north, Swami Rāmānujar went to Gokulam, Mathurā, Vrindavanam, and Govardhanam. Continuing north, Swami Rāmānujar visited Muktinath, Badrinath, Joshi Mutt, Devaprayāga, and then proceeded to Pushkaram.

To complete his yatra, he traveled to Kashmir in search of the Saraswati Bhandaaram, a renowned library that housed many sacred texts of Sanathana Dharma. Swami Rāmānujar, along with Kūrattāzhvān, went to the Saraswathi Bhandaaram, which was holding the Vrithi Grantham written by Bodhāyana. The Vrithi Grantham was a book that served as a commentary on all the Brahmasutrams. Swami Rāmānujar reached the Saraswathi Bhandaaram, which was being guarded by two pandits. The two pandits asked Swami Rāmānujar why he had come to the library. When Swami Rāmānujar told them that he wanted to take the Vrithi Grantham, the two pandits laughed and guided him and Kūrattāzhvān to an idol of Devī Saraswathi. The idol posed a riddle to Swami Rāmānujar.

The riddle was as follows:" tasya yatha kapyasam pundarikam evam akshini. " Swami Rāmānujar immediately gave a detailed answer, as this was the very same statement that he had first given a commentary on under Yādava Prakashar's education. The word "kapyasam" in Sanskrit grammar has multiple meanings. One can be interpreted as the posterior of a monkey. Another interpretation is that of the thin disk of light that envelopes the sun during sunrise. Another interpretation is something that is blown up and out of proportion. When Swami Rāmānujar provides these three explanations, he states that none of these explanations can be used to describe the eyes of the Lord. Swami Rāmānujar describes that the word kapi, in Sanskrit, refers to the sun. The word kapyasam refers to kapya: aayasam, which can be described in the following scenario. Imagine a pond filled with still freshwater, where lotus flowers bloom. When the sun's rays fall on the pond's surface, the water evaporates, causing the lotus to bloom with all its resplendence. Thus, the eyes of the Lord can be described as equivalent to those of the sun and possess a gaze that is as soft as the petals of the lotus.

Saraswathi Devī tells Swami Rāmānujar that she was impressed by his answer and that She would grant him access to her library and allow him to take the Vrithi Grantham. Thus, Swami Rāmānujar took the Vrithi Grantham and started his journey back towards Sri Rangam. By night, Swami Rāmānujar and Kūrattāzhvān reached Kāshī and decided to spend the night there. Swami Rāmānujar fell asleep, saying he was tired from the travel. Later in the morning, when both Swami Rāmānujar and Kūrattāzhvān awoke from their sleep, they saw that the Vrithi Grantham was missing. Swami Rāmānujar was heartbroken as he understood the pandits must have stolen the Grantham from them when they were sleeping.

Kūrattāzhvān then tells his Āchārya not to feel bad, as he had read the entire Grantham in the night before falling asleep. He told his Āchārya that his curiosity to know what was in the Grantham did not let him sleep; thus, he read every last word in the Grantham before going to sleep. Swami Rāmānujar decides to test Kūrattāzhvān and asks him to recall whatever he can remember from the Grantham. Kūrattāzhvān recited the entire Grantham before Swami Rāmānujar and told him that he could remember anything he read in a single attempt. Swami Rāmānujar and Kūrattāzhvān returned to Sri Rangam.

After returning to Sri Rangam, Swami Rāmānujar began writing another magnum opus, a commentary on the Brahmasutras written by Bhodayana. Swami Rāmānujar used the references of Āzhwār Pāsurams, Brahmasutra-Artham, which he was taught by Tirukacchi Nambi, and the Vrithi Grantham through Kūrattāzhvān to write the great Sri Bhasyam.

title: Kulothunga Chola and the migration to Melukote
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: Kulothunga Chola and the migration to Melukote

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Kulothunga Chola and the migration to Melukote

Now we reach that stage of the story where Swami Rāmānujar is reaching his mid-to-late fifties in age. At around this time, Kulothunga Chola I became the king of Kanchipuram and sought to establish Shaivism as the state religion. He managed to convert all the Vaishṇavas who were residents of Kanchipuram to Shaivism by force. He intended to extend this with an iron fist further, but noticed that Swami Rāmānujar posed a great hindrance to this movement. Thus, he summoned his two most trusted aides, Tirukacchi Nambi and Kūrattāzhvān, to his court and held a great philosophical debate.

When he noticed that both Tirukacchi Nambi and Kūrattāzhvān were not budging from their claim of Nārāyaṇa being the greatest among the trinity, he asked them to substantiate how anyone or anything in existence could rival Lord Shiva's presence in the universe. Kūrattāzhvān immediately spoke up, citing drona-charcha, which says that the drona-pushpam, which sits atop the matted locks of Lord Shiva, is more significant than Lord Shiva. Hearing this, Kulothunga Chola became furious and decided to punish both Tirukacchi Nambi and Kūrattāzhvān. The king ordered his soldiers to gouge out their eyes. The soldiers gouged out Tirukacchi Nambi's eyes. Still, before they could get to Kuratazhwan, he said: "Whoever thinks/says that Supreme Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇan is equivalent/on par with or inferior to other devathas, that paaapam would catch me!" He then said there would be no bigger sin. Thus, he gouged out his own eyes and placed them in the hands of the soldiers.

Kulothunga Chola felt terrible for his actions and paid a beggar who was residing outside the palace to escort both of them to Sri Rangam. Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ, by this time, was very old and said he could not face Swami Rāmānujar as he had disgraced him and his principles, and decided that it was time for him to depart to Paramapadam. Thus Tirukacchi Nambigaḷ departed for Paramapadam. Soon, the news reached Swami Rāmānujar that Kulothunga Chola was planning to annex Sri Rangam and take Swami Rāmānujar's life. Therefore, Swami Rāmānujar departed from Sri Rangam and started to head north into Karnataka. By the time Swami Rāmānujar and a few of his disciples reached Karnataka, it was late at night, and they were in a dense forest. In the darkness of night, a hunter's tribe offered to protect Swami Rāmānujar and his disciples.
As they continued their journey, they reached a house by evening, where they decided to stay the night. A few of Swami Rāmānujar's followers went into the house and found a woman who was deeply immersed in bhakti.

She was performing aaradanam to a set of paduka. The disciples told her that they had come from the south and were seeking shelter for the night. The woman obliged. The disciples saw the paduka and asked her who her Āchārya was. She told them that she had once visited Sri Rangam and had received divine instructions from an Āchārya, but she soon forgot what she had learned. As luck would have it, she ran into her Āchārya once again, but she did not see his face. She fell to his feet and told him that she had forgotten his instructions, and she wanted to learn his teachings once more. She said her Āchārya recognized her bhakti and gave her his paduka, and she has been performing aaradanam to the paduka since that day.

The disciples further probed her to see if she was speaking about Swami Rāmānujar. They asked to describe the face of the Āchārya she talked about. She said she never saw his face and only fell at his feet as a mark of respect. She said that her Āchārya's feet were like those of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, like a lotus, and she could recognize his feet if she were ever to see them again. As she said this, Swami Rāmānujar entered the room, and she saw his feet and immediately started to prostrate herself before him, saying he was the Āchārya whose paduka she had been serving earnestly. She gave Swami Rāmānujar and his disciples shelter and guided them to Melukote (Tirunārāyaṇapuram).

title: Tirunarayanapuram Vaibhavam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Tirunārāyaṇapuram Vaibhavam

Cheluvanarayana

Yadugiri Thaayaar

Swami Rāmānujar reached Melukote (Tirunārāyaṇapuram), and one night he had a divine dream in which Sriman Nārāyaṇa appeared and told Swami Rāmānujar that he was very near him on the Yadugiri hill. He told Swami Rāmānujar that He was awaiting Swami Rāmānujar's arrival and that Swami Rāmānujar would find Tiruman at the site where He was present. Swami Rāmānujar immediately sent out word to King Vishnuvardhan, who helped clear out the forests in the Yadugiri area. In clearing the woods, the soldiers found the Tirukalyani and a set of kaashayam at the site. They immediately returned to Swami Rāmānujar, who had come to the Tirukalyani, and upon seeing the kaashayam, understood that this was the site where Swami Dattatreya had taken up Sanyasam.

Swami Rāmānujar took a bath in the Tirukalyani and changed back into kaashayam. When Swami Rāmānujar had left Sri Rangam, his disciples insisted that he wear white-colored clothing to avoid getting caught by Kulothunga Chola's soldiers. Swami Rāmānujar found the Tiruman on the northwest banks of the Tirukalyani but was unable to locate the Lord's idol. When Swami Rāmānujar returned to his hermitage, he was disappointed as he could not find the Lord's idol.

That night, the Lord again appeared in Swami Rāmānujar's dreams.
He told him he could see the idol inside an anthill, which would be flanked by a Champaka tree, a Vakula Tree, and Swami Rāmānujar would find tulasi growing on the anthill. He also told Swami Rāmānujar that the anthill would be located on the southwest bank of the Tirukalyani. Swami Rāmānujar returned to the banks of the Tirukalyani the following day and discovered the divine anthill. Swami Rāmānujar sent information to King Vishnuvardhan, who immediately rushed to Yadugiri to see the Lord. Swami Rāmānujar performed ksheerabhishekam (an abhishekam with milk) to the anthill.


As the milk was poured on the anthill, it dissolved, showing a divine idol of the Lord. Swami Rāmānujar personally performed punar-prathishtaapanam to the idol over three days. Soon, the forests around the area were cleared entirely, and streets were constructed. A temple was erected at the site where the anthill stood, and sets of festivals were instituted.


The only missing entity at the time was a Utsava Murthy. Swami Rāmānujar decided to recast the idols of Perumāl and Tāyār using panchaloham (a mix of five holy metals in a particular proportion). That night, Sriman Nārāyaṇa once again appeared in Swami Rāmānujar's dreams and told him that His Utsava Murthy, Ramapriya, whom Lord Rāma worshiped, still existed and that the idol was residing in Delhi, which was under the Turkish regime. The Lord told Swami Rāmānujar to journey to Delhi and claim Him from the Turks.

Ramapriya/Selvapillai

Vairamudi Utsavam

Swami Rāmānujar made his journey to Delhi and went to the royal court of the Turk king. He explained his situation. The king showed Swami Rāmānujar the way into the treasury, where all the idols and plundered wealth were being kept.

Swami Rāmānujar searched the entire treasury but could not find the Lord's idol. Swami Rāmānujar returned to the king's court and informed him that he was unable to find the Lord's idol. The king then personally took Swami Rāmānujar to the queen's palace. The king told Swami


Rāmānujar that if the idol was still intact, it had to have been with one of the queens or one of the royal women. Swami Rāmānujar began searching for the Lord's idol and discovered that it was in the possession of a princess. When Swami Rāmānujar saw the Lord, his eyes welled up with tears of joy, and he immediately called out to the Lord, referring to Him by the name of Selvapillai.

The idol of the Lord then jumped from the windowsill and ran into Swami Rāmānujar's hands. The king did not know what he had just seen. He was awestruck. The princess did not want to be separated from the idol, as she had come to believe that the Lord was her husband and did not want to be separated from Him.


The king then explained to his daughter that the idol did not belong with her and that they were foreigners who had to return to their land. Saying this, the king gave Swami Rāmānujar his leave. Soon, the princess started chasing after Swami Rāmānujar and followed them to Tirunārāyaṇapuram.


Swami Rāmānujar recognized the bhakti in the princess's intentions and allowed her to stay by the Lord's side, dubbing her Bibi Nachiyar.

Bibi Nachiyar

title: Swami Ramanujar's return to Shri Rangam and attaining Paramapadam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: Swami Ramanujar's return to Shri Rangam and attaining Paramapadam

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Rāmānujar's return to Sri Rangam and attaining Paramapadam

After Kulotunga Chola died in 1118, Swami Rāmānujar decided to return to Sri Rangam. The people of Yadugiri could not bear to part with Swami Rāmānujar. Thus, Swami Rāmānujar instilled his qualities into a panchaloham idol. Swami Rāmānujar and his disciples first made a stop at Tirumāliruñchōlai, where he fulfilled his vow to Sri Andal and presented the Lord with 100 gangalams of butter and sweet rice. After fulfilling his promise, he visited Srivilliputur, where Sri Andal is said to have appeared before him and bestowed upon him the title of Godaagraja. Swami Rāmānujar then safely returned to Sri Rangam.


When Kūrattāzhvān received the news of Swami Rāmānujar's return, he rushed to see his Āchārya. When Swami Rāmānuja saw the plight of Kūrattāzhvān, he told Kūrattāzhvān to visit Varadaraja Perumāl to regain his lost eyes. Kūrattāzhvān followed Āchārya's instruction and restored his sight through the grace of Varadaraja Perumāl. Kūrattāzhvān then served Swami Rāmānujar for a period of two more years before attaining Paramapadam.


Seventeen years after Kūrattāzhvān's demise, a time came when Swami Rāmānujar sensed that his time on bhu-lokam was coming close to the end. It was at this time that Swami Rāmānujar appointed Kūrattāzhvān's son Parāshara Bhattar as the successor to propagate the Vishishṭādvaita Philosophy and made his final journey towards Paramapadam.


The gist of his last teachings is as follows:
Worship all holy men precisely as you would do in the case of your spiritual preceptor. Have sincere faith in the teachings of the previous acharyas and Āzhwārs. Never become enslaved by your senses. Be not satisfied with the acquisition of worldly knowledge; spend your time reading literature that deals with the greatness of God and the wonders of His creation. By the Guru's grace, the attraction of the senses will cease to torment you. Learn to maintain composure in feelings of joy and sorrow, charm, and aversion. Enjoy the names and chanting of the glories of God's devotees with as much relish as the chanting of God's names and glories. Never forget that service to the devotees of God is more significant than service to God Himself. He who renders service to God's devotees speedily attains God Himself. Do not take to the life of a devotee as a means for acquiring any selfish advantage.


Three idols of Rāmānuja are especially associated with him. In the Tamil language, Tirumeni means 'idol' or 'figurine'. Ugandha means be worthy, be right, fit, rise to the occasion, and be suitable.

Sri Perumbudur, near Kanchipuram, got Thaan Ugandha Tirumeni – an idol that became sanctified on its own while Rāmānuja was in Shrīraṅgam.

Melkote, near Mysore, is home to Tamar Ugandha Tirumeni – an idol fashioned and sanctified by Him for His disciples.

Shrīraṅgam, near Trichy, got Thane Aana Tirumeni – an idol that is He, Himself.
He was a celebrated saint of His time who had codified the worship system itself.

After his passing, a life-size idol of his form has been kept in a sitting posture in a shrine within the Prakaram, a circumambulatory path of the Shrīraṅgam temple complex. Such an honour has not been bestowed on any other saint.

title: Birth of Swami Deshikan
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Birth of Swami Deshikan

Swami Vedānta Deshikan

Swami Vedānta Deshikan is considered the Ghantavataram (reincarnation of the divine bell) of Lord Venkateshwara of Tirumala.


Anantha Somaiyaji was one of the 74 simhaasanaadhipathis chosen by Swami Rāmānujar to spread the message of the Vishishṭādvaita philosophy. He lived in Kanchipuram with his son Pundareekaksha and his grandson, Anantasuri, who had studied all the shastras. When Anantasuri reached marriageable age, Pundareekaksha approached Kidambi Appullar, the grandson of Kidambi Aachan, who was responsible for the kitchen duties of Swami Rāmānujar. Pundareekaksha approached Kidambi Appular with a wedding proposition to give his son's hand in marriage to Kidambi Appullar's sister Tottarambha.



Kidambi Appullar prayed to Kanchi Varadaraja to provide him with guidance on whether he should accept the proposition or not. That same night, Kanchi Varadaraja appeared in Kidambi Appullar's dreams and told him that the child born of the union between Anantasuri and Tottarambha would be a great Āchārya. He would achieve greatness in his life. The next morning, Kidambi Appullar approached Pundareekaksha. He told him about his dream, in which the Lord appeared and prophesied the child's future, to be born of the union between his sister and Anantasuri. The marriage was conducted on the next auspicious date.


Anantasuri and Tottarambha lived a very prosperous life in a house opposite the Deepaprakashar Temple in Tiruttankaa. As the years passed, the couple's desire to have a child grew. Thus, to have their wish fulfilled, they traveled from one sthalam to the next, bathing in each pushkarani and praying to each Lord, asking to be blessed with a well-mannered child. Soon, they reached the shores of Swami Pushkarani in Tirumala. The couple bathed in the pushkarani, went to the temple, and offered their prayers to the Lord. The couple decided to spend the night in the holy kshethram of Tirumala. That night, Tottarambha had a dream wherein the Lord appeared and handed her the divine bell that was being rung during the daily aaradhanam.



The dream further progressed, showing Tottarambha a vision that made her feel as though she had swallowed the sacred bell. Simultaneously, the Lord had shown this dream to Anatasuri as well as the temple priest. The next morning, when the couple visited the temple, they noticed the priest saying that the temple bell was missing. It was at this moment that Tottarambha shared the events of her dream with Anantasuri. Anantasuri was stunned by what he heard and told his wife that he had had the same dream the previous night. As the couple conversed, the priest overheard their conversation and said to them that the Lord had appeared in his dream as well.


The priest then declared that it was the Lord's divine will, and from that day on, the smaller ghanta bell would no longer be rung. Even today, when one visits Tirumala, only the larger bell is rung. Twelve years later, Swami Deshikan was born. The twelve years here are of great significance. The significance lies in the fact that each year corresponds to one of the twelve Adityas. Swami Vedānta Deshikan was born possessing the knowledge of all the twelve Adityas combined.  Swami Deshikan was born in the Tamizh month of Puratasi under the nakshatram of Tiruonam on Vijayadashami in the year 1268 AD.

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Childhood and Education of Swami Deshikan

As discussed previously, Swami Deshikan was born in the year 1268 in the Tamil month of Puratasi, on the tenth day of the Shukla Paksha (Vijayadashami), under the nakshatram of Tiruonam, in the Thoopul agrahaaram, opposite the Deepaprakashar Temple, in Tiruttankaa.


Upon birth, Swami Deshikan was named Veṅkaṭanātha by his maternal uncle Kidambi Appullar. As Swami Deshikan grew, his uncle became his guru. When Swami Deshikan was just five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Kidambi Appular, to attend a discourse by Nadadhoor Ammal, a revered Sri Vaishṇava Scholar at the time. As soon as Nadadhoor Ammal saw Veṅkaṭanātha, he saw a divine radiance in the child and stopped the lecture he was delivering to hug the child affectionately.


After this, when Nadadhoor Ammal said that he had forgotten where he had stopped his lecture, Veṅkaṭanātha reminded him of the point at which he had stopped. This act astonished the crowd, as they had never seen a five-year-old boy comprehend the deep intricacies of the philosophical knowledge being discussed. It was then that Nadadhoor Ammal predicted and blessed Veṅkaṭanātha, saying he would become the torchbearer to spread Sri Vaishṇavism everywhere.


By the age of seven, Veṅkaṭanātha was initiated into Brahmacharya by Kidambi Appullar, who performed the Upanayanam and Pañcha-Saṃskāram. Upon being initiated into the Brahmacharya ashramam, Veṅkaṭanātha was taught the Vedas as well as the Naalaiyira Divyaprabandham.

title: Swami Deshikan's Return to Kanchipuram
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Deshikan's Return to Kanchipuram

After composing Hayagriva Stotram, Swami Deshikan composed various other stotrams, such as Garuḍa Panchashath, a fifty-shloka treatise on Lord Garuḍa, Devanaayaka Panchashath, a fifty-shloka treatise on Devanatha Perumāl, and Vaikuntanaayaki Thaayar, Achyutha Shathakam, a hundred-verse stotram dealing with various ideas of philosophy. Swami Deskian has written Achyutha Shathakam using Naayika Bhavam. Naayika Bhaavam is the process of writing where one imagines oneself as a woman who is in love with the Lord. Swami Deshikan composed the above stotrams and various other magnificent pieces before returning to Kanchipuram. On the way to Kanchipuram, Swami Deshikan first made a stop at Tirukkovilur. At Tirukkovilur, he composed Dehaleesa Sthuthi. Dehaleesa Sthuthi is a stotram in praise of Trivikrama Perumāl, the presiding deity of this nadu naadu Divyadesam as seen through the eyes of the mudhal azhwars, namely Poigai Āzhwār, Bhoothaazhwar, and Pei Āzhwār. Upon returning to Kanchipuram, Swami Deshikan composed Nyasa Dashakam, a ten-verse stotram on the doctrines of prapatti. Another magnum opus composed by Swami Deshikan is the Artha Panchakam.

The Artha Panchakam is a set of 11 Pāsurams dedicated to Sri Varadaraja Perumāl of Kanchipuram. The 11 Pāsurams are assigned to two each of the five doctrines or truths of the Artha Panchakam.

The five doctrines discussed  are as follows:

1. The Svarūpam of Parabrahman.
2. The Svarūpam of the jeevaathma.
3. The obstacles that prevent us from reaching Paramapadam
4. The means to moksham: Bhakti and Prapatti
5. The supreme goal of Bhagavat Anubhavam

title: Swami Deshikan's Yātrā of Vadu Nadu Kshethrams
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: Swami Deshikan's Yātrā of Vadu Nadu Kshethrams

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Deshikan's Yātrā of Vadu Nadu Kshethrams

In the year 1317 AD Swami Deshikan and his wife Kanakavalli were blessed with a son named Varadacharya. Just like his father, Varadacharya was a learned soul. It was as though a lamp was lit from an already bright and shining lamp. Soon after the birth of Varadacharya, Swami Deshikan undertook a yatra of all the Vadu Nadu Kshethrams. The first stop made by Swami Deshikan was that at Tirumala. Here, Swami Deshikan composed the Dayā Shatakam, a hundred verse treatise on the characteristics of the Lord's quality of showering limitless daya or mercy on all of His devotees. When Swami Deshikan presented this work in front of Lord Srinivasa, the Lord is said to have been so moved by the rendition that He conferred Swami Deshikan with the title of Vedantaacharya.

Swami Deshikan then continued his journey north and visited many kshethrams such as Tirukadigai, Tiruayodhyi, Kāshī, Mathurā, Avantika, Badarikashramam, Puri, Brindavan, Dwārakā, Triveni, Gaya, Salagramam, Purushothamam, Srikoormam, etc. Before returning to Kanchi, he also visited Tiruvallikkeni and Tiruvallur.

title: Miracles Performed by Swami Deshikan
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Miracles Performed by Swami Deshikan

A magician is said to have confronted Swami Deshikan. As the magician drank the water of a pond, Desika's belly bulged, filled with water, and caused unbearable pain. Desika just scratched with his fingernail a pillar nearby, and all the water flowed out therefrom, and Desika's belly regained the normal position. The magician begged to be excused and disappeared, but not before the Swami thanked him for helping in cleaning the streets of Kanchi without any effort on his part!

 In Kanchipuram, a snake charmer brought a few snakes and asked Desika if he could control them. Desika drew a line on the floor with a piece of chalk. The serpents could not cross the line. But when a poisonous snake crossed and threatened him, he uttered the Garuḍa Mantra. Immediately, a Garuḍa bird appeared and picked up all the serpents and flew away. Deprived of his only means of livelihood, the snake charmer begged to be excused. Desika recited his "Garuḍa Dandakam' and the bird brought back the snakes.

 Instigated by some jealous people, with the intention of embarrassing Swami Deshikan sent a bachelor to Swami Deshikan for financial help for his wedding, knowing full well that Swami Deshikan had no means to provide any financial support. Swami Deshikan took him to the Sanctum Sanctorum of the divine mother and sang the famous 'Sri Sthuthi'. Immediately, the sky opened up, as it were, and rained gold coins. Swami Deshikan asked the bachelor to take them away. And, the mischief-makers were aghast at this wonder.

title: Getting the title of Vedānta Deshikan and Brahma Tantra Swatantra
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: Getting the title of Vedānta Deshikan and Brahma Tantra Swatantra

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Getting the title of Vedānta Deshikan and Brahmā Tantra Swatantra

Once a band of Maayaa Vaadhis landed in Shrīraṅgam for a debate condemning Rāmānuja Darsanam. Periya Vaachaan Pillai, Pillai Lokaachaarya, and others resorted to the Grand old Master Sudarsana Bhattar for advice. Sudarsana Bhattar said that only Swami Desika could save the situation, and a letter was sent to Kanchi inviting Thooppul Pillai to face the opponents. Swami immediately set forth for Shrīraṅgam, but on the way, he halted at Sriperumbudur and prayed to Yathirajar, composing the famous Yathiraja Saptadhi. On reaching Shrīraṅgam, Swami fell at the feet of Sudarsana Bhattar and sought his blessings. Bhattar blessed him, saying that the Perumals (Sri Rangam Ranganathar, Tirumala Srinivasar, and Kanchipuram Varadar) commanded that he should re-establish our Siddhanta as Rāmānuja had earlier. The debate lasted for seven days, during which Swami demolished every single argument of the opponents. The Maayaa Vaadhis accepted defeat, became Srivaishṇavas and his Sishyas. The essence of the debate is what we now have as "Satha Dushani".It was at this time that Periya Perumāl conferred the title "Vedānta Deshikan" and Periya Piraatti the title "Sarva Tantra Svatantra." Sudarsana Bhattar and Periya Vaachaan Pillai commended on this and declared that he was the one who deserved the honorific most eminently.

title: Swami Deshikan's Move to Sathyagala
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Deshikan's Move to Sathyagala

In approximately 1327, during the Muslim invasion of Shrīraṅgam by Malik Kafur, the General of Allauddin, Sultan of Delhi, a great commotion ensued. The Srivaishṇavas, who were Satvic by nature, were no match to the Muslim plunderers. Fear gripped everyone's minds as to what might happen to the temple and the Lord's Archa murthis. The Āchāryas deliberated under the guidance of the Centenarian Master, Sudarsana Bhattar. It was decided that one group under Pillai Lokacharya ( who was equally advanced in age) was to take the Utsava Murthi and His consorts covered up in a palanquin to Tirupati. The party under Sudarshana Suri was to stay put at Shrīraṅgam, after erecting a stone wall in front of the Sannidhi of Moolavar to cover him from the sight of the marauders. Swami Deshikan took Sudarshana Bhattar's two sons and the manuscripts of Sruta-Prakaasika (the elaborate commentary on Sri Bhashyam chronicled by Sudarsana Bhattar during the Kalakshepams of Nadadur Ammaal) to safety at Tirunārāyaṇapuram via Satya Mangalam. But, before he could do that, the Muslim army attacked them and massacred many of them. Swami hid with his wards in the midst of corpses and spent the night. In the morning, they moved towards Satyagala village in Karnataka en route to Tirunārāyaṇapuram.

It was at this time, during his stay at Satyagala, that Swami composed the famous Abheeti Sthavam seeking the Lord to restore the worship of the Lord at Shrīraṅgam. He lived there for nearly 12 years (reciting the Sthavam incessantly) until news of the restoration of the Lord in Shrīraṅgam reached his ears. The Aswatha tree under which Swami rested in Satyakaalam can still be seen in the village even today. The stone slab on which Swami sat is kept preserved in the temple of Lord Varadaraja in the village. There is also the image of Swami, which is unique. Unlike in other places, the Swami is seen in a standing posture as if he was on his toes ever ready to move to Shrīraṅgam, awaiting the good news of reinstallation of the Lord there. At Tirunārāyaṇapuram, Swami Deshikan's son, Kumara Varadachariar, delivered discourses on Pillaans commentary of Tiruvoimozhi called 6000 Padi with the help of the notes of Swami Deshikan called "Nigama Parimalam."

One peculiarity which can be seen here is that one will see the idol of Swami Deshikan in a standing posture instead of his usual sitting posture, as seen everywhere else. This is because he was longing to return to Sri Rangam and worship Lord Ranganatha and Perundevi Tāyār.

title: Swami Deshikan's Return to Shri Rangam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: title
fields.text: Swami Deshikan's Return to Shri Rangam

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Deshikan's Return to Sri Rangam

After the threat of the Muslim invaders receded, Swami Deshikan returned to Sri Rangam. After returning to Sri Rangam, Swami Deshikan reinstated the procedure of performing Adyayana Utsavam and composed the magnum opus known as Paaduka Sahasram. 

Reestablishing the practice of Adyayana Utsavam:

When some of the orthodox people objected to the recital of Divya Prabandam in the temple because they included the works of Non-Brāhmaṇa Āzhwārs, written in Dravida Baasha (Tamizh), and Tiruvoimozhi in particular dealt with Kaama, which was taboo for them. Swami Deshikan argued with them and convinced them that the holy collects were equal to the Vedas since they contained all that was in the Vedas, that since they were in praise of the Lord, the language did not matter, and that the Kaama spoken of was nothing but absolute devotion to the Lord. He re-instituted the practice of 'Adhyayana Utsavam'- the ceremonial honoring of the Āzhwārs.



Composition of Paaduka Sahasram:

Azhagiya Manavaala Naayanaar, brother of Pillai Lokachaarya and our Swami Deshikan, went to worship Lord Ranganatha. The Naayanaar was captivated by the Lord's feet and wanted to compose a Stotra praising the same. Our Swami felt that the Divya Mani Paadukaas of the Lord were equally captivating and offered to write a Stotram on the Sandals of the Lord before daybreak the next day. But he had slept almost till the wee hours of the morning of the appointed day. When there were hardly a couple of hours to go before sunrise, the agitated disciples woke him up to remind him of his promise. Instantly, he commenced pouring out with bewildering rapidity an epic 'Paaduka Sahasram' and completed it well before daybreak. The 1,000 verses of this epic are examples of literary excellence and lofty thoughts- an incredible masterpiece of how a single subject like the Divya-Paadukai of the Lord could be expressed in so many different ways and yet hold up the audience's imagination and interest!

The Chitra Paddhati section of Swami Vedānta Desika's Pādukā Sahasram is a stunning fusion of devotional poetry and mathematical brilliance. Among its most remarkable feats is a 64-syllable Sanskrit verse (no. 929) that solves the Knight's Tour Problem, wherein a knight must visit every square on a chessboard exactly once without repeating. Each syllable in Desika's verse corresponds to a square on the 8×8 board, and their sequence traces a valid knight's tour—crafted not merely as an intellectual exercise, but as a hymn in praise of Lord Ranganatha's divine sandals (pādukās). This composition is an early example of algorithmic thinking expressed in poetic form, blending bhakti, kāvya, and gaṇita in a way few thinkers have ever achieved.

What makes this even more extraordinary is that Desika composed this work in the 13th century, nearly four centuries before Leonhard Euler and other European mathematicians began studying the Knight's Tour in the 18th century. While Euler approached the problem through formal mathematical inquiry, Desika embedded the same solution within a lyrical, devotional framework—demonstrating that sophisticated combinatorial reasoning was already alive in India, articulated through culturally rich and spiritually meaningful expressions. His poetic solution stands as a powerful testament to the interdisciplinary genius of pre-modern Indian scholars, where devotion, aesthetics, and logic seamlessly converged.

title: Swami Deshikan's Attainment of Paramapadam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Swami Deshikan's Attainment of Paramapadam

When in Srivilliputtur, he composed "Godha Sthuthi." The Choodik Kodutha Naachiyaar was so pleased that she ordained the Stotra to be recited during her Utsavam days, along with the Divya Prabhandams.

Having lived a whole and rich life for 101 years and satisfied with his work on earth, Swami Desika cast his tabernacle of flesh, praying to Udaiyavar and Appullaar by placing their Paadukas on his head which he kept on the lap of Nainarachar and his feet on the lap of Brahmā Tantra Svatantrarar, while his Sishyas chanted Tiruvoimozhi and Upanishads. He attained Paramapadam in Sowmya year in the month Kartigai in the Tamizh month of Kartikai. In the Kali yugam year 4471, which corresponds to 1369 AD.

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Present Day Sri Vaishṇava Mutts and Āshramams

To help aspirants seek out an Āchārya, the mutts and Āshramams and their Jeeyars help and serve the Sri Vaishṇava community. At present, several Sri Vaishṇava Mutts and Āshramams are serving the community. In addition to the Āchāryas of these mutts and Āshramams, many independent grihastha-acharyas are helping society.
Each of the Āshramams and mutts trace their roots back to Swami Rāmānujar. Swami Rāmānujar had appointed seventy-four Simhasanadhipatis to monitor, maintain, and propagate the Sri Vaishṇava Paramparā. Under Swami Deshikan, the Parakala Mutt was established. The Ahobila Mutt, Srimad Andavan Āshramam, and the Sri Poundarikapuram Āshramam were established by the various successors of Swami Deshikan. In the Tenkalai Sampradāyam, Sri Maṇavāḷa Māmunigaḷ founded the Vanamamalai Mutt.
All one has to do is seek out and surrender to their Āchārya, who, out of their infinite compassion, always welcomes the disciple and guides them in their spiritual journey.

title: Varāha Charama Shlokam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Varāha Charama Shlokam

The Varāha Charma Shlokam can be found in the Varāha Purāṇam. The Varāha Purāṇam is one of the 18 celebrated Purāṇas of Indian literature. The Varāha Purāṇam is a conversation between Lord Varāha and Bhoodevi as the Lord lifts Bhoodevi from the ocean of deluge after defeating Hiraṇyāksha.


The Varāha Charama Shlokam is as follows,

Lord Varāha addresses Mother Earth or Bhoodevi (who expresses concern for the well-being of all Her children):
If anyone thinks of Me, when the mind is sound (sthite manasi), with the body in good health (suswasthe shareere), and with all mental and physical faculties working correctly and intact (dhaatu saamye sthite) - thinks that I am indeed the very cause of this universe (or the form of this universe, vishwaroopam), that I am without birth (ajam) - then I assure (You, Devī) that I will remember this devotee of Mine when they are on their death bed, lying (helplessly) like a stone or a log of wood, and personally take them to the Supreme Abode.

The doctrines of karma establish the laws that govern each jeevaathma. The aathma dwells in the body, which includes the senses and the mind. At death, when the soul departs from the body, it takes with it a load of character as developed by the activities it has so far undergone in its human host. This marks the beginning for its next host. As established by Bhakti Yogam, to achieve salvation, one must think of the Lord in one's final moments. In the age of Kali Yugam, where people find it difficult to follow the established doctrines established in the scriptures, Bhoodevi, in her emotional attachment for all those born by her to reach Vaikuṇṭham and end the cycle of life, asks the Lord what has to be done. The Lord then tells her to stop the cycle of rebirth; one must perform sharanagati unconditionally to the Lord. If one unconditionally surrenders to the Lord and fails to remember him in their last moments, then the Lord Himself will remember that jeevaathma and grant the soul salvation.

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Charama Shlokas

In the Vedānta school of thought, three shlokas stand out as a guiding factor to the three philosophies of Dvaita, Advaita, and Vishishṭādvaita. These three shlokas are referred to as charama shlokas.
The word charama in Sanskrit translates to ultimate or the total extreme. These shlokas are of such high regard as these were shlokas rendered by Lord Sriman Nārāyaṇa in different situations but hold a fundamental and universal purpose. One can find three charama shlokas, namely,

1) Varāha Charama Shlokam
2) Rāma Charama Shlokam
and
3) Krishna Charama Shlokam.

The three charama shlokas form the basis for the Sri Vaishṇava school of thought as given to us by Sri Rāmānujāchārya.

title: Rama Charama Shlokam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Rāma Charama Shlokam

The Rāma Charama Shlokam can be found in the Rāmāyaṇa. This shloka is given to us by Lord Rāma when Vibhīshaṇa approaches Rāma and asks to be a part of his army.
When Vibhīshaṇa approached Lord Rāma to be a part of his army, Lord Rāma asked the senior members of His military as to whether or not to accept his proposal. Lord Rāma asks Sugrīva, Nal, Neel, Angad, and Jāmbavān. All of them refuse to accept Vibhīshaṇa saying he was Rāvaṇa's brother. Finally, Lord Rāma asked Hanumān for his opinion as he had traveled to Lankā and had seen the situation at ground zero. Hanumān tells the Lord that among all the people he had seen in Lankā, Vibhīshaṇa was the only truly trustworthy person. He told the Lord that he was a pure bhakta, and the Lord could wholeheartedly trust him and harbor him. This was when the Lord gave us the second Charama Shlokam. The Rāma Charama Shlokam is as follows,

The meaning of the shloka is as follows,
To all those beings that wholeheartedly seek My shelter and plead for My mercy and say I am yours, I shall undoubtedly offer My protection to all of them. This is My vow.

title: Krishna Charama Shlokam
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Krishna Charama Shlokam

The Krishna Charama Shlokam is considered to be the most revered among the three Charama Shlokas. Many scholars have given commentary on it from across different countries and across time immemorial.
This Charama Shlokam can be found in the Bhagavad Gītā, the divine discourse given to Arjuna by Lord Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Arjuna becomes overcome by emotion upon seeing members of his family in the opposition's army. It is then that Lord Krishna tells Arjuna about Karma Yogam, Jnāna Yogam, Bhakti Yogam, and various other methods on how to lead life. As a final commandment, the Lord tells Arjuna the Charama Shlokam, which is the principal guiding factor of Sri Vaishṇava philosophy.
The Shloka is as follows,

The meaning of the shloka is as follows,
Give up all (the other) dharmas and seek Me alone and My refuge. I will absolve you of all sins and liberate you. Do not despair. The Lord here tells Arjuna if one is not able to adhere to the principles of Jnāna, Karma, and Bhakti, but in all profound heart surrenders his belief to the Lord, He will grant liberation from the cycle of life and death.

title: Stages of Bhakti Yoga
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Stages of Bhakti Yoga

There are three stages to bhakti yogam, namely:
(i) Para bhakti
(ii)Para jnanam
(iii)Parama bhakti
Saamanya Bhakti, or ordinary bhakti, leads to Para bhakti, where the seeker of moksha known as the mumukshu develops a keen desire to experience the Lord after climbing up the ladders of Karma Yoga, Jnāna Yoga and necessarily realizing the nature of the jeevaathma and its relationship with the Paramātma. The second stage of bhakti-yoga is Para jnanam, in which the intense desire of para bhakti is rewarded by the Lord when He grants Paripurna sahakaaram, which is full of bliss and enjoyment of His presence for a limited period. If, in this period, the practitioner develops a complete appetite for the Lord, His presence, and His form, then such a person becomes entitled to parama bhakti in which the mumukshu expresses his single desire, which is to be with the Lord at all times. The Lord acknowledges this desire and provides permanent saakshatkaaram wherein the Lord responds to any prayer made by the mumukshu granting him the final boon of eternal union with Himself or moksham.

The path of bhakti-yogam is very drawn out and often can start in one lifetime and continue to take roots in the following lifetimes. Hence, it becomes challenging to practice bhakti yogam in its entirety. Those who do not possess the knowledge or power to practice bhakti yogam in the time of kali-yugam are many. To help gain the fruits of bhakti-yogam, one can perform prapatti or sharanagati. The paths of prapatti are open to everyone and are not limited by any means to any varna-ashrama. As prapatti or sharanagathi are the only alternatives to bhakti yogam, the acharyas now adopt this means for us to attain moksham.
Prapatti provides a simple and straightforward path that is bereft of the restrictions imposed by bhakti-yoga, which is very difficult and drawn out. There are three modes of prapatti, namely:
(i) Sva-Nishta: Applicable to the Āzhwārs, Āchāryas, and sages who have full knowledge of the Lord.
(ii) Ukti-Nishta: Applicable to others who get initiated through an Āchārya. The Āchārya initiates the seeker through an Archaamurthi of the Lord.
(iii) Āchārya-Nishta: Applicable to those who cannot adopt any of the above two categories. In this case, the aspirant surrenders to an Āchārya, and the Āchārya, through his compassion, prays to the Lord on his behalf to grant him moksham.

title: Conclusion
parentTitle: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: parentBookTitle
fields.text: A Brief Insight to Visishtadvaita Philosophy

fields.name: body
fields.text:
Conclusion

The object and goal of life is that every human being should internally realize the divinity within himself and realize the unity with the Lord. The devotee who understands that he lacks the qualifications or the ability to follow Karma, Jnāna, and Bhakti yogas as stipulated, but possesses a longing desire to be united with the Lord, has a sure and easy path laid out. All one has to do is seek out an Āchārya and surrender to him with complete confidence, absolute faith, and devotion. The disciple must learn to appreciate the teachings of the Āchārya and see the Āchārya as an equivalent or a representative of the Lord Himself. Through being initiated by the Āchārya and following his instructions, the disciple gains the fruits of dharma, artha, kama, and moksha. Ultimately, the Lord will shower his grace on such a person, granting moksham or eternal bliss.
I would like to end this journey by paying obeisance to my Āchāryas and the Lord.
